en: Oṃ. The Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The First Chapter.
Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the examination of the ground;
one should plow and clear the auspicious ground, which should slope toward the northeast.
Devoid of bones, hair, and the like, and free from skulls and limbs;
[and likewise] free from reptiles and the like, tigers and the like, and whatever other wicked creatures there may be.
One should always avoid that ground where [such things] are seen;
a site crowded with dogs and jackals at its commencement brings about the destruction of one's kinsmen. (Vis 1.3)
The ground of excrement always brings suffering to everyone, including the doer, with its husks, ashes, bones, hair, wood, clods of earth, and potsherds. (ViS 1.4)
Ground infested with worms, insects, moths, and gravel brings inauspiciousness and misfortune; therefore, one should examine it with great care. (Vis 1.5)
One should carefully avoid a woman endowed with such and other inauspicious marks.
For a Brahmin, the ground [of the womb] is white; for a Kshatriya, it is indeed red.
The [scent] of a Vaiśya is said to be yellow, while that of a Śūdra is black.
A Brāhmaṇī woman has the scent of ghee, and a Kṣatriyā woman has the scent of blood.
A prostitute has the smell of urine; a Śūdra woman smells like excrement; a Brāhmaṇa woman is said to be sweet-smelling, while a Kṣatriya woman is remembered as having an astringent scent.
The Vaiśya woman is indeed declared to be bitter, while the Śūdra woman is pungent;
having thus examined them with effort by means of their color, smell, taste, and so forth.
One should cause a pit one cubit deep to be dug and then fill it with earth;
where the earth exceeds [the original level], that ground bestows all desires. Vis 1.10.
Where the dust is indeed level, it is the best, for it yields half the fruit;
where the dust is uneven for men, it is middling, yielding the lowest fruit. (Vis 1.11)
Indeed, that ground upon which all seeds, once moistened, sprout within the space of three nights is considered the most excellent. Vis_1.12.
The middling [type] takes five nights, and the inferior takes seven nights; however, one should carefully avoid that soil in which [the seeds] do not sprout. Vis_1.13.
When the crops are ripe, the best of practitioners should ensure that the cattle are satisfied;
thereafter, he should worship the guardians of the world.
O Lord of Śacī, at midnight one should thus offer the bali-oblation with rice, cakes, and parched grain,
either separately or combined together.
Thereafter, one should excavate that site into a square on all sides;
having dug it to the depth of two men, one may even dig it to half that depth.
Or, according to the measurement of a sword, it should be half the height of a man;
having thus dug the earth, one should fill its center with water.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs and other instruments, and provided with lutes and flutes—
having thus honored the ritual procedure, one should begin the consecration (adhivāsana).
To its right, or in the west, or even in the north,
the practitioner should construct a pavilion in the midst of that [area] for the Vasus and the other deities.
One should place a full water-jar in the center, shaped like a ripe bimba fruit,
filled with two *droṇas* [of grain], and adorned with three threads.
Having filled it with scented water and provided with fragrant flowers,
and having spread out eight *droṇas* of rice, he should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
One should place the water-pot upon the pericarp, wrapped in a pair of cloths,
endowed with the nine gems, and equipped with the five golden weapons.
Then the best of preceptors, using the mantra of Vāsudeva,
should install [the image] equipped with all weapons and surrounded by all the gods.
Gold is the knower of all beings, situated in the heart of all beings;
it is the Self, the inner self, and the imperishable supreme self.

One should thus meditate upon Viṣṇu, the Puruṣa, who is subtler than a grain of nārāyaṇa-atom, whose prowess consists in the creation and destruction [of the universe], and who is the cause— within the center of the *kumbhaka* breath-retention.
Having meditated thus and worshipped them with delightful perfumes and other offerings,
one should place the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) individually around the top of the *droṇa* measure of śāli rice.

As before, the practitioner, having worshipped the substances joined together within the jars with their respective mantras and with pleasing offerings such as perfumes and so forth, [should proceed]. (Viṣṇu-purāṇa 1.28)
Having thus worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), one should commence the ritual of the fire-oblation (homa).
To the east of the water-pot (kumbha), there should be a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
One should have it fashioned by an artisan or perform it upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
at the time of commencing the construction of the temple, O Lord of Śacī, one should do so at midnight.
Accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments, and joined with hymns of auspiciousness (svastisūkta),
the preceptor, taking hold of the palāśa wood, shall pacify all obstacles.
One should offer oblations once in the middle [of the rite], either one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times, with the Nārasiṃha mantra. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.32)
Or, one should likewise perform the offering with twenty-eight pieces of *udumbara* wood,
each with the root mantra, and likewise offer clarified butter (*ājya*).
One should offer the excellent sixteen oblations of the *caru* into the center of the sacrificial pit using the *Puruṣasūkta*, which brings about all prosperity and happiness. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.34)
Having thus performed the ritual procedure,
the knower of mantras should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the sacrificial ladle (sruk) using the root mantra known as the twelve-syllable one.
O Lord of Śacī, having taken a *kuḍuba*, or half of that, or half of that again—either *kapila* ghee or ordinary ghee—one should perform the oblation according to the ritual sequence. (Viṣṇu 1.36)
Having burned the enclosing sticks and the rest, he should then accept the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
At the conclusion of the fee-offering, O Lord of Śacī, he should cause a proclamation to be made with conch shells and other instruments in due order.

One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), accompanied by dance, song, and the like, preceded by the auspicious day (supuṇyāha), and joined with the recitation of the Vedas. (Vis 1.38)
Having thus completed the rites up to the end of the fire-oblation, one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) during the first watch of the night;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, the preceptor, composed in mind, shall bathe.
As before, the wise one should worship the jars and sprinkle the ground in the center,
as well as at the boundary in all directions, each with its own respective mantra.
The knower of mantras should offer the *bhūtakrūra* bali sacrifice in all eight directions;
thereafter, he should perform the binding of the quarters with the *astra* mantra.
One should gradually lead the remainder of the water from the jar into the center of the earth;
then, having filled the pit in stages with earth mixed with sand.
Having properly caused [the ground] to be leveled with mallets by Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas,
one should dig the lines and stakes in the month of Caitra on an auspicious day.
Afterwards, the preceptor, together with skilled artisans, should indeed lay out the lines with a cord and subsequently have the temple constructed.
The practitioner is fit for the mantra, while the master is fit for the ritual work;
this supreme and auspicious sprinkling is for the purpose of purifying the ground. (Vis 1.45)
Thus, O Lord of Śacī, the purpose of the temple has been briefly explained;
whoever should construct it according to this very procedure shall partake in meritorious karma.
Freed from all evils, he goes to the supreme goal;
it brings about the prosperity of the kingdom and increases merit, longevity, and health.
Wealth and grain increase, and the kingdom and the king’s realm flourish;
thereafter, one should honor the teacher with garments and even with ornaments. (ViS 1.48)
There, one should honor the artisan with garments and golden earrings;
afterwards, one should honor the astrologer with new clothes and finger-rings. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 1.49)
Thereafter, one should honor the members of the assembly, beginning with the offering of mouth-perfumes;
having thus worshipped them in this sequence, [one should present them] together with garments and ornaments.
Then, having had a house constructed by a skilled artisan during an auspicious moment and a favorable planetary conjunction, one should begin the construction of the child's chamber.

Having first established the site for the children, one should subsequently and in due order construct the main temple, especially ensuring it is provided with the ritual deposition of jewels (ratnanyāsa).
O Lord of Śacī, having dug a pit one cubit deep at the Brahma-spot,
one should place [the image] there with a thousand niṣkas, or a hundred, or half of that, or even half of that again.
The practitioner, having gathered emeralds and other gems, should place supreme refined gold in the center of the earth with the Astra mantra.
One should install [the deities] from Brahmā down to Īśāna with their respective mantras at midnight, together with the patron who remains well-concealed.
One should perform the rite of conception (garbhādhāna) accompanied by the sounding of conch shells and other instruments;
having made a lid out of copper, one should cover the pit and fill it. Vis_1.56.
Having gradually covered the pit with stones or bricks,
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, accompanied by the sound of a bell.
The supreme practitioner should accomplish all that by means of the seed-syllable of Brahmā;
thereafter, for the sake of supreme and auspicious prosperity, he should worship the Goddess.
Thereafter, one should worship in due order with the mantra of Vāsudeva (or *vaṃ* *sva?*).
Thus has the unsurpassed examination of the ground been briefly described. Vis_1.59.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Procedure for Examining the Ground," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Second Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall duly explain the construction of the pavilion and other structures in their proper sequence.
The pavilion, the sacrificial pits, the large and small ladles, and the eight auspicious objects.
The archway (toraṇa) and its name, the ritual procedure for their worship in sequence, the gatekeepers and banners, and the ritual procedure for their installation in sequence. (Vis 2.2)
O Lord of Śacī, by means of this secret rite, more secret than the secret,
performed in due order on the eastern side of the pavilion, there shall be an increase in prosperity and glory.
It pacifies all obstacles in the southern direction, brings fame in the south,
bestows victory in the western quarter, and grants wealth in the northern direction.
One should likewise construct the pavilion in the southeast, the southwest, the northwest, or the northeast; among these, each preceding direction is more excellent than the one following it.
One should act according to the wish of the patron; one should not have it performed in another location.
The pavilion is said to be of three kinds: inferior, middling, and superior.
Furthermore, for an inferior [site] an inferior pavilion should be constructed, for a middling one a middling one,
and for a superior one a superior one, according to the prescribed ritual.
One should have a pavilion constructed in due order, measuring either fifteen, ten, or even eight cubits, and provided with sixteen pillars.
One should know that to be the lowest; now listen to the middle, O observer of good vows.
They know the pavilion to be of sixteen or twelve [parts] as the middle.
One should know that the best [size] is from twenty-four cubits down to twenty cubits; now hear the procedure for laying out the lines.
O Lord of Śacī, [the image] may be one cubit, two cubits, or three cubits in size, whether it is from a palace, a pavilion, a wall, or even a pedestal.

Having dismissed [the previous assembly], the preceptor should construct an auspicious consecration pavilion, endowed with all the required characteristics and according to the teacher's desire. Vis 2.12.
One should drop the Brahma-thread as far as the area of the pavilion;
having divided that into three parts with the thread, one should cause four lines to be drawn.
Having constructed three peaks extending east and west as well as south and north, one should then arrange the divisions therein.
One should fashion pillar-frames at all the corners,
and one should fashion other pillars at all the junctions of the threads.
O Lord of Śacī, all the components of the pavilion and all other elements should be constructed according to the rules, employing both general logic and specific technical reasoning.
Equipped with four doors and adorned with canopies and other ornaments—
one should construct the pavilion in this manner at least seven days prior [to the ceremony].
One should have an altar constructed in the center according to the proportions of the pavilion;
one should construct the altar in due order using both unbaked and baked bricks.

One should apply the superior [method] to the superior, the middling to the middling, and even the inferior to the inferior; having done so according to that measure, one should form a packet from the measured [substance]. (Vis 2.19)
Having constructed an altar (vedikā) that is two cubits in height and resembles the surface of a mirror,
one should then prepare the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in due order.
On the altar, however, all [obstacles] have been removed from every side;
having cleared away four *tālas* or two *tālas* on all sides in due order. (Vis 2.21)
Having cleared three *tālas* around the altar in due order, [the objects] should be placed at a distance of four *tālas* or two *tālas* on all sides. // Vis_2.21* //
The practitioner should cause fire-pits (kuṇḍas) to be made, beginning with those that are square,
first in the east and ending with those situated in the west.
Thereafter, one should strike a line across it from south to north, extending as long as required; having determined the measurement, whether one cubit or two cubits, one should mark it.
Then, one should mark each corner-fish with two [lines] at a time;
having carefully stretched and struck the directional threads through them in sequence.
The field made square is auspicious, with four equal corners;
it is twenty finger-breadths larger than the square [of the previous one]. (Vis 2.25)
Having marked out the site with a cord, one should then dig the earth there;
or, having had it dug by a skilled craftsman, one may dig half of it.
One should cause the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be constructed in due order according to the rules, starting with the square shape;
all the pits around [the site] should be made according to the measurement of one tāla in their respective sequence.
One should cause it to be made square and so forth, equal in width and length;
having marked out the site with a cord, one should then dig the earth to that extent.
The girdles for the pit should be made, leaving a space of two finger-breadths;
the first is declared to be *sāttvikī*, and the second is considered *rājasī*.
The first [of the three] is of the nature of darkness (tāmasī), twelve finger-breadths in height;
the second is eight finger-breadths, and the third is four finger-breadths.
All [the parts] should be made continuously with a width of four finger-breadths;
the womb (yoni) is beautiful with a length of ten finger-breadths, and its tip measures six, four, or two finger-breadths.
The shape of the vagina should be like that of a vulva, or perhaps resembling the trunk of an elephant;
it should be made four finger-widths long and gradually tapering inward. (Visuddhimagga 2.32)

The root [of the sacrificial post] should be known as three finger-breadths, and its tip six finger-breadths; this is the description of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit and so forth. Vis_2.33.
In a pit measuring two cubits, it is said that both the navel and the girdle are doubled;
or, for a rite performed in brief, the pit may have only a single girdle.
Having carefully marked the midpoint of the pit and the midpoint of the corner portion in the northern direction, as well as [the midpoints] from east to west from the center; // Vis_2.35 //
A pit rotated in every direction clearly becomes a half-moon;
that pit is for the sake of all accomplishments and increases all prosperity. (Vis 2.36)
The wise one should perform the pacification of all obstacles on the right;
the thread situated thus from the pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth is that which extends to the corner.
For that purpose, having established it in the direction [of the deity], it should be rotated until it becomes circular;
this supreme circle should be known as the warder-off of all suffering. (Vis 2.38)
There is no fear of drought, nor likewise fear of excessive rain;
everywhere it is shaped like a lotus, while the girdle is circular. Vis 2.39.
The practitioner should draw each one above the girdle of Śacī’s lord;
he should draw either a twelve-petaled lotus or an eight-petaled one with a pericarp.
That pool is called Padma by those learned in all the scriptures;
it should be known as that which increases Brahmanical merit and bestows growth in sacrifice and Vedic study.
In that same way, it may be square; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Or it may be triangular or a lotus-shaped pit (kuṇḍa), according to the practitioner's desire.
The wise one, however, should have [the mandala] constructed as the destroyer of all obstacles;
it may be thirty-five finger-breadths or even twelve finger-breadths.
Having taken up the cord from the preceptor and having stretched it out,
one should carefully strike it and mark the fish-shaped figures at the corners in the southwest and the northwest.
In that very same way, one should mark the eastern [sector] so that it becomes an auspicious triangle;
the wise man should then have a pit constructed by a skilled artisan.
O Lord of Śacī, the practitioner who knows the supreme truth should have the girdle made around the pits in their respective forms, proceeding in due order. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.46)
This is declared to be the triangle; the remainder shall be common [to all].
This row of fire-pits (kuṇḍa) is fully described as having the nature of the three guṇas.
O Lord of Śacī, that is the source of all beings for the sake of their accomplishment;
it is the cause of the multitude of vidyās and mantras, as well as of liberation.
The head is said to be in the east, while the two arms are situated in the corners known as the northeast and southeast; the two feet are in the northwest and southwest.
The belly is said to be the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and the womb is prescribed as the source (yoni);
the three girdles are declared to be the three qualities (guṇas).
Thus has the characteristic of the sacrificial pits been briefly described in sequence;
likewise [the characteristics of] the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the auspicious items, and the arches.
Now I shall declare their characteristics;
it is said that they should be made of aśvattha, khadira, or other such woods, measuring twenty-four finger-breadths.
And for the purpose of the fire-oblation during festivals such as consecrations, one should have a *sruva* ladle made;
it should be five or seven finger-breadths in length, square in shape, and of equal width.
One-third of that [measurement] should be a very beautiful circular pit in the center;
one should dig it either level with the horizontal and vertical dimensions, or half of that, using a sacrificial ladle (sruva).
Having set aside a fourth part of a finger's breadth at the edge of the pit,
one should properly fashion the girdle (mekhalā) around the edge of that pit in due order.
One should fashion a single girdle and its height in the same manner;
around the girdle, one should draw the shape of lotus petals.
One should also cause a twelve- or eight-petaled [lotus] to be made upon the base of the girdle;
one should draw the pericarp in the middle of the pit according to the proportions of the craft.
At the edge of the petals, one should fashion a square enclosure on all sides;
it should have a width of half a finger-breadth and be adorned with the digits and dots.
Adorned with all ornaments, one should perform [the drawing] with two lines;
or likewise, having drawn twelve or eight [lines] according to one's preference, one should proceed in sequence.
The neck should be three parts in width and one and a half finger-breadths in length;
or it may be two finger-breadths in length, and at its tip there should be the opening.
It should be four finger-breadths in width, or perhaps five;
it should have three ridges, each measuring two finger-breadths, with a very beautiful channel in the middle.
There should be a hollow in the region of the throat, like a small tube;
on the right and left sides of the stream, one should draw a circle at the opening. 2.62.
Above the throat, one should then draw a very beautiful face;
it may have either a single nose and mouth, or indeed the face of a boar.
It may indeed have the form of a tiger or a cow's face; one should perform it according to one's preference.
Having cleansed the back of the *sruk* ladle, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus around it.
Then, one should place a square foot-measure outside that, measuring exactly two finger-breadths;
likewise, at the base of the staff, one should perform the placement of the foot-measure according to the rule.
One should fashion its circular base with a measurement of one thumb-breadth;
there is a lotus at the end of the second staff and below the third.
One should draw [the mandala] provided with eight petals upon a wooden board;
in the central portion, one should arrange ghee and other substances in sequence all around.
At the base of the staff, one should fashion a lotus bud and three lines representing the lifespan;
O Lord of Śacī, that [staff] should be twenty-four finger-breadths in length.
Thereafter, one should have a *sruva* ladle made, provided with a mouth;
its handle should be two finger-breadths in circumference, circular, and very beautiful.
Just as a cow's footprint might be submerged in shallow mud, so it should be;
at the base and at the tip of the *sruva* (or *sruca*), there should be three lines measuring one *yava* each.
O Lord of Śacī, one should have that sacrificial ladle (sruk) made; it bestows all accomplishments.
Having set aside three finger-breadths from the mouth and so forth, one should fashion the base at its end.
On the back, there should be a very beautiful rounded base according to the measurement of the fingers of that body;
likewise, at the base of the *sruva* ladle, the foot should have the same width and length.
One should fashion the base of the *sruva* in the shape of a lotus bud;
alternatively, one may have the *sruk* and *sruva* fashioned with [the measurements] reduced by two eyes and four feet [of the other].
This is declared to be the *sruk* and *sruva*; it is called the "Eight Auspicious Items.
One should make them from metal alone, or, if those are unavailable, from wood.
[The staff] should be made of aśvattha, palāśa, khadira, or even vaṭa wood;
it should be twenty-five finger-breadths in length and twelve finger-breadths in width.
The pedestal should be known to be two finger-breadths thick and four finger-breadths square;
upon it, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
The conch, the discus, the banner, the śrīvatsa, the mirror, the bull, the pair of fish, and the jar—these are considered the eight auspicious signs (maṅgalāṣṭaka). Vis_2.77.
The wise one should prescribe a length of twelve finger-breadths for conch shells and the like, and should determine their width according to their respective forms.
One should arrange chowries and great lamps at their sides,
and one should place auspicious objects such as conch shells and a parasol above them.
Now, the characteristics of the archways shall be described in due order:
the Aśvattha archway is in the east; it belongs to the Ṛgveda and has Indra as its presiding deity.
Likewise, in the south is the Audumbara tree, dedicated to Yama and the Yajurveda;
and in the west is the Nyagrodha tree, dedicated to Varuṇa and the Sāmaveda.
To the north, there should be a Plakṣa tree dedicated to Soma and belonging to the Atharvans;
or, in its absence, an Aśvattha tree in each of the four directions starting from the east.
One should fashion the forms of those respective trees according to their own names, measuring seven cubits or even five cubits. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.83)
Or one may perform it with a length of four cubits, according to one's preference;
the crossbar should be half that size and provided with three tridents.
O Lord of Śacī, I have declared the length of the *śūla* to be two *tālas*, or less by one-quarter; the *pāda-śūla* is eleven finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*). (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 2.85)
Or nine finger-breadths, O Lord of Gods, one may act according to one's preference;
those two feet and the crossbar are twenty-two finger-breadths in total.
One should construct it either circular or square according to the rules and with proper skill;
one should place archways at the gates and in their respective locations, made from the appropriate trees.
Having dug two *tāla*s deep into the ground in the pavilion with the root mantra,
one should then dig a pit in the earth measuring one *tāla* in size.
Having erected the archways in their respective pits in due order,
that which is in the east should be most beautiful, while the one in the south is named Subhadra.
The best of instructors should worship Subandhu in the western [direction] and the one named Suhotra in the northern, using their respective names as mantras.
Kumuda and Kumudākṣa are recorded as the two gatekeepers in the east;
Puṇḍarīka and Vāmana are known as the guardians of the southern gate.
Śaṅkukarṇa and Sarpanetra are the two gatekeepers in the west;
Sumukha and Supratiṣṭhita are the two gatekeepers of the north.
Having placed them within the archway according to the eight directions:
a red banner in the east, and a yellow one in the south.
In the west, resembling collyrium, and likewise in the north, which is white in color;
there, Kumuda and the other lords of the spirits are proclaimed to be upon the banners.

Thus, O Lord of Śacī, the construction of the pavilion and so forth, up to the sacrificial ladles (sruk and sruva) and the banners, has been briefly described; now hear about the collection of timber.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Rules for the Characteristics of the Maṇḍapa and Other Structures," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Three. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme collection of wood;
having fed the Brahmins, the teacher, with a pure mind, [should proceed].
The preceptor, having adorned himself with new garments and finger-rings, and the patron, O Lord of Śacī, being pure and of purified inner heart; Vis_3.2.
Having honored the artisan with perfumes, flowers, garments, and the like,
and having adorned the Vaiṣṇavas with food, clothing, and other such gifts.
Having taken up the axe and other implements together with the Vaiṣṇavas, the knower of mantras— pure, wearing new garments, accompanied by his wife,
and wearing a turban— should proceed in due order.
Having reached a tree, the practitioner, together with the artisans,
should depart after reciting the great eight-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times.
Then, with kusha grass in hand, having prostrated, he should gaze at the wood with a concentrated mind on a clean,
secluded spot, free from hair and charcoal.
Having gazed upon the tree thus established and bowed down while remembering Hari,
one should take that tree with the mind and avoid the thorns.
During the eight months beginning with Kārttika,
the highly wise one, having observed an auspicious tree at the prescribed time, should collect the excellent timber.
One should take the *khadira* wood from among thorny trees and avoid that which is pithless;
I shall now describe, in brief, the sequence of trees and their supreme essence.
Khadira, devadāru, badarī, the two types of sandalwood, śiṃśupā, rājavṛkṣa, bilva, and yūpavana; thus [are the trees].
Madhuka, lohita, svandana, and svandaka; likewise tumbaka, śāmalya, and the śāla tree. Vis_3.11.
The *asana*, the *vakula*, the *śirīṣa*, and the *āmalaka*,
as well as all trees suitable for sacrifice, are prescribed for the purpose of making images.
And those others which possess pith, being free from worms and insects, burnt by fire, dried up by themselves, or likewise fallen of their own accord. || Vis_3.13 ||
Likewise, it was split and shattered by a thunderbolt from below;
moreover, it sloped toward the south, while those born in other regions were avoided.
Having conceived the image of one [deity] upon a stone or even on a tree, one should gradually take possession of it; thus, only one [image] is to be made here.

One should not make an image otherwise, for the ritual action would be fruitless. I shall now describe the procedure for the consecration and the offering of oblations for images made of stone or wood.
Below that, in the western direction, the wise one should draw a mandala upon the earth,
having sprinkled it with scented water while reciting the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
At the foot of that tree, the mantra-knower, having donned new garments,
and the preceptor should hang banners there in the four directions.
There, having invoked Viṣṇu— Hari situated within the sun—
one should worship Puruṣottama with the Puruṣasūkta itself.
One should also smear the place where the stone is to be placed with cow dung;
having decorated it as before, one should cover it with new cloths.
Here, one should worship the imperishable Hari according to the previously described path;
the knower of the tantra should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the evening on the eastern side of that [shrine].
Having lit great lamps in the four directions and adorned all the people with unbroken rice grains and incense, they should be made to wear the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and face upward.
The preceptor, taking up a water-pot that is flawless, wrapped with thread, provided with *aśvattha* sprouts, containing gems, and filled with water; Vis_3.23.
Having wrapped it with a pair of garments, one should place it upon a heap of grain;
having worshipped Brahmā therein, one should set eight jars around it.
One should place them separately upon a heap of grain, together with their lids and cloths;
one should worship the guardians of the directions, from Indra to Īśāna, in due order.
One should perform the rite of oblation starting from the east and ending at the north,
for each of the forms beginning with Vāsudeva individually, using their respective names.
One should offer one hundred and eight oblations of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, respectively,
into the tongue of the fire with the Vidyās of Vāsudeva and the others.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), there remains nothing further in this;
in this supreme Great Mantra (or Tantra),
the transformation into Vaiṣṇava occurs through the sequence.
Just as it was proclaimed by Nārada himself, one should likewise produce [the fire] here;
having produced the Vaiṣṇava fire, one should perform the oblation (homa) in that fire.
Alternatively, while recollecting the fourfold form in the eastern section,
one should perform the fire-offering rites in the eastern fire according to the sequence as before.
One should offer the bali-oblation all around, casting the fierce bali for the bhūtas;
it should consist of milk-rice mixed with jaggery, accompanied by the subtle sound of a bell.
Having had the proclamation of an auspicious day made, one should first and lastly, in due order,
consecrate the axe by adorning it with new cloth and other offerings.
One should draw an eight-petalled lotus in the center of a mound of *droṇa* rice;
in its center, one should lay [the image] with either the Weapon-mantra or the eight-syllable mantra.
Having covered it with a new cloth, the practitioner, the most excellent knower of mantras,
should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, while the knower of mantras recites the Astra mantra.
The teacher, having become well-established, should utter this mantra:
"Oṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the source of all worlds, the sovereign lord. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.35)
Salutation to the one who is all-pervading, who possesses all forms, the lord of dreams;
to the rākṣasas, piśācas, and nāgas who dwell here perpetually.
"May they all depart; may Hari be ever present.
Having spoken thus, desiring sleep, he should lie down at night during the final watch. (Viṣṇusmṛti 3.37)
Having observed what is auspicious and inauspicious here, as proclaimed in this chapter on dreams,
one should accept [the result] even when there is no visible sign, and should turn back from it if it is the opposite.
The teacher, having risen in the morning, should perform his bath according to the rules;
knowing the mantras, he should take a water-pot to the foot of a tree or to a stone slab.
Having consecrated the unsurpassed Sudarśana with the weapon-mantra,
having proclaimed "Sahasrāra," and immediately thereafter the syllable *huṃ*, [he should perform the rite].
Ending with the syllable *phaṭ*, this is the mantra of the King of Weapons, the Sudarśana, the great weapon that is unbroken; it is supreme, bestowing glory, fame, and victory. (Vis 3.41)
Having been consecrated, having sipped water three times, and having put on new garments,
one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and should perform a conciliatory rite.
"For the sake of the world's peace, go to the auspicious abode of the gods;
there you shall attain divinity, free from burning and cutting."
By offering water and flowers, with fine incense and sacrificial oblations, people will worship you; through that, you shall attain liberation.
Having thus offered consolation, O Lord of Śacī, you should likewise offer consolation even while seated upon a stone at the foot of a tree.
Having uttered the name of the stone, the stone shall indeed become a source of consolation;
and having paid homage to the axe with the mantra of the weapon (astra), the practitioner [should proceed].
Taking that [axe] with both hands, he repeatedly cut down a tree;
thus, having taken a wooden [image], he stayed in the forest together with the forest-dwellers.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and the like, as well as drums and the resonance of cymbals,
one should proceed gradually to the temple, joined with song and dance.
From the moment he takes hold of the wooden vessel, he should constantly have an image fashioned there; until that task is completed, he should subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
The patron, being composed, should not perform any other work;
nor should the master artisan or his descendants, who are experts in the authority of the scriptures. (Vis 3.50)
O Lord of Śacī, having examined what is essential and what is not here with a skilled craftsman, listen now to the gathering of wood in his absence.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra,
the knower of mantras, having brought them together, should cause them to receive the root vidyās.
Having taken that, O Lord of the Rakshasas, one should go to the forest for the sake of wood,
[seeking out] Vaishnavas, devotees of the Blessed One, who are strong and intent on ritual action.
Having reached the forest, one should go forth after cutting down a tree while remembering Hari;
placing that tree upon one's head, one should remember the Lord Nārāyaṇa.
Then, accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, one should go to the sacrificial hall;
there, one should cause a full water-pot to be placed to the east of the primary shrine.
One should place [the vessel], provided with aśvattha sprouts, covered with a lid, wrapped in cloth, filled with water, and containing jewels, upon heaps of grain.
And one should sequentially recite the mantras, beginning with the root mantra, into that jar,
as well as the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, which expounds upon creation and other such topics.
Likewise, one should recite the Puruṣasūkta together with the Vaiṣṇavas over the waters contained within the pitcher, [visualizing] Viṣṇu, the complete and imperishable.
Having meditated and worshipped with incense and other offerings, as well as with the Puruṣasūkta,
one should smear the eastern part of the pitcher with cow dung.
One should scatter two *droṇas* or half that amount of rice grains in sequence;
in the center of that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus even with the ring finger.
One should apply the great eight-syllable mantra to the pericarp and other parts;
there, in the center of the pitcher, one should sprinkle it while reciting the Astra mantra.
One should sprinkle [it] again with water from a conch using the root mantra;
having sprinkled it three times, repeatedly, while recollecting the form of Viṣṇu.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] again with the five Upaniṣadic mantras, the practitioner, composed in mind,
should sprinkle him thoroughly with water from the pitcher while reciting the two root mantras.
One should bathe the excellent wooden image with mantras previously consecrated;
one should worship it with fine incense, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in the same sequence as before.
Having covered [the image] with a new cloth, one should offer oblations all around,
starting from the east and proceeding in order, using the Sudarśana mantra.
The offering of the oblation with sacrificial food is indeed for the sake of all-pervading peace; know that this oblation bestows auspiciousness, prosperity,
and the warding off of all obstacles.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform an offering (bali) here;
and when the night has turned to dawn, one should wander about the sanctuary.
Taking an excellent tree accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments,
the preceptor, the most proficient in mantras, should proceed together with the Vaiṣṇava disciples.
Having installed [the image] in the inner sanctum,
one should then fasten the door for three nights, five nights, or even seven nights.
Or else, O Lord of Śacī, one should not open the door for nine nights from the time the rite of sowing seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) is commenced.
The practitioner, having constructed a pavilion, a peaked roof structure, or a water-shed to the northeast, south, or north of the Ālaya, should proceed.
It was covered with a canopy of cloth, adorned with ornaments,
provided with strings of pearls, and decorated with flower garlands.
It should be provided with a vessel and a sprout, joined with lamps in the eight directions,
furnished with coconut leaves, and adorned with chowries. Vis_3.73.
In the afternoon, the knower of mantras, together with the Vaiṣṇavas, should bring a tree endowed with such characteristics to the pavilion, O Lord of Śacī.
Accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, and joined with dance and song,
one should reach the inner sanctum and open the door.
Having worshipped the wooden image with perfumes and other offerings while recollecting the root mantra,
the wise practitioner should sprinkle it with scented water and perform the rite for an auspicious day.
O Lord of Śacī, one should gradually dig a pit in the middle part of the pavilion, measuring two cubits, or half of that, or half of that again.
Having taken a preeminent tree, the practitioner should establish it with the Astra-mantra;
then, with the root mantra, he should place Śrī upon the right side.
In the north, however, one should place Puṣṭi and her respective root-mantra in due order,
recollecting the supreme tree whose lifespan extends for a thousand years.
Having placed water at their base with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā, or with their respective root-mantras, one should thereafter offer libations of water according to one's preference.
Having propitiated that entire, immutable one with white flowers,
you ought to forgive everything— whether it be deficient in mantra or deficient in ritual action.
Having spoken thus and paid homage to the foot of the tree, the knower of mantras, having performed this,
should then proceed once more with the gathering of wood.
In this regard, one should perform all the rites beginning with the formal acceptance (*adhivāsa*) as previously described;
then, having honored the artisan, one should cut the wood again and again.
Joined by those very Vaiṣṇavas while recollecting the Root Form,
he attains the fruit; otherwise, there is the destruction of the village and the loss of wealth.
In that case, the destruction of the site would occur; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, having taken a wooden [image], one should proceed through the sequence of rites involving its re-consecration.
One should have the supreme image fashioned according to the treatises on iconography;
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with gold, garments, and rings.
In that very manner, having honored the artisan, one should begin the taking up of the stone.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Wood," in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
The Fourth Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme method for the selection of the stone.
However, two kinds of stone are to be taken from mountains and from the earth. (Vis 4.1)
First I shall describe the mountains, among which these peaks are found:
Trikūṭa, Hemakūṭa, and Kailāsa, the best of mountains. (Vis 4.2)
Mandara, Mālyavat, Niṣadha, the Nīla mountain,
Meru, Sahya, Vindhya, and Kiṣkindha, the best of mountains.
Having observed Veṅkaṭa, Dardara, Śrīgiri, and Citrakūṭaka— such places as these— one should always bow down before them.
Taking a leaf and a flower, one should cast them at the foot of a mountain,
having paid homage to Hari and meditated upon the mountain that destroys sins.
One should perform all the rites of acceptance (adhivāsanā) in this regard as previously described.
Now, the characteristics of those stones that are said to be found on the ground are being stated. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 4.6)
The Vāruṇī, the Māhendrī, the Āgneyī, and likewise the Vāyavī—these four stones are proclaimed; their characteristics are now described. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 4.7)
That ground which is filled with flowering groves and surrounded by reservoirs of water should be known as Vāruṇī; the stone found there is likewise Vāruṇī.
That which has its northern boundary [marked by] a field of rice to the south and milk-trees to the west is proclaimed as Māhendrī.
To the south were palāśa and khadira trees, kāśmaryas, and puṣparyas;
there were also partridges, pigeons, and vultures that feed on fat.
Where bees and boars are constantly seen sporting, there is water located nearby, though it may be only a small amount.
They declare that [state] to be the fiery one.
Abounding with bilva and śleṣmātaka trees, as well as snuhi and vibhītaka;
where jackals are seen, and likewise mirages.
That ground which is devoid of grass and water, and filled with gravel and saline soil, is said to be of the nature of wind; one should avoid such a stone-like place.
On the bank of a river, on the shore of a lake, or surrounded by the salt ocean;
in the middle of a village, in a cremation ground, and likewise at a crossroads.
Stones should never be taken from impure ground, from anthills, from saline soil, from places defiled by corpses, or from those scorched by wind, sun, or fire. (Viṣṇusmṛti 4.15)
If one, deluded by greed, should make or cause to be made an image using stones that have been discarded, for him there will be the effect of malevolent magic.

The preceptor, having first fed the brahmins and had them perform the recitation of auspicious blessings (*svastivācana*), should go out together with the artisans for the purpose of measuring. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 4.17.
Having taken up an iron axe or similar tool, facing either east or north, he should look at a stone as soon as he has gone outside; from that time forth, he should do so constantly.
One should perform the work of making the image, consuming sacrificial food (haviṣya) until the completion of that task;
and the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) is declared in the chapter on the collection of wood.
In that regard, everything should be applied; I shall tell you the specific method:
having had the ground excavated by artisans, one should look at the stone with a concentrated mind.
Its length extends from south to north as well as from east to west;
the southern neck bestows peace, while the eastern neck grants victory.
The western neck of the [image] always brings prosperity to the maker;
the northern neck bestows nourishment, but one should avoid the corners.
When it is being torn away, sparks are seen there like those from a fire, and sounds like that of a bronze bell arise; this is considered the head of the stone. (Vis 4.23)
That stone whose sound in its middle part is like that of bell-metal, but at its base is like that of a bronze cymbal, is proclaimed as "Pumān" (the Male).
Therefore, if it is slightly deficient and has a hollow sound, that stone should be known as female; if it is even more deficient than that, it is neuter.
When masculine, it is called the image; when feminine, the footstool;
but when below the placement of the jewels, it is declared to be neuter.
In that regard, one should examine for a fetus even by means of cutting or piercing;
wherever circular marks are seen, there one should diagnose a fetus.
A frog arises there in a spot resembling the color of madder; in a yellow circle, a lizard;
and in a black one, a black snake.
In a tawny [spot], a mouse is indicated; likewise, in a reddish one, a chameleon;
in a yellowish one, a stone; and in a variegated one, a house-lizard. (Vis 4.29)

In [the vein] resembling a sword, it is known as a water-jar; in one resembling a lotus, it is sand; in the variegated [vein], it is a scorpion; and in the blue and yellow [veins], it is a moth. Vis 4.30.
A wise person should identify a firefly-like circle as being honey-colored;
furthermore, I shall explain the defects arising from the appearance of the embryo exactly as they are. Vis 4.31.
Through a frog there will be ill health; through a lizard one will become destitute;
through a snake one dies by poison; and through a mouse one will be childless. (Visuddhimagga 4.32)
In a chameleon there is short life; on a stone, death by lightning;
in a female earthworm, loss of wealth; and in water, indeed, the destruction of the fetus. (Vis 4.33)
In the *sikātā* year there is an absence of water; likewise, in the *vṛścika* year there is strife.
In the *śalabha* year there will be the destruction of the kingdom, and in the *khadyota* year, the ruin of one's family.
Therefore, one should constantly and vigilantly examine the fetus with effort;
for if, out of greed, one fashions an image together with the fetus, [it will result in misfortune].
The king who is the lord of that mandala is both the creator and the establisher; these [obstacles] become uprooters. Therefore, one should purify the womb.
O Lord of Śacī, whether made of jewels, metal, or wood, a [water] vessel that always reflects the interior within its interior bestows growth and auspiciousness. Vis_4.37.
In this latter portion of the Tantra, I have proclaimed in due order the characteristic of Pramīma, which was told to Nārada; it is the most secret of secrets and unsurpassed.
Therefore, having understood what precedes and what follows, one should cause the measurement to be performed in due order.
Thus has been declared the procedure for the mountain, the most excellent among the excellent.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Collecting Stones," in the venerable Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā of the Pāñcarātra.
The Fifth Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme installation of the Śūla.
One should place the spear of the image upon the deposit of jewels.
One should take woods such as khadira, especially those suitable for sacrificial rites;
O Lord of Śacī, listen first as I shall describe their characteristics. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.2)
Fifty-five and a quarter finger-breadths is said to be the length of the trident;
it is measured in successive finger-breadths, free from the defects of the wood.
The face is said to be twelve finger-breadths in measurement;
the portion below it may be one and a quarter [finger-breadths], or twenty-seven [in total].
The thigh-shaft is said to be twenty-five finger-breadths in length, with its lower end directed downward and measuring half a finger-breadth [in thickness]. Vis 5.5.
The knee should be one and a quarter parts; the shank is equal to the thigh.
Two *golaka*s are prescribed below, and likewise two intervals between them.
The width of the chest-pillar should be twenty-five finger-breadths;
the width of the hip-pillar is said to be sixteen finger-breadths. (Vis 5.7)
The length of the upper arm-staff should be twenty-five finger-breadths;
the length of the lower arms, however, should be seventeen finger-breadths.
The wrist is one *kalā* in length; it is fashioned so as to shine like a binding. The length of the middle finger is recorded as five *aṅgulas*. (Viṣṇu 5.9)
This is the measurement for the trident; other [measurements] have been mentioned, but one should observe further [details].
O Lord of Śacī, however, one should employ the tridents of the goddesses even if they have not been specifically described.

One should have the characteristics of the trident fashioned according to the treatises on arts (śilpaśāstra), O Lord of Śacī; for if the trident is worn out by clay, cloth, rope, or similar materials, [it is ineffective]. 5.11.
Furthermore, having produced another [image], one should have it made exactly as previously described;
one should not make it inferior or superior, but should act like the "worn-out staff. (5.12)
Thus has this been declared by me regarding the rite of restoring what is decayed;
it is performed with logic and specific methods by those who are unwearied in this matter.
O Lord of Śacī, I shall now proclaim the preliminary consecration of the sacrificial stake (śūla) and other rites;
listen with a one-pointed mind, secluded from distractions, as I speak. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.14)
In front of the palace, one should construct a square pavilion,
provided with four doors and adorned with four archways.
Covered with a canopy of cloth, adorned with ornaments,
it was one hundred and five cubits in width and exactly that much in length.
In the middle of that, O Lord of Śacī, having constructed an altar measuring ten tālas, it should be ten cubits or twelve cubits in size.
Having divided that pavilion (or its platform) into three parts, one should construct the altar in the center with a measurement reduced by ten *tālas*.
One should have an excellent altar constructed.
Having constructed an altar two palm-trees high, resembling the surface of a mirror,
one should duly fashion the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) upon that altar in due order.
At a distance of four *tālas* or three *tālas* from all sides,
one should arrange square and other shapes around the pedestal (*vedikā*).
Or, for the rite of installing the stake, it should be performed upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having properly constructed the pavilion in this manner, one should carry out the water-shed (prapā) ceremony therein.
Having first performed the rite of offering the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should install the supreme trident;
likewise, having made the appropriate adjustments for the male and female deities of the trident and so forth, one should proceed in due order.
One should arrange for a stay in the water for either three nights or one night;
listen, Śakra, Lord of Śacī, to this secret preliminary consecration in the water.
O Lord of Śacī, one should practice dwelling in water in a river, or a lake, or a mountain spring, or in a river flowing toward the ocean. Vis_5.24.
Having established the imperishable Hari on that delightful shore,
the practitioner who knows the supreme goal meditates upon Hari within the center of the trident.
The supreme practitioner should install either a mere metal image;
having worshipped it with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, he should commence the rite of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Vis 5.26.
Having understood the great eight-syllable mantra, the expert in mantras,
having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his own body, should thereafter perform the placement upon the deity in due order.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the order of emanation (sṛṣṭi) therein; one should not here recollect the order of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
The wise one should perform the six-syllable placement and then perform the placement of persistence (sthiti) in due sequence.
Then, in front of the deity, one should smear the ground with cow dung;
having strewn rice grains in its center, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
O Lord of Śacī, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the center upon the pericarp;
having placed scented water in the east, one should place water with flowers in the south.
One should place coconut water in the west and kuśa-grass water in the north;
having placed curd in the southeast and milk in the southwest.
In the northwest, however, one should place water with *maṅgala* [grains], and in the northeast, water with barley;
thus, one should arrange these nine [substances] in sequence within the center of the lotus.
One should arrange the eight world-protectors around the lotus;
one should place water inside each vase in due order.
And having covered them with new cloths upon the jars,
O Lord of Śacī, let there be one new cloth for each, or even three for each.

Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, he, the best among those who know mantras, should likewise utter the *Svastisūkta*, having worshipped [the deity] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, under his own name.
Afterward, while recollecting Nārāyaṇa, one should bathe [the image] according to the sequential method,
using jars containing the five products of the cow and other substances, with the *parameṣṭhi* mantra as before.
Having adorned it with flower garlands, one should wrap it in variegated cloths;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should remain mindful of the Lord Nārāyaṇa. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.37)
Having constructed a water-shed in the midst of the water, adorned with canopies,
measuring either seven cubits or five cubits in size.
Having wrapped it with darbha grass threads, one should then wrap it again with garlands;
O Lord of Devas, it should be four cubits in length and equal in width.
Adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass, embellished with strings of pearls,
decorated with flower garlands, and graced by banners.
Having thus decorated the water-shed, one should place a seat in its center—an unsurpassed wooden seat provided with four legs. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.41)
Having invoked the deity into its midst while recollecting the Ocean of Milk,
the knower of mantras should cause the Lord of Śacī to lie down with the Mūrti-mantra.

The preceptor, who has mastered the tantras and knows the five Upaniṣads, should cause [the deceased] to lie either with the head toward the east or toward the south, O Lord of the Pitṛs. (Viṣṇudharmottara 5.43)
Then the person should worship Hari with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
he should place the eight jars of the world-protectors around the deity.

One should worship all [the deities] by their own names, following the sequence beginning with Indra, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, accompanied by the sound of the bell. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.45)
The practitioner who knows the ultimate truth, having offered everything from perfumes up to lamps,
should cause the bali offering to be made in sequence to the eight directions around that drinking-water station.
Recalling the world-protectors with this [mantra], the best among those who know the tantras,
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, should perform what has been taught or whatever else [is required].
"O Lord of Śacī, the procedure for dwelling in the water has been explained by me in due order.
On the following day, O Indra, at the afternoon hour, you should remain composed. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 5.48)
Having emerged from the water, the knower of the tantras, together with conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments,
should worship the two deities after adorning them with garlands and other ornaments.
One should place [the image] in the northeast portion of the pavilion in the bathing pavilion;
having performed the ritual bath according to the rules, one should worship it in sequence with perfumes and other offerings.
In this subsequent tantra, I have explained the ritual bathing in its proper sequence;
having performed that bathing in sequence, one should then prepare the bed in due order.
Having prepared a bed, one should lay out the collection of tridents;
in the center of it is the trident of the God, and the trident of the Goddess on the two sides.
One should cover the tridents with cloths and worship them with fragrant flowers;
then, one should perform the *sṛṣṭinyāsa* using the Puruṣasūkta. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 5.53)
In that [state], withdrawal is not desired; one should apply the principles (*tattva*) there.

The twenty-five principles are: root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*), the great one (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), ether (*ākāśa*), wind (*vāyu*), fire (*vahni*), water (*vāri*), earth (*vasuṃdharā*), speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, mind (*manas*), prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna, and the individual soul (*jīva*).
Having thus arranged the principles, one should assign their names.
Then, on the altar, with a concentrated mind, he should place full water-pots upon a heap of grain, following the sequence starting from the east.
Having worshipped Varāha and the others by their respective names in the eight petals (or jars),
the consecration of the Brahma-jar on the altar is not required.
One should not recall here any unmentioned varieties of ritual placement (*nyāsa*);
rather, having worshipped with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, one should remain mindful of Hari, Nārāyaṇa.

The guardians of the forms (mūrtipāḥ) should offer oblations separately into either the fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), according to the sequence starting from the east for the forms beginning with Vāsudeva.
One should offer oblations in sequence one hundred and eight times with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, honey, milk, curd, and ghee. Vis_5.59.
With the Puruṣasūkta itself, according to the sequence starting from the east and so forth,
one should perform sixteen oblations for each and every fire-pit.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should bring the fire-sacrifice (homa) to completion;
he should present milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, and rice mixed with cow's milk to the Lord of Gods.
At that time, one should employ the sounding of conchs and drums;
for the sake of protection, one should perform an offering to the eight directions with the weapon-mantra and sacrificial oblation.
Accompanied by the sound of bells, one should cause the conch and the drum to be sounded;
then, one should wrap it from above with new cloths in successive layers.
Having offered fragrant flowers and prostrated with the añjali mudrā,
one should spend the remainder of the night in due order with song, dance, the lute, and so forth.
When the night has turned into dawn, the preceptor should perform his bath;
having applied the vertical *puṇḍra* marks in due order, he should be adorned with garments and ornaments.
Rising together with the image-worshippers while recollecting the base of the trident,
he should honor it with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, and then offer the oblation into it.
Performing the circumambulation of the universe in a counter-clockwise direction, he should cause [the deity] to enter the inner sanctum;
then the preceptor should install the trident with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra.
Having established the Devīśūla with its own name, such as Śrī and so forth,
one should extract the Vedas along with their accents and recite them at that time.
Having invoked Vārāha and the others, one should sprinkle them in sequence upon the tip of the trident;
then the seat by Puṃs, and then the bed by Viśva.
Furthermore, the holder should sprinkle the vehicle with the *nivṛtti* [water] upon its head;
from the head down to the feet, he should [sprinkle] Vārāha and the others in successive order.
One should assign the trident (*śūla*) to the body with its own name individually;
one should likewise establish the trident at the two sides of the deity, [namely] Śrī and Puṣṭi.
One should have an image made from half-stone and half-wood, complete with its primary and secondary limbs; one should install it there as previously described for the trident.
Having taken a new, smooth cloth there, free from blue fibers and the like,
one should cover the image with it while reciting the *praṇava* alone.
The wise one should have the image restored according to its previous appearance,
having performed the re-consecration in due order according to the scriptures on installation.
In this [body], the marrow is the stake; therein, the sinews are the rope; the flesh is the clay, and the skin is the cloth; thus is this known to be like a body. 5.75.
Just as one might conceive of sixty-four veins within the body,
so too should one extract the essence from the husk of a coconut for the purpose of making rope.
Nooses should be fashioned upon the stake by auspicious artisans skilled in that work;
having thus prepared it with cords, one should wrap it well all around its limbs.
In brief, the most auspicious method of binding with ropes has been described;
having performed this according to the rule, the supreme installation upon the stake is accomplished.
Thereafter, one should honor the teacher with wealth and golden earrings;
thereafter, one should likewise honor the artisan with new garments.
One should first honor the astrologer with garments, gold, and rings;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas who are Vaiṣṇavas and masters of the Vedas. (Viṣṇu 5.80)
Thus has the installation of the supreme trident been briefly described.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Śūla," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Sixth Chapter. Viṣvaksena said: Now I shall describe the preparation of the clay; listen with a one-pointed mind.
It is declared to be of two kinds, the cooked and the uncooked, respectively for the Brahmins and the others.
All the world does not praise an image made of burnt clay;
an unbaked image is praised, and that alone should be made by the wise.
One should never make it with lime nor ever with stone powder;
one should make the earthen image with clay alone, according to its appropriate color.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the clay is traditionally held to be white and soft; for a Kṣatriya, it is remembered as reddish;
for Vaiśyas, it should be yellow and soft; and for a Śūdra, it is declared to be black.
One should take clay produced from a sacred field according to the sequence of colors,
and [prepare it] with curd, clarified butter, milk, and linseed oil.
Having first ground sugar, iron, and stones into powder,
one should then mix these powders in equal proportions with clay.
One should grind śrīveṣṭaka, resin (sajjarasa), saffron (kuṅkuma), and koṣṭha with a decoction of khadira and arjuna.
And these juices, including *kunduru*, are all endowed with every flavor;
they are found on the banks of river confluences and in sacred groves.
Having taken clay from that place mixed with oily powder,
and having let it sit for a month, one should then fashion the image.
If ground for three nights, that clay becomes as hard as stone;
I have thus described the preparation of the clay, by which one should fashion the image in due order.
One should have a very firm and beautiful image made by a craftsman in accordance with the vision of the scriptures, complete with all its primary and secondary limbs.
One should wrap a very smooth new cloth over the image,
and upon that, one should write [the mantra] in a smooth manner according to the sequence of the syllables.
Therefore, I shall explain that in the sequence of its colors:
white, yellow, red, green, and black.
These five colors are said to have the earth and other elements as their presiding deities;
those produced from minerals are declared to be supreme, while those originating from trees are middling.
The inferior [caste] born from a union should be known; the collection of castes is threefold:
the caste itself, the sub-caste, and likewise the mixed caste.
In this treatise, I shall describe the threefold combination of castes;
those who are pure are called "castes" (varṇa), while others are produced through activities such as royal service and the like.
Those phonemes which, among the vowels, are generally devoid of purity are called *anuvarṇas*; I shall now describe the *saṃkaras*.
It is of four kinds: white, red, black, and blue.
That which has the luster of the color of a conch shell or cow’s milk is designated as "white. (ViS 6.18)
Green and yellow—the yellow-colored [pigment] is of two kinds:
realgar (manaḥśilā) and yellow orpiment (harītāla) are proclaimed to be green. (Viṣṇu 6.19)
That which has the luster of turmeric or saffron is called yellow;
thereafter, the dark complexion is considered to be of two kinds: the dark and the black.
One [complexion] has the luster of durvā grass and emerald, while another resembles sapphire;
that which is red mixed with white is designated as "harit" (yellowish-green).
Yellow mixed with white is called "fair" (gaura);
that which is mixed with red is designated as "tawny" (kapila). (ViS 6.22)
Black mixed with white is designated as "smoky" (dhūmra);
black mixed with yellow is designated as "dark" (kāla).
White joined with yellow and black is called "pale-white" (gaura);
white joined with yellow and red is declared to be "variegated" (karbura).
A complexion joined with yellow and black is proclaimed to be the color of Hari;
thus, through such a mixture, the complexion remains firmly fixed for that duration.
The form described as resembling something is a description of its color and configuration;
it arises from an unseen place, is intermediate, and is produced by time.
Thus has the classification of the castes been proclaimed in due order:
Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha.
In the Kali age, O Lord of Śacī, one should have that image made with a dark complexion; know that it bestows auspiciousness,
prosperity, and increases the king and the kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort in the Kali age, one should have [an image] made of Śyāma;
otherwise, one incurs misfortune and brings about the destruction of the king and the kingdom.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Purification of Clay," in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Seven. Viṣvaksena said:
Henceforth, O Lord of Śacī, I shall proclaim the chapter on dreams—supremely secret and intended for those who are secluded; listen to it in due order, O Lord of Śacī. (Vis 7.1)
A dream in the first watch yields its ripening after one year;
in the second, after eight months; and in the third, after three months.
In the period from dawn until midnight, the fruit [of an action] occurs within ten days;
beyond that, I shall declare what is meritorious and what is non-meritorious—listen indeed!

Mounting bulls, elephants, palaces, mountain peaks, or trees; being smeared with excrement; and approaching women who should not be approached—these are declared to be auspicious in dreams. (Visuddhimagga 7.4)
But he who sees at the end of a dream a king, an elephant, a horse,
gold, a bull, or a cow—
his household increases.
If one climbs alone a tree that bears both fruit and milk, and while staying there one becomes aware [of its nature], one will quickly obtain wealth. Vis 7.6.
Whether one eats while staying in a palace, or crosses the ocean,
even if born into a family of slaves, such a person shall become a king.
He who, at the end of a dream, obtains a lamp, food, fruit, a lotus, a maiden, an umbrella, or likewise a banner, will certainly attain prosperity through the mantra.
Now listen as I describe the fruit for one who, at the end of a dream, eats human flesh—whether raw or well-cooked. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 7.9)
If one eats his foot, the gain is a hundredfold; if one eats his arm, a thousandfold;
and if one eats his head, one shall obtain a kingdom or a hundred thousandfold.
If one awakens having obtained sandals and an umbrella,
or a stainless, sharp sword, one should predict a journey for him. (Vis 7.11)
He who boards a boat or crosses over rivers shall be sentenced to exile, with a swift return required.
If one's teeth fall out or appear to fall during a dream,
it portends the loss of wealth or suffering from arrows in battle.
One who anoints [the head] with oil, or with milk, or with ghee, or with any other unctuous substance— for such a person, one should predict disease. (Visuddhimagga 7.14)
If horned or tusked beasts, or even monkeys or boars, charge at one in a dream,
there will be danger from the royal family.
A woman wearing red garments, with red perfumes and ointments,
who embraces one in a dream— one should designate that person as a killer of a Brahmin.
If a woman dressed in white garments, anointed with white perfumes,
embraces one in a dream, prosperity shall attend him from every side.
If one sees the solar disc or the moon in a dream, one who is ill is freed from disease, and one who is healthy shall attain prosperity. Vis 7.18.
He who, having encountered a female mule, a female crane, or a female curlew, awakens himself,
shall obtain a sweet-speaking wife brought from a distance of one krośa.
Furthermore, he who is released from shackles as well as from the nooses of his arms—
there a son shall be born, or one should predict that he will attain a firm foundation.
But he who is bitten by a white snake on the auspicious right [hand] obtains a thousand pieces of wealth on the completion of the tenth day.
If one dreams of a village or even a city surrounded by entrails,
one will become a sovereign king of the mandala in that village, or a ruler in that city.
If in a dream one drinks blood or even liquor,
a Brahmin will obtain knowledge, while another shall obtain wealth. (Vis 7.23)
If one drinks the frothy milk of cows during milking in a dream,
that person shall partake of the drinking of Soma and, at the end, [attain] the earth through sacrifice.
Upon seeing curd, there shall be joy; upon seeing wheat, the arrival of wealth;
one should know that from barley comes the acquisition of ghee, and likewise from white mustard seeds.
But he who, seated upon a lotus leaf in the middle of the lake, should eat honeyed milk-rice— him one should know to be a lord of the earth.
Having worshipped that *liṅga* and beheld it, especially the gods,
one attains victory in legal proceedings.
And there shall be abundant wealth.
One should know that when it is flowering, it is in bloom; when it has borne fruit, there is supreme intelligence. When it is emitting smoke, that is ruin; when it is blazing, it brings prosperity.
Whether on a seat, in bed, in a vehicle, in the body, in a carriage, or in a house—when these are ablaze, he awakens; his prosperity shall face every direction.
Whatever deities, twice-born brahmins, cows, ancestors,
or ascetics tell a man in a dream, one should declare that to be exactly so.
All white things are to be welcomed, with the exception of cotton, ashes, bones, and buttermilk;
all black things are not auspicious, with the exception of cows, elephants, gods, Brahmins, and horses.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for Dreams," in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
The Eighth Chapter.
On the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk, [he beheld] the golden one performing austerities.
The sage Nārada [approached] the commander of the army on Viṣṇu’s mountain of sport.
Having seen him, bowed down, and honored him, the Blessed One— impelled by the power of devotion to Viṣṇu—
questioned him who stood there as if he were the very embodiment of devotion.
But previously, the characteristics of the forms of the Supreme Self and others were explained,
as well as the characteristics of the mantras, the meters, and likewise the sages.
O General, if I am worthy of your favor, you should explain these and other matters, such as the types of dwellings and so forth, in their proper order.
Viṣvaksena said: Listen, O best of divine sages, to all that you have asked.
I shall explain it in its entirety and in due order; be attentive.
This tantra has its root in the Śruti and is an authoritative source, like the Kalpasūtras;
this alone is established as the sole authority even among the Āgamas.
It bestows long life and health upon men, and brings about fame, prosperity, sons, and offspring;
it effects the destruction of evil, constitutes great merit, and is indeed the means for accomplishing yoga.
Therefore, in that regard, the northern portion always bestows prosperity and auspiciousness;
from the initial laying of the bricks onwards, it eternally grants all desires.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for smoothing the bricks,
as well as the plowing, the dwelling of the cattle, and likewise the purification of the ground.
I have already explained in the earlier portion of this tantra that,
preceded by the ritual of offering seed-sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) during the first watch of the night.
Having constructed a pavilion as before, one should smear it with cow dung and adorn it with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
In the first part of the night, however, the four primary bricks are prepared;
they may be made of stone or clay, and should be endowed with the proper characteristics.
Bricks free from defects, twice as long as they are wide, are prescribed for a very large [stūpa];
they should be six, five, or four finger-breadths thick.
These [bricks] are of the sequence beginning with the best, twice as long as they are wide;
their thickness is said to be half their width according to the measurement of the bricks.
Having sprinkled [the site] with the five products of the cow and likewise strewn it with *kuśa* grass,
one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made and then sprinkle [the area] with water mixed with *kuśa*.
The wise one should bind the auspicious thread with golden [threads] using the root-mantra;
having covered each [thread] with cloths, he should place it at the front.
Thereafter, one should place the water jars, provided with cloths and lids;
and the central jar should be very firm and endowed with the five jewels.
The supreme practitioner should consecrate the water-jar with the root mantra;
he should fill the jars in sequence, joined with the lords of the vidyās.
The Vārāha, the Nārasiṃha, the Śrīdhara, the Hayaśīrṣaka,
Rāma the son of Jamadagni, the Vāmana, and the Vāsudeva.
In this manner, one should worship the aforementioned Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) in sequence within the jars;
having placed coral in the jar of Vārāha and cat's-eye (pravālaka) in that of Nārasiṃha.
Having placed emerald in Śrīdhara, lapis lazuli in Hayaśīrṣaka, sapphire in Rāma, and ruby in Vāmana-Nairṛta; Vis_8.21.
One should place a topaz on Vāmana and a conch-shell on Vāsudeva;
in the absence of these, a golden one, and if even that is unavailable, a pearl.
The wise man should have [the image] prepared with a beard, adorned with all ornaments;
then, at dawn, he should worship it along with the master craftsman and the carpenters.
The *sthāpaka* is fit for the mantras, while the *sthapati* is fit for the ritual work;
there, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should bathe the bricks with the root-vidyā.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should honor the astrologer;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor there with gold, garments, and rings.
Then, having worshipped Takṣaka, one should begin the laying of the bricks;
this location is prescribed on the right side of the door.
The wise one should place the bricks around [the altar] in due order during three muhūrtas;
and he should install them in the four directions with the vidyā-mantras of Vāsudeva and the others.
Afterwards, having adorned the artisan with garments, gold, and rings,
and having established him together with that very [image], one should place bricks in the four directions.
In the midst of those, one should fill the pit with water;
a clockwise swirl is indeed auspicious, while a counter-clockwise swirl is inauspicious.
Likewise, one should perform a hundred oblations with the root mantra while turning counter-clockwise;
at that very time, one should place the nine gems in their proper sequence.
One should place, in sequence, diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, conch-shell, crystal, topaz, moonstone, sapphire, and ruby.
On an elephant’s tusk, or in a conch shell, an anthill, or a crab’s dwelling;
on a bull’s horn, in a lake, at a river, at a sacred ford, or likewise on a mountain.
And having taken earth from the ocean, one should likewise fill the pit;
then, after having the Brahmins recite the "Auspicious Day" formula, one should feed them.
In this first celestial palace, all of this should be performed without sloth;
however, in the pavilion it may be devoid of jewels, and in the rampart as well, it should be devoid of jewels.
If this is done,
it bestows the abundance of all prosperity;
if it is not done in this way, then one may be possessed by piśācas and the like.
There will be great fault for both the one who performs [the act] and the one who causes it to be performed;
therefore, with every effort, one should practice according to the prescribed injunctions.
O great sage, he who first undertakes the work together with the carpenters and architects, with the consent of the patron, [should begin] with the plowing and so forth. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 8.37.
Furthermore, whether it be the restoration of what is dilapidated or even work such as painting,
the wise man should have it executed by that very person and never by anyone else.
That which was produced by the carpenter through pride and so forth has been extracted once again by the carpenter himself,
by means of his carving.
"Nothing at all would have to be done"—this is the certainty of the scripture.
Therefore, with every effort, the installers and carpenters should perform the installation;
