otherwise, whether out of delusion or greed, it must not be done by anyone other than the installers and carpenters.
Whoever should cause this to be done or perform it himself would destroy the king and his kingdom;
thus, having examined [the site] in many ways, the wise and best of practitioners [should proceed].
Having become tranquil in mind, one should perform the rite for the first brick;
then, at the conclusion of the first brick, one should gradually commence the temple.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Rule for the First Brick," in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*.
Chapter Nine. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the child’s initiation;
listen briefly, O Nārada, to both the first and the second. Vis_9.1
One should construct a small temple for the deity in front of the palace, facing the great celestial mansion (mahāvimāna), at a distance that is neither too far nor too near. Vis_9.2.
One should arrange it facing the great house— or perhaps the entrance to the house— at the eastern gate; however, in the absence of a palace to face, one should arrange it toward the south.

O best of sages, one should construct the temple for the young [deity] either to the north, or between Soma and Īśāna, or in the northeast; however, in the absence of these, one may fashion it elsewhere.
O best of sages, in the east it brings about the increase of the kingdom and bestows wealth, grain, and happiness; in the south, there shall be the prosperity of the village and the nation.
O Sage, for the sake of attaining Brahman and supernatural powers, for bringing happiness through sons and grandsons,
and for the destruction of the fear of famine, one should [worship] between Someśa and Īśāna.
In that [direction], in the northeast, there shall be the site of the village, which brings about prosperity;
in the palace, the location for children is in the west, at the western gate.
In that [mandala], one should perform everything according to the sequence beginning with the south, as previously described;
immediately thereafter, one should take the location of the primary site.
O best of sages, first one should construct the temple;
it should be made of bricks or even of clay, as prescribed by the scriptures. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 9.9)
Having ascertained [the proportions], let the practitioner fashion it at six, five, seven, or even nine cubits, according to the desire of the patron. (Vis 9.10)
One-third of the measurement of the sanctum is recommended as the measurement for the door;
the height of the door should be twice the measurement of its width.
The preceptor, together with artisans, should have a house for the child constructed either with a peaked roof or in the shape of a pavilion. Vis_9.12.
One should have the laying of the first bricks and so forth performed here as before;
having constructed a pavilion in front, well-protected and enclosed by a wall.
One should perform the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), but the deposition of jewels (ratnanyāsa) is not desired;
having constructed a pedestal (pīṭha) there in the center, either with wood or likewise with bricks.
Or, having prepared a very firm and smooth altar made of clay or wood, one cubit in height, provided with eight petals and a pericarp; Vis_9.15.

Having thus constructed a house for children according to the practitioner's desire, and having likewise built an excellent temple for the Youthful One (Kumāra) according to the prescribed rite; Vis_9.16.
Now listen to the characteristics of the forms of the Supreme Self and the others.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Child-Abode," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Tenth Chapter. Nārada said:
What is the definition of an image, or what is the definition of the different types of forms? And how [is it so]?
O best among speakers, tell me the arrangement of the sun.
Viṣvaksena said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom! This question is for the benefit of the world.
Listen with respect and effort, and remain attentive. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.2)
The Supreme Self (Paramātman) is the first,
and Vāsudeva is the second.
Saṃkarṣaṇa shall be the third, and Pradyumna the fourth.
The fifth, however, is Aniruddha; these indeed are the primordial forms.
They have been described according to the sequence of the four forms; now hear the sequence of the ten forms.
The Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, the Man-lion, and the Dwarf;
Rāma, son of Jamadagni, Balarāma, and Kṛṣṇa, who is worshipped by the gods.
"Kalki is declared to be Viṣṇu; such is the sequence of your ten forms.
O sinless one, I shall now describe to you the distinction of the twelve forms."
O Sage, among them Keśava is the first, and Nārāyaṇa is supreme;
then there is Mādhava, and Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama shall be by name, as well as Vāmana and Śrīdhara;
Hṛṣīkeśa shall be another, and after that, Padmanābha.
Therefore, O great sage, it is traditionally held that the form of Brahmā resides within this;
listen as I speak of this reality, the glorious form known as Dāmodara. Vis_10.9 //
One shall be Viśvarūpa, the second shall be Yajñamūrti, and the third shall be Vedamūrti; thus there shall be a triad of forms.
O best of sages, I shall describe to you the various forms beginning with Śrī;
first is the form of Śrī, and after that, the form of Puṣṭi.
Medhā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Vighneśa, and the six beginning with Śrī—such shall be the division starting with Śrī; I shall describe it according to the measurement of finger-breadths.
Eight sesame seeds are said to be one barley grain; eight barley grains are traditionally held to be one finger-breadth (aṅguli).
Alternatively, it may be the height of three rice grains, or simply eight barley grains laid side by side.
Alternatively, O ascetic, hear from me the measurement of the finger:
it is equal to the middle line of the middle finger of a teacher, O Sage. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.15)
O Sage, the measurement of a finger (mātrāṅgula) is the circumference of the middle joint of the middle finger of an average-sized hand. Vis 10.16.
Thus, O Sage, the threefold finger-breadth has been described; now, by means of those preferred fingers, the measurement for the temple as well as for the image (bera) should be performed.

Then, during the ritual arrangement of the eight auspicious vessels, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, the archway, the altar, the pavilion, and the fire-pit, as well as the sacrificial fuel sticks; 10.18.
And thus, at the beginning of the ritual of bathing, the wise preceptor, being well-prepared, should diligently perform the rite according to the rules using pure measures of finger-breadths. 10.19.

Alternatively, O divine sage, it was for the purpose of explaining the measurements of the eight auspicious symbols and so forth, according to the rules for the path of measurement, as the Sage was speaking. (Vis 10.20)

O Great Sage, this [measurement] is to be measured right here by the four fingers of the teacher’s hand, beginning with the little finger, as they slide obliquely across the middle joint of the middle finger. (Vis 10.21)
Twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) in measure is indeed called a palm (tāla); those who know measurement understand that two palms make a cubit (hasta). 10.22.
Thus has been described the threefold measurement according to the distinctions of the fingers; I shall now speak of the characteristics of the image—listen always with focused attention.
Whether by the measurement of the portable image, or again by the measurement of the door,
or by the measurement of the inner sanctum, it should be known according to the proportions of the primary image.
Whatever the measurement of the width of the main temple on the outside,
half of that is said to be the best, and half of that is remembered as the middling.
Half of that, they say, is the minimum height for the image here;
such is the measurement of the temple, so now hear the measurement of the door.

The height of the image should be one-quarter greater than the door for the best, equal to the measurement of the door for the middling, and one-quarter less than the door for the inferior. (Vis 10.27)
I shall proclaim the measurement of the womb; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth.
An image that is three-quarters or two-thirds as long [as the base] is considered the best. 10.28.
An image that is five parts as high as the [temple] is considered medium; that which is half the height of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) is the height of an inferior image. Vis_10.29.
The measurement of the womb has been declared, as well as the variegated [mandala] and the half-variegated;
now listen, O Nārada, to the procedure for the "semblance of the variegated. Vis 10.30.
An auspicious image should be made according to the measurement of the appropriate time; it may be a full painting, a half-painting, or likewise a mere appearance of a painting.
Those who know the treatises declare that there are three kinds of image-making:
wherein the limbs of the image are visible on all sides. (Vis 10.32)
It is recited that she was marvelous in her height, breadth, and proportions;
yet, as for her when she was in the form of stone, her back could not be seen. (Vis 10.33)
That which is joined with the measurements of honor is known as the "Half-Picture" (sārdhacitra), whether it exists in the form of a painting or is even drawn by artisans. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.34)
When joined with the correct measure of pride, that is called the "variegated appearance" (citrābhāsa).
The superior fruit is the "variegated" (citra), while the middling is the "half-variegated" (ardhacitraka).
Painting is declared to be the lowest [form] in the sequence of rites for consecration.
Thus has been explained the rite concerning images; O Sage, now hear the procedure for the pedestal. Vis_10.36.
Having divided the height into three parts, one part is for the height of the pedestal;
and one part out of four is for the height of the seat in the standing posture.

From the door, the base should have a width of one-quarter [of the door's measurement] and a height equal to that;

The circular [shape] is declared to belong to Śiva, while the square belongs to Pitāmaha; its length is one cubit, and its circumference is said to be of that same measure.
This has been declared regarding the standing posture; now the seated posture is described:
the height of the lotus-feet should be two parts of the womb-door.
Its length and width are as previously described; the remainder is stated here:

"O Sage, thus has the characteristic of the primary images, such as the root-liṅga, been described;

The *kautuka* (auspicious thread) may be of three kinds—superior, middling, or inferior—depending on whether it consists of one part of the Veda or one part of the elements. (Viṣṇudharmottara 10.45)

For a Śūdra, the images may be made of copper, or for all castes, they may even be made of copper; images made of iron are declared to be faultless when properly described.
The jewel-born [fires] are said to be of three kinds: the lunar, the solar, and the combined.
That which consists of moonstone is the lunar; the other, consisting of sunstone, is the solar. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.59)
The "crystal" [type] is said to be equal [in height]; the former is superior to the former, and the latter is the most excellent.
Its height should be two finger-breadths or four finger-breadths.
The image of the jewel is said here to be three finger-breadths in measure;
know that such was the former characteristic of the images for one's own sake. Vis 10.61.

For the characteristics of ritual actions, worship, and so forth, have been explained previously according to the threefold division of superior and so on; therefore, by that [explanation], the procedure may also apply for one's own sake.

The characteristics of those [images] painted on a board, a cloth, or a wall are the same as the characteristics of the ritual worship; that which has been stated regarding their proportions is authoritative. Vis_10.63.
In this matter, there is a certain distinction [to be made] regarding the *kramuka* and other such materials, or again,
with regard to the *pālāśa*, the *bilva*, or the *khadira*. (Viṣṇu 10.64)
Or with an udumbara tree, or with a bakula, O Great Sage, or especially with a panasa, if any of these trees are obtained. // Vis_10.65 //
It should be two finger-breadths thick and four finger-breadths long;
it may be either square or circular, and should be encircled by three girdles.
Upon that, one should again draw an eight-petaled lotus,
or else one endowed with twelve petals, possessed of all beauty.
One should specifically place the nine jewels upon its pericarp;
or else, one should place the pericarp upon that [image], or at the tip of the pericarp, or upon the panels and so forth.
Having invoked the deity, one should worship him for the sake of one's own sacrifice;
O Sage, hear now the distinction regarding the locations of the primary image and the other icons.
O Sage, when the interior of the temple is divided into seven parts, there are forty-nine squares;
the center of these is called the Brahma-square.
Outside of that is the region of the gods (the divine station);
outside of that would be the human [region];
and outside of that, the realm of the Piśācas should be known—thus has the distinction of the stations been declared. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.71)

O Sage, in the Brahma-rite there should be worship of the pedestal (*pīṭha*) and likewise of the image (*bera*); in the rite of many images (*bahubera*), there is the installation of the pedestal and the chowrie-fringe (*cāmarāṃśaka*). (Viṣṇu 10.72)

if a seat is to be prepared, one should resort to something human.

if one should do so out of negligence at a time other than those prescribed places, [it is improper].
For the lord of the mandala and for the king, as well as for the establisher [of the mandala], misfortune is certain;
no ritual actions bear fruit there—of this there is no need for deliberation. (Vis 10.75)
The son of the sacrificer will die; of this there is no doubt.
A terrible famine arises, and the entire kingdom perishes. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 10.76)
Therefore, with every effort, one should install images and the like;
O Nārada, the proper location for the images used in daily festivals and other rites is now described.
The wise one should place the *bali* image to the right of the ritual image (*karmārcā*),
and the bathing image (*snānabimba*) with care to the right of the *bali* image.
The location for the festival image is to the left of the ritual image; indeed,
the procession image and the pilgrimage image are both placed on the left side of the festival image.
The preceptor, most knowledgeable in the tantras, should install [the images] precisely in the correct sequence;
otherwise, if they are installed incorrectly, the performer shall encounter great danger.
"The king incurs strife and the village perishes as well"—thus has the division of the site for the perpetual festival and other forms of worship been demonstrated. (Viṣṇu 10.81)
Alternatively, listen to the characteristics of the primary image and the other icons:
the primary image, the ritual image, the daily worship image, and thereafter the festival image.

O celestial sage, the great festival, as well as the ritual bathing and worship, is called the "New Temple" (*taruṇālaya*); thus the sixfold cycle of the image (*pratimā*) has been described. (Vis 10.83)
Now listen, O Nārada, to the measurements of these:
the height of the best [image] shall be ninety-six finger-breadths.
The height of the middle [type] shall be reduced from this by the width of a finger;
it is said that the height of the inferior [type] shall be fifty-one [finger-breadths].
Thus it has been stated that the height of the primary images (bera) is of three kinds;
in the case of the consecration of a single image, the lowest [height] is prescribed.
"O Sage, it is said that the measurement of a stone image is not the highest; rather, it should be according to that [other] measurement when a stone image is installed. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.10.87)
In that regard, this procedure is prescribed according to the rule for a single Liṅga;
thus has been stated the characteristic of the height for one, two, or many Liṅgas. (Viṣṇudharmottara 10.88)
O Sage, the width should be made in proportion to the height;
now hear the characteristics of the goddesses for the installation of many beams.
O best of sages, the height [of the image] is taught to be up to the base of the arms of the god, or up to the breasts of the goddesses.
One should place a lotus bud in the right hand of the goddesses;
if there were a lotus in the left hand, one would encounter great fear.
The king incurs strife; therefore, he should avoid it with great effort. Hereafter, I shall explain the raising of the ritual image and so forth. 10.92.
Know, O Nārada, that the best [image] is twenty-four measures (twenty-four finger-breadths) in height;
the medium image is indeed twelve finger-breadths in height. Vis 10.93.
That which is eight finger-breadths in length is proclaimed as the lowest;
for an image intended for a perpetual festival, the length should be twelve finger-breadths.
"Or eight finger-breadths, or even four finger-breadths;
having understood this, O best of sages, one should perform the *bali* offering. (Viṣṇudharmottara 10.95)
For a great festival, twenty-two cubits or one cubit is said to be the length;
or it may be less by one and a half finger-breadths, or less by two finger-breadths. *Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa* 10.96.
Or it may be three finger-breadths less than the festival [measurement], O Great Sage;
beyond this, however, it is not [permitted].
O Nārada, one must indeed perform [the rites] with either deficiency or excess.
O best of sages, for the purpose of visiting sacred sites, for bathing, and likewise for festivals, it is sufficient even with a single image in the absence of a [full] form.
I shall describe the characteristics of this image; listen, O Nārada.
That which is proclaimed as the best is measured at twenty finger-breadths.
That which measures sixteen finger-breadths is declared to be the medium;
that which measures twelve finger-breadths is declared to be the inferior.
Hear now another [instruction] regarding the supreme image (*beraka*):
that which measures sixteen finger-breadths is called the best image. (Vis 10.101)
That which is twelve finger-breadths in measure is called the medium-sized image;
it may also be seven or eight finger-breadths, or even four finger-breadths.
One should have [the image] made endowed with the [proper] characteristics; this is declared to be the lowest [grade]. Hereafter, O Nārada, listen now as I shall explain [the others]. Vis_10.103.
O best of sages, O Nārada, the essential form of the images, such as the primary icon (mūlabera), may have eight arms, four arms, or even two arms.
The primary image and the others should be fashioned according to the wish of the patron;
one may likewise arrange them in a standing, walking, sitting, or reclining posture.
In this regard, O best of sages, there is a specific distinction concerning the bed:
one should worship either Aniruddha or the form of Padmanābha.
Having recognized that it possesses the required characteristics, one should have it laid down according to the prescribed injunctions;
O best of the twice-born, having thus fashioned the primary image, if it is indeed two-armed— ||| Vis_10.107 |||
The characteristics of the images for ritual worship and so forth may be four-armed;
however, O Lord of Sages, if the primary image (*mūlabera*) is for ritual worship, it should be two-armed.
Furthermore, the characteristic of the images of children and others may be four-armed;
for an image of a Great Festival, it may be either two-armed or four-armed.
O best of sages, I have thus declared the specific details regarding the bed;
in the manner described, one should have the image fashioned in due order.
If the root image has eight arms, the ritual image and others should have four arms;
if it has two arms, then [the others] should be the cause of universal destruction.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not fashion [the deity] as two-armed;
nor should one fashion a recumbent posture for an image that has eight arms.
Likewise, one should not perform the ritual of reclining for the forms of Matsya and the others,
nor for the forms beginning with Śrī and ending with Vighna, according to that same procedure.
But this I shall tell you, O Sage, which is more secret than the most secret:
he who is Nārāyaṇa in person is indeed called Vighneśa.
He who is called Vighneśa is indeed remembered as Nārāyaṇa,
O great sage, because he consists of Vāsudeva and because he is all-pervading.
Even the sages who perceive reality do not know its distinction;
however, O Nārada, I do not consider this [distinction] to be inferior, for it is one secret among secrets.
Out of affection for you, the knowledge imparted by the gods has been revealed;
therefore, [worship] Śrī, Durgā, Vāṇī, and Vighneśa as well.
The wise one should worship [the deities] independently for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals;
however, the characteristics of Śrī and the others should be understood by those most proficient in the tantras.
Therefore, when the forms of Śrī and the others act out of their own autonomy for the sake of others,
the characteristic previously mentioned should apply to worship performed for one's own sake.
The wise know from the Tantra that the height of Lakṣmaṇa and likewise the height of Bharata is up to the arms of the principal image.
The end of Lakṣmaṇa’s arms shall be the elevation of Śatrughna.
O Nārada, listen now to the truth regarding the sacrifice performed for one's own sake. Viṣṇu 10.121.
A height of sixteen finger-breadths is declared to be the best;
the middling should be half of that, while the smallest is two finger-breadths. Vis 10.122.
One should understand that the measurement of objects made of gold and so forth, as well as of paintings on wooden panels and the like, is proclaimed to be for one's own benefit. Vis 10.123.
The characteristic of its width should be made in proportion to the stated height.
Listen now to the materials, such as gold and others, and their respective fruits.
Gold, silver, copper, brass, stone, wood, and clay are recommended materials for the fashioning of images. (Vis 10.125)
One should give these [images] made of gold; through their recitation, they grant prosperity, fame, and happiness to men.
That [image] made of silver or iron, however, bestows happiness everywhere.
An image made of copper bestows sons, grandsons, and wealth; an image made of silver burns away all sins, afflictions, and sufferings. (Viṣṇudharmottara 10.127)
An image made of stone bestows good fortune, long life, and happiness directly;
an image made of wood grants strength, health, and fame.
"An earthen image is especially a bestower of all desires;
such are the varieties of objects and their respective fruits, O Nārada. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.11.29)
Out of affection for you, O Great Sage, the instructions regarding the making of images have been declared;
hereafter, I shall explain to you the collection of stone.

O Sage, the gathering of wood, the erection of the stake, the preparation of the clay, and all such preliminary tasks—O Great Sage, [these were performed].* Vis_10.131 *The Sanskrit text provided in the prompt is incomplete; this translation reflects the standard version of the verse.
In the eastern section, one should indeed cause five [images] to be made exactly as previously specified;
or else, O tiger among sages, listen to the procedure for the images.
The taking up of the stone is performed according to the procedure prescribed in the Padmodbhava Purāṇa;
that which begins with the taking up of the stone and ends with the consecration of the clay is [the first part]. (Viṣṇudharmottara 10.133)
Following the instructions prescribed by Viśvakarman and characterized by the technical definitions of the arts,
the artisan, with a concentrated mind, should perform the work at the command of the practitioner.
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautiful in all its limbs,
adorned with every ornament, and graced by a halo of light.
The practitioner, together with a craftsman, should fashion [the image] so that it shines, joined with the limbs beginning with the feet and adorned with ornaments and a crown.
"O Brahmin, tell me the characteristics of that supreme image which is fashioned for the sake of the vision of devotees;
it is impossible to describe them all."
Nārada said:
O God of gods, Lord of the world, everything you have spoken has been understood;
now, sever the doubt that dwells within my mind.
"O Lord, tell us this: is an image established in one place not also appropriate elsewhere? By that [explanation], we shall have our purpose fulfilled."
Viṣvaksena said: Listen, O Nārada; I shall speak that which you have now rightly spoken.
It is more secret than the secret itself, O one whose wealth is austerity, and must not be disclosed.
That which was previously [established] by means of the ritual within the celestial palace during the five nights;
In that regard, an image that is devoid of worship should be fashioned according to the rules of that scripture.
When the shrine has been constructed according to one's own tantra, the worship should take place there within that temple;
it would not be valid if performed according to another tantra—such is the certainty of the scripture. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.11.42)
In whichever celestial palace (vimāna) one is established according to a single tantra, in that very place the worship should be performed; it does not arise from another tantra.

When an image or a temple has been worshipped according to one tantra, at no time should there be worship according to another tantra; if one were to do so, it would cause great danger. (Viṣṇu 10.144)
O Sage, wherever there is no [proper] worship here due to the occurrence of a mixture of tantras, in each such case there is great fault; the king and the kingdom perish. (Vis 10.145)
Therefore, with every effort, one who desires the welfare of the entire world should act in such a way that no arising of faults in the tantra occurs.
Nārada said:
O Lord, if these [rites] are performed by one who has avoided all [forbidden things], what is the fruit thereof?
[Regarding] the worship of the image to be avoided...
Or rather, speak, O best among speakers!
Viṣvaksena: Out of delusion, fear, or greed, [one may act] with censured materials such as stone and the like.
One should worship the images and so forth with emanations alone, and not even with those [offerings] prescribed [in the scriptures].
If one should perform or cause to be performed [a rite] with prohibited materials such as stone and the like, that village will perish, as will the image for as long as it remains there. (Vis 10.149)
One should speak of strife even regarding the kingdom, for the king himself will perish therein;
therefore, a wise person should avoid what is forbidden with every effort.
Thus, the characteristics of the images have been briefly explained to you;
hereafter, I shall explain the distinctions beginning with the Paramātman.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Rules for the Characteristics of Images and Other Matters," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Eleventh Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
O best of sages, [tell me] the colors and other attributes of the weapons, as well as their arrangement.
O Nārada, first hear [this] for the sake of realizing the nature of the Supreme Self.
O Sage, [he sees] the Tridaśa, resembling a white mountain, seated upon Garuḍa; saluted by all the gods and worshipped by those such as the Lotus-seated One (Brahmā);
adorned with all ornaments, possessing two or four arms and two feet; resplendent with his own body, O Sage, and bearing a supreme golden radiance.
Thus, O best of sages, one should meditate upon that which consists of all the gods;
by so meditating, O Nārada, perfect knowledge arises for him.
Thus has the supreme self been shown to you directly in embodied form;
I shall now describe the arrangement of this embodiment and of its weapons.
On the tip of his right hand is a wheel, while his lower hand,
O Nārada, is positioned in the *svāgata* (welcoming) gesture or holds a lotus, O Hari.
One should place a rosary in the hand of the figure standing below;
in this same manner, it is prescribed for the right hands and the left side as well.
Above the hands on the left side, there should be a conch and a hand granting boons;
the hand at the waist should hold a mace—such is the form of the Supreme Self.
I shall describe to you the form and the weapons of Vāsudeva;
his form is either like cow’s milk or crystal, or else it is dark-complexioned.
Either wearing yellow garments or red robes,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should contemplate Vāsudeva, complete in all his limbs, adorned with four arms, and endowed with every ornament.
O great sage, I shall describe to you the arrangement of his weapons:
a discus at the tip of his right hand and a lotus situated below it.
Upon his upper left [hand] he should place a conch shell, and upon the other [upper right hand] a mace, both facing downwards;
he should then install Śrī on his right side and Puṣṭi on his left.
Or, O best of sages, one should place Tuṣṭi on the left side;
in this same manner, the image of Janārdana must also be fashioned.
Thus has been described [the form] of Vāsudeva; now hear that of Saṃkarṣaṇa.
He is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa, resembling the rising sun.
Wearing yellow garments, he was manifestly resplendent with four arms;
endowed with all limbs, he was adorned with every ornament.
"Always adorned with all ornaments and bearing the conch and the discus"—
this indeed is the form of Saṃkarṣaṇa in his right hand.
The wise one should place a discus on the upper [hand] and a mace in the lower hand;
it is said that a conch is on the upper left hand and a lotus in the lower [left] hand.
The wise one should establish Śrī on the right and Puṣṭi on the left;
thus Saṃkarṣaṇa has been described—now hear about Pradyumna, O Nārada.
Wearing yellow garments, four-armed, with all his limbs complete,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and adorned with all ornaments.
Thus, one should fashion the form of Pradyumna endowed with all ornaments;
in his upper right hand one should place a lotus, and below it, the Kaumodakī mace.
One should place the conch and the discus in the left hand, positioned above and below;
thus, O divine sage, the form of Pradyumna has now been described by me to you. (Vis 11.21)
We speak here of the Unobstructed; listen to this in truth, O Nārada:
he resembles a dark cloud and is like a mass of black collyrium.
The god who holds the conch and the discus, clad in yellow garments, four-armed, endowed with all ornaments, and beautiful in every limb. Vis_11.23.
Adorned with all ornaments, he is called Aniruddha;
in his upper left hand he holds a conch, and in his other hand a mace.
One should place the discus in the upper right [hand], while elsewhere the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) is desired;
[one should meditate on] Aniruddha, the Lord of the World, reclining upon Ananta.
One should place Śrī on his right side and Puṣṭi on his left;
when there is a bed, the primary image should have two or four arms.
O tiger among sages, one should fashion [the seat] which brings about all prosperity and happiness;
one should then place Śrī and Puṣṭi at the side of the feet of the deity.
Alternatively, O Sage, one may fashion Śrī at the side of the god’s crown;
she may be painted in full detail, or in half-detail, or even as a mere outline, O Sage.
One should perform the characteristics of the goddesses in sequence according to the desire of the sacrificer.
Thus, among the forms beginning with Śrī, each preceding one is more venerable than the next.
He is called Aniruddha; now hear, O Nārada, about the fish and the others.
In the center of a lotus made of a hundred petals— Vis 11.30.
Seated in the lotus posture, surrounded by eight fish, with a golden luster,
three eyes, two arms, facing eastward, and holding a lotus.
The form [of the deity], complete in all its limbs and adorned with all ornaments,
possessing the conceit of being a fish.
And thus it was said, O Nārada: (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 11.32)
The wise one should place a golden fish on the eastern petal of the lotus,
and then he should place a silver fish on the petal in the southeast direction.
In the middle of the petal in the southern direction, one should place a fish resembling copper;
in the petal in the southwest direction, one should place a black-colored fish.
One should place a red-colored fish in the petal of the western direction,
and one should place a dark-colored fish in the petal of the northwestern direction.
One should place a fish of smoky color on the petal in the northern direction;
one should place a fire-colored fish on the petal in the northeastern direction.
Thus, by means of the fish situated upon the petals of the eight directions,
the embodied form of the one who identifies with the fish has been shown to you out of affection, facing you directly.
On his right side one should place Śrī, and on the other side Puṣṭi;
then one should indeed place the form of the Fish, and after that, hear about the form of the Tortoise.
Resembling a mountain of black collyrium, with three eyes and beautified by his own limbs,
he possesses four arms and is adorned with all ornaments.
With a form resembling collyrium-ointment, seated upon a lotus carved from a twelve-petaled lotus,
and occupying his seat known as Padmasana, Viṣṇu dwells here in the body of a tortoise.

His form is surrounded by twelve tortoises, whose bodies have the appearance of the color of collyrium, who stand facing him, and whose bodies are mounted upon twelve-petaled lotuses arranged in a forward progression.
Holding a conch and a discus, and likewise with a lotus in his hand,
the god was then brought face-to-face by twelve tortoises.
In his upper right hand is a wheel and a lotus held between the fingers;
it is said that in the upper left hand is a conch, and in the lower left hand is a lotus. Vis 11.43.
Having placed Śrī on his right side, the wise one should likewise place Puṣṭi on the left; thus is the Kūrma form described.
O Sage, listen as I describe the Vārāha [image]: it resembles the color of rājāvarta stone, or it may be the color of a conch shell or dark blue, endowed with all the auspicious marks. Vis_11.45.
The goddess was in the full bloom of youth, beautiful in all her limbs,
the most excellent of women, with lovely hair and a face like a lotus.

Or she may have the luster of a flash of lightning, or she may be dark-complexioned; she is joined with all ornaments, and she has submerged herself in the auspicious earth with palms pressed together in reverence.
Embracing her with his left arm and lifting her up, the Lord embraced her as she stood firm;
clasping her with his left arm, he smelled the face of the Goddess.
O storehouse of asceticism, having embraced her shoulder with his left hand and firmly grasped her thigh with his right hand, [he spoke]. (Vis 11.49)
One should place the Lord, whose body is like that of a boar and who has four arms, holding the conch and the discus;
one should place the discus on the right and the conch on the left.
Thus, your first manifestation is recited as the form of a boar;
or else, it is the face of a boar, with a massive body and excellent tusks.
The form of that Great-Souled One is indeed endowed with all the primary marks, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa, and his sūtra-measure established across his body.
O storehouse of austerity, the medium version of the Varāha has been described in brief;
or rather, listen as I shall describe the form of the one who possesses the form of Varāha.
Having raised the left hand to the level of the nose,
one should always gaze at the space beyond the elbow on the half-portion of the left side.
Supporting the region of his hips with his right hand—
such was the form of Mahāviṣṇu, who bears the conch and the discus.
"In the palm of his right hand there is a discus, and in the other [hands] a conch";
thus the threefold form of the Varāha incarnation has been shown.
O Nārada, having been told that the form [of the deity] is thus threefold in aspect,
listen now to how the form of Nṛsiṃha must be fashioned.
Bearing a human form below the neck and his own true nature as a lion-faced being above,
he possesses terrifying eyes that shine with the splendor of fire and the sun.
Bearing the conch and the discus, adorned with all ornaments,
complete in every limb, he is auspicious and the bestower of all accomplishments.
The wise one should place a discus in the right hand and a conch in the left;
[the deity] resembles a white mountain and is the destroyer of all suffering.
His limbs were smeared with red sandalwood paste; his roar was like the crashing of dark clouds;
his tusks were like the crescent of the autumn moon; and he was enraged, with a jaw made of refined gold.
O Sage, having first fashioned such a form of Nṛsiṃha out of clay—with a perpetually blossoming face yet extremely terrifying to the wicked—[he was filled with joy]. Vis_11.62.
Having assumed the paryanka posture, seated upon an auspicious seat,
one should place the two hands, with palms upward, over the knees.
Thus has your form as Nṛsiṃha been described, which is worthy of your praise.
O great sage, listen now as we describe here the form of Vāmana. Vis_11.64.
He was smiling gently, with a lotus-navel,
short in stature and dwarf-like in form; resembling a young elephant, he had broad shoulders and mighty arms.
Dark-complexioned, with lotus-like eyes and long, stainless gaze,
he seemed, O Nārada, to cause the surface of the earth to tremble with his footsteps.
Endowed with a forest of matted locks and enchanting to all, he has two arms; with his right hand in a fist, he holds a staff. (Vis 11.67)
O Sage, your left foot is drawn up, while your right arm is extended in welcome; you are adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets.
Adorned with a long sacrificial thread and a triple girdle,
the young Brahmin Kāśyapa appeared perfectly suited to his state as a religious student.
Wearing either a loincloth or yellow robes,
he had assumed a dwarfed form for the sake of protecting the worlds.
Thus, O Great Sage, one should create a form endowed with these auspicious marks;
hereafter, I shall describe the form of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
His complexion is the luster of gold; he has two arms and is white and red;
he is seated with a serene countenance, encompassed by the splendor of Brahmā.
Complete with all the marks, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with every decoration, and graced by a circle of matted locks.
In his right hand he holds an axe, and in his left a bow with an arrow;
or else, he may hold a water-pot in the left and a rosary in the right.
O Sage, thus has the form of Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, been described to you;
now we shall describe here the form of you, the son of Daśaratha.
They were exceedingly endowed with beauty, with dark, wavy hair;
broad-chested and with sloping shoulders, they were adorned with armlets and bracelets.
Long-armed, endowed with splendor, gentle, and with smiling faces,
their eyes reaching to their ears, they were manifestly in the prime of youth.
As if sprinkling the world from all sides with the nectar-like waters of their beauty,
they held swords in their hands and bows in their grasp, their prowess celebrated throughout their arms.
O Sage, with their leather finger-guards and arm-guards bound on, they resembled Vaiśravaṇa;
by virtue of their magnanimity and perfection of form, they captivated the hearts of men.
The two heroic sons of Daśaratha, who grant joy to Kausalyā and Sumitrā, are most valiant and are like the scorching sun to the darkness of the Rākṣasas.
Those two delights of the Raghu dynasty, known as Nara and Nārāyaṇa,
have assumed human form for the sake of protecting the worlds.
O great sage, both of them had eyes as wide as lotuses, were dressed in yellow garments, carried quivers fastened to their upper arms, and held arrows in their hands.
Dwelling together with Śrī in the ocean of Vālmīki’s poetry,
those two were like death itself to the Rākṣasas, being far more terrifying than Rāvaṇa.
The two princes, the best of the Raghus, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
endowed with all auspicious marks, should be installed by those most skilled in the Tantras.
Sītā, the beloved of Rāma, endowed with all auspicious marks,
born pure and not from a womb, was manifested for the destruction of the Nairṛtas.
Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas and is established as the root-prakṛti,
is known by the name of the Manifest (vyakta) in its manifest form, yet it is directly the Unmanifest (avyakta) in its unmanifest form.
The illustrious Padmā, devoted to her husband, the most excellent of women and a goddess of fortune,
with hands like red lotuses and a face resembling a lotus.
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, whose divine limbs were unrestrained by youth,
endowed with the virtue of devotion to her husband, the beloved of Rāma.
Adorned with every ornament, her hair was dark and curled at the ends;
her braided tresses were bound with a garland, and her eyes wandered with intoxication.
Wearing black and yellow garments, she should be placed at Rāma’s side,
with her left fist raised toward the forehead, its opening facing upward.
O best of sages, cause him to place that firm bow, which is bent in three places and thick with a multitude of arrows, along with the Vāsava weapon, upon his left arm.
The arrow was fastened to his waist-string with his left hand;
it was a firm shaft, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, capable of bringing an end to the descendant of Pulastya.
Placing his face between them,
let the *golaka* become formidable as he crushes Rāvaṇa’s city along with his own army and his life-force.
Having struck [the drum] with the hand held by Rāma,
the wise one should place it on the right hand,
using either an eight-beat rhythm (vasutāla) or the sequence of a nine-beat rhythm (navatāla).
One should indeed carry all the weapons in accordance with their respective forms;
the left foot should be bent, while the right foot is well-placed.
The thumb should rest upon the place marked by the little finger;
the left foot should be positioned with the knee slightly bent.
O Nārada, best of sages, because he possesses three bends in these three parts— the face, the body, and the waist— he is celebrated as "Tribhaṅgī."
The face is bent to the right, while the middle of the body is bent to the left;
with the waist also bent to the right, this is declared to be the threefold bend (tribhaṅga).
The left hand should hold a bow and the right hand an arrow;
such shall be the characteristic of Lakṣmaṇa, while that of Bharata is as follows.
Furthermore, it is determined in the tantras that Śatrughna should be likewise;
having established Rāma in the center, one should place Lakṣmaṇa on his left side.
One should place the goddess Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, on the right;
Śatrughna and Bharata should be placed on the north and the south, respectively.
"With their arms occupied by chowries even while performing the act of attending," thus it is taught in the *Svatantra*; now I shall speak according to the *Paratantra*.
And in an image fashioned from metal, O Sage, according to the sequence of the highest and other classes,
the height should extend from the big toe up to the forehead.
O twice-born one, know that the best kautuka is thirty-two finger-breadths in height;
the medium-sized image (bera) is seven finger-breadths less than this in elevation.
"O best of sages, that which is nine finger-breadths less than this is proclaimed as the inferior [measure] for the stature of the son of Daśaratha. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 11.105)
O divine sage, I shall now tell you the dimensions of Sītā, Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna as well.
They declare the height of the Goddess to be as far as the base of the god’s arms;
likewise, the height of Lakṣmaṇa is said to extend to the end of Rāma’s mouth.
"The arm-length of Lakṣmaṇa shall be the height of Śatrughna";
thus the long measurement is declared, and the remainder should be performed as previously described.
The characteristics of you, the Independent One and the Dependent One, have been spoken by you;
now I shall describe the characteristics of Balarāma—listen, O Nārada.
Balabhadra was known as Nibhā (or Sitā), possessing a radiance white as the kunda flower and the moon;
he had lotus-like eyes, a face like that of a beautiful woman, and was adorned with all the marks of physical perfection.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with every kind of jewelry,
his every limb was perfectly formed, and he was graced by a halo of light.
The wise one who knows the mantra of Balarāma should place a mace on his right arm and a plow in his left hand.
One should place the goddess Śrī on the right and Garuḍa on the left;
Balarāma, likewise described as yellow and with palms joined in reverence, should be placed there.
Hereafter, I shall describe Kṛṣṇa, who has the luster of black collyrium;
his installation must be performed, and his specific stationing is especially important.
O great sage, that supreme Hari was seated upon a throne in the tribhaṅgī posture, accompanied by the Goddess and holding a play-staff.
One should establish the Omniscient One, the cause of all things, in the divine place;
thus has it been briefly declared in its secluded form, O Sage.
Therefore, one should meditate upon Vāsudeva, who resembles the color of a dark cloud, is clad in yellow garments, possesses curly hair, and is adorned with all ornaments.
The deity holds a play-stick and is endowed with the *tribhaṅga* posture;
his right foot is well-placed while his left foot is drawn up.
One should likewise cause the sole of the left foot to extend horizontally in sequence;
one should then place the big toe in the position where the little finger was.
The left knee should be slightly bent while the foot remains on the ground;
likewise, one should maintain this posture in the face, the limbs, and the pelvic region.
Because of the bending in three parts (or paths), the state of being "three-fold bent" is established:
the face bends to the right, while the middle of the body bends to the left.
When there is a break on the right side of the waist, three breaks are described;
one should fashion the right hand as a beautiful staff, adorned with bracelets.
The left [hand] is joined with the arm of the Goddess; the left hand is turned downward, and one should join the left palm along the line of the navel.
One should join the right hand on the hip with the facial sūtra;
the length [of the face] is three parts, and the face at the head consists of three spheres.
The jaw and neck are known to be three and a half mātrās, and the throat is said to be half a mātrā; the region from the heart to the navel is established as the middle body. Vis 11.125.
The penis faces the navel, and from there the two thighs face outward;
thus the measurement has been stated in brief, while the remainder is considered to be common [to all]. Vis 11.126.
One should also install two goddesses on either side of him in due order;
on the right side of the god, one should place Rukmiṇī, who resembles gold.
And one should place Satyabhāmā on the left, resembling a dark cloud;
she should hold a lotus as before and be endowed with the quality of sattva.

This has been stated regarding the independent [tantra]; now I shall tell you concerning the dependent [tantra], O tiger among sages, according to the sequence beginning with the superior [and so forth] by means of metal.
O Sage, having thus described the characteristics of Rāghava, one should likewise produce here the characteristics of the Lord of the Yādavas, beginning with his height and so forth.
O best of sages, the characteristics of the [divine] forms include the dance for the sake of butter, or likewise the serpent-dance, and so forth. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 11.131)
According to the wish of the patron, one should have an image fashioned in that [place] through one's own creative play;
by means of skillful methods and specific techniques, one should have the image made in due order.
Thus, O best of sages, the characteristics of Yādavasiṃha have been proclaimed in brief; now hear from me those of Kalki Viṣṇu.
Resembling exceedingly red blood, three-eyed and of terrifying form,
he has four arms holding a conch, a discus, and a mace, and wears a crown.
Adorned with a forest garland, decorated with all ornaments,
endowed with every kind of finery, and clothed in yellow garments.
Thus Kalki has been described by me; now I shall tell you the placement of the weapons (*hetinyāsa*):
the discus in the upper right hand, and the conch in the upper left.
One should place a black noose in the left lower hand,
and one should fashion a staff of death (kāladaṇḍa) facing downward in the right hand.
The wise practitioner should place Śrī on the right side and Puṣṭi on the left;
this constitutes the second enclosure, accompanied by the eight attendants.
Having reflected thus, one should worship Kalki according to the prescribed rite;
O twice-born, one should especially worship Kalki in the Kali age.
Whether it be a king or one equal to a king, whoever should worship [it] day after day attains all desires and attains the fortune of victory.
And here a specific distinction has been proclaimed; the remainder is remembered as common to all.
Thus have I proclaimed the characteristics of Kalki, which grant all accomplishments.
I shall describe the characteristics of the forms, distinguished according to the various scriptures:
the primordial form is the supreme, eternal deity Vāsudeva.
The second supreme form is known as Saṃkarṣaṇa;
the third eternal form is that which is called Pradyumna.
The fourth form, however, shall be known as Aniruddha;
these are the four forms of the Pratiṣṭhā, each distinct from the others.
Vāsudeva is the supreme form to be installed by the best of the twice-born;
the second form is installed by Kṣatriyas who desire liberation.
O best of Brahmins, the form known as Pradyumna should be installed by Vaiśyas seeking liberation;
the form Aniruddha, the teacher of the world, is to be installed by Śūdras.
O Brahmin, each one of these is further divided by groups of three;
thus, the divisions of the letters are proclaimed through the various applications of the nyāsa.
Listen now to the sequence for the forms of Keśava and the others, which is distinct:
they are either like a conch or jasmine, or indeed dark blue.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, with his chest marked by the Śrīvatsa,
his every limb perfectly formed, and adorned with all ornaments.
O best of sages, one should thus meditate upon Hari, who is endowed with yellow garments, possesses four arms, wears a crown, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
And I shall explain the various arrangements of the weapons; listen in due order:
he bears the discus in his upper right hand and the conch in his upper left.
O Sage, hear now of this manifestation of the Primordial Being called Keśava: he holds a mace in his lower left hand and a lotus in his lower right hand. Viṣṇu 11.152.
Now I shall describe Nārāyaṇa; listen, O best of men, Nārada!
He is like the kunda flower, or dark blue, or even red.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, with four arms, wearing a diadem,
clad in yellow garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
[He beheld] Hari, the Lord of the three worlds, whose every limb was perfectly joined, who was adorned with all ornaments, who consists of all the gods, and who is subtle.
Having thus reflected upon the form, now hear concerning the placement of the hand-gestures (mudrās): one should place a closed lotus bud in the raised right hand.
O Sage, on his lower [arm] there should be a discus resembling the fire of time;
having placed a mace on the upper left [arm], one should place a lotus in the hand below.
Such is the arrangement of his weapons; now hear concerning Mādhava, who resembles the petals of a conch-flower and bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Complete in all his limbs, adorned with every ornament,
fully endowed with all jewelry, four-armed, and wearing a crown.
Now Mādhava has been described as the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha;
O great sage, hear now the specific arrangement of his weapons.
In the upper left hand, one should place a white conch shell;
in the lower left hand, one should place a red lotus with ten petals. (Viṣṇu 11.161)
O Nārada, in the third form known as Mādhava, one should place a discus in the upper right hand and a club in the lower one.
I shall describe to you this distinction of Saṃkarṣaṇa from Vāsudeva:
he may resemble the rising sun, or be dark-complexioned, or like a cloud.
Wearing yellow garments, four-armed, adorned with all ornaments,
possessing all limbs complete, one should meditate upon Govinda, the delighter of Gokula.
In this way, O best of sages, one should meditate upon Hari, the granter of all desires;
now listen, O most excellent Nārada, to the specific application of his weapons.
One should place a mace in his upper right hand and a discus below it;
on the upper left side, one should place a lotus in the hand, and a conch in the other.
O Govinda, having been thus addressed, now hear about the one named Viṣṇu:
he resembles the petal of a red lotus, or is dark-complexioned, or indeed red. (Viṣṇudharmottara 11.167)
Or, O tiger among sages, [one may meditate on] Kṛṣṇa, endowed with all the primary marks,
complete in all his limbs, and adorned with all ornaments.
One should meditate upon the eternal Viṣṇu, who holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, who is four-armed, clad in yellow garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
In the first hand, one should indeed place a lotus, and below it a mace;
in the left hand one should place a conch, and below that a radiant discus.
Alternatively, O tiger among sages, hear of the eternal Viṣṇu:
he stands upright, exceedingly gentle, with his hands placed upon his hips.
Endowed with a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness, clothed in yellow garments,
with all limbs complete and adorned with every ornament.
One should meditate upon Viṣṇu, the unsurpassed, endowed with all ornaments;
I have thus described the two-fold Viṣṇu, both the manifest and the immutable.
O best of sages, meditate thus according to the will of the practitioner:
[the deity] resembling the petals of a red lotus, clad in yellow garments, and four-armed. Vis 11.174.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, beautiful in all his limbs,
endowed with all ornaments, and adorned with every kind of jewelry.
Complete in all its limbs, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with every decoration, and supreme as the bestower of all accomplishments.
In the first right hand, one should place a conch shell below a discus;
in the left upper hand, a lotus, and in the lower hand, a mace.
Know, O Nārada, the characteristics of the form of Madhusūdana; this is the distinction from Saṃkarṣaṇa. Now hear about Trivikrama.
Resembling molten gold, or dark like a cloud, or indeed like fire,
he is adorned with all ornaments and beautiful in every limb.
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing yellow garments, and possessing four arms,
he holds a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and is saluted by all the gods.
The characteristics of Trivikrama have been fully described; they bestow prosperity. He carries a mace in his first hand and bears a discus below it.

O best of sages, wherever it may be seen, there is a lotus in the left [hand] and a conch below; or else, O most excellent of Munis, the arrangement of the weapons may be according to one's preference.
Thus has the arrangement of weapons been described; now the Vāmana [form] is spoken of:
it resembles the petals of the Karṇikāra flower, is red in color, and has four arms.
Complete in all its limbs, adorned with all ornaments,
endowed with every decoration, and supreme as the bestower of all accomplishments.
In his first right hand a wheel is seen, and below it a conch; in his left hand there is a mace, and below that a lotus shines beautifully.
O best of Brahmins, he who is named Vāmana should be known as possessing auspicious marks;
his complexion resembles molten gold, and his chest is marked with the Śrīvatsa.
Complete in all his limbs, adorned with every ornament,
wearing yellow garments, four-armed, and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
I have described the characteristics of Śrīdhara, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation:
one should place a discus on the upper hand and a lotus on the right hand.
In the left hand, a mace should be known [to be held], and below it, a conch shell shining brightly;
thus is the form of Śrīdhara to be understood by the best of teachers.
In this way, the manifestation of Pradyumna is called Aniruddha;
he resembles the petals of a blue lotus, has four arms, and wears a crown.
Hṛṣīkeśa, the eternal one, who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest.
In his right hand is a great discus, and below it a mace;
in his left hand is a great lotus, and below that a conch shell.
O Nārada, that form should then be known as Hṛṣīkeśa;
I shall now describe the characteristics of Padmanābha, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Or else, O best of sages, having recognized there the blue-colored or dark-hued [sign], one perceives the All-Knowing One, the cause of all. (Vis 11.194)
O tiger among sages, the practitioner should have it fashioned by artisans,
endowed with all the auspicious marks and adorned with all ornaments.
With all his limbs complete, four-armed, wearing a crown,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and clad in yellow garments.
Know him as Padmanābha, endowed with the Śrīvatsa on his chest;
in his first hand there is a lotus, and below it, indeed, a conch.
And on the left, a discus is seen with a mace situated below it;
that form is called Padmanābha and should be saluted by the wise.
Or one may arrange the placement of the weapons here according to one's preference;
or rather, O observer of good vows, hear now the characteristics of Padmanābha.
O best of sages, one should meditate upon him there as having two arms, lotus-eyed, and either dark-complexioned or like the color of fire, endowed with all the auspicious marks. Vis_11.200.
O Nārada, since the topic of the bed of Padmanābha has been fully explained,
the characteristics of the ritual acts, worship, and so forth will now be described.
O best of sages, one should have the image for ritual worship made joined with the *yogamudrā* and endowed with the conch and discus, or otherwise as previously described.
Thus has the characteristic of Padmanābha been fully described;
on the side of his wall, above the navel, is a red lotus with a beautiful stalk.
O Nārada, one should have a most beautiful lotus made with a pericarp, consisting of one hundred petals, or half of that, or even a quarter of that.
O Nārada, one should meditate upon the ritual procedure at the tip of the pericarp along with its characteristics;
I shall explain those characteristics which bestow both worldly enjoyment and auspiciousness—listen! (Viṣṇudharmottara 11.205)
Seated in the lotus posture, golden-hued, four-armed, seated, four-faced, and eternal. Vis_11.206.
Complete in all its limbs, adorned with every ornament,
consisting of all the gods, subtle, and characterized by the nature of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
One should then meditate upon Brahmā, born from the lotus, in this form;
one should place the *sruk*, *sruva*, and rosary in the right hand of Brahmā.
O Sage, one should place a lotus in the left hand and a water-pot above it; or else, the lower part of the left hand may display the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Having thus meditated upon Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus, one should then perform the ritual placement (nyāsa);
hear now the sequence for that which is above the secret [level].
O best of sages, one should touch the base of the thighs with both hands turned upside down; this is called the yoga-mudrā.
I have taught the yogamudrā; one should employ it in all yogas.
On its right side, however, is Medhā, and on the left, Sarasvatī.
One should perform the placement [of mantras] in one's own tantra, but not in another's;
having thus performed the ritual procedure, [one should worship] Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus.

O tiger among sages, the embodied form of Padmanābha is traditionally known as dependent (*paratantra*); however, in the independent (*svatantra*) system, the knower of mantras [should perform it] together with artisans. *Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa* 11.214.
Having established the lotus-seat, one should fashion the lotus according to the rules in the place of Brahmā, or in the east, the south, or the west.
Or, O best of sages, he should gradually prepare his dwelling on the northern side of a village, or on the bank of a river, or on the shore of a lake.
The temple should be constructed according to the donor’s wish, following the prescribed rules and sequence;
one should have the lotus-seated deity fashioned there, whether in the Brahma or the Daivika style.
One should install it according to the prescribed rite, either with six beras or three beras;
then one should worship it with devotion by means of Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas.
O Sage, [one should perform it] there either with those [mantras] associated with the Pañcarātra that are capable of reasoning and refutation, or independently, or with the Brahma-sūkta.
Or, O Brahmin, one should worship according to the prescribed rite with the Puruṣasūkta;
one should worship there in this manner, while the remainder is considered common to all.
O Sage, one should cause a swan to be fashioned at the front of Brahmā’s celestial chariot and upon his foot for the purpose of a vehicle, or decorated in various ways according to one's desire.
I shall explain the specific retinue within the inner sanctum; listen now to this unsurpassed secret regarding the Piśāca [deities] at the entrance. Vis 11.222.
Kapila, Kāśyapa, Dakṣa, and Dakṣiṇa occupy the right wing; Rudra, Vahni, and Marut likewise occupy the left side.
Bhṛgu and Nārada are the gatekeepers of the first celestial chariot;
O best of sages, Candra and Āditya are the gatekeepers of the second.
Śaṅkha and Padma are the two gatekeepers of the third door;
their worship, O tiger among sages, is performed by one who has completed the rites of sacrifice and Vedic study.
It brings about divine power for men, bestows all prosperity and happiness,
destroys all suffering, and grants the increase of both the king and his kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the ritual according to the rules;
a specific distinction regarding this has been proclaimed here, while the remainder is remembered as being common to all.
Thus, O tiger among sages, the procedure for the independent worship of Brahmā has been briefly declared; now listen to that of Dāmodara.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, wearing yellow garments, four-armed,
with all limbs perfectly formed, and adorned with every ornament.
Adorned with every ornament, his chest marked with the Śrīvatsa,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and resplendent with a garland of forest flowers.
In this way, one should meditate upon his own form as being free from disease and possessing a belly that is slightly protruding;
in his first hand there is a conch, and indeed below it, a lotus.
In his left hand is indeed a mace, and below that is a discus;
this is the manifestation of Aniruddha, known as Dāmodara.
And the divisions of the four forms have been fully proclaimed:
the first form is called Pratiṣṭhā, which is to be worshipped eternally in age after age.
In the Tretā age, however, he is Dvitīya; likewise, in the Dvāpara age, he is Tṛtīya;
and in the Kali age, he is Aniruddha—or rather, all [of these] exist in all [ages].
One should install them in due order with mantras beginning with *parameṣṭhin*;
thus is the characteristic of the twelve forms recited.
Resembling the *kiṃśuka* flower, with three eyes and a terrifying form—
one should [meditate on him] a thousand times, or half of that, or one hundred and eight times.
Alternatively, one may have him fashioned with eight arms, most beautiful to behold,
clad in yellow garments, and adorned with all ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon Hari, who consists of the universal form, endowed with all ornaments and equipped with all weapons.
In her upper right hand there is a discus, and in another arm a pestle;
below that there should be a noose, and in the other [lower left] she should place a goad.
One should place a discus in the left lower hand and a club above it;
in the hand above the club, however, one should place a conch shell resembling cow’s milk.
Above the conch, one should place a bow with an arrow; in this manner, one should assign the weapons, and all the remaining missiles may be assigned to the hand as desired.
The characteristics of Viśvarūpa have been fully described; they grant victory and prosperity.
He resembles pure crystal, has three feet, and seven hands.
He had the Vedas as his horns, two faces, three eyes, and was clad in yellow garments;
he held a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and was adorned with all ornaments.
With all limbs complete and adorned with every ornament—
thus has the Lord of Sacrifice, the destroyer of evil, been described in brief.
In his upper right hand, he holds a discus resembling the fire of cosmic destruction,
and having placed a staff in the other [right hand], he carries a conch shell in his upper left hand.

O Sage, one should meditate on him holding a hand in the gesture of granting fearlessness (*abhaya*) or the gesture of giving boons (*varada*) upon his lower lip, with three hands, assuming the posture of one who receives a portion of the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhāga*). Vis 11.246.
Thus should one meditate upon Hari, the supreme Lord of Sacrifice, during the three junctions of the day;
or a twice-born man should worship the Lord of Sacrifice at the three junctions or even at a single junction.
One attains all desires and obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
through the arising of meditative concentration, perfect knowledge is attained.
Therefore, with every effort, a twice-born man should worship the Lord of Sacrifice.
The Lord of Sacrifice has now been described; now hear about the Embodiment of the Vedas.
Dark-complexioned, resembling a mountain, with four arms and a diadem,
his every limb was perfectly formed and adorned with all manner of ornaments.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, three-eyed and of terrifying form,
he was clad in yellow garments and adorned with every ornament.
Consisting of all the Vedas, subtle, more secret than the secret, and unsurpassed—this has been declared by me as the Embodiment of the Veda (Vedamūrti). Now, listen to the Hetinyāsa.
O great sage, one should place a discus, radiant like the fire of time, in his upper right hand, and a bow in his lower right hand.
In his upper left hand he holds the Pāñcajanya conch, and below it the mace;
such is the arrangement of the weapons. Now hear [the description] of Śrī and the others.
[He saw her] made of molten gold, endowed with four arms,
complete in all her limbs, and adorned with every ornament.
Endowed with all powers, resplendent with a crown and other ornaments,
adorned with every kind of decoration, and shining with all manner of jewels.
The goddess holds a red lotus, is arrayed in red garments,
is seated upon a lotus throne, and is the goddess Haripriyā herself.
One should thus contemplate Lakṣmī herself, adorned with all ornaments, resplendent with every kind of jewel, and holding a conch, a discus, and a lotus.
In the upper right hand is a wheel and below it a radiant lotus;
in the left is a conch and below it a lotus, or else [the hands display] the gestures of granting boons or fearlessness.
O best of sages, one should meditate in this manner during the independent rite of worship;
however, I shall now describe the characteristics associated with nourishment (puṣṭi) for the dependent rite.
Having set aside the conch and the discus, one should visualize Śrī; having placed the two-armed Śrī, who has a golden luster, on the right, one should arrange Puṣṭi.
One should place Puṣṭi on her left; hear her characteristics, O Nārada:
she is dark-green like dūrvā grass or deep red, two-armed, and has a lotus-like face.
The goddess, complete in all her limbs, radiant with a crown and other ornaments,
seated upon a red lotus, and adorned with every kind of jewelry.
One should meditate upon the goddess Puṣṭi, the beloved of Hari, who wears divine garlands and garments, is resplendent with celestial jewels, and holds a red lotus in her hand. Vis_11.264.
Having meditated thus, O best of sages, one should fashion a most beautiful [image], having likewise contemplated this nourishment which destroys the mass of all suffering. (Vis 11.265)
Next, I shall describe Medhāmūrti, who bestows all branches of knowledge;
she resembles the petals of a red lotus, is seated upon a lotus throne, and is auspicious.
The goddess Medhā, endowed with all the [auspicious] marks, adorned with all ornaments,
two-armed, two-eyed, and wearing a crown.
I have now described Medhā; listen now to Vāgdevī.
She resembles pure crystal, is auspicious, and is seated upon a white lotus.
Seated upon a lotus posture, endowed with four arms, clad in white garments, and adorned with ornaments of pearls; Vis_11.269.
She has either three eyes or two eyes, holds a rosary, and is auspicious.
One should visualize the goddess of speech, adorned with a crown, joined with the book of commentary.
Thus one should meditate upon Sarasvatī, the supreme, who consists of all goddesses;
if I am to explain the procedure for the dependent [form] of Sarasvatī, I shall do so.
Endowed with all the primary marks, beautiful in every limb,
adorned with all ornaments, she is supreme, possessing two arms and two eyes.
And here a specific distinction is proclaimed; one should perform the remainder as before.
Thus is the characteristic taught in the Paratantra.
In his upper left hand he holds a rosary for counting, and above it a water-pot;
in his lower hand is a book containing the nectar of the ocean of all knowledge.
O Best of Sages, in the *Paratantra* [tantra], she has the gesture of bestowing (*pratipādanamudrā*) in her lower right hand, holds a lotus in her hand, and possesses an auspicious face.
Taking hold of a cloth by the side of her foot, one should fashion the speech in this way.
Thus has it been briefly explained; now hear concerning the form of Durgā.
O best of sages, she has the form of a dark mountain peak, possesses three eyes, and has a lotus-like face; she may have two eyes or eight hands. Vis_11.277
With all her limbs perfectly formed and resplendent with a crown and other ornaments,
she holds a conch, a discus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands,
and is seated upon a lotus.
Thus Durgā has been described by me; now hear the placement of the weapons (hetinyāsa):
in her upper right hand is a discus, and in her other [right] hand is the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya).
Having placed a conch in the upper left hand and a hip-hand (waist-grasper) below it, thus the four-armed form is described; now listen to that which has eight hands.
Upon his upper right hand is a wheel resembling the fire of cosmic destruction;
beneath that is a conch shell, and on his lower right arm is a sword.
One should place a trident resembling coral on the other auspicious hand;
thus it has been taught for the right side, but now hear concerning the left.
A bow should be in your upper left hand, while a conch shell is indeed in the one below it;
a club is in the lower right hand, and a mace is in the other (upper right) hand.
Thus has the auspicious Mahiṣāntakarī been briefly described;
herein lies a certain specific detail regarding the sequence of the ritual for the worship of Durgā.
Holding the *saṃhitā* in his hand, he should perform the worship as prescribed by the rules;
the specific details here have been fully explained, while the remainder is considered to be common to all.
I shall describe the Vaiṣṇava Vighneśa, the destroyer of all obstacles;
listen briefly, O Nārada, to his origin and characteristics. Viṣṇu 11.286.
Manifest as a portion of Nārāyaṇa, consisting of the nature of space, imperishable,
and joined with the elephant-faced [Gaṇeśa], he was born from the fire through his divine play.
For the purpose of utterly destroying the wicked, [I shall describe] the supreme Hari in the sacrificial fire;
therefore, I will state its characteristics—listen attentively in due order. 11.288.
O best of sages, having recognized one that is white, black, dark, or red, and endowed with the proper characteristics, one should have the elephant-faced [image] fashioned. Vis_11.289.
One should have him fashioned here with all limbs complete, adorned with all ornaments, having four arms and two eyes, or else three eyes.
His body is adorned with a serpent as a sacred thread, he is clothed in white garments,
equipped with a conch and a discus, granting boons, and holding a girdle and a goad.

O tiger among sages, one should install [the deities] in sequence according to the will of the practitioner; one should likewise install Vighnanāyaka for the purpose of destroying obstacles to the sacrifice. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 11.292)
One should place a wheel in his right [hand], and in the other hand (the left) the gesture of fearlessness;
one should place a conch in the left [hand], and indeed a club above and below.
Thus has that which is proclaimed as the wheel and so forth been explained; now hear the other [arrangement].
Having placed an axe on the right, one should place a noose and a goad below it.
O tiger among sages, one should place a rosary on the left [hand] and a noose on the lower lip;
one should place a fruit upon the tip of the elephant's face.
"I have declared two types of weapons for Vighneśa;
O tiger among sages, one should deploy them according to the desire of the practitioner."
In both the independent (svatantra) and dependent (paratantra) [mandalas], one should contemplate form in this way;
a rat is said to be its vehicle, or one should visualize Garuḍa in front.
And because he is a portion of Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Birds (Garuḍa) is proclaimed there;
furthermore, O twice-born one, the devotee should worship Vighneśa there with the three Ṛgvedic verses dedicated to the Gaṇas.
One obtains all desires and victory shall belong to the king;
however, there is a certain distinction in this matter—listen to it, O bull among sages.
The characteristics of celestial palaces, the materials for images, the characteristics of the images themselves, and the characteristics of their retinues. // Vis_11.300 //
O bull among sages, having understood the common procedure for all the rites of worship and so forth for the images, one should perform them just as for the primary image.

O great sage, one should worship the forms beginning with the Supreme Self (Paramātman) and ending with Vighneśa, according to their respective vidyās, both in the independent (svatantra) and dependent (paratantra) systems. Vis_11.302.
O Lord of Sages, if one installs Vāmana and Vighnarāja as independent deities in a single form,
one should worship them day after day.
O Sage, having established [the deity] according to the ritual procedure as either six-faced or three-faced, Śrī and the others are not required here; the supreme installation is that of the Śakti.
And here a specific distinction is proclaimed; the remainder shall be common [to all].
One should indeed worship Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, Vāgdevī, Medhā, and Durgā there.
One should worship both in the independent (svatantra) and dependent (paratantra) [systems] with their respective vidyās;
the specific distinction here has been proclaimed—therefore, hear now the different types of worship.

I shall now describe the forms, such as the temples and so forth, as before; [I shall also describe] the specific distinctions in the modes of worship for the forms of the Supreme Self and others. (Vis 11.307)
When there is a reclining image, the primary image (mūlārcā) and the ritual image (karmārcā) should serve as the seat;
or one may also fashion that image in a standing posture with four arms.
One should likewise provide a festive offering and a ceremonial bath;
in this same manner it should be done for the stationary image, or one may also have a portable image made. Vis_11.309
When the Mahābera is seated, everything else should likewise be seated; or one may adopt the standing posture; in all cases, every [deity] should thus have four arms.
O best of sages, the worship-image of the ten forms beginning with Matsya is four-armed, exactly as has been described for the primary image (mūlabera).
Or else, one may perform the worship of an image at the time of descent;
in this regard, O Nārada, there is indeed a specific distinction concerning the Fish incarnation and the others.
O best of sages, listen as I shall describe the incarnations beginning with the Fish in their proper order;
the wise man should construct the temple of these incarnations in the outer enclosure.
Whether in a pavilion, at a city gate, or on a rampart, [this] independent [rite] bestows all desires, is meritorious, and increases longevity and health. (Viṣṇudharmottara 11.314)
For the sake of increasing the fortune of victory for both independent and dependent [practitioners], the fruit of worshipping the incarnations is proclaimed throughout the worlds. (Vis 11.315)

O Sage, one should have [the images] fashioned according to their proper sequence and endowed with the correct characteristics, whether on a mountain, in a forest, in a village, or even in a city. Vis_11.316.
O Sage, one should have an image fashioned there, either independently or dependently upon this [tantra], using the materials previously mentioned.
Having installed them according to the prescribed rules,
one should worship them day after day. Now, listen to the procedure for the different forms of the deities according to the ritual for independent worship.
One should perform the festivals for the bali-offerings, the images, and so forth, as well as those for Vāsudeva and the others;
however, one should not do so for an avatāra-form unless it follows the pattern of the primary image (mūlamūrti).
And according to the desire of the sacrificer, one should perform all the attendant rites in this [rite] as one wishes, following the sequence as before. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 11.320)
One should arrange the manifestations according to the independent rite of worship;
and in the independent [rite], one should likewise perform all the enclosures beginning with the doors.
A wise person should perform this here with logic and specific reasoning;
if one fashions the image in the manner thus described, [verse 11.322].
He attains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
