Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Rule for the Arrangement of Castes and Weapons," in the *Śrīpāñcarātra-viṣvaksenasaṃhitā*.
Chapter Twelve. Viṣvaksena said:
Listen, O best of divine sages, to the supreme sequence of mantras, along with their extraction (uddhāra), as well as the seer, the meter, the deity, and the initial phonemes.
I shall explain it briefly according to my understanding, O Great Sage:
there may be another [method] than that of the Tathāgata, which is the withdrawal of fire through weapons. (Vis 12.2)
The Supreme Self is the second, while Vāsudeva is the third;
after that is the mantra of Saṃkarṣaṇa, and likewise that of Pradyumna.
The Vidyā of Aniruddha, followed immediately by the Matsya-mantra;
then the Kūrma-vidyā, then Kroḍa, and the tenth is the Nārasiṃhaka.
After that, the mantra of Vāmana; after that, the one of Jamadagni's son;
thereafter the knowledge of the son of Daśaratha; and immediately following that, the mantra of Balarāma.
And again and again [he taught] that Vidyā of Kṛṣṇa, of Viṣṇu, of Keśava, of Nārāyaṇa, and of Mādhava, in due order.
O Sage, for Govinda as well as Viṣṇu, there are the [mantras] known as Traivikrama, Vāmana, and Śrīdhara, by means of the Madhusūdana-vidyā.
Then Hṛṣīkeśa, the mantra of Padmanābha,
the Brahma-mantra, and likewise the Dāmodara-mantra, in due order.
Furthermore, [he taught] the mantra of Viśvarūpa and that of Yajñamūrti;
then the mudrā-mantra of Vedamūrti, as well as the Śrī-mantra.
The Puṣṭi-vidyā, as well as the Medhā-vidyā, Sarasvatī,
and also the vidyā of Durgā and Vighneśa, as well as that of Parameṣṭhin.
Furthermore, O best among those who know mantras, beyond this is the mantra of Puruṣa and Vidyā, which possesses all sovereignty and is characterized by cessation.
As it has been said: "Out of a desire for the welfare of my devotees, I shall extract [the mantra];
I will proclaim the extraction of the mantra exactly and in due order. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.12)
Listen with focused attention, O Sage, to that which is more secret than the secret;
having extracted the Viṣṇu-pañcaka, thereafter [I shall teach] the Bhānumanta.
One should join the final letter of the *yajuṣ* mantras—whether it ends in *l*, *s*, or *m*—with that same final letter;
having encased it with the *praṇava*, the second [syllable] is joined with the nasal drop (*bindu*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.14)

With reverence, one should offer the supreme mantra consisting of eleven syllables to the Blessed One: *namaḥ*, ending with *ṇa*, ending with *ma*, to the Self (*ātmane*), ending with *viśveśa*, ending with *ṇa*, and ending with *la*. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 12.15)
One should extract [the mantra] from Vāsudeva by means of the eleventh and second [syllables],
ending with the letter *la* preceded by *ya*, joined with the foot of the *yantra* and the syllable *ma*.
The wise one should extract the mantra beginning with the first [syllable], which is secret and accomplishes the secret purpose;
having placed the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, and the word "namaḥ" immediately thereafter. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 12.17)

The first [syllable] ending in *m*, likewise beginning with *m* and ending in *m*, reaching the end of the *kalā*s; beginning with the fourth [vowel], accompanied by *sa* and *ha*, together with *ī*, *hā*, and ending with *ṣa* along with the crest-jewel (*cūḍāmaṇi*).

The supreme practitioner should extract the letter *ma*, which is the first of the groups (*varga*), immediately after the letter *śa* (the end of the *ta*-group), and likewise the letter *ma* at the end of the *pa*-group, as well as the letter *a*. Vis_12.19.

Having ceased from loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables], one should immediately utter the word "namas," joined with the fifth vowel (u) and the letter following the wind (m), ending in the fourth case, directed toward the Blessed One.
The third of the fourth [vowel] joined with the fifth of the wind (v), ending with the fifth [vowel] and ending with the fourth [vowel], having two morae, and preceded by the wind (v). Vis_12.21.
The letter *a* with the visarga, the *praṇava*, and likewise *namaḥ*;
the fifth, the fourth, and the third of the first [vowel]. Vis_12.22.
Then the letter *la* preceded by the fourth [vowel], joined with the eleventh vowel;
then Viṣṇu, which is the final letter of the fourth group, adorned with the third vowel.
By means of the application of the fifth vowel, one should extract the fourth [consonant] as the third and fourth [syllables];
then, after the wind [the letter *ya*] ending in the final [vowel], one should extract the sixteenth vowel.
Then, having extracted the syllable *a* from *anila* and so forth,
and likewise the syllable *o* from *anala*, one should utter the word *namaḥ* with the same vowels as those preceding it.
The letter *k* ending in *ā*, followed by *lānta* (the letter *m*) and *te* (*e*), and then the fourth letter of the series beginning with *ya* (*j*);
the eleventh [letter] (*ṇ*) joined with the second (*i*) and the fifth (*u*) ending in *l* (*lu*). Vis_12.26.
First, one should extract the letter *va* with the vowel *a*; likewise, the letter *ṣa* with the vowel *u*;
then the letter *va* with the vowel *u*; and thereafter, one should extract the letter *ra* with the vowel *ā*, as well as the mantra-syllables and so forth.
One should place the second [syllable], ending with *la*, above the Lord (*nātha*) by means of the head of the *bindu*;
and the word *bhagavat* and the word *viṣṇu* as before, preceded by *namaḥ*.

The best of mantra-knowers should extract the letter *ka* with six crests, then the fire (*ra*), then the elbow (*ma*) by means of the letter *ma*, and then the sixth vowel (*ū*) ending in *pa*. (Vis 12.29)
One should extract the word "nikāma" beginning with 'na' and ending with 'ba', adorned with the sixth vowel, followed by the word "namaḥ" with the visarga, and then the word "bhagavat. (Vis 12.30)
That which ends in *e*, begins with *ś* and ends in *m*;
that which ends in *s* and is joined with the second [consonant]; and that which begins with *v* and ends in *y*—this is "Bhūḥ. (Vis 12.31)

Having extracted the syllable beginning with *ā* and ending with *ya*, and the syllable beginning with *lā* [ending] with fourteen dots (*bindu*s), just as in the *mātṛkā*, so too at the end; likewise, "Homage to the Blessed One. (Vis 12.32)
By the first [syllable], however, the elements beginning with space (viyat) are joined with the Bindu;
by the second, space as well as wind, and then fire within the ether.
From *analā* (A) to the end of the fourth (*turyānta*), adorned with *bindu* and *nāda*,
from the end of the thirteenth (*trayodaśānta*) to the end of *sva* (S), and beyond that, ending with *ga* (G).
In the eleventh [syllable], there is that which ends in *ṇ* and that which ends in *ṇ*; indeed, the supreme [syllable] ends in *ś*.
With the second of the eleven, there is that which ends in *l*, followed immediately by that which ends in *bh*.
Having extracted the final letter and the letter *mā*, one should write the first [letter] at the end;
O best of sages, hear now this mantra of Jamadagni.
One should utter the *īśvara-bindu* at the beginning and likewise at the end,
and the words "Bhagavat" and "Viṣṇu," each ending with the fourth vowel (*ū*), again and again.
One should expel the wind, which is joined with the earth-element, fire, and likewise the sun,
by means of the second and first [parts] of the breath-cycle.
The letter ending in *r* (ra) joined with the fifth vowel (*u*), conjoined with the letter *ma*, [is placed] at the foot and at the peak; likewise, the word *namaḥ* is added in its entirety.
For the sake of the world, he [praised] Rāma with glory, [and] Anila, Anala, Lāntaka, and Kāntaka—
ending in *ṇ* by means of the first and second vowels, and likewise ending in *k*.
Immediately after [the words] "rakṣātmajāyām" and "sarvaṃ ca rakṣoghnāya," having joined them together with "viśvāpi" ending in "śāṇāntena," it was indeed made manifest.
O best of sages, one should likewise place the letter *la* along with the poison-foot (*viṣatāṅghri*) and the eleven digits; now hear the extraction of power and knowledge.
Having first uttered "Oṃ padaṃ" and having performed that with its splendor (śrī), [one should place] "vābhraṃ" at the beginning and the end, and again "namo bhagavate. 12.43.
One should extract the first [syllable] from *gānādi* by means of *nādi*, and the fire [syllable] joined with wind;
listen further to the extraction of the Kṛṣṇa-vidyā.

niya............................................. / Oṃ Āṃ Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, the Supreme Self, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the Self of All; Oṃ Om. Aṃ Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. Vis_12.44,3.
Oṃ āṃ oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Saṃkarṣaṇa; āṃ oṃ. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Pradyumna; āṃ oṃ. Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Aniruddha; āṃ oṃ.

Aṃ Oṃ Kaiṃ! Homage to the Blessed One Vāsudeva, who is the Fish, who has the form of a fish; Krenda Oṃ. Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, who is the Tortoise, who has the form of a tortoise; Vāṃ Oṃ.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Boar!
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Man-Lion, kṣaiṃ oṃ!
Oṃ īṣi, homage to the Blessed One, the Dwarf, dhī oṃ!

Riṃ! Homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Paraśurāma; rīṃ oṃ. Oṃ lūṃ! Homage to Śrī Rāma, the one whose name is known throughout all the worlds, the destroyer of Rāvaṇa, the son of Daśaratha, the slayer of all demons, the one true to his promise, Viṣṇu, the sovereign lord; hrīṃ oṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, Balirāma; hrīṃ oṃ.
Oṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the son of Devakī, Kuṃ Om.
The Protector, Om.
Oṃ Gaiṃ. Homage to Puruṣottama, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, Kalkī.
Salutation to Viṣṇu, hrāṃ oṃ.
Oṃ oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Keśava, āṃ oṃ. Oṃ, salutation to the Blessed One Nārāyaṇa, oṃ.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Supreme Person, to Mādhava, to Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva; kṣuṃ, oṃ.
Āṃ, oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Govinda; āṃ, oṃ.
Obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu; bhūṃ, oṃ.
Āṃ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Madhusūdana, Āṃ oṃ.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One... the god, thus to the one who has fulfilled his vows, Trivikrama, aṃ namaḥ oṃ.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu Vāmana, aṃ oṃ. Vis_12.44,22–24.
Oṃ aṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva, to Śrīdhara; aṃ oṃ.
Oṃ aḥ oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, to Hṛṣīkeśa; aṃ oṃ.
Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Viṣṇu, to Padmanābha, to the lotus-handed one; oṃ ām. Vis_12.44,25–27.
Aḥ Oṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, Dāmodara. Aṃ Oṃ. Oṃ tat sat. Homage to Brahman.
Tat sa Oṃ. Oṃ Khaṃ. Homage to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the one of universal form, the all, the one in all, who abides within all beings. Oṃ. 30.
Oṃ oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One, Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the sacrifice, the leader of the sacrifice, the enjoyer of the sacrifice; salutations, salutations!
Oṃ, salutations to the infinite one, the thousand-formed Viṣṇu, Vāsudeva, the Veda, the embodied one; salutations! Oṃ!
Oṃ, salutations to all the mudrās! Vis_12.44,31–33.
Oṃ, homage to Kamalavāsinī. Vis 12.44.34.
Oṃ bhuṃ, homage to Puṣṭi. Vis 12.44.35.
Oṃ hrīṃ, homage to Medhā; hrīṃ oṃ. Vis 12.44.36.
Oṃ saṃ, salutation to Sarasvatī; saṃ oṃ.
Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ saṃ oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Durgā;
oṃ hrīṃ oṃ hrīṃ, salutation to Sandā; oṃ. Vis_12.44,37–38.
Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati, the leader of obstacles; oṃ.
Oṃ kṣaiṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the Self who is the Parameṣṭhin;
oṃ yāṃ, obeisance to the Supreme, obeisance to the Self who is Puruṣa. Oṃ. Vis 12.44,39–41.

Oṃ rāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the Universal Self. Oṃ vāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the Self of Cessation. Oṃ lāṃ, salutation to the Supreme, salutation to the All-Self.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Enumeration of Mantras," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Thirteen:
Viṣvaksena— the ritual procedure for all branches of knowledge, beginning with the mantras such as the *praṇava*.
I shall explain everything regarding the seers, the meters, and so forth, exactly as it is.
The inner controller is the sage; the meter is the goddess Gāyatrī; the supreme self is the immortal syllable; and the beginning of the Vedas is remembered as the "I" (asmitā). 13.2.
The sage Viśvāmitra is Viṣṇu; the deity is the Supreme Self (paramātman);
the meter is the Supreme Self itself, and its color is traditionally held to be white.
The sage is Jāmadagnya, the metre is Anuṣṭubh, and Vāsudeva is the deity;
for Vāsudeva, the color is declared to be white.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh, the sage is Bharadvāja, and Saṃkarṣaṇa is considered the deity;
for the science of Saṃkarṣaṇa, the color red is said here to be its attribute.
The sage of Pradyumna is Gautama, the meter is Paṅkti,
the deity is Pradyumna, and his color is remembered as golden-hued.
For the vidyā of Aniruddha, the sage is Atri and the metre is Triṣṭubh; the deity is Aniruddha, who has the color of a dark blue cloud.
Vasiṣṭha is the seer of the Matsya-mantra, and its metre is remembered as Jagatī;
Vāsudeva is the deity, and blue is said to be its color here.
One should know the sage Kāśyapa as the tortoise; the Virāj is its meter. The deity is the dark Nārāyaṇa; this is said to be the color of the Vidyā.
In the Vārāha-vidyā, Agastya is said to be the seer, the Gāyatrī the metre, and the immortal Viṣṇu the deity; he is described as being of dark-blue complexion.
Nārada is the seer of the Nṛsiṃha-vidyā; Hari is remembered as its deity;
the meter is that of Nṛsiṃha, and the deity is white in color.
...one should know Maṅkaṇaka as the *ṛṣi*, and likewise the *chandas* and the *muni*.
In this mantra, Vāmana is said to be the deity, and Añjana is the color. (Vis 13.12)
One should know the Bhārgava [mantra] in the Bhārgava [kalpa]; it is said to belong to the gods. The Bhārgava deity is the Sage; his color is said to be yellow. (Vis 13.13)
The *Ṛgvedic Gāyatrī* of the science of Rāma composed by Vālmīki is thus described:
its sage is [Vālmīki], its meter is *Gāyatrī*, and its deity is the Supreme Self, resembling the ocean.
Bṛhaspati is known as his strength, and Supratiṣṭhā is remembered as his sage;
the meter belongs to the deity Vāyu, whose color is golden.
Bhṛgu is the sage of Kṛṣṇa’s Vidyā; the meter is the Chandas, and the deity is the Supreme Self (Paramātman). Its foundation is said to be silver, and its color is white.
The sage Yājñavalkya is remembered as the sage of Kalki-Viṣṇu;
his meter is the Gāyatrī, and the color of Viṣṇu is smoky-grey.
The sage is Śātātapa, the metre is Paṅkti, and the deity is Keśava;
for the lore of Keśava, the phoneme is said to be Rītikā.
The mantra of Nārāyaṇa is said to be the Devīgāyatrī;
its inner controller is one's own self, and its color is emerald.
For Mādhava, Saṃvarta is the seer; Mādhava is remembered as the deity; Jagatī is the meter; and the color is like crystal. Viṣṇu 13.20.
The sage of Govinda is Vyāsa; his meter is Virāṭ and his deity is Govinda himself.
His color is said to be like a diamond.
The sage is Sanatkumāra, and the deity of the Viṣṇu-mantra is Viṣṇu himself; the meter is Virāṭ, and the color is ruby-red.
For the Madhusūdana-vidyā, the sage is Dakṣa and the deity is Madhusūdana;
the meter is Anuṣṭubh and the color is coral-red.
The *māṇikya* of Trivikrama is said to be the sage Saṃvarta;
the meter is Bṛhatī, and the color is... [as specified].
But the deity is Trivikrama.
The sage of Vāmana is Parāśara; the meter is remembered as Triṣṭubh.
The deity is Vāmana, and his color is said to be like a pearl.
The sage of Śrīdhara is Kaṇva; the meter is Tūṣṇih;
it is desired by those who know it; the deity is Śrīdhara; and its color is like that of lapis lazuli.
The sage is Aṅgiras; the meter is remembered as Jagatī; the deity is Hṛṣīkeśa, who is blue-hued and belongs to the Kaukiśi family. (Vis 13.27)
The sage of Padmanābha is said to be Vaiśampāyana;
his meter is to be known as Triṣṭubh, and his color resembles silver.
Śuka is said to be the sage (muni) of the Bṛhatī meter within the Brahmavidyā;
its presiding deity is Brahmā, and its color is like the luster of the moon.
For the Vidyā of Dāmodara, the sage is Mārkaṇḍeya;
the meter is Anuṣṭubh; the color is like a lotus; and the deity is the immortal Dāmodara.
The color of Viśvarūpa is cyavana, resembling the sun;
his meter is the threefold gāyatrī, and he is the immortal sage Vāsudeva.
Pulastya is the sage of Yajñamūrti; his meters are three, and his presiding deity is Vidyā; he is yellow in color, and Saṃkarṣaṇa is remembered as his sage.
The sage Aitareya is remembered as the Virāṭ meter of the Veda’s embodiment;
his color is like refined gold, and he is called the immortal Pradyumna.
The sage Pippalāda is said to be the meter of the Mudrā-vidyā;
its foundation is Agnivarṇa, and Aniruddha is the presiding deity.
O best of sages, for the Lotus-Vidyā, Dakṣa is remembered as the seer, Virāj as the meter, Kamalā as the deity, and its color is like a lamp. Viṣṇupurāṇa 13.35.
For the Puṣṭividya, Kaṇva is the seer, the Gāyatrī is held to be the meter, Puṣṭi is said to be the deity, and the sage’s color is recorded as white. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 13.36)
The sage Saṃvarta is said to be the seer of the Medhā-mantra; its meter is declared to be Triṣṭubh, and its presiding deity is Śaṅkha, who is described here as being white in color.
Maitreya, however, is remembered as the *jagatī* meter of the Sarasvatī-vidyā; its metre is Sarasvatī, its deity is Sarasvatī, and its color is like cow’s milk. (Vis 13.38)
The sage of Kāśyapa is Triṣṭubh; Durgā alone is the deity. His color is declared to be dark blue; now hear [the details] of Vighneśa. 13.39.
The sage of this *gaṇaka* [mantra] is Triṣṭubh, its meter is remembered as Gaṇapati;
its deity is Dhavala, and its color is likewise that of the Vidyā of Gaṇapati. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 13.40)
The seer is Āditya, the color is blue, and it is said to be in the Gāyatrī meter;
likewise, Viṣṇu is always the deity, while the meter of Parameṣṭhin is [the same].
The sage is Puruṣa, the Sūta is the white color, and the deity is Vāsudeva; likewise, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī.
The sage is Ravi, who resembles the rising sun;
likewise, Saṃkarṣaṇa is the deity, and the meter is declared to be Uṣṇih. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 13.43)
When the color has ceased from the King, Pradyumna is called immortal;
likewise, the sage is Anumā, and the meter is recited as Gāyatra.
Mārtaṇḍa is said to be the sage of all knowledge, with the complexion of a cloudless sky; the Uṣṇih is the meter, and Aniruddha is declared to be the deity. Vis_13.45.
O best of sages, for those whose seer (ṛṣi) and other details are not mentioned in this mantra, one should know that, by general rule, their seer is Āditya himself.
The Gāyatrī meter alone should be used, and Sadāviṣṇu the deity;
likewise for the seed-syllables, the seed-colors, the meters, and the deities.
If that [worship] is performed for one who does not know the Sage, it would be as if it were not performed at all.
Therefore, having understood the sequence of the sciences and so forth, the supreme practitioner— Vis_13.48.
As it has been said: "O Sage, one who has acquired knowledge and is pure should worship constantly;
otherwise, he who worships out of delusion incurs a mass of sin and the destruction of his lineage. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 13.49)
It brings about the destruction of the king; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, having understood [this] through hardship, the wise one should worship the mantras and so forth.
For the further increase of all vows, I shall hereafter proclaim the [mantras] of the most secret sciences, as well as those of the Sūkta and the Puruṣa.
O best of beings, Nārada, hear in brief the deity, the meter, and the sage and so forth of this hymn, which begins in the *anuṣṭubh* and ends in the *triṣṭubh*. Vis_13.52.
The Puruṣa who is the seed of the universe is remembered as the seer Nārāyaṇa;
for it has been declared regarding the collection [of verses], so listen to each verse, O Nārada. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 13.53)
For the first [mantra], the sage is Vāsudeva; the meter is said to be Uṣṇih;
the supreme self, the immortal, is designated as the syllable, and its color is white.
Saṃkarṣaṇa is the sage; the meter is Anuṣṭubh; its deity is Matsyaka.
O best of sages, the color of the second [form] is declared to be smoky-gray.
The third is the Gāyatrī meter of the Goddess; its color is remembered as ruddy.
They say Pradyumna is the seer, and the deity is said to be the Tortoise.
The sage of the fourth [quarter] is Atiruddha; the meter is Virāj;
its deity is Vārāha, and its color is declared to be blue.
For the fifth, the sage is Chandas, Keśava is said to be the meter,
Narasiṃha is the deity, and the color is like cow’s milk.
One should know that for the sixth [chapter], the seer is Nārāyaṇa, the metre is said to be the *nicṛt-gāyatrī*, and the deity is Māndhātṛ; furthermore, Dhūmraka is the deity of the sixth itself.
The color of the seventh [syllable] is that of a sage (muni); Mādhava is remembered as its white [color].
One should know Rāma to be its presiding deity; the Uṣṇih meter is declared for it.
Govinda is the seer of the eighth [verse], its metre is indeed uṣṇih,
its deity is Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, and its color is like the fire of cosmic destruction.
The sage of the ninth [chapter] is Viṣṇu; Balarāma is its presiding deity.
The color of the Gāyatrī meter is said to have the appearance of cow’s milk.
The sage Madhusūdana is said to be the deity of the Gāyatrī;
that which is the presiding deity of the tenth [mantra] is Kalki, who is like fire in appearance.
Trivikrama is the sage, Virāj is the meter, and he is like fire;
this Viśvarūpa is the deity for the tenth [chapter], which is exclusively dedicated to him.
One should know the twelfth [digit] as the Sage (Muni), resembling fire;
his meter is Virāj, he is immortal, and he is recited as the embodiment of sacrifice (Yajñamūrti).
For the thirteenth, the meter is Uṣṇik, the sage is Śrīdhara,
the deity is Vaikuṇṭha, and the color is like refined gold.
The fourteenth [chapter] consists of the Gāyatrī meter; its deity is the one whose form is like that of Añjana;
its sage is Hṛṣīkeśa, who is remembered as the god Mahāviṣṇu.
The sage Padmanābha is remembered as belonging to the fifteenth [tattva];
his presiding deity is Vedamūrti, his metre is Uṣṇih, and he is remembered as white.
The seer of the sixteenth [chapter] is remembered as Dāmodara;
the great seer is Hayagrīva, and the meter is Agni, who resembles a god.
Thus has been proclaimed the seer and the other [details] of the Puruṣasūkta;
as well as the seer, the meter, the deity, and the phoneme of each verse.
If one worships out of ignorance or delusion, even a well-performed rite becomes as if unperformed;
therefore, with every effort, one should correctly identify the seers and other elements in their proper sequence.
The seer (ṛṣi) of the Atharvaṇa hymn that sets forth the creation and so forth is Nārāyaṇa, and its metre is indeed the Devīgāyatrī.
O best of sages, the color of the supreme Self, the immortal, is designated as white; for those [deities] not mentioned in this mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) and other attributes are likewise understood.
One should know that for these [mantras], the sage is traditionally held to be Nārāyaṇa;
the metre is indeed the Gāyatrī, and the Supreme Self is the presiding deity.
The color of the *ṛcs* is yellow; thus has this secret been declared by me.
Thus have the seers (*ṛṣi*) and other details been proclaimed for the *ṛcs* that have been linked together.
This secret has been told in brief, indeed for the benefit of practitioners.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Seers, Metres, Deities, and Other Attributes of the Mantras," in the *Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā* of the illustrious *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Fourteen. Viṣvaksena said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for cooking the sacrificial oblation (caru).
Listen, O omniscient Nārada, to [the description of] the fields of rice and so forth, in their proper order.
One should not store grain on saline soil, near the houses of outcasts and the like, or on ground near a cremation ground. (ViS 14.2)
Grain produced from a fertile field, whether three years old, five years old, or even one year old,
or six months or three months old, is auspicious when it has been properly stored for some time.
Then, O best of sages, in this collection [of offerings], one should include red rice, white rice, and likewise black rice; however, white rice is the most excellent. Vis_14.4.
One should cook rice grains made from that [substance], which resemble jasmine, the moon, or pearls,
in the house of Hari.
In the southeast, in the kitchen. // Vis_14.5 //
One who knows the mantras, is born of a noble lineage, is devoted to the morning bath, is fit for cooking the sacrificial oblations, is strong, and is intent upon ritual action. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 14.6)
Now I shall speak of pride and the rest; listen to this unsurpassed secret:
it is filled with two hundred and twenty-five grains of rice. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 14.7)
One should calculate the measure known as a *śukti* by that very [unit];
two of those are called a *tala*, and two *talas* make a *prakubja*.
Two of those are called a *prasṛti*, and two *prasṛtis* are a *kuḍuba*.
Two of those are called an *añjali*, and two *añjalis* would be a *prastha*. (ViS 14.9)
A *pātra* is said to be two *prasthas*; two of those make an *āḍhaka*. Two of those are called a *śiva*; one should know that two *śivas* make a *droṇa*.
Two droṇas make one khārī, and three khāris make one bhāra;
thus has the measurement been declared by me. Now listen to the purification of the vessels.
Two vessels for the sacrificial pap (caru) are prescribed: either made of copper or of clay.
O best of sages, in the absence of copper, one should have them made of clay.
Day after day, the best of practitioners should prepare fresh domestic offerings;
and the attendant, having gathered vessels and bowls, [should do likewise].
Having washed it thoroughly with pure water, one should sprinkle it again with scented water using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī and, in sequence, with the five Upaniṣads.
This is declared here to be the purification of the vessel; [now follows] the enumeration of the sacrificial oblations (*havis*).
They declare that which is filled with eight *droṇas* to be called the "most excellent of the excellent."
That which is prepared with six *droṇas* of rice is considered superior;
that which is less than a *droṇa* is called inferior among the superior. (Vis 14.17)
That which is said to be middling-superior consists of two *khārīs*;
with two *droṇas*, the food offering (*naivedya*) becomes middling-middling.
The middling and the lowest are said to be two *droṇas* and one and a half *droṇas* respectively; one *droṇa* and its half, and half of that again, constitute the three grades of the lowest.
One should not prepare an offering of food that is deficient by one āḍhaka of rice;
the sacrificial porridge (caru) is said to be two prasthas, and the oblation (havis) is called one āḍhaka.
O best of sages, one should offer either an *āḍhaka* or even half of that amount of rice to the goddesses Śrī and the others; now hear the ritual procedure for the rice.
One should construct a granary for threshing grain either in the second enclosure or even in the third enclosure, in the region of the northeast.
Either in the south, or in the northwest, or in the southwest, or likewise in the interior;
having adorned the hall with beautiful canopies and other such decorations.
Having smeared it with cow dung, one should decorate it with rice flour;
the Brahmin woman, being of virtuous conduct and endowed with Brahmanic qualities, [should perform this].
One should perform the threshing of the grain right there, using an excellent mortar;
having consecrated the mortar and other implements by reciting the mantra "Hari" in succession.
One should cause all grains to be destroyed, and afterwards even the rice;
whether raw or cooked, in this very manner day after day.
Having consecrated all the rice grains and gathered them together with the *praṇava*,
he should thereafter gaze upon the rice grains and all the sugar and other ingredients.
O Sage, by remembering Hari and gradually becoming pure and concentrated, a true Śūdra who worships Viṣṇu for the sake of others is indeed a Vaiṣṇava.
One should not touch cooked food with raw food; one may act according to one's preference.
In the absence of that, O best of sages, [one may seek it] in every house of the Vaiṣṇavas.
O best of sages, rice must be prepared day after day by those who are not Śūdras; for if one, out of delusion or greed, should obtain it in a Śūdra’s house, [the rite is spoiled]. 14.30.
If one offers rice as an oblation, that worship will become fruitless;
one incurs total ruin, therefore one should avoid it with effort. (Vis 14.31)
One should cause the deity to be offered, according to one's desire and with devotion, for the sake of one's own purpose;
likewise, rice grains that are unbroken and unhusked should be accepted.
They were free from husks and stones, devoid of worms and insects; they were without broken grains, free from dust, and untouched by soil.
Other grains of rice that are uncooked must not be offered under any circumstances;
one should offer only cooked *caru* and avoid that which is uncooked. (Viṣṇusmṛti 14.34)
O Sage, if one offers the sacrificial oblation (caru) that has been excluded [from the ritual] out of delusion,
the rākṣasas and piśācas will joyfully seize that oblation.
Even Hari becomes angry; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, one should always avoid that which is to be avoided with every effort. (Vis 14.36)
O great sage, one should lift up all the bowls with the *praṇava*,
after having previously washed the bowls according to the procedure mentioned before.
One should smear [the vessel] with clarified butter using the eight-syllable mantra,
and afterwards touch the rice grains with the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Having meditated on Hari within his heart, he should cast twelve handfuls [of flowers] in sequence with the twelve names, joined at the end with the word of salutation (namaskāra).
Then, one should cast four handfuls [of water] while reciting the names of the forms,
and having performed the rinsing with the six syllables of the Parameṣṭhin-bīja.
Afterwards, the practitioner should place [the substance] upon the hearth with the seed-syllable of the male nature;
thereafter, he should kindle the fire with the seed-syllable of Viśva.
Having sprinkled [the offerings] with the *nivṛt* mantra, one should then pour them down using either the entire [mantra],
O Sage, or with the *mūrti-mantra* for all [deities], or with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*).
O tiger among sages, O great sage, one should perform all these mantras in due order for both the daily and occasional rites within this procedure for cooking the *caru* oblation.
The best of mantra-knowers should employ [the ritual] even for those who are devoid of prostrations;
I shall explain, in due order, the rules regarding what is to be avoided and what is not to be avoided in relation to the sacrificial oblations and other elements.
One should avoid grain that has turned blue, as well as that which is overcooked; likewise, one should avoid that which is entirely uncooked and that which is only half-boiled.

That which has changed color, that which is foul-smelling, that which has been fumigated, that which has been cooked twice, that which has been set aside, that which has been smelled, and that which is vomited—[these should not be consumed]. Vis 14.46.
That which is sneezed upon, struck by breath, or likewise affected by the air from the mouth;
that which is touched by another, looked upon by a dog, or gazed at by one who has not been initiated.

Furthermore, [water] that has been struck by drops of sweat, or likewise by the hand of one who is ill, or that which has been stepped over, or is cold, or excessively hot, or has been placed in a broken vessel; Vis_14.48.
[An image] containing worms, hair, and the like; joined with wood, clods of earth, and so forth;
devoid of mantra, devoid of ritual action, devoid of devotion, and [thus] unsatisfied. (Vis 14.49)
One should also carefully avoid sacrificial porridge placed in a vessel made of *arka* wood;
likewise, fruits that have been cooked with effort must be avoided in every respect.
Among those fruits that have been carefully ripened, one plantain fruit is selected;
however, one should offer here a fruit that is unripe and destroyed by fire.
When it has been said that pure food is thus [prepared], the milk-rice (pāyasa) is now described;
according to the desire of the patron, the practitioner takes rice for that purpose.
Milk should be double the amount of rice, and the essence of mung beans should be equal; this cooked preparation is called *pāyasa*. One should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
Having added ground sesame seeds amounting to one-fourth of the rice,
and having added ghee amounting to one-fourth of that, one should cook it according to the prescribed rule.
"Kṛsarānnam" has thus been described; now hear about "gaulyānna.
Having prepared milk-rice (pāyasa) as before, with an equal amount of sugar and rice.
One should add half a *guḍa* of clarified butter and add fruits such as plantain;
this is declared to be "rice with jaggery. Now, "rice with mung beans" is described. (Viṣṇu 14.56)
Mudga beans mixed with rice and coconut slices are declared to be "mudgānna"; here, "haridrānna" (turmeric rice) is now described.
This is called *pācitam* when it is prepared according to the rules with *marīci*, asafoetida, cumin, and mustard seeds; it is known as *haridrānna*. (Vis 14.58)
O Sage, listen now as I describe the procedure for that [cooking], which increases by one part;
take one *droṇa* of rice that has the brilliance of jasmine or the moon. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 14.59)
Having cooked it as before, one should add the spices beginning with black pepper;
one should throw in a quarter-prastha of black pepper and three times that amount of turmeric.
One should add double the amount of mustard seeds and half of that amount of cumin;
this is what I have taught regarding one *droṇa*, and the remainder should be applied according to reason.
Thus, O best of sages, I have described to you the successive portions of the turmeric-rice; now I shall describe the accompaniments—listen! (Visnu Purāṇa 14.62)
Fresh ghee, endowed with fragrance, color, and flavor, and strained through cloth—
of which the clarified butter (ājya) should consist of thirty-two parts— one should take cow's ghee for this purpose.
One-sixteenth part is the measure for a gulma-portion, and half of that is desired for a gulma;
all ripe fruits and roots should likewise be mixed with salt.
O Sage, one should cook it properly with ghee until it resembles molten gold,
O Great Sage, along with black pepper, turmeric, and mustard seeds.
Having cooked the side dishes, one should offer them to the Lord of Gods;
the remaining side dishes may be cooked according to the wish of the patron.
It is declared that [the preparation] should be mixed with curd, sugar-candy, and juices in eight parts;
and one should likewise prepare the soup according to one's means.
Therefore, O best of sages, I shall describe its measurement:
in that [rite], the practitioner, according to the wish of the patron, should take cow's milk and curd.
Having added half of that amount of jaggery, one should likewise add sugar-cane juice;
in its absence, however, there should be clarified butter, along with black pepper and powdered long pepper.
One should place the cooked soup there according to the prescribed rite,
as well as the fully ripened fruits of the plantain, the jackfruit, and the mango.
Mango should be used as a side dish; listen now to the ripe side dishes:
plantain, breadfruit, and likewise the two types of kāravallī.
As well as the two types of karkavallī, the kūṣmāṇḍa,
the urvāruka, the bṛhatī, the kṛṣṇabṛhatī, and likewise the karavarta.
One should likewise take the *karkarī*, the small *bṛhatī*, the two types of *alasanti*,
as well as the black *alasanti*, and those that are sweet.

O Nārada, among all sweet fruits, one should avoid the palmyra fruit; having extracted the essence from plantains, jackfruit, and the like— *Note: The Sanskrit text provided contains a corruption in "kadalīpanasādyeṣu(-dyānāṃ?)". Based on the context of classical dietary lists, the intended reading is likely "kadalīpanasādīnām" (of plantains, jackfruit, and so forth).*
Having placed it in a vessel, one should offer it to the deity, avoiding skins and such;
O Sage, one should carefully avoid what is forbidden even if it is being presented as an offering.
That worship becomes fruitless and causes the increase of all diseases;
therefore, one should diligently avoid skins and such, always remaining free from them.
One should avoid horse-gram, black gram, and flat beans, as well as legumes with two leaves; likewise, one should avoid the two kinds of mung beans, śība, and black lentils.
Having combined it with two kinds of sugar, properly cooked, and well-cooled,
one should place it upon the food and offer it to the God of gods.
One should avoid the *kośātakī*, the *alābu*, and various kinds of leaves;
the fruits have been described here, so now hear about the roots.
Vallī, Mahāvallī, and likewise Vanavallī;
Piṇḍā, Mahāpiṇḍā, and likewise Kṣudrapiṇḍā.
The fragrant root of the utpala lotus, which is auspicious and dear to the Lord of Gods—
one should take these roots and offer them to the God of Gods.
If these are not obtained, one should avoid all the remaining roots, including the vanasūraṇa.
In the same way, O best of sages, one should offer a yam in the daily worship.
If an offering is presented out of greed or delusion, that worship will be fruitless; therefore,
one should avoid it with effort and completely renounce the surana root.
O great sage, during a rite for desired objects, at a great festival, and indeed at a feast of great food,
one should offer surana according to the wish of the sacrificer.
O great sage, Viṣṇu, Mahāviṣṇu,
and likewise [the others] are satisfied here by the great food; being delighted, they partake of that sacrificial porridge (caru).
One should cook it with pungent, sour, and especially bitter side-dishes (upadaṃśa),
using whatever is available, while observing the prescribed characteristics.
One should add one *kuḍuba* of *marīci* and powdered salt into its midst;
they call this "sour relish," which brings all prosperity and happiness. (Vis 14.87)
Only those things mentioned [in the scriptures] should be offered, and never others;
one should also ensure that the vessels and bowls are used and that external purification is performed.
On all external vessels, one should apply the vertical mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) with ashes using the *mūrti-mantra*, in due order starting from the east and so forth.
One should mark the bowl with the Viṣṇu-mantra on the front part of the vessel,
beginning from the kitchen and ending at the inner sanctum.
Having sprinkled the vessels with water using the first [mantra], the wise one should raise them all up in sequence, employing that same mantra. 14.91.
At that very time, however, they blew three conch shells separately;
and on the northern side of the gate, one should place all the vessels.
One should make the vessel out of gold, silver, copper, or even a plantain leaf, or from pure bell-metal weighing one hundred palas.
Or half of that, O best of sages, or even thirty-two *palas*;
having taken up the vessel according to his means, the practitioner [should proceed]. (Vis 14.94)
Taking up a ladle or a mallet, one should sprinkle it with clarified butter;
one should fill the vessel with food, such as flour-cakes, parched grain, and molasses.
One should offer clarified butter, ghee, and curd along with side dishes;
having divided this into four parts, one should assign one portion to the deity.
One should offer the portion prepared for the deity to the Lord of Devas;
having made the offering at the proper time, the knower of the Tantra should present the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and so forth. Vis 14.97.
Having offered a flower and paid homage to the feet of Hari, the practitioner,
knowing the mantra, should wash his hands with the weapon-mantra of the deity.
Then, having performed the sprinkling as before, the supreme practitioner,
having washed his own hands, should touch them with the root mantra.
O great sage, having performed the remaining rites as before, beginning with the oblation,
the preceptor should face north while seated in the svastika posture before Upendra.
One should place the five Upaniṣads upon the fingers of the right hand;
one should offer oblations there five times with the Parameṣṭhi mantra.
O Sage, having performed prostrations, one should thereafter recite the five Upaniṣads;
then, having carefully washed one's hands, one should offer [the food] separately into a vessel.

O divine sage, for the God of gods, there is [worship] accompanied by the sounding of conchs and drums, and joined with dance and song, both as a regular (nitya) rite and on special occasions (naimittika).
Having offered well-prepared incense with devotion, one should again present curd;
and having given water once more in a clean and auspicious vessel for play.
Having again offered the libation and the rinsing of the mouth for each respective recipient,
he should rub his hands with fragrant pastes and wipe them with a very white cloth.
Having covered [the image] with fragrant paste, the best of practitioners should again offer water for rinsing the mouth; then, having offered mouth-perfume according to the rule.
Furthermore, with the second portion of the oblation, one should perform a fire sacrifice in the sacrificial pit using the root mantra,
preceded by fuel sticks and clarified butter.
With the third [verse], one should offer the bali-oblation, facing either east or north;
having again properly offered water and performed a circumambulation while paying homage.
Having offered that, the preceptor, the most excellent knower of mantras, should cast the remainder of the bali onto the bali-pīṭha, having set aside one-fourth portion.
Facing the east, one should consume the most excellent remains of the vessel;
those remnants destroy all sins and cut away all diseases. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 14.110)
Therefore, the knower of mantras should consume the supreme *chedaṣa*, which bestows all holy fords (*tīrtha*),
either to the north or to the southwest of the temple.
O best of sages, having eaten, one should perform the remaining rites as before,
O Brahmin, according to the sequence in the ritual for daily worship and the ritual for cooking the sacrificial oblation (caru).
One should cause this to be performed day after day in the manner thus described.
Now I shall explain the procedure for the great oblation; the smallest consists of eight *droṇas*.
Twofold is declared to be the middling; threefold is the lowest-of-the-high;
fourfold, fivefold, and sixfold—these they know as the three [grades] of the middling.
It is said that for the superior [type], three [medicines] consisting of seven, eight, or nine [ingredients] are prescribed;
having cooked them as before, one should cause all of them to arise separately.
Then, one should place the vessels in due order on the northern side of the pavilion;
or alternatively, one should set out the great sacrificial offering in the southwest or the west.
Having constructed a square pavilion and adorned it with unbroken grains,
one should decorate it with flour-powders and fashion a lotus together with its pericarp.
Having covered the ground with a cloth and placed plantain leaves upon it,
one should perform the rites for the deities, such as the ritual bathing, in sequence as before.
Having placed the deity before him, the practitioner should slowly announce his purpose;
then, having raised the Lord of Devas from his seat, he should worship Him with his two sandals.
Accompanied by the sound of a conch shell, one should bring the seat for the meal;
having offered water for the feet, the respectful offering, and water for sipping, one should worship with perfumes and flowers.

Having sprinkled [the offerings] with water and then poured clarified butter over them, he should likewise prepare the vessels for the *caru* offerings in due order: milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice-and-pulse (*kṛsara*), sweet rice (*gaulya*), and mung-bean porridge (*mudgānna*).
Pure rice and soup, curd-rice, and the great oblation;
clarified butter, jaggery and sugar-candy, and the three fruits beginning with the plantain. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 14.122.
One should offer all the side dishes cooked in ghee into the vessel;
then, having performed the sprinkling, one should touch [the food] with the *Annasūkta*.
One should place that [offering] in his right hand with the gesture for consuming the sacrificial oblation (haviḥ-prāśana-mudrā),
and having given fragrant, sweet-smelling water, one should offer excellent drinking water.
Having given water for sipping once more, he should wipe his hands with a cloth;
having rubbed them with a paste of fragrant substances, he should then lead him to another seat.
Having first removed the previous rosary, one should then wrap it with the [new] rosary;
having again offered water for sipping (ācamana) and purified the hands with a cloth.
One should offer various oblations ending with cakes;
then, having given a coconut fruit, one should provide water for drinking and rinsing the mouth.
Having again offered water for sipping, one should present mouth-perfume:
namely, a split areca nut, whether unripe or ripe. (Viṣṇudharmottara 14.128)
O Lord of Sages, whether sprinkled with camphor oils or not,
it should be gradually washed along with the leaves of the betel vine.
Elā, kakkola, and jātī, together with camphor in due order, combined with the fruits of the mātuluṅga and accompanied by coconut water. Viṣṇu 14.130.
One should offer mouth-perfume prepared with powdered sugar combined with camphor, consecrated by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ). Vis_14.131.
And having given [the offering], one should worship Hari properly like a king and like a father;
then, rising from the seat, one should circumambulate the temple of the Lord of Gods.
Having circumambulated the palace accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums and joined with benedictory hymns, one should cause it to enter the inner sanctum.
O great sage, the procedure for the Mahāhavis has been declared in brief;
I shall now explain in detail the procedure for the Mahānna sacrifice in its proper sequence.
O best of sages, O most excellent Nārada, listen to this secret even among secrets:
[it is attained] through the previously mentioned offerings that increase the sacrificial oblation, as prescribed in the rules for cooking the *caru*.
The great oblation (mahāhavi) consists of one hundred and ten measures of fine rice;
half of that is recorded as the middling [oblation].
Of that [milk], half-prepared is called the inferior great oblation by those who know it;
from cows that have been milked, there should be six āḍhakas, which is a sixty-fourfold quality.
There should be one āḍhaka of ghee and five prasthas of cooked mung beans;
[one palāśa of ghee and five prasthas of cooked mung beans?];
there should be two āḍhakas of water for the cleaned and split [beans]. (Viṣṇu 14.138)
Two *kaṃsa* measures of rice grains are desired for the preparation of milk-rice balls;
half of this is excellent, half of that is mediocre, and half of that would be inferior.
This milk-rice (pāyasa), cooked according to the prescribed method without jaggery or ghee,
and cooked with the essence of mung beans, is equal to a meal of śāli rice with the essence of mung beans.
A cake prepared from sugar-cane flour cooked with ghee is prescribed,
along with *kakkola*, nutmeg, betel nuts, and the leaves of the white *bhujaga* plant.
Stone powder mixed with citron peel and coconut fruit,
combined with camphor oil, is declared to be a complete mouth-freshener.
O Sage of the Thirty-three, all the water scented with cardamom, campaka, and ketaki, as well as the great offerings and so forth that have been prepared, [are for you]. (Vis 14.143)

That which has been accomplished in a temple or even in its vicinity would be suitable for the mantra; however, if one out of delusion accomplishes it for a deity with a mantra in another house... [Vis_14.144]
For he who gives food as an offering would be a sinner and a destroyer of the kingdom;
whatever cooked food has been prepared elsewhere, even if it comes together [with him], [he should not give it]. 14.145.
Having displayed each of these before the image, one should indeed offer them to those who have been cooked;
having performed this properly, it becomes a great oblation most dear to Hari.

The devotee who performs [the practice] to a middling degree attains proximity; one who performs it to a lesser degree attains similarity; and the highest attainment is co-residence in the same world.
Having offered milk-rice with devotion, one attains peace through Hari;
indeed, the supreme portion enters the middle, fulfilling all desires.
O Sage, a great distinction has been proclaimed here regarding the ritual for Nādividhi;
one should perform the remainder according to the common [rule]— this is the certainty of the scripture.
And here, regarding the performance of the great fire-sacrifice (mahāhoma), two types of measurement have been taught;
the knower of the tantras should practice both kinds as appropriate.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Cooking the Caru," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Nārada said:
O Lord of Harisenā, tell me in detail [the ritual] regarding the root mantra.
O support of compassion, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, [please explain] the sequence of the fire sacrifice for me who desires to hear it.
Viṣvaksena said: Listen, O Sage Nārada, to the truth according to the first section,
concerning the sacrificial pits, the *sruk*, and the *sruva*.
And indeed, I have spoken this quite clearly. (Vis 15.2)

One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to one's ability, either following that sequence, or without it, or together with the root-vidyā; in every way, one will surely attain accomplishment (siddhi).
Therefore, first hear that which is endowed with Vaiṣṇava instruments: one should prepare a fire-drill consisting of a *pippala* wood encased within *śamī* wood. Viṣṇu 15.4.
Having produced fire by churning using Vaiṣṇava mantras, or having brought fire born from jewels, or even ordinary worldly fire, one should sprinkle it with the twelve-syllable mantra.
The preceptor, having taken up the fire, should withdraw it into his own self by means of that seed-syllable using the index finger and thumb, O Sage.
Having paid homage to the fire again and again with the añjali-mudrā,
one should cause the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) to be made square.
For the purpose of making [the site] Vaiṣṇava, one should, without sloth, have a pit dug in the earth by the hand of Agni to a measurement of four finger-breadths.
Leaving two finger-breadths from the edge of the pit, one should fashion the girdle;
its width should be four finger-breadths, and its height likewise.
A single girdle made of the skin of a tiger or a lion should be placed all around;
thus, the "single-girdled" sacrificial pit (*mekhalā-kuṇḍa*) is proclaimed in this tantra. (Vis 15.10)
The circle of the Vaiṣṇava fire-pit is the conceptualization of the womb;
the womb should be fashioned according to one's desire, like the leaf of a Pippala tree.
O best of sages, the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) have been fully described for all activities, such as plowing and so forth, for the purpose of making them Vaiṣṇava.
Having sprinkled and thoroughly moistened [the site] according to the scripture, the practitioner, most excellent in mind,
should smear it and draw the lines of the bolt.
She who is named Sacrifice. Vis_15.13.
The first [line] of that [diagram] has its tip facing north; of those two [lines], their tips face east.
In the middle, there are three lines of the same form, proceeding in the order starting from the south.

Having thus drawn [the lines] and sprinkled [water], the preceptor, knowing the mantra, should first meditate upon the bed in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by means of the syllable Om alone.
Having placed Dharma and the other [triads] at the feet, and likewise Adharma and the other three,
one should place Ananta in the center; thereafter, the three qualities (guṇas) are the nooses (pāśas).
Then, according to the prescribed procedure, the practitioner [should dissolve] the elements beginning with earth, as well as the instruments and the agent, by means of the root mantra.

One should meditate upon Lakṣmī in the midst of that [maṇḍala], which is covered with a layer of grass and well-perfumed with the fragrance of incense— she who is primordial nature, consisting of the three guṇas.
In the midst of that bed, however, he saw her who had reached the bloom of youth,
endowed with supreme beauty, and whose eyes were rolling with intoxication.
She is the power of Viṣṇu, endowed with the capacity for creation, possessing an auspicious form,
wearing divine garlands and garments, and resplendent with celestial jewels.
Her limbs were anointed with divine perfumes and adorned with celestial ornaments; she was full of longing, having bathed after her menses, and was entreating Hari.
Having thus reflected upon the goddess who holds a lotus,
[he offered] perfumes, garlands, water, and so forth, ending with mouth-fresheners.
Having meditated on all those articles of play and enjoyment on every side,
[he saw one] exceedingly endowed with beauty, standing in the prime of youth.
His body was variegated with a crown and armlets, his hair was dark and curled,
and he wore divine garlands and garments, resplendent with celestial jewels.
His chest was marked with the Śrīvatsa, he was resplendent with a forest garland,
and he shone with the Kaustubha gem which emitted a network of light from all kinds of jewels.
With shoulders broad like those of a lion, a chest wide and expansive, and eyes reaching as far as his ears;
with arms reaching down to his knees, he was glorious, serene, and possessed of a smiling countenance.
One should meditate upon the four-armed Lord, who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace, and who seems to sprinkle everything on all sides with the nectar-water of his loveliness.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess and likewise the god in that form,
one should worship them with pleasing services such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Then, free from desire, he himself should worship with devotion, having meditated upon them as lying together on one bed, embracing one another. (Vis 15.29)
Thereafter, having attained supreme joy through the practice of sexual union,
the practitioner [should visualize] the seed-syllable of fire situated in the middle of the white [syllable] of the deity.
With that seed-syllable, the wise one should install the unsurpassed fire;
having established the womb-couch, it should be endowed with that jewel.
After the rite of conception has been performed, one should dismiss the deity;
thereafter, one should kindle the fire with dry wood immediately.
Having made the fuel-sticks a span in length, one should then perform the placing;
then, having swept around with darbha grass, one should strew them in three rows of three.
Just as one should cover the root with the tips starting from the east in sequence,
so too should one place the vessels upon it, as well as the two sets of fuel and sacrificial grass.
And having placed the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles here with the *praṇīta* water, the practitioner [should proceed].
There are two *praṇītā* vessels for sprinkling, as well as two *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pots). // Vis_15.35 //
Having arranged them in pairs, and having sprinkled everything else that is required, he should then take up the *prokṣaṇī* vessel.
Having filled [the vessel] with water and purified it, and having placed that water in his hand while a purifier is held between the fingers,
the practitioner should sprinkle himself with it.
Having performed that [action] in the sprinkling-water itself and having meditated upon the imperishable light,
one should establish the fire as before, after purifying it with water from within.
Then, having sprinkled everything three times and loosened the entire fuel-bundle,
the practitioner [should offer] it along with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains, together with the water from within the purifying vessel.
Having placed the *praṇītā* water in front, one should install Hari along with his limbs within it;
having worshipped the Lord, the performer of all protection, with perfumes and other offerings.
Having meditated and led [the fire] to the northern part, the wise one should establish it and worship it;
then, having filled the vessel for clarified butter with ghee, he should place it in front.
One should perform the consecration of the clarified butter by means of dipping in and lifting out;
two blades of kuśa grass, unbroken at the tips, cut, and a span in length, [should be used].
With those two hands turned upward, using the thumbs and ring fingers, one should grasp them at their bases,
lead them away three times, and then bring them back three times.
Having cleansed both the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and washed them again, the practitioner,
having heated them and set them down, should do so with the *praṇava* alone.
With that seed-syllable, the wise one should perform the fire-oblations for the rites beginning with conception:
the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the rite for a male child (puṃsavana), and likewise the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana). (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.15.45)
The birth-rite, the naming ceremony, the first feeding of solid food,
as well as the tonsure, the initiation, the Prājāpatya rite, and the Soma sacrifice.
O Sage, the Vaiśvadeva, the Śukriya, the Samāvartana, and the Vivāha— these indeed are to be known as such, and after these [follows] the highest.
The sequence of the purificatory rites has been declared; their performance shall now be described.
Having worshipped the fire with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the oblations for the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*). *Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa* 15.48.
O Sage, the preceptor should begin with only these seven tongues of fire;
otherwise, it would be as if it were not done at all, yielding contrary results.
Nārada said:
"Tell me, O Sage, what was previously mentioned that I should hear: what is the name of this 'seven tongues,' what is its state, and what is its quality?"
Viṣvaksena:
Listen, O sage; I shall correctly declare the supreme secret, as well as the name "Jihvā," its form, its location, and its application hereafter. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 15.51)
Kālī is the first [flame] of the fire of the tongue; Karālī follows immediately after that; Manojava is the third, while Lohitā is the fourth. 15.52.
The fifth is Sudhūmra; the sixth is called Sphuliṅginī;
the seventh is named Viśvarūpā—these are proclaimed as the seven tongues of flame. Vis 15.53.
Kālyā’s abode is the middle [direction], Karālī’s shall be the eastern quarter, Manojava’s the south-west, and Lohitā’s place is the western [quarter]. (15.54)
Deep smoke-colored, resting in the blue moon, possessing sparks, abiding in fire,
she who possesses all forms.
O Sage, such is the state of Śavasati, attained through these stages in succession.
For these [women], one should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* up to the end of the marriage ceremony at dawn;
however, in the form of the Vaiṣṇava fire, one should offer clarified butter while reciting the *praṇava*.

The practitioner of mature mind, recollecting each [of these] with its specific visualization, should especially perform the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) with eight oblations for each. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 15.57)
Taking up sixteen pieces of fuel wood while reciting the *praṇava* once,
one should offer them into the center of the sacrificial pit at the time of Kālī and at the conclusion of the meal.
Having again offered an oblation of clarified butter (ājya) eight times with the Praṇava,
one should then offer the sacrificial porridge (caru), pouring one oblation at a time, each as large as an akṣa berry, in due order.
Then, having offered the full oblation with the ladle using the eight-syllable mantra twenty-eight times according to the root [mantra], the practitioner [should proceed].
One should utter the *praṇava* with a protracted vowel at the end of the mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should pay homage to the fire with its own mantra.
Having taken the fire from the [central] pit, one should place it in the eastern pit;
then, having deposited it in the southern one, immediately thereafter in the western one.
Having cast the fire into the northern [pit] with the root mantra,
O best of sages, or else, in this case, the practitioner should indeed perform everything with the first [mantra].
Having placed a fire in each pit, the knower of the supreme truth,
having thus consecrated the purifying fire of Hari according to the ritual rule, [proceeded].
Thus, the consecration by fire (agnisaṃskāra) is prescribed for all sacrifices;
and likewise, in the process of making [the recipient] Vaiṣṇava, there shall then arise the Vaiṣṇava fire.
O Nārada, having burnt the enclosing sticks and the other materials with the *praṇava*, the practitioner should then generate the Vaiṣṇava fire according to this sequence.
One should cause everything to be performed according to the rules in activities such as plowing and so forth;
or else, O tiger among sages, one should have it performed at the eastern sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

All the rites for making [the deity] Vaiṣṇava, as well as the remaining common rites, should be performed in either a fire-pit or on a sacrificial mound. Perform the rite of making [the deity] Vaiṣṇava there.
But if one should, out of delusion, produce fire in an improper place, that rite should be known as fruitless, and it will result in the destruction of crops and other such things. (Viṣṇu 15.69)

Therefore, with every effort, one should have the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) shaped as squares and so forth constructed according to the injunctions; having sprinkled them with water while reciting the Astra-mantra.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) in due order with the syllables beginning with *śaśāṅka* (the moon) according to the prescribed method;
O Nārada, listen as I describe the sequence of that placement within the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*).
Whether in a sacrificial pit or on a consecrated ground, once the sprinkling with the *praṇava* has been performed,
one should sprinkle [the area] with the "Vasusūtra" line, starting from the south and ending at the north.
Having divided and partitioned the space from the west up to Indra (the east),
one should spread cooked rice in the central square by means of a *kuḍuba* measure.
One should draw a moon disc here with unbroken rice grains;
having inscribed the seed-syllable in its center, one should write the eight syllables starting from the east.
Outside of that, one should write the vowels ending with *ṝ* within the eight squares;
outside of that, from Indra to Īśāna, one should place them in the vowel-squares.
One should place the letters beginning with *ja* and ending with *na* from the east to the northeast;
then, one should write the letters beginning with *jha* and ending with *sa* in the squares for the elements outside of that.
From the east to the northeast, and then indeed upon the enclosures (mekhalās),
one should recite the Sudarśana mantra from the east to the north.
O best of Brahmins, the practitioner should place the unsurpassed seed-syllable of Viṣṇu five times within the center of the womb using the ring finger.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence for the benefit of practitioners,
if the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is performed without such placement, that rite shall be fruitless.
That village goes to destruction, and those residing there shall meet their end;
therefore, a wise person should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with every effort.
O best of sages, at every sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or on the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), being unwearied,
one should worship with offerings beginning with perfumes and ending with lamps, and perform the gesture of the joined palms (*añjalimudrā*).
Having shown [the mandala] according to the rule, one should perform the five hundred [offerings] in sequence;
likewise, one should worship the yoni within the girdle (mekhalā).
Henceforth, O best of sages, I shall explain the supreme sequence of fire-offerings (homa) for all ritual activities, beginning with the plowing of the field.
The preceptor should proceed with the fire-offering, as well as the sacrificial grass,
the fuel-sticks, the enclosing sticks, the large and small ladles, the food, the clarified butter, the parched grain, and likewise the sesame seeds.
Then [he should prepare] the fuel, the sacrificial substances, incense, flowers, excellent incense, a lamp, the vardhanī vessel, fragrant water, and likewise the prokṣaṇī vessel.
Then, having set aside the consecrated clarified butter and other substances,
the practitioner should place them in pairs to the north of the location of the wind, using a pair [of fingers] for each.
O Sage, having poured the water from the *vardhanī* vessel into the *prokṣaṇī*, and having sprinkled the ritual materials with the root mantra, one should then invoke the fire.
Having sprinkled the fire as previously described,
one should contemplate the form of Agni; having sprinkled that fire situated in the pit, [one should do so] with the seed-syllable accompanied by the anusvāra.
Having placed the fire with both hands according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should kindle the fuel, sprinkle it, and spread the sacrificial grass around the center of the fire.
Having meditated upon an eight-petaled lotus, one should invoke the Lord of Gods there from the primary image and worship him according to the prescribed rite.
In this matter of the fire-offering ritual, O Nārada, there is a certain distinction:
one should [visualize] the deity as resembling a white mountain, having three feet and seven arms.
He saw Hari with the Vedas as his horns, two faces, wearing yellow garments,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, possessing seven tongues, and beautifully adorned.
The wise one should meditate on the gentle [deity], surrounded by all divine ornaments,
as being present within the fire in the form of fire, facing the mouth of the sacrificial flame.
Therefore, having offered the guest-water (arghya) and other honors, one should place the ritual vessel (vidhi) to the south of the fire;
after worshipping it according to the rules, one should then place the oblation materials in the center.
Having placed the vessel for the *praṇītā* water, one should place Hari there along with his limbs;
having worshipped the God with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the rite of *homa*.
In the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites, one should use fuel-sticks and clarified butter in their proper order;
the fuel-sticks are from the palāśa, khadira, bilva, udumbara, and pippala trees.
The wise should select excellent wood; its length should be twelve finger-breadths.
It should be as thick as the little finger, free from crooks, knots, and other irregularities.
The enclosing fence (paridhi) should be one cubit long, whether on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) or in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa);
they know its thickness to be equal to that of the middle ring (mekhalā), measured by the thumb.
One should cause the enclosures for the gods to be made in all four directions,
especially in the Viṣṇu sacrifice and in the fire-rituals of the twice-born.

O Sage, in the sacrifice of Viṣṇu, the ritual up to the end of the oblation (homa) is performed in the three [fires] starting from the west; however, for both [the sacrificer and the priest], darbha grass is used for Mahendra and the others in all directions.
O best of sages, for the protection of the night-stalkers and of Mahendra and the others who seize the sacrificial materials, there is this special rite.
Having understood this, O best of sages, the knower of mantras should perform the fire sacrifice with fuel and other materials;
having offered the sacrificial wood into the Karālī fire, he should do so with the root mantra.
The preceptor should offer oblations of clarified butter with the first mantra of the Vedas into Manojava;
likewise, he should offer oblations of food with the Mūrti-mantras into Lohitā.
Likewise, having prepared parched grains (lāja) over the Sudhūmrā fire with the second mantra,
one should likewise offer sesame seeds over the Sphuliṅginī fire with the third mantra.

On each successive day, one should perform the *viśvarūpī* rite with the fourth [finger]; the ring finger together with the middle finger, joined with the downward-pointing thumb, [is used for] that respective substance. *Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa* 15.105.
One should take [the vessel] up to the middle joint and perform the ritual action with that very [vessel];
one should perform the oblation with the substance for oblation, and the offering of clarified butter with the *śuktikā* ladle.
Then, one should again offer the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścittāhuti*), the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and likewise the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and so forth;
furthermore, everything whose location was not previously specified should be offered into the *Kālī* fire.

One should perform one hundred and eight oblations of the substances beginning with fuel-sticks and ending with sesame seeds as an expiatory rite, using the root mantra and the vidyā for each single offering.

Then, having offered the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the sacrificial ladle (*sruc*) by means of the root mantra known as the twelve-syllable mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, the practitioner [should proceed].
One should likewise offer all the peripheral oblations (paridhi) and so forth, ending with *vauṣaṭ*;
one should fill [the vessel] with a handful of clarified butter using the root mantra ending in *svāhā*. 15.110.
The best of practitioners should offer oblations according to the scriptures;
at the conclusion of the final oblation, he should recite the root mantra one hundred and eight times.
O Sage, at the conclusion of a festival, one should burn the enclosing sticks during the festival;
likewise, in the perpetual fire, one may perform all occasional rites according to one's desire.
Whether during a festival or when there is no festival, the wise man should perform the occasional rite (naimittika) in the fire;
thereafter, he should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the teachers according to his desire.
If this [rite] is devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is indeed entirely fruitless;
therefore, for the sake of satisfying the preceptor and for the prosperity of the king and his kingdom, [the fee must be given].
The teacher should honor the disciple even with ornaments and garments;
being honored by the patron with grains and wealth as well.
The patron should give a sacrificial fee to the preceptor according to his ability;
if this is not done, the entire kingdom will perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform what is prescribed by the rules;
one should worship the deity residing in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) diligently with ritual offerings.
Immediately thereafter, having entered and formed the gesture of the *añjali* mudrā,
the one who knows the ritual procedure should then transfer [the deity] from the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) into the primary image (*mūlabera*).
During festivals such as the plowing ceremony, at the time of the regular festival rites, and in other such occasions,
the wise practitioner should perform the fire offering (homa) according to the manner described above.
One should cause all people, who are exceedingly dear to Hari, to undergo transformation;
however, during the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma), one should not burn the enclosing sticks (paridhi) nor the sacrificial grass (barhis).
O Sage, this secret concerning the sequence of the fire-offering ritual has been told;
whoever performs it, or even causes it to be performed, acts in a manner exceedingly dear to Hari.
Through devotion to the guru, everything shall be attained; he is Hari—of this there is no doubt.
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for *Jhṛhom*," in the *Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā* of the glorious *Pāñcarātra*.
Chapter Sixteen.
Viṣvaksena said: Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme characteristics of consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
Endowed with all the [auspicious] marks, having a small body, and possessing four arms.
One should have it made beautiful according to each respective form;
listen briefly, O observer of noble vows, to both the first and the second.

And for the benefit of practitioners, having properly performed the rite of offering the ritual sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) seven or five days prior to this, one should perform the sequence of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 16.3.
Having performed the ritual immersion in water as prescribed therein,
one should construct an altar according to the rules in the center of the previously mentioned pavilion.
One should have all the rites performed with a concentrated mind according to the vision of the scriptures;
O best of sages, hear now the characteristics of the pavilion in case those [scriptures] are unavailable.
It should be either one hundred and five cubits or twelve cubits in size,
provided with four gates and adorned with four archways.
Covered with a canopy and adorned with ornaments,
one should wrap the pillars all around with new cotton cloths.
One should also have archways and water-pots constructed, and in the center, one should cause an altar to be made;
it should be ten spans in width and one cubit in height.
O Nārada, one should cause fire-pits (agnikuṇḍas) to be constructed according to the rules in the four directions all around the altar (vedikā), starting with the square shape.
Or, in the absence of a sacrificial mound, one should perform it in a small temple;
having raised Hari from his preliminary immersion in water, one should bring him into the pavilion.
There, one should perform the opening of the eyes with a golden needle;
reciting "taccakṣur" for the left eye and "citraṃ deva" for the right.
Having shown two cows, one should then perform the ritual bathing;
the bathing, whether inferior or superior, follows the sequence of eighty-one [verses].
One should perform [the rite] with twenty-five jars, or seventeen,
or twelve, or nine, according to what is available.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then prepare the bed;
there, one should scatter rice measuring five *bhāras*.
One should place half that amount of rice upon the śāli grain;
above that, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
In its center, the knower of the tantra should cover [the area] with a woolen blanket;
the bed is said to be of three kinds: made of linen or cotton.
And all that [should be] made of wool, with an upper covering of tiger skin;
or else three garments of variegated cloth, or indeed three garments of new cloth.
According to one's means,
one should construct it by a single path,
provided with a head-cushion and equipped with foot-basins.
Having thus prepared a bed with the two beautiful cheeks as its left and right sides, and having honored it with perfumes and flowers; Vis_16.19.
Having adorned Janārdana with garments, ornaments, and garlands,
the preceptor, together with the guardians of the images, should perform the rite accompanied by words of auspiciousness.
One should place [the image] upon a bed provided with a parasol and fly-whisks;
using the twelve-syllable mantra, one should lay it down with its head toward the south.
O Sage, the one who assumes the form [of the deity] should first perform the Vaiṣṇavīkaraṇa;
thereafter, the practitioner should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) using the Mūrti-mantra.
Accompanied by dance and song and joined with the study of the Vedas,
one should face either the east or the north while standing upon the southern part of the altar.

Having performed the breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) in sequence, the preceptor should perform the placement of creation (sṛṣṭinyāsa), the placement of maintenance (sthitinyāsa), and the placement of withdrawal (saṃhṛtinyāsa) by means of the syllable Om alone.
O tiger among sages, one should place those [elements] upon that image exactly as they truly are;
thereafter, one should place the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) upon the statue.
Having performed the placement [of mantras] with the five Upaniṣads together with the Praṇavas, the knower of mantras [should proceed];
or else, listen to the sequential placement of mantras for the God of gods.
The teacher, reciting the Nārāyaṇa hymn consisting of twenty-four verses in sequence, should touch the feet of the deity.
At its conclusion, O Brahmin, one should recite the Puruṣa-sūkta consisting of sixteen verses;
thereafter, from the Atharvaveda, that which sets forth the origin of creation and so forth.
One should recite the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad three times and touch the words;
one should mutter eight hundred times the mantra beginning with "ātman" and ending with "namaḥ."
During the worship, the consecration, and the installation, the instructor should perform the placement of the six-syllable mantra upon the heart of that image.
Otherwise, everything is fruitless; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the recitation of the six-syllable mantra at intervals.
O best of sages, a wise person should perform each and every thing that has been prescribed.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in the proper sequence, one should wrap [the image] with nine new cloths.
Having paid homage with a handful of flowers, one should worship Puruṣottama;
one should worship him with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, and with dances and songs. Vis_16.33.
Then, the knower of mantras should invoke the deity upon his head with the root mantra—
[the deity] who holds the conch, discus, and mace in his hands and is adorned with yellow garments.
One should meditate upon the eternal God according to each respective form,
offering water for the feet, the respectful oblation, and water for sipping, followed by perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order.
Having offered to the God rice mixed with molasses, milk-rice, and mung-bean porridge, along with side dishes and soaked in ghee, one should then offer curd.
One should offer water for drinking, water for sipping, and mouth-perfume;
then, having paid homage, the preceptor should cause the deity to lie down. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 16.37)
Filled with fragrant water, well-wrapped with three threads,
provided with *aśvattha* sprouts, and filled to the brim with a *droṇa*.
