[He saw] clay jars shaped like ripe bimba fruits, endowed with auspicious marks,
filled with the five jewels, and provided with the five golden weapons.
One should also meditate upon the golden Śrīvatsa mark accompanied by a golden Garuḍa,
as well as the conch, the discus, and the tortoise, using the root mantra.
With its beard and its lid, and wrapped in a pair of cloths,
one should place it upon heaps of grain on the right side of the deity.
Taking the principal jar, facing either east or north,
one should meditate upon the fivefold form [of the deity], having invoked it into that jar, O Nārada.
One should worship that pitcher with perfumes and flowers using the Brahma-seed syllable.
Ritual worship, the festival, the ceremonial bath, and the offering—this is the fifth [chapter].
O best of sages, during the bathing, the consecration, and the preparatory rite (*adhivāsa*), one should perform them at the same time, having united [the image] with the deity and the goddesses.
Then, one should place eight jars of knowledge in the eight directions—
auspicious jars filled with gold and jewels and wrapped in cloth.
One should install [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna and Vārāha and the others;
one should worship them by their own names and install auspicious objects such as the conch shell.
Having wrapped the perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata) in a cloth,
and having performed it according to this rite, one should carry out the image-oblation (mūrtihoma).
O twice-born one, it was accompanied by the Rigveda and other Vedas in the directions beginning with the east,
joined with the sounding of conchs and other instruments, and endowed with dance and song.
One should perform the fire-offering rite accompanied by lute and flute;
having taken up the Vaiṣṇava fire, one should cause it to be placed within the sacrificial pits.
One hundred and eight fuel-sticks of *pālāśa*, *khadira*, *bilva*, and likewise *audumbara* wood are prescribed; one should arrange them separately, starting from the east.
In the absence of palāśa or khadira wood, one should indeed use bilva;
O best of sages, in the absence of bilva, one should then use udumbara.
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) for the fire-pits starting from the east is thus proclaimed;
the clarified butter (ājya) is prescribed as being like the sacrificial pap (caru), and their respective quantities are specified individually.
Likewise, one should meditate on a lotus with filaments and petals in the center of the fire;
having visualized the deity residing there, the wise practitioner should perform the fire offering (homa).
Facing the east, all of them, wearing upper garments and well-adorned, should perform the oblation;
at night, they should feed twelve devoted Brahmins rice-milk porridge.
In this case, one should cause the study of the Vedas to be performed in the four directions, as well as the four kinds of food: milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, sweetmeats, and turmeric rice.
One should arrange them starting from the east and ending in the north according to their respective order;
then, having performed the propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma), one should proceed at the conclusion of the homa in due sequence.
One should offer sixteen oblations for each verse with honey, milk, curd, and ghee, using the *Puruṣasūkta*. (Or: one should also offer [them]... Vis_16.57.
Having offered oblations repeatedly into the sacrificial pit in due order, starting from the east and ending at the north, they should touch the image with the root mantra.
Having offered honey, one should touch the feet; having offered milk, one should touch the belly;
having offered curd, one should touch the mouth; and having offered clarified butter, one should touch the head. (Viṣṇu 16.59)
One who assumes that form should sprinkle [the deity] in the east with a branch of the *palāśa* tree;
then, one should sprinkle in the south with a branch of the *khadira* tree.
The bearer of that form should sprinkle [the deity] with a bilva branch toward the west,
and the bearer of that form should sprinkle with an udumbara branch toward the north.
The preceptor, having offered a handful of flowers and paid homage with the root mantra, should sprinkle water with a branch of cane at the corner of the site. (Viṣṇu-purāṇa 16.62)
The preceptor should offer the "three sweets" into the northern fire;
the three sweets are said to be sugar, clarified butter, and honey mixed together.
One should offer eight oblations for each [deity] in sequence with the root mantra,
accompanied by dance, song, instrumental music, and the recitation of the Vedas and sacred discourses.
One should complete the remainder of the night with lamps that do not go out;
then, when the night has turned to dawn, the diligent preceptor, having bathed, [should proceed].
On the right side of the door, upon a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice, offering fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru).
For the sake of pacifying yakṣas, rākṣasas, and piśācas, one should offer oblations separately with fuel-sticks of apāmārga, śamī, and khadira.
The best of those who know mantras should offer oblations with his own mantras beginning with the *praṇava*,
and he should perform directional fire-offerings all around the temple.

In this very same manner, one should offer oblations into the fires upon the sacrificial altars, meditating again and again on the lords of the directions with their respective mantras, offering fuel sticks and other materials in due order.
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, plakṣa, nyagrodha, bilva, udumbara, and kāśmarya— these are proclaimed as the eight kinds of sacrificial fuel (samidh).

Having thus duly completed the Vāstu-homa and other rites in their proper sequence, from Indra in the east to Īśāna in the northeast, one should also offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (caru).
O bull among sages, having caused [the rites] to be performed, the preceptor should subsequently offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the western fire with the mantra ending in "vauṣaṭ."
One should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the twelve-syllable mantra using the sacrificial ladle (sruva),
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, accompanied by the sound of the bell.
Having performed the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) in due order while recollecting the mantra three times,
one should smear the area around the child’s place all over with cow dung.
Or else, at that primary location, the knower of mantras should diligently cause banners to be erected in the eight directions according to rule, using the root mantra.
One should set up archways prescribed by the scriptures in the four directions,
adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and the like, and decorated with strings of pearls.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with flower garlands, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day and worship those worthy of worship. Vis_16.77.
One should properly cause garments and ornaments to be given to the preceptor;
the satisfaction of the preceptor’s mind brings about the attainment of supreme success.
A golden sacred thread, a golden ear-ornament,
as well as a ring for the finger and a bracelet for the forearm.
Having thus adorned the teacher, one should cause him to receive a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
twenty-five niṣkas of gold is the highest sacrificial fee.
Half of that is the middle [gift], and half of that again shall be the lowest;
in this very manner, the sequence of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) should be performed during a festival.
O best of sages, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) has been declared according to the sequence beginning with the highest; or rather, O sage, one should give the fee in accordance with one's own wealth.
Whatever substance has been used here, except for the ornaments of the deity, such as clothing, grain, and so forth, should be given to the preceptor. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 16.83)
The fee for the Sthāpaka (the installer) is equal to half the fee of the Ācārya;
that of the Mūrtipas (the image-protectors) is half of that, as is the fee for the one who performs the Vāstu-śānti rite.
The southern half [of the site] should belong to the officiating priests (hotṛs), while the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) belongs to those who have studied [the texts].
Furthermore, a pair of new and auspicious garments should be given to all of them.
Afterwards, one should honor the astrologer, for he provides the auspicious moment;
then one should indeed honor those who perform song and dance, as well as the Vaiṣṇavas.
When an auspicious moment arrived, with the permission of the brahmins,
he beheld the Lord, the Master Nārāyaṇa, situated in the center of the solar disc.
Having invoked [the deity] into the water-pot and the five-pronged [liṅga] with the syllable Om,
and having worshipped him with the offering of water for the feet and other honors, one should contemplate him as the single embodiment.
O best of sages, having himself performed the worship while free from desire,
he should then worship Śrī and Puṣṭi within the middle of the pitcher.

The practitioner, the best among those who know mantras, should place the deity residing within that jar, preceded by the syllable *praṇava* and his own name; he is the most excellent of practitioners. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 16.90)
O Lord of Sages, either the installer or the preceptor should lift up the pitcher;
having raised it, one should extract the supreme pitcher together with the uṣṇīṣa.
In that very same manner, O best of sages, having adorned it, the preceptor, joined by the image-makers, should gradually raise up the statue.
And those performing the fire-offerings for the quarters should likewise raise auspicious sounds,
accompanied by the resonance of conchs and drums and the recitation of benedictions.
It was accompanied by dance and song, provided with incense and lamps,
endowed with showers of flowers, and furnished with canopies and banners.
Then, having beautifully adorned auspicious Vaiṣṇava vessels before the deity,
they should be filled with scented water and well-wrapped with three threads.
Taking a *vardhanī* vessel filled with a *droṇa* measure of water mixed with *aśvattha* shoots,
the knower of the tantra [should perform the rite] before the deity with an unbroken stream.
Having circumambulated the house clockwise, the best of mantra-knowers should cause the child to enter its place; he should then install the image with the mūrti-mantra.
Then, having established the five mantras according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor, most skilled in the tantras, should place a water-pot before them.
Then one should sprinkle water upon the head of the image with the root mantra;
for Śrī and the others,
one should sprinkle it in sequence according to their respective mantras, as one would for a deity.

One should perform the ritual worship of the images as with the primary image (mūlabera). Having taken the remaining water from the pitcher and poured it into a shallow bowl (śarāva), [one should proceed]. Vis 16.100.

Furthermore, the knower of mantras should perform a circumambulatory sprinkling all around with an unbroken stream [of water] no thicker than a blade of grass, using the root mantra. (Viṣṇudharmottara 16.101)
Having displayed the añjali gesture, one should recollect all the mantras;
then, on the northern side of the door, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) and the fire offering (homa) with one's own mantra.
O tiger among sages, on the sacrificial ground, those learned in the Pañcarātra should perform oblations of fuel-sticks and other materials, one by one in sequence.
Then the best of practitioners should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) as before;
likewise, the officiant should cause that supreme placement to be performed upon it.
Thereafter, the supreme practitioner, having taken refuge in the Lord, should worship Janārdana with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and bow down to him. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 16.105)
Saying, "Please remain present," he should prostrate himself on the ground like a staff;
at that time, the one of great wisdom should perform the study of the Vedas. (Viṣṇu 16.106)
Having paid homage with a handful of flowers, the preceptor should recite the mantra:
"Whatever was previously performed by me that was deficient or excessive."
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master, you should forgive all of that for me.
Then, O tiger among sages, the wise one should sprinkle the temple with water.
But when the water in the jar has been entirely exhausted, both outside and inside in every respect,
it becomes pure simply by sprinkling with the *puruṣasūkta*.
One should offer milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, jaggery-based sweets, and mung-bean porridge;
one should also provide betel-leaf for refreshing the mouth and arrange for the retinue.
O best of sages, the knower of mantras should indeed arrange the world-protectors in their proper sequence, both internally and externally, preceded by the fire-oblation (homa). Vis 16.111.
One should not imagine other obstructing deities in the house of a child;
rather, the sequence of fire offerings (homa), festivals, and ritual oblations (bali) must be performed day by day.
One should offer the bali separately to each [deity] beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Īśa;
its measurement should be half that of the great *pīṭha*, and its width and length should be the same.
To the east of the child’s house, O Sage, one should prepare an excellent pedestal;
upon the pedestal, a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
As before, the wise one should place the remnants of the offering upon the two offering-stands where all the attendants stand, joined with the mantras as previously described.
O Lord of Sages, one should perform the festive ablutions and other rites as prescribed by the scriptures; the remaining [rites] should be performed in the common manner at the place of the Child.
One should not construct the primary foundation before the preliminary foundation;
if one should do so, there will be a great fault that destroys both the builder and the country.
One should not worship an image consecrated in the house of a child within the primary temple;
if one were to worship that image, both the maker and the kingdom would perish.
Therefore, O best of sages, one should not perform worship in the root temple with all effort; rather, at the conclusion of the consecration, one should hold a festival in due order.
On the day the festival begins, one should immediately prepare a banner— measuring five, seven, or nine cubits, according to one's means— on that very day.
At the edge of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), one should perform the ritual ablution according to the previously mentioned procedure;
however, O Great Sage, the ritual of offering flowers is not prescribed in this case.
Thus, O Sage, the rite for the station of the Child has been briefly explained;
in this very same way, the supreme characteristic of the installation of the second [station] is established.
And here, O great sage, I shall state the specific distinction regarding the second [type of] nakṣatra-consecration:
on the eve of the rite, at midnight, in a small house.
O best of sages, having caused a square sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) one cubit on all sides to be prepared, the wise practitioner should thereafter lead the deity there.
Recalling the root mantra, one should place the water-pot according to the ritual rules upon a sacrificial mound in the center before the image, and within that pot, one should meditate upon Hari.
One should bring [the deity] with the mūrti-mantra and worship him with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
one should lead the deity residing within the pitcher into the center of the sun in an instant.
O great sage, having subsequently invoked the deity into the great pitcher,
the wise one should then place the deity residing within that pitcher into the primary image (mūlabera).
As before, the one skilled in tantra should sprinkle the root site;
then he should arrange all the attendants as prescribed by the scripture.
Having installed the deities of the directions according to the rules, one should worship them day after day;
the specific procedure for this has been fully explained, while the remainder shall be as in the general ritual.
O Nārada, best of sages, one should perform these actions here with logic and specific reasoning during both the first and second stages of the rites.
When this has been performed according to the rules for the king, the inhabitants of his realm,
the performer, and the one who causes it to be performed, their lifespan and prosperity will increase.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Installation," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Seventeenth Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the mobile [deity].
Furthermore, a stationary image is secondary, whereas a mobile image is supreme.
O tiger among sages, if all ritual actions are distinct, one should perform the rites for the image, such as its bathing and so forth, solely for the sake of purifying the image.
While this time is occurring for the purpose of performing rites such as the bathing festival,
one should perform the ritual water-dwelling in due order and the preparatory consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the pavilion.

O twice-born one, having performed the fire-oblation as before—excluding the sesame oblation—and having performed the ritual bathing according to the rules, O sage, excluding the placement of jewels; Viṣṇu Purāṇa 17.4.
In that [temple], one should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) without the deposition of mantras (mantranyāsa),
having omitted the central thread in the temple by means of the Supreme Lord (parameṣṭhin).
Having recited the *Pauruṣa-sūkta*, the wise one should install [the images] separately;
the specific locations for the forms have been demonstrated in the chapter on the *bimba*.
O Nārada, having installed each [image] in its respective place with its own mantra, one should perform worship and other rites;
whatever was the form of the primary image (mūlabera) and whatever marks it had previously been characterized by—[those should be reflected].
The form which was previously established as the primary image (mūlārcā) by the great-souled ones—
how and by what arrangement of weapons was it fashioned by those best among the wise?
One should likewise cause all that to be performed upon the images [made of] clay, metal, and so forth;
this procedure for one who has fallen asleep is proclaimed as the ritual for installation and the like.
For one who is lying down, however, the ritual worship may be performed while standing or seated;
having installed the deity known as Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa is not required.
Likewise, having installed Saṃkarṣaṇa, a wise person should not worship Pradyumna;
for in the installation and worship of Pradyumna, there is no ritual worship without Aniruddha.
The ritual image should be fashioned in every respect according to the primary icon;
the specific details here have been fully explained, while the remainder should be performed as previously described.
Thus, O Sage, the installation of mobile images has been briefly described;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and bestows the fruit of all desires. (Vis 17.13)

I shall now fully explain the installation [of the image] upon a multicolored painting, a half-painting, a wall, a wooden board, or a cloth; for it is said that the manifestation [of the deity] is threefold. 17.14.
Likewise, if there exists a half-painted image on a wall, on stone, or even on wood, or if there is an image made of metal for these [deities], [one may perform the rite]. // Vis_17.15 //
O best of the twice-born, having performed the entire ritual in the case of the action-image as before, the placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) must then be performed upon the primary image.
The wise one should sprinkle [the image] with water from the consecration jar,
and then with the Puruṣasūkta and also with the five Upaniṣads.
In this very context, those who have mastered the tantras do not desire the sixteenfold placement on either a wooden board or a cloth; I shall now explain the specific distinction regarding these.
Having constructed a pavilion as before and having prepared an altar as before, O Sulocanā, one should place [the image] upon a divine couch.
The wise do not accept the preliminary immersion in water nor the ceremonial bathing;
rather, having performed the fire-offering for the image, one should omit the fire-offering for the directions.
Then, having worshipped the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) in the pitchers upon the altar,
the preceptor should perform the rites of dissolution and emanation in due order.

One should sprinkle [the site] with water from the Brahma-vessel using its own mantra; employing skillful means and specific techniques, one should perform the remainder of the rite as previously described.
Now I shall describe the proper location for an image placed upon a wall, as well as for one on a wall, a cloth, or a painting, which is adorned with colors and ornaments. Vis 17.23.
Having prepared a pavilion with its full furnishings before the deity on a cloth [painting] that is either radiant or half-finished, O fair-eyed one, || 17.24 ||
There, one should have a railing constructed by a skilled artisan according to the previously mentioned procedure, measuring either two or three cubits.
Then, one should place a heap of śāli rice in the middle of the altar;
in the center of the śāli rice, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp.
Then [he brought] a radiant Brahma-vessel filled to the brim with Droṇa-measures of water, purified by cloth, complete with a tuft of grass and a lid.
Wrapped in a pair of garments along with its thread, joined with jewels, endowed with eight powers, and equipped with five golden weapons; Vis_17.28.
One should place that pitcher, filled with *aśvattha* sprouts and honored with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains,
in the center of the lotus using the *praṇava* alone.
Then, one should place eight jars around the lotus petals,
filled with water as before, containing gold and wrapped in cloth.
One should worship them with their lids and strainers, and with *aśvattha* sprouts placed at the openings,
using perfumes, flowers, lamps, and various other offerings.
One should worship the flawless Nārāyaṇa, Viṣṇu of unblemished deeds, the Supreme, with the root mantra in the central jar.
One should place Vāsudeva in the east, Saṃkarṣaṇa in the south,
Pradyumna in the west, and Aniruddha in the north.
One should place Lakṣmī in the southeast, Sarasvatī in the southwest,
Rati in the northwest, and Śānti in the domain of the northeast.
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rule, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
or else, O best of sages, one should place water-pots all around here.
In the midst of that, the best of practitioners should bring forth the eight Lords of Knowledge:
Vārāha in the eastern quarter and Nārasiṃha in the south.
Śrīdhara is in the western region; Hayaśīrṣaka is in the north;
Bhārgava Rāma is in the southeast; and Rāma himself is in the southwest.
Having worshipped Vāmana in the northwest and likewise Vāsudeva in the northeast—
each of these individually in their respective jars— one should worship them by their own names.
Having thus performed the worship, one should carry out the rite of fire-oblation (homa);
one should arrange the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) starting from the east and ending in the north.
One should first worship Vāsudeva in a square sacrificial pit;
one should worship Saṃkarṣaṇa in the southern [pit], which is shaped like a half-moon or a flame.
In the western circular pit, the wise one should worship Pradyumna;
and in the northern lotus-shaped pit, he should then worship Aniruddha.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations each, made of palāśa, khadira, bilva, and udumbara wood, starting from the east and proceeding separately in order; Vis_17.42.
The guardians of the forms (mūrtipās) should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain into the fires in sequence;
or else, O best of sages, the most excellent practitioner should do so here in the eastern fire.
The wise preceptor should perform the oblation with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge—either in a fire-pit or upon a sacrificial mound. Vis 17.44.
The fire oblation (homa) should be performed at night, and the sprinkling with water during the day.
One should not perform the sprinkling at night, nor should one perform the oblation during the day.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the fire-oblation at night when the auspicious moment has arrived, with the permission of the Brahmins.
One should sprinkle with water contained in the *kumbha* vessel while reciting the *parameṣṭhi* mantra;
then one should invoke the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment.
One should meditate upon the Teacher of the World, Hari, who holds the conch and the discus, who wears yellow garments,
and whose form has been visualized upon the wall.
Having done this, one should sprinkle Mahāviṣṇu with scented water;
then, one should sprinkle the image again with the Puruṣasūkta.
One should worship with water for the guest-offering (*arghya*) and water for the feet (*pādya*), as well as with various kinds of sacrificial porridge (*caru*);
and according to one's means, one should give a teacher’s fee (*ācāryadakṣiṇā*).
Thus, the installation supported by a wall has been briefly described.
Then, having constructed a fine pedestal, one should proceed in due order around the base of the pedestal.
Having formed the mental resolve and having invoked the retinue there, one should worship them day by day, O best of sages, at the three junctions of the day or even once.
Thus, the arrangement of the wall-image has been briefly explained.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Mobile Image and Other Icons," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The Eighteenth Chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the supreme installation of the goddesses.
Listen now to their marriage and the fire-oblation, a secret [teaching], in due order.
O Sage, having first installed the deity, one should at that time sprinkle [it] with water from the great jar using the respective mantra of Śrī and the others. (Vis 18.2)
O tiger among sages, if one should perform the installation of the Goddess separately,
one should construct a pavilion measuring ten cubits, as described previously.
Having constructed the altar as before, in accordance with the dimensions of the pavilion,
one should arrange sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around it in sequence, measuring either one cubit or half a cubit.
The practitioner should have them constructed by artisans according to that procedure;
all [the mandalas] are proclaimed to be square, following the sequence of Śrī.
The sacrificial pits for the Earth and likewise for her limbs are situated in the fires starting from the east— namely Śānti, Lakṣmī, Vāgdevī, and Rati.
Having meditated upon Śvetā, who is dark like a white lotus and a blue lotus, one should perform oblations in sequence for Lakṣmī,
Sarasvatī, Rati, and likewise Prīti.
Kīrti, Śānti, Tuṣṭi, and Puṣṭi likewise—
these are the deities of the pitchers located in the east and other directions upon the altar.
Having established the Great Vessel (Mahāmudrā), one should lead its power into the center—
that which is endowed with all powers, possessing all limbs, and performing all actions.
One should worship the deities of the banners, the archways, and the water-pots with their own respective mantras, using fragrant and most delightful perfumes and other offerings. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.10)
Indeed, those previously mentioned should be worshipped here in this very sequence:
the archways, the gate-pitchers, and also the altar-pitchers.
On the railing of the pedestal, likewise the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala),
one should cover them in sequence with cloths and worship them with perfumes and flowers.
One should place those respective forms within golden jars;
[these include] the bathing, the laying to rest, and the consecration.
Having invoked the Goddess with diligence, one should perform everything previously mentioned and conduct a grand worship when the auspicious time has arrived. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.14)
I shall here describe a special [instruction] that bestows auspiciousness upon all the world, generating devotion in everyone and increasing longevity, prosperity, and fame. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.15)
It generates nourishment for those who perform it, especially for the village;
it removes all suffering for men and bestows the fruit of all desires. (Vis 18.16)
One who has mastered the tantras should, in due order, perform the marriage fire-sacrifice;
for both the divine powers (śaktis) of Viṣṇu and those that are human have been declared [as such].
O great sage, where those powers [of Lakṣmī] have their former abode and supreme limit, there is the partial incarnation of the Earth known as Puṣṭi.
One should apply either the earth or nourishment to the left side when the marriage of the two goddesses occurs at the same time.
Having first caused the [shrines] of Lakṣmī and then of Bhūmi to be constructed, the wise man,
upon the passing of the auspicious moment (lagna), should perform the ritual water-offering according to the prescribed rule.
In that sequence, the practitioner should again accomplish the remainder;
furthermore, he should perform it by means of the sequential yoga upon a single sacrificial mound.
Having diligently adorned the Lord of Gods and the Goddess with a pair of garments and various ornaments in due order, [one should proceed].
Having led the Goddess to her divine throne, one should commence the rite of fire-offering (homa),
after having had the Brāhmaṇas perform the auspicious day ceremony accompanied by benedictions.
One should perform the offering of water accompanied by all ritual services;
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) and standing before the deity.
Having thus requested permission, the wise one, being granted leave, should perform the fire-oblation;
taking twenty-five fuel-sticks, they should be anointed with clarified butter.
One should cast [the oblation] once with the eight-syllable mantra ending in *svāhā*,
having offered a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the Gāyatrī mantra known as Viṣṇu.
The preceptor, having circumambulated the fire just as the domestic priest does for kings,
should offer three oblations of parched grain with the syllable Om.
Moving around the purifying fire of Hari from time to time,
one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) with clarified butter while reciting the syllable Om.
O best of sages, having performed sixteen excellent oblations for each individual according to the prescribed rite, one should cause dancing, singing, and other such performances to take place.
Having thus performed the marriage ceremony, one should worship Puruṣottama according to this very procedure, or even by means of a mere consecration.
O best of sages, the knower of the tantras should join [the image] with the deity and perform worship; this is declared for the metal images of the goddesses. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.31)
One should worship [the deities] day after day according to the sequence beginning with Lakṣmī;
this very procedure shall apply to all the goddesses.

O best of sages, for the installation of the principal image and the goddesses, even the mere rite of consecration is sufficient; the sequence beginning with marriage and so forth is not required there.
O best of sages, the installation of forms such as Medhā, Sarasvatī, Durgā, and others should be performed using their own respective seed-syllables.
O Sage, this sequence beginning with the installation (pratiṣṭhā) should be performed for those who speak thus;
one should sprinkle [them] with water from the Brahma-vessel using their respective mantras. Vis 18.35.
Having established them with their respective mantras, one should worship them according to the prescribed rule.
Thus has the procedure for the installation of the goddesses been briefly described.

Thus, whoever should cause the supreme installation of the Śaktis to be performed with devotion shall obtain all desires, including long life, sovereignty, sons, and so forth. (Viṣṇudharmottara 18.37)
Having obtained happiness in this world and likewise in the next world,
and having attained supreme royal splendor, he will once again become wise.
In this regard, there is a certain distinction concerning the Śrīvatsa, which is dear to Hari:
its defining characteristic, its specific location, as well as its mantra and its mode of worship.
And other such distinctions, O Great Sage, I shall briefly proclaim; listen to this unsurpassed secret. (Viṣ 18.40)
For the sake of the complete fulfillment of all prosperity, and for the bestowal of all auspicious desires,
[it may be made] with gold, silver, or likewise with copper.
One should have the seat made according to the supreme sequence;
its length as well as its width should be six finger-breadths.
It may also be five finger-breadths long, and its middle part should be equal to that;
its width should be two finger-breadths, or perhaps one finger-breadth for the crown.
Knowing this, O best of sages, one should construct an excellent receptacle;
for such is declared to be the characteristic of the highest form of the fruit.
That which is reduced by one finger-breadth is taught as the medium size;
that which is reduced by two finger-breadths is declared to be the smallest.
One should make that [measure] three finger-breadths less; that is the lowest of the low.
In this task of the middling-low, one should indeed employ the lowest of the low.
O best of sages, the practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should fashion its width in proportion to that [mandala], having first meditated upon it in the center. Vis_18.47.
One should accomplish the goddess Kamalā, who resembles molten gold,
endowed with all the auspicious marks, and seated upon a lotus throne.
The auspicious goddess Śrī, lotus-handed, beloved of Padmanābha,
adorned with jewels and pearls, and decorated with all ornaments.
Having thus reflected upon that goddess Śrī, the leader of the three worlds,
O best of sages, he placed her at the side of Hari’s chest on the right.
One should establish that goddess Śrī for the purpose of protecting the world and for the sake of the increase of all prosperity; such is the certainty of the scripture. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.51)
And regarding this preliminary consecration of the water, I shall tell you a special detail:
an excellent water vessel filled with two bhāras.

Having collected [the materials], O tiger among sages, one should let them soak in that vessel; having brought the previously mentioned water and filled the container, [one should proceed]. Vis_18.53.
Having worshipped with fragrant flowers, one should meditate upon the ocean of nectar;
in its midst, as before, one should perform the ritual of dwelling in the water according to the rules.
O great sage, one should perform this either in sequence or before the image of Acyuta,
especially when it is present in a mirror, a statue, a painting, or similar representations.
O Sage, one should have a smaller water-vessel made from a bronze mold for the sake of one's own welfare and the welfare of others; that is declared to be the "lesser" [vessel].
O best of sages, the specific procedure for the consecration of the water has been declared;
it has been taught by me in two ways, which one should perform according to what is appropriate.
Having invoked that goddess from the root image, the wise practitioner should join her right here with the root mantra, using water from the ritual jar upon his two hands.
O best of sages, the practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should join [the syllables] right here with the mantra;
this has been declared by me in this tantra as a treasury of mantras.
Having recited this supreme mantra, which is more secret than the secret and bestows boons,
one should sprinkle the Goddess with the water contained in the great jar.
The best of those who know the Tantra should place the twenty-five principles and that very five-syllabled mantra upon his body by means of the ritual of placement (nyāsa).
The one most skilled in the tantras should display the mudrās of the conch, the discus, and the lotus;
thereafter, he should worship the Goddess with the eight services beginning with the water offering (arghya).
He should offer water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), as well as water for sipping (ācamana), and likewise perfume and flowers;
and incense, a lamp, and an oblation consisting of milk-rice mixed with jaggery.
In the manner thus described, one should cause the offering of the bali to be performed, accompanied by bells and drums; it is auspicious and bestows all desires.

One should worship her whose abode is the lotus with a lotus flower combined with bilva leaves and unbroken grains (akṣata), or with a palāśa leaf or an utpala, or joined with karavīra and other such flowers. (Viṣṇu 18.65)
O best of sages, one should worship in this very manner day after day,
offering milk-rice mixed with jaggery and accompanied by sprouts of bilva leaves.
The offering substance for the bali here is said to be mixed with sandalwood water;
it should be accompanied by bells and dundubhi drums in the manner thus described.
O Sage, one should cause the offering of bali to be performed at the root of a bilva tree, a palāśa tree, or an aśvattha tree; it bestows all desired results and is auspicious. Viṣṇu 18.68.
Having fashioned a square or circular pedestal, the knower of mantras should worship Lakṣmī in its center, saying, "Salutation to Lakṣmī. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.69)
The five-syllable mantra is traditionally taught as being joined with the Praṇava at its beginning;
one should offer a bali-oblation before it according to the previously mentioned procedure.
Having thus performed worship provided with perfumes and flowers, along with incense and lamps, one should then offer mouth-freshener.
O best of sages, at the conclusion of the offering, one who is skilled in the tantras should recite the Śrīsūkta three times,
or otherwise recite the Śrī-mantra or its hymn of praise.
Then, O best of sages, one should cause the five great sounds to be proclaimed again and again; and in the evening, one should worship the Goddess as before.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice (caru),
using any one of the [fruits] such as bilva, in a lotus-shaped hearth according to one's desire.
Having formed a single resolve, O best of sages, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in their midst,
offering sixteen oblations each of *bilva* and *pālāśa* fuel-sticks.
One should perform the oblation with the root mantra; one should offer it with the ghee of a tawny cow.
Likewise, O Brahmin, one should offer sixteen oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa).
In the same manner, one should offer oblations again and again with bilva leaves, with single-petaled lotuses, and with karavīra flowers accompanied by unbroken grains of rice.
Having performed the fire sacrifice according to the rules, one should summon the Goddess from the sacrificial pit;
that sacrifice is supremely secret and brings about the prosperity of both the village and the king.
The auspicious one who liberates from all diseases and grants all desires—
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the fire-oblation at night. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 18.79)
At the conclusion of the fire offering, one should give a sacrificial fee according to the extent of one's wealth;
thereafter, one should honor the preceptor with gold, garments, and rings.
Thereafter, one should honor the Brahmins and subsequently honor the astrologer;
if, however, one should act out of negligence by employing someone who lacks the aforementioned characteristics, [the rite will fail].
In that case, there is the destruction of the village, the king, the kingdom, and the sacrificer;
actions bear no fruit there—of this there is no need for deliberation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause that which is enjoined by the ritual rules to be performed;
thus has it been briefly explained for one's own sake and for the sake of others. Vis 18.83.
The specific distinction here has been fully declared; the remainder should be performed as previously described.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Goddess," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Nineteen.
Viṣvaksena said: Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and other such rites.
Listen with a secret mind, indeed, for the benefit of practitioners.
The sequence for the placement of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), as well as the characteristics of the mudrās, and various fruits herein, which illuminate all vidyās. (Vis 19.2)
The teacher, having become purified, facing either eastward or northward,
should assume the lotus posture (paṅkaja), the sitting posture (āsana), or the svastika posture, as he desires.
At the commencement of the worship, having joined the palms in añjali and paid homage according to the rule,
one should place the right hand directly across the upturned palm of the left hand.
Having touched the circular shape with the left hand and the other [hand],
one should then form a fist with the left thumb pointing upward, O Sage.
Having formed a fist, he went to his abode, meditating on the mantra with a concentrated mind;
likewise, touching the heart of the deity with three measures, he did so for the head as well.
Having bowed down and again formed the mudrā by crossing the hands,
the knower of mantras, having entered with the añjali-mudrā, [should proceed] with the worship mantra.

Having meditated upon the mantra ending with *namaḥ* at the heart, on the head, at the crest-lock (*śikhā*), likewise at the armor (*kavaca*), and at the weapon (*astra*) and the eyes, the wise practitioner should then perform the placement (*nyāsa*) using those respective symbols.
Now hear also the characteristics and the etymological explanation of the *mudrā*,
by means of which, once obtained, the practitioner [overcomes] the enemies of the gods.
Because it causes joy to flow forth, it is called a *mudrā*; hear now its defining characteristic:
with the fist closed, the thumb is extended straight outward.
Having thus formed the middle fingers, one should touch the heart at its base;
then, having properly drawn back the index fingers and bound them with the thumbs to form fists.
Then, at the end of the thumb and the forehead, one should likewise place a large [finger] above the crest;
by means of the two broad tips alone, there is the binding of the small seal.
Having raised the two hands upward and formed the circle of the navel, one should mentally assign the seal of the armor (*kavaca-mudrā*) with the thought that it is the armor itself. Vis 19.13.

This is said to be the mudrā for the Aparāstra: having formed a fist with the tips of the fingers pointing toward the right, one should then touch the tip of the index finger to the line of the thumb.
Having touched [the heart], one should cast the *sphoṭa* gesture toward the ten directions, beginning with the east;
then, having joined the little fingers and ring fingers, they are struck together while resting in the middle of the palms.
The eye-mudrā is formed by the tips of the index and middle fingers at the eyes;
having raised the middle finger and carefully contracting the hand.
Having contracted the little finger, [one should place it] upon both of the remaining fingers;
then, with the left hand, one should hold the face with the remaining fingers.
Having touched the right [hand] with the left, one should rotate the lamp-seal;
then, properly forming the hollowed cupped hands (saṃpuṭa) in the shape of añjali, one should raise them toward the forehead or the heart.
This should be known by name as the *añjali-mudrā* for prostration;
it is prescribed here for those already mentioned, and with effort for others not yet mentioned.
If one is unable even to show [the previous gestures], one should instead display the añjali;
this mudrā called añjali is dear to all who consist of mudrās.
This is the mudrā of salutation to Viṣṇu; it bestows all desires.
O Sage, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on all limbs with these [mudrās], one should perform recitations, fire offerings, and other rites.
He who performs self-protection shall obtain long life, fame, happiness, sovereignty, strength, and supreme dignity. Vis 19.22.
For, O Sage, by even one of those various and excellent sciences that have been proclaimed, a king may attain both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 19.23 ||
By means of the method of the embodied mantra, the practitioner should worship once;
his every intention will surely be accomplished, there is no doubt.
There is no fear of drought, nor likewise fear of excessive rain; nor is there plague, famine, thieves, and the like, nor suffering, nor untimely death.
What is the use of much talk here? Whatever a person on earth desires for himself, he shall accomplish it all. (19.26)
One should properly offer each of those things to that very Hari;
or else, the practitioner, being restrained and full of devotion, should worship Him correctly. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 19.27)
In this way, O Sage, one shall obtain all of that—delicious food, or even kingship or the status of a king—through Vedic mantras; of this there is no doubt.

O best of sages, if one is unable [to perform them] with the mantras of the forms, one should have the worship and other rites performed with one's own materials by a practitioner according to the rules. Vis_19.29.
Having attained the fruit of his well-performed deeds, he reaches the state of having the same form as Viṣṇu.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Placement of Limbs (Aṅganyāsa) and Other Rites," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty.
Viṣvaksena said: Listen, O Nārada, in truth and for the benefit of practitioners indeed.
I shall now describe the various types of worship for the forms beginning with the Supreme Self (Paramātman).
In a pure and delightful place, or even in a most sacred forest, at a holy bathing site, or in an excellent field, or even in a village or a city; ||| Vis_20.2 ||
Whether in a hamlet, a small village, or a city, on a riverbank or by the shore—
especially in a great village, or even in one that is western or central.
One should properly have a temple built for the gentle Lord Viṣṇu, the master of the flowers; one should fashion it with many porticos according to the previously described method.
Regarding the characteristics previously mentioned, if there is only a single central image (*ekaberaka*) therein,
one should calculate [the proportions] for three Rāmas and so forth, even if there are many images (*bahuberaka*).
O Sage, is there any difference in the types of worship between one who acts for their own sake and one who is independent or dependent? To that it is replied: Vis_20.6.
In the *svatantra* [tantras], there is invocation (*āvāhana*) and dismissal (*visarga*) at the three junctions [of the day];
in the *paratantra* [tantras], there is the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and the offering (*bali*), but without those two.

Having diligently painted [the deity] upon a wooden board or a cloth for one's own sake—endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics—and having performed the consecration according to the prescribed sequence; ||| Vis_20.8 |||
Having sprinkled [the site] with water, one should invoke and worship the nine jewels upon an altar, an image, or a metal vessel, according to one's preference.
Sapphire, emerald, crystal, and diamond, as well as ruby,
coral, lapis lazuli, and pearl.
Regarding the nine gems known as *māṇikya*, I shall now describe their respective times for worship, namely at dawn and at midday. Vis 20.11.
The evening, the onset of night, midnight, and likewise dawn—this group of six is remembered as supreme for worship performed for the sake of others. Vis 20.12.
In the case of a middling [vessel], one should avoid the evening and the dawn;
for a low [vessel], one should avoid midnight and the late afternoon.
One should perform the circumambulation with offerings in the morning, at midday, and in the evening;
not at other times, even during the highest worship or the middling ritual.
Now listen to the different types of worship when the time for the *bali* offering has passed:
the invocation, the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācāma*), and the fragrant flowers.
Incense, lamps, offerings, mouth-fresheners, and dismissal—thus will the time for the channels (nāḍī) of the supreme rites and so forth be explained. Vis_20.16.
The first [period] shall be seven nāḍīs, the middle one five nāḍīs, and the shortest three nāḍīs; such is the certainty of the scripture. (Viś 20.17)
Before the rising of the sun, the teacher should perform his bath;
at sunrise, O best of sages, he should perform the rite of worship.
All ritual actions preceded by bathing are the causes for the successful attainment of results;
therefore,
I shall first explain them for the benefit of practitioners.
The practitioner should perform his bath in waters such as those of a river flowing to the ocean, in a lake, a stream, a pond, or even a spring. Vis 20.20.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and contemplating the goals of dharma and liberation,
the practitioner should proceed toward the northeast direction and perform his ritual bath.
The wise person should perform the bath in the north-eastern part of the body of water;
he should discharge [the water] in the north-west, the south-west, the south-east, and toward the west.
If one should perform a bath out of delusion in water that is devoid of living beings, that bath becomes fruitless; one should perform the bath again.
Having risen in the morning, the practitioner should perform his bath with the mantra for the worship of whichever specific form he himself worships among the various forms.

Having immersed oneself in the midst of the water with the Viṣṇu-mantra, or with its ancillaries, or else with the root-vidyā, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times while reciting the mantra.
Having discarded the wet garment, one should wrap [the image] with another pair of cloths;
then, with a *pavitra* in hand, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) while reciting the mantra.
One should wear a golden ring or the like on the right arm;
with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should sprinkle water over one's own head.
One should satisfy [the deities] with their respective mantras and perform the rite of bathing;
however, if one is unable, one should instead perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while recollecting the prescribed vidyā.
Having sprinkled himself and performed the rites of bathing, the wise one should enter the place of activity;
having entered and performed the necessary purification, the knower of mantras should proceed with the mantra for worship.
O Sage, having opened the door-panel with the first mantra,
or else with the wind-mantra, one should open the door-panel in due order.
Having divided that gateway into two parts, the practitioner, most skilled in mantras,
should place his right foot upon the northern side of the cord.
Having prostrated and recollecting the six-syllable mantra,
the practitioner who knows the mantras should then light the perpetual lamp with the Viṣṇu-mantra.
On the right side of the thread, facing north himself, on a level and pure spot, upon a spread of black antelope skin and *kuśa* grass, [he should sit]. (Viṣṇusmṛti 20.33)
Seated upon a plank or sitting comfortably with a pure internal mind, he should assume either the lotus posture or the swastika posture, according to his preference. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.34)
With that mantra, one should establish the binding of the directions in the eight quarters for the protection of the sacrificial site; so say those who perceive the meaning of reality.
Having thus performed the binding of the directions, one should then begin the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma),
reciting the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras.

Having restrained the breaths three times, one is considered to have performed the highest form of breath control; having restrained the breaths twenty-five times within, it is called mental breath control.
The repeated recitation of the eight-syllable mantra once constitutes a middling breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
*Prāṇa* is the wind residing within the body; its *āyāma* is that which restrains it. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.38)
Inhalation, retention, and exhalation are known as the threefold [breath control];
having circumambulated the knee, neither too quickly nor too slowly.
The snapping of the fingers is proclaimed to be one *mātrā*;
likewise, inhalation (*pūraka*) is performed gradually through twelve *mātrās*.
Therefore, the wise perform *kumbhaka* with breath-holds of double that duration;
likewise, having performed *recaka*, the wise who perceive the meaning of reality [perform it] in the same manner.
O best of those seeking liberation, this is declared to be the inferior *prāṇāyāma*;
one should perform it here according to its possibility within this threefold regulation.
Having performed three, five, or seven breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), one should practice breath-restraint, O best among those who know breath-restraint. (Viṣṇu 20.43)
Then, for the sake of purifying the body, one should assign the qualities beginning with smoke-colored [smoke, white, red, yellow, and black];
these are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth.
One should lead the self, joined with the ego, mind, and intellect, ever into Viṣṇu; having thus united it, one should thoroughly purify the body of the elements.
One should meditate on the seed-syllable situated in the center of the navel, smoky-grey in color and consisting of fierce wind,
which completely dries up all the impurities residing within the body.
One should meditate on the seed-syllable, full of light, situated within the center of the heart-lotus made of linen;
then, with flames blazing upwards and across, one should burn away all impurity.
The wise one should cause his own karma to revolve by means of rays [of light] pervading the heart-lotus, directed toward the ocean of nectar situated in the sky in the form of the moon. Vis 20.48.
Subsequently, by means of the *suṣumnā*, the path of yoga, one should join the objects of the senses, such as sound, which have spread through all the channels, to the center of the head. (Vis 20.49)
And thus, O Nārada, this form of the nectar has been proclaimed by me;
one should place its seed-syllable at the navel with the ring finger, O Nārada.
One should place the seed-syllable of Kṣauma at the heart with the thumb and the ring finger;
however, this supreme seed-syllable [of Īm] should be placed on the head with all the fingers.

Having thus purified the body— [visualizing it] as smoky, pale-red, and black, beginning with the letter *ya* and ending with the letter *va*— one should apply the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*).
I shall describe the procedure for the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra*; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth.
It is meritorious, the destroyer of all sins, and the bestower of the fruit of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.53)

With the mantra for worshipping one’s own form, [he should apply] sandalwood, white clay, and water from the roots of *bilva* and *tulasī* to the forehead and so on, up to the back of the head. (Vis 20.54)
The wise practitioner should draw the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) with the ring finger for the sake of purification,
using twelve names corresponding to the twelve months.
O Sage, one thus becomes purified by the wearing of the *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* marks,
as well as by the two types of hand and limb placement (*nyāsa*), according to the principles of creation, maintenance, and so forth.

O Nārada, even without formal worship, [the practice] becomes fruitful through the power of the form and the mantra; I shall now describe the sequence of propitiation, beginning with the worship of the gateway.
The practitioner, with all his limbs perfected, fortunate, free from disease, and rid of leprosy and epilepsy, should perform the worship at the gateway. (Vis 20.58)
Caṇḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Garuḍa— ending with the dative case and followed by "namas"—
are placed at the southern, northern, and eastern gates, together with the *praṇavas*.
On the lower lip of Caṇḍā there should be a wheel, and on the lower lip of Pracaṇḍā there should be a lotus;
in this manner, one should perform the worship of the gate with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Alternatively, O great sage, hear the sequence for the worship of the gates:
having worshipped Caṇḍa and the others as before, but without the wheels and other [ornaments].
One should worship Dhātṛ on the left and Vidhātṛ on the right;
the preceptor, most skilled in mantras, stands on the right side of the thread.
One should worship Śrī on the ground at the lower part and her limbs above;
one should also worship Durgā and Gaṇapati situated upon the door panels.
One should place the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures at the base of the two branches,
and one should place the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers upon the supports of the door-panels.

One should worship the door with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, incense, lamps, and other offerings, while [visualizing] the upward-pulling and downward-pulling [forces] within the internal mechanism above and below.
Then one should worship Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa, ending with Garuḍa;
the mantra is said to consist of their respective names preceded by the syllable *praṇava* (oṃ). Vis_20.66.
The expert in the Tantra should worship the deities of the gateway as before;
he should perform the practice according to the three types I have taught, as appropriate.
And here, O Nārada, one should worship with the syllable *praṇava* and their own names;
thus has the sequence of the ritual for the worship of the gateway been briefly described.
Having sounded the bronze bell and covered the door with a cloth,
the practitioner, with his senses restrained, should enter into the presence of the deity.
Having assumed the previously described posture, O great sage, one should prepare the seat for the deity, whether it be made of gold, silver, or copper.
Having prepared a seat for Hari with either kuśa grass or flowers, and having placed it before the God, one should remain with the senses restrained. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.71)
The *praṇava* should be known as the support, and likewise the goddess Vāgīśvarī as the power (*śakti*).
Having recollected the bulb (*kanda*) as the earth,
one should consider the stalk to have the nature of space.
At the tip of the nose, one should remember the lotus, the heart-lotus which is the supreme abode;
for all the [chakras] beginning with the *ādhāra* are indeed the seats of the Great Sage. (Vis 20.73)
If one should conceive [the supports and so forth] out of ignorance or delusion, it will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should conceive the supports and the rest.
Having first placed the *ādhāra* and then the *śakti*,
the wise one, O great sage, should place the *kanda* upon the *śakti*.
Having placed the stalk, which has the form of space, upon the bulb,
one should then place the [elements] beginning with Dharma at the tip of the stalk in their proper order.
In the midst of those [elements], however, is a white eight-petaled lotus for Dharma and the others:
the fourfold set consisting of Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
One should place these four in the corners, beginning with the southeast;
having placed Rudra in the center, in the middle of the base of the stalk.
And one should place the fourfold set— non-dharma, ignorance, non-detachment, and lack of sovereignty—
in the four directions, starting from the east, in due order.
First, one should place the [elements] beginning with Dharma, conjoined with the first mantra; and by means of their own names for all of them, it is designated as the "mantra. (Vis 20.80)
The practitioner should also place Adharma and the others in the four directions— starting from the east— in their respective order, each according to its own name.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) in sequence, beginning with the foundation (ādhāra), O great sage, Nārada said:
"O Lord, I desire to hear about the forms of dharma, jñāna, and the rest. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.82)
"You ought to describe the weapons of them all according to their true nature.
Viṣvaksena said:
"Listen, O Nārada, knower of reality, you who are devoted to the feet of Viṣṇu. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.83)
I shall describe the essential forms and the weapons of Dharma and the others:
four-faced, four-armed, two-legged, and with a dark countenance.
He holds the conch and the discus, is gentle in appearance, clad in yellow garments,
resembling the petals of a jasmine flower, and adorned with all ornaments.
I shall describe to you the embodiment of knowledge, renowned as the embodiment of Dharma—
eternal, with two feet, four arms, and four faces.
Resembling the petal of a blue lotus, bearing the conch, discus, and mace,
and renowned as the embodiment of knowledge— this, I declare, is dispassion.
Endowed with three red eyes, four faces, and four arms,
he wears yellow garments, is serene, and always holds a conch and a discus.
Resembling the petals of the *karṇikāra* flower and situated in the northwestern direction,
it is designated as "of detachment"; now I shall speak to you of sovereignty.
Resembling the petals of a red lotus, with four faces and four arms,
possessing a yellow lower garment, gentle in appearance, and always bearing the conch and the discus.
Joined with a white face and adorned with a pearl necklace—this is designated as the [mudrā] of sovereignty; I shall describe it to you as belonging to Īśvara.
Resembling a jasmine flower or a pearl, having two feet and four arms,
endowed with three red eyes, and wearing a crown of matted hair.
Wearing yellow garments, gentle, bearing an axe (and) a trident,
endowed with all ornaments, and beautified by every splendor.
"O celestial sage Nārada, know the form of Hara to be thus;
in this way, the nature of his dharma, knowledge, and so forth has been briefly described."
I shall describe the limbs such as Adharma; listen, O Nārada!
He is red in color, of massive body, with a neck like a conch shell and four arms. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.95)
Having one face and a large belly, endowed with three eyes,
wearing red garments, fierce, and bearing a sword and a mallet.
Thus has it been told regarding Adharma; now I shall describe Ignorance to you:
yellow in color, with a large belly, a massive body, and four arms.
Holding a spear and a sword, fierce, and adorned with all ornaments—this is the form of ignorance; I declare this to you as the absence of dispassion.
O Brahmin, he resembles the dark-green color of durvā grass; he has two feet and four arms, holds an axe and a noose, is fierce, and always wears red garments.
Endowed with three eyes and wearing a crown of matted locks—this would be the form of one who lacks dispassion; I shall describe to you that which is devoid of sovereignty.
Smoke-colored, with a large belly, four arms, and a great jaw;
having one face and a massive body, he is endowed with disheveled hair.
O Sage, that which is inauspicious, ungentle, and endowed with three eyes has now been described as the form of a lack of sovereignty.
O Nārada, one should constantly recollect the forms of the five [elements] beginning with Dharma and those beginning with Adharma; one should then place them therein in their proper sequence.
If one should, out of delusion, conceive of it otherwise as defining the support and so forth, that worship becomes fruitless and there will be danger from fire for the village. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.104)
Therefore, O Nārada, the practitioner should, with every effort, remember the forms [of the deities] and place an eight-petaled lotus upon them. Vis 20.105.
Therein, one should arrange the sun, moon, and fire one above the other;
one should place the solar disc, which is circular in shape and red in luster.
There, having meditated upon a white circle resembling the moon, one should place it above;
and having meditated upon a triangle resembling fire, one should place it upon the mandala.
Having thus reflected upon the form of the mandala, the sun, and so forth, O Nārada,
one should place the three qualities, beginning with tamas, upon the mandala.
The tamasic, the rajasic, and the sattvic [forms] are respectively as follows:
the tamasic is black in form, while the rajasic has a red appearance.
One should recollect these colors as being sattvic and white;
having contemplated that color there, one should place it upon the mandala.
Having placed Tāmasa and the others, the wise one should assign the two Ātman-s—
the Ātman and the Antarātman— both of whom have Vāsudeva as their ultimate refuge.
The Self (ātman) should be white in color, and the inner self (antarātman) likewise; having contemplated their respective colors, one should place them within the Self and the inner self.
Now listen to the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa) from the foundation (ādhāra) up to the innermost self (antarātman).
Having first placed the foundation, which is white in color and joined with the three forms (trimūrti), [one should proceed].
The placement of the *śakti* is in the second, while the placement of the *kanda* follows thereafter;
the stalk has the nature of space and is dark-colored as the fourth.
O Nārada, one should place the fifth, the embodiment of Dharma, in the south-eastern corner of Nāla,
and the sixth, the embodiment of Jñāna, in the south-west.
In the seventh [position], the wise one should place detachment in the region of the wind;
the best knower of the tantra, having placed sovereignty as the eighth, [should do so] in the northeast.
One should place the ninth [deity], the form of Rudra who is Sadāśiva, at the base of the stalk;
and the tenth, Adharma, one should place at the front of the tip of the stalk.
Having placed the form of ignorance on the right in the eleventh [position],
one should thereafter place non-detachment in the west, O Nārada.
In the northern direction, one should place the deity Anaiśvarya;
the wise man should meditate upon a lotus at the tip of the stalk as his supreme abode.
This is declared to be the lotus posture (padmāsana), which is always honored by the gods;
upon that, O Nārada, one should subsequently place the mandala, the sun, and so forth.
One should place the three qualities—beginning with tamas—in the center in their proper order;
then, within the midst of the qualities, the wise one should place the Self and the Inner Self.
Thus, I have briefly described the sequence for the seat;
now I shall explain the worship of the seat concisely according to the ritual rules.
O best of sages, one who is composed should worship all the forms, from the foundation (ādhāra) up to the innermost self (antarātman), either individually or collectively.
One should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other pleasing offerings;
one should present everything in due order with the mantras consisting of their respective names.
This, O best of sages, is what should be prepared; and I shall now describe the invocation:
a vessel made of gold or some other metal, filled with two *kuḍuba* measures [of grain].
Thus, O Nārada, the characteristics of all vessels have been declared;
that vessel [for the rite] consists of five, six, or seven [units], beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Having placed them before the worshipper, one should sprinkle them with the root mantra;
however, if even these are unavailable, one may use a conch shell or a mother-of-pearl shell instead.
O Sage, one should wash all the vessels with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
[the vessel] should be filled with two āḍhakas and shaped like a ripe bimba fruit.
Having placed the *vardhanī* on the left side,
the wise one should fill it with filtered water and place within it fragrant flowers.
The remaining ritual substances for worship should all be placed in order on the right side, or around it, or even in front. Vis 20.130.
O best of sages, having gathered those into a single vessel from among the various bowls,
one should sprinkle it repeatedly with the six-syllable mantra.
Having sprinkled that vessel again with scented water, one should fill it;
then, one should place a flower upon that [vessel] and pour the water together with the flower onto the head.
Having extracted [the deity] with the worship mantra and meditated upon it here, O Great Sage,
the practitioner should contemplate that very form which was correctly visualized. Vis_20.133.
Once the great image has been brought down and arrived,
one should sprinkle water upon its head and offer a seat for the Teacher of the World alone.
Then, having scattered a handful of flowers at the root of the discourse,
and having paid homage with palms joined, O best of sages, he should thereafter show his respect.

Having offered the water for the guest (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamana) to the deity, the knower of mantras should then provide the attendants with the remainder of the vessel.
O Nārada, I shall explain the sequence of the retinue according to reality;
one should arrange it in due order with water that is a portion of the invocation.
To the east, however, is Vāsudeva, resembling pure crystal,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and adorned with yellow garments.
One should place Saṃkarṣaṇa in the southern direction, resembling the moon, a young elephant, and the sun,
endowed with a conch and a discus, and resplendent with four arms.
O Sage, having placed Pradyumna in the west— one who resembles molten gold,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and adorned with yellow garments— Vis_20.140.
One should place Aniruddha upon that northern [side], having a blue form,
equipped with a conch and a discus, wearing yellow garments, and possessing four arms.
Śrī, with a golden complexion; Sarasvatī, white in form;
Rati, red in color; and after her, Śānti, resembling saffron.
O Nārada, one should place the forms of the Śaktis in the corners beginning with the southeast (Āgneya),
and thereafter, one should place the conch and the other [emblems] in the northeast (Paiśāca) corner.
One should place a white conch shell, accompanied by worship and sound, in the east;
and in the south, the supreme wheel, having a form like the fire of cosmic destruction.
Having placed an unsurpassed mace, yellow like turmeric, in the west,
the wise one should place a lotus resembling the color of blood in the north.
One should place the pestle, which is black in color, in the southeastern direction;
there, one should place the sword, which resembles the sky, in the southwestern direction.
The best knower of the tantras should likewise place a five-colored Śārṅga bow in the northwest,
and a forest garland composed of all colors in the northeast.
This is proclaimed as the inner enclosure within the sanctum;
and to the south of the door is Caṇḍa, black in color and four-armed.
Having thus visualized [the deity] with three eyes and red eyes, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands— now hear about Pracaṇḍa.
On the northern side of the door, one should [visualize] the three-eyed one of terrifying form, red in color, with four arms holding a conch, a discus, and a mace.
And in front [of him] was Vainateya, golden-hued, with palms joined in reverence,
wearing a crown and a basket, clad in blue garments, and lovely to behold.
Having thus meditated upon Garuḍa, who possesses a blue-tipped nose and is adorned with serpent ornaments, like the very embodiment of Balarāma.
Whoever should worship the Lord with devotion should likewise worship Garuḍa;
having first placed the Blessed One at the forefront, one should subsequently employ Garuḍa.
O Lord of Sages, he is red in color, with either four arms or two arms,
adorned with all ornaments and graced by every beauty.
One should worship the presiding deity of the wheel in this manner on the side of the gate: having a form resembling the fire of cosmic destruction (kālāgni) and adorned with a crown bearing a wheel.
Having the luster of a conch shell, with a gentle form, adorned with all ornaments, wearing a sacred thread, white, holding a conch, and endowed with a crown; Vis 20.156.
One should meditate on Dhātṛ, who has four arms or two arms, on the left side of the door;
he is yellow in color, while Vidhātṛ has the radiance of dawn.
The ground should be dark green in color; one should worship Haripriyā as red-colored, Durgā as soft green, and Vināyaka in white form.
O Sage, the Śaṅkha and Padma treasures appear white and red respectively;
and the Gaṅgā and Yamunā rivers appear white and black, O Sage.
One should visualize the goddess Utkarṣaṇī as red and Karṣaṇī as red in color at the gate, and worship them thus during the three junctions of the day.
One should not worship Caṇḍa and the other gatekeepers during the twilight;
if one worships them out of ignorance or delusion, there will be the destruction of the sacred site.
Famine arises in the kingdom, causing the destruction of wealth and grain;
therefore, one should perform with every effort that which is prescribed by the ritual injunctions.
In the southeast and southwest corners of the celestial palace, and in the center of that,
one should visualize Gaṇanāyaka as before, with the face of an elephant, four arms, and the appropriate colors.
In the southern celestial palace, one should place the Lord Dakṣiṇāmūrti—
the God who holds a rosary and is devoted to the eight-syllable mantra.
Three-eyed, white in appearance, gentle, and bearing the crescent moon,
he was attended by hosts of sages such as Nārada and others, and was facing the south.
Thus, this secret form is prescribed for you in brief;
on its right side, however, [is the place] for the Mothers, facing north.
O tiger among sages, one should arrange [the deities] which bring all prosperity and happiness;
O lord of sages, one should arrange the Mothers to the north of the Ālaya.
Now listen attentively as I state their names in order:
Vāgīśvarī, Kriyākīrti, Lakṣmī, and likewise Sṛṣṭi. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.168)
Vidyā and Kānti—these seven are declared to be the mothers of Viṣṇu;
furthermore, Hayāsya and Śrīdhara are located in the north and the west respectively.
Alternatively, Vīrabhadra and Gaṇeśa may be the door-keepers of the Mothers;
one should arrange the Mothers of Viṣṇu according to the practitioner's desire.
The Mothers are golden-hued, and Śrīdhara is dark-complexioned;
Hayaśīrṣa is golden-hued— these are proclaimed to be their respective colors.
In the same way, the description of Vīrabhadra and the others is recited;
then, on the upper part of the celestial chariot, the practitioner [visualizes] Ananta.
Above the five-faced serpent, he is surrounded by [beings] with five faces;
he is four-armed, seated, and holds the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Thus, one should worship Durgā, who possesses these characteristics and is saluted by all the gods,
in the space between the gentle-faced [Viṣṇu] and Īśāna, appearing dark-hued.
To the north of that, however, one should place my eternal form as the Lord of the Army— dark-complexioned, with tawny eyes and a tawny beard.
Holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, four-armed, wearing a crown,
clad in yellow garments, gentle, and endowed with wide-open eyes.
Threatening the world with your left index finger held near the tip of your nose—
thus indeed is my form described to you, O best of sages. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.177)
Then, one should place those prescribed in the ritual for the retinue on the exterior;
one should visualize the conch and the wheel at the right and left sides of the door.
On the right, one should always place the conch-colored [deity], who holds the conch, discus, and mace, possessing four arms and three eyes, with the conch upon his head.
On the left side, one should place the discus, which has the form of fire, four-armed, three-eyed,
of terrifying appearance, and bearing a conch, a discus, and a mace.
One should place the discus upon his head, adorned with a blue garment and a crown;
such is the described characteristic of the forms beginning with the conch and the discus.
One should assign [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna in their respective places:
[Indra], who holds a vajra in his hand, has a thousand eyes, is gentle, and has a dark complexion.
One should meditate on Indra, whose divinity is beauty,
as wearing a crown, possessing three points, radiant with a red hue, and adorned with red garlands.
O Sage, he has three feet and eight arms, with three red eyes;
his hair, nails, and beard are red, he has the form of fire, and he is accompanied by Śakti.
Then one should meditate upon Dharmarāja, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
having the appearance of a dark cloud, two-armed, and holding a staff in his hand.
Adorned with a crown, necklaces, armlets, a tiara, and other ornaments—
this is the description of the Lord of all pretas that has been told by me.
Then [he saw] Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas,
with red hair, a sword in his arm, a massive body, a red face, and three eyes.
Then, this description of the lord of the Rākṣasas was proclaimed:
he was endowed with all auspicious marks and adorned with every ornament.
[He saw] Varuṇa, the lord of the waters, dark-complexioned, holding a noose in his hand, seated upon a lotus,
with a form resembling the color of smoke, bearing a banner, and possessing great arms.
"Two feet and two hands—this is what is designated as 'living beings' for all;
thus, O tiger among sages, is the characteristic recited. (Vis 20.190)
The wise one should meditate upon the unsurpassed Lord of Yakṣas in the northern quarter,
resembling molten gold and endowed with all auspicious marks.
Two-footed and two-armed, holding a staff in his hand, the Lord of Wealth has the form of the peak of a white mountain; he is two-footed and four-armed.
One should meditate thus on all [the deities] in sequence— the one whose banner is a bull, the three-eyed, the trident-handed, and the moon-crested— and worship each separately by their own name.
In this third enclosure, on the moon and sun at the sides of the door,
[is the deity] red in color, with a massive body, a shell-like neck, and four arms.
One should meditate on the Sun at the third gateway on the right side, holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, possessing three eyes, and having a formidable form.
One should meditate on him as having the appearance of a *kundapuṣpa* flower, bearing a conch, a discus, and a mace; four-armed, three-eyed, and clad in yellow garments.
