On the left side of the door, one should contemplate the supreme form of the moon, and behind the crown of the head, the form of a mandala beginning with the sun.
Having thus meditated upon the Moon and the Sun on the two sides of the third gate,
one should place Kumuda and all the others in succession starting from the east.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarpanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
Their characteristics have been proclaimed; one should meditate upon them during this great festival.
Having understood them in that way, the best of practitioners should worship the lords of beings here.
One should place all the many attendants of Viṣṇu in front;
they all bear every kind of color, and all hold weapons and missiles in their hands.
Having recollected all the hosts of spirits within the great seat (mahāpīṭha),
the worshipper should then meditate upon his own form in sequence at the time of worship.

O Lord of Sages, one should worship the retinue by their own names, preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, using offerings such as *arghya* and *pādya*, or alternatively, with perfumes (*gandha*) and other articles.
One should perform worship during the daily ritual while recollecting the mantra beginning with the *praṇava*;
in this tantra, the worship of the enclosures beginning with Caṇḍa has been proclaimed by me.
During the festival, the procedure for worshipping the retinue is supreme;
likewise, having worshipped the retinue with diligence, the wise one [should proceed].
Having thus worshipped the lords of beings, one should thereafter perform the ritual worship;
one should wash all the vessels according to the previously stated procedure.
Having sprinkled all the ritual substances and gazed upon them with the first mantra,
one should proceed through the entire sequence of services, beginning with the invocation.
Having worshipped the God of gods, he goes to the supreme goal;
I shall describe the sequence of ritual services exactly and in their proper order.
First, one should perform the invocation, and then again the offering of a seat;
thirdly, the scattering of flowers, and fourthly, the prostration.
The fifth is the añjali-mudrā, and the sixth is likewise the arghya;
one should perform the pādya as the seventh, and the ācamana as the eighth.
One should know that the ninth is the ceremonial bath; the tenth shall be the garment;
the eleventh shall be the ornament; and the twelfth is the sacred thread.
The thirteenth is the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), the fourteenth is fragrance (gandha),
the fifteenth is flowers (puṣpa), and the sixteenth is incense (dhūpa).
The lamp is the seventeenth, and the mudrā is said to be the eighteenth;
the oblation is the nineteenth, and likewise, the water is the twentieth.

The twenty-first is likewise the rinsing of the mouth (ācāma), and the twenty-second is the betel (tāmbūla); the twenty-third is the service (upacāra), and immediately after that is the rinsing of the mouth.
The twenty-fifth is mouth-perfume; the twenty-sixth is said to be song;
the twenty-seventh is the Purāṇa; and after that, the dance-offering.
The circumambulation with offerings is the twenty-ninth;
after that, O tiger among sages, one should offer water for the feet (arghya) or flowers, according to one's desire.
The thirty-first is the offering of mouth-perfume, and after that is the dismissal;
thus, O Great Sage, have the thirty-two modes of service been described.
I shall describe the ritual procedures;
listen and be attentive.
First is the invocation, and after that, the seat. Vis_20.218.
The third is the water for the feet (pādya), the fourth is the water for the guest-offering (arghya), and the fifth is recorded as the water for rinsing the mouth (ācāma).
One should know that the sixth is the bath (snapana), and the seventh is the garment (vasana).
The eighth is the sacred thread (upavīta), the ninth is said to be perfume,
the tenth is the arrangement of flowers, and the eleventh is incense.
Thereafter, one should know the lamp; then the offering of the sacrificial porridge (caru);
then the mudrā of the fourteen-fold añjali; and after that, the circumambulation.
The dismissal shall be the sixteenth; such is another sequence.
Thus, O Nārada, the ritual services (upacāras) are said to be sixteenfold.
O great sage, hear the sequence of the eleven services:
the first is the invocation, and the second shall be the seat.
One should know that the *arghya* follows immediately after, and the *pādya* comes after that;
the wise one should know that the fifth for the deity is the *ācamana*.
One should know that incense comes immediately after [the previous offering], and the flower is the seventh;
one should know that incense is the eighth, while the lamp is recorded as the ninth.
The tenth [item] should be the offering (nivedya), and after that, the dismissal (udvāsana).
Now hear the application (viniyoga) according to the sequence of primary and secondary [elements].
Wherever there is the highest worship, one should perform the primary service;
however, where the worship is middling, one should employ the secondary service.
"Wherever the image is smallest, there it should be employed with the eleventh [mantra]; this is the firm conclusion of the scripture for the most excellent practitioners. (Viṣṇudharmottara 20.228)
O bull among sages, one should perform worship either to all [deities] everywhere, or according to the specific place and time, or in accordance with the practitioner's own desire.
Whatever the supreme practitioner desires to accomplish, he should perform every ritual service with that very form-mantra. Vis 20.230.
O best of sages, there is a difference in the mantras for the *snapana* (sprinkling) of the forms [of the deity],
whether it be the daily (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) rite, as well as for the *viṣṇornuka* hymn.
The Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad, the twelve-syllable mantra,
the Nārāyaṇa Brāhmaṇa,
or the [Hymn] to the Goddess (Ato Devī).
Or again, thus: Vis_20.232.
Either the thousand-headed god consisting of eight syllables,
or the "Thousand-headed Puruṣa" mantra of Parameṣṭhin.
Performing even one of these ablutions while pure, the practitioner,
having uplifted his own kingdom, shall attain the world of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Person, the worshipper should honor [the deity] with the root mantra alone,
as well as with all the ritual services beginning with the invocation.
One who possesses good qualities, is born of a noble lineage, is faultless, and free from disease—
[such a person] is always fit for all these rites, beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
Or, O best of sages, one may perform [the rite] for the images with the eight-syllable mantra,
O great sage, because of the excellence of the worshiper and because of its faultlessness.
In this case, the Lord of Gods is satisfied by a mere flower alone;
that worship becomes fruitful and brings prosperity to both the village and the kingdom.
Thus, O best of sages, whether he be an ascetic, a student of sacred knowledge, or a worshipper, whoever performs this with devotion attains the supreme goal.
One obtains double the fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus one should worship Viṣṇu, the all-encompassing and imperishable, with devotion.
Having attained prosperity in this world and likewise in the next world, one obtains all desires; it shall be the fruit of all sacrifices.
I shall here explain the distinction between one's own purpose and that of others,
as well as the entire sequence of ritual service, for the benefit of practitioners.
One should offer to the deity in sequence everything from the *arghya* up to the *mukhavāsa*:
the *arghya*, the *pādya*, the *ācamana*, and again the *madhuparka*.
Betel, fragrant flowers, unbroken grains, incense, a lamp, the añjali mudrā, and the food offering—these, O Great Sage, [are the requisites]. Vis_20.244.
Water for drinking, water for sipping, and likewise mouth-perfume—O best of sages, this is the sequence; or one may worship according to that order.
The one most skilled in the tantra should wash all the vessels as before;
having placed the respective substances into each vessel and filled them with flowers.

One should smear the face of Hari with the water for the *arghya* offering using his own mantra; likewise, the water for washing the feet (*pādya*) should be offered at the god's feet using their respective vidyās.
Into the right hand of the deity [he places] water for sipping (ācamana) and the honey-mixture (madhuparka);
likewise, he offers water for sipping and betel-leaf again and again.
One should take *jāti* and *śrīkaṇṭha* (or *khaṇḍa*) and grind them into a paste like mud,
combined with camphor and filling [the vessel] with two *kuḍuba* measures.
One should offer either pure sandalwood or six handfuls of fragrance,
along with four *prastha* measures of flowers for each of the individual forms.
The practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should diligently cause fragrant incense—pervaded by sweet scents and emitting high, rising flames—to be offered. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.251)
One should cause a lamp to be offered that has many lines, is not lacking in purity, and measures ten finger-breadths;
it should rise seven finger-breadths high and be illuminated with ghee and camphor.
One should cause incense and fragrance to be offered at the right nostril;
one should devotedly offer all these in due order to Vāsudeva.
The wise one, knowing the mantra, should rub all the remaining parts, beginning with the *kāla*, with his left hand; being composed, he should take a flower. (Vis 20.254)
With the right hand alone, one should place [the offering] at the feet of the deity;
one should offer a handful three times with one's own vidyā-mantra.
Then one should offer unbroken rice grains (akṣata) again and again, placing them between the middle and ring fingers together with the thumb.
With a concentrated mind, one should offer incense at the nose of the god;
the knower of mantras should offer a lamp on the right side, near the eye of the god.
The display of the mudrā should be performed three times while looking toward the south;
having sprinkled [the offering] with tawny clarified butter, one should touch it with the *Annasūkta*.
Having sprinkled [water] with the mantra beginning with *pariṣicya*, one should place the hand [of the disciple] with one's own hand;
one should place it in the right hand using the mudrā for consuming the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥprāśana*).
Water for drinking, water for sipping, and likewise mouth-perfume—thus the sixteenfold special service is proclaimed. Vis 20.260.
One should offer everything in due order with a mind purified by devotion;
thereafter, the practitioner, having bowed properly with the añjali-mudrā, [should proceed].
With a concentrated mind, he should touch the feet of the deity with his two hands;
then, according to the Atharvaveda, specifically by the Śaunaka recension.
Having recited the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad again and again,
O great sage, one should likewise recite it with the mantra in its three sections.
The Lord of the Gods is indeed satisfied; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
There shall be prosperity for the king and the kingdom, as well as for the villages and other settlements.
One should worship [her] otherwise; through delusion, one would become a performer of malevolent magic.
That worship is indeed fruitless, and there will be an increase in disease.
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship by means of the three sections;
moreover, the expert in the Tantra should perform the fire-ritual as previously described.

One should offer sixteen oblations each of the fuel sticks with the root mantra, the clarified butter with the clarified butter according to the mantra, and the sacrificial porridge with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Having repeatedly offered oblations into the midst of the fire, the practitioner, most skilled in mantras,
should perform all the remaining rites with the remaining substances exactly as previously described.
Having thus completed the fire-ritual (agnikārya), the offering of oblations (balidāna) is now described;
the entire sequence for the offering of oblations will now be explained in brief.
Now the characteristics of vessels made of gold and other materials are described, which bring about all prosperity and happiness in both daily and occasional rites. (Viṣṇudharmottara 20.270)
The *tāla* is said to be the pericarp (*karṇikā*), and its base (*tala*) is half of that;
one should make a foot (*pāda*) outside of it, and at its end there should be a circle (*valaya*).
The vessel for the offering is declared to be made of copper, silver, or gold;
it may be superior, inferior, or middling, according to one's means.
The artisan should have the offering vessel made from a single material;
then the preceptor, properly adorned, taking the vessel, [enters] the mandala.
After it has been consecrated and sprinkled,
one should then prepare a very firm seat for the sacrificial oblation in the midst of that [place] with water that has been strained.
O Nārada, the width of the food-stand is said to be the same as the size of a karṇikāra flower, while its height is four finger-breadths.
And here the characteristic of the perpetual worship festival has been fully explained;
however, during a great festival, one should not perform it upon the food-offering pedestal.
One should have the supreme procession of offerings performed on palanquins and other vehicles;
one should arrange it with its retinue stationed within the inner enclosure.
O best of sages, having placed it upon that vessel under your own name,
and having laid the cloth over the food and scattered other flowers, [proceed].
Adorned with various garments, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers,
and embellished with variegated golden blossoms, it was endowed with a brilliance that eclipsed all else.
Adorned with garlands such as jasmine and others, it is most delightful;
it may be made of gold, silver, or copper, and is exceedingly beautiful. (Vis 20.280)
In that [stūpa], one should place an image according to its respective form;
or, if such is unavailable, one made of gold, silver, or even copper.
One should offer rice, sacrificial porridge, and flowers in the morning and at midday, and perform the bali offering at dusk, according to the appropriate sequence.
The preceptor should offer the eightfold offerings beginning with *arghya*, or those ending with *mukhavāsa*,
or those ending with the lamp, using his own respective mantra.
But in another vessel, the knower of mantras should place food together with water,
combined with perfumes and flowers, and accompanied by the recitation of auspicious verses.
O best of sages, at each sacred seat (pīṭha) one should perform the offering of oblations (balidāna),
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and provided with incense and lamps.
Adorned with canopies and banners, beautified by parasols and yak-tail whisks,
it resounded with the sounds of musical instruments and was accompanied by shouts of victory.
Having honored the disciple with perfumes and other offerings, the Guru himself should meditate upon Garuḍa;
then, with the first mantra of the Vidyās, the Guru should raise up the vessel.
One should place the unsurpassed vessel of offerings upon the head of the disciple;
one should install the deity within that vessel and imagine it as departing (or arriving).

O best of sages, at the time of the circumambulation with offerings, one should present the offering before the image, accompanied by the sound of conch shells and other instruments played slowly and gradually. Vis 20.289.
O Sage, if one out of delusion performs the rite of offering (balikarma) in a place devoid of an image, that location goes to ruin, and those situated there shall go to hell. Vis_20.290.
Therefore, with every effort, one should present the bali offering before the image;
from that point on, one should avoid walking between the image and the preceptor.
If there is a journey to that place, one should perform a bath with the five products of the cow;
at its conclusion, one should bathe that image with scented water.

O Sage, it should be accompanied by the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), joined with the sounds of hymns for well-being (*svastisūkta*), and [consecrated] with either the first mantra of the mantras or the form-mantra (*mūrtimantra*). Vis_20.293.
Having offered one oblation at a time, in sequence, with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice,
he should offer each into its respective fire in due order, ending each with the word "svāhā."
Afterward, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should perform the remaining rites;
first, having performed a circumambulation accompanied by dance and song.
And having circumambulated a second time accompanied by songs and musical instruments,
he then circumambulated a third time joined by various kinds of musical instruments.

And having worshipped [the deities] beginning with Caṇḍa and Pracaṇḍa up to the great seats (mahāpīṭha) with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, as well as with perfumes and other substances mixed with water; Vis_20.297.
Having worshipped the retinue as previously arranged, and having performed everything up to the distribution of offerings, one should circumambulate the great pedestal.
Having gone to the third libation, one should again perform a circumambulation;
having reached the city gate, one should produce the sound of three conch shells.

Having reached the door of the celestial palace (vimāna), and having offered either an arghya offering or a flower with the mantra of that deity's form, one should cause [the deity] to enter the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra).
On the right side of the pedestal, one should propitiate the image of Bala;
likewise, in the ritual worship, one should offer the four [services] beginning with water for the feet.
The wise one should place the flower situated in the offering vessel before me;
he should then place the food-offering and water upon the great pedestal.
Having washed his feet and hands and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) again according to the rule,
he should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the procedure, as before, with the Mūrti-mantra.
One should assign the *kakudanta* and the *lalāṭa* and so forth upon the body in their proper sequence,
reciting [the mantra] a thousand times, or a hundred times, or even twenty-eight times.
One should recite each respective mantra in sequence according to one's ability;
having performed prostrations in sequence, one should proceed with the hymns of praise to those forms in sequence.
The practitioner of mantra should recite his own mantra in the presence of the God of gods;
at this time, the Lord of Gods is satisfied—
of this there is no doubt.
One obtains all desires and brings about the prosperity of both the village and the king;
otherwise, O Lord of the Gods, he becomes angry—
of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, the wise person should chant the hymn of praise to the Form;
having offered a flower and paid obeisance, he should lead Hari to the primary image (mūlabera).
Perform the dismissal just as the invocation was done before;
having observed this, they say it is the supreme and most excellent offering of the bali.
I have spoken briefly; now I shall describe the bestowal of the glance, or else the sequential procedure for offering the bali-oblation to the retinue.
I shall proclaim it, O best of sages; listen to that which is more secret than the secret.
It is accompanied by jhallarī and maddala drums, and provided with various musical instruments.
Prior to the perpetual festival, one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation,
provided with all ornaments and accompanied by a canopy and a banner.
Accompanied by dance and song, one should subsequently circumambulate the image;
and with vigilance, one should offer the intermediate oblation to Caṇḍa and the others.
The rite named Dattāvalokana brings prosperity to the king and his kingdom;
in this manner, one should perform the sequence of offerings to the retinue day by day.
Thus has the delusion regarding the constant festivals and offerings been briefly explained;
I shall now describe the specific details here concerning the ritual of offering for the sake of others.
Listen with focused attention, O Sage, to that which is more secret than the secret;
one should invoke Indra and the other world-protectors according to the sequential method.
If one performs the sequence of the retinue offerings for a single enclosure path,
one should perform it in the first enclosure, omitting Vighneśa and the others.
Having established [the deities] from Caṇḍa up to Śarva, one should perform the bali offering;
afterwards, O Sage, having first established the bali upon the great seat (mahāpīṭha).

One should cause Hari to be circumambulated a second time accompanied by songs featuring conch shells and other instruments; one should cause Hari to be circumambulated a third time accompanied by various musical instruments.
Afterwards, the illustrious one, having led the deity [inside], should worship Him with water for the hands (arghya) and other offerings;
then, accompanied by the singing of conch shells and other instruments, he should cause the second image of Hari to be circumambulated.
Accompanied by various musical instruments, one should cause Hari to circumambulate for the third time;
thereafter, the illustrious one, having led the deity back, should worship him with the arghya and other offerings.
Having taken water for the feet and sprinkled it over the devotees, the knower of mantras should perform the rite of the bali offering;
thus is the procedure for the worship of a single enclosure described.
Furthermore, O Lord of Sages, if a rampart is likewise imagined right here,
one should place [the deities] beginning with Caṇḍa and ending with Īśāna in the first enclosure.
The remaining retinues in the second and third [circles],
from Indra to Supratiṣṭha, should be re-established by the knower of mantras.
One should perform the offering of the bali-oblation according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thus that worship becomes fruitful, and prosperity increases day by day.
There shall be prosperity for the king, for the kingdom, and likewise for the residence;
thus one should perform [this] day by day, protected by the third enclosure.
In this very manner, one should perform the bali offering in the abode of the second enclosure;
one should place [the offerings] up to the arghya, according to the previously mentioned path, in the first [enclosure].
O best of sages, one should first perform the bali offering to Vidhneśa and the others.
Thereafter, one should offer the bali-oblation to Indra and the other deities in the first enclosure.
In the third enclosure, one should subsequently offer the bali-offering to Kumuda and the others;
that bali is middling, while this [preceding] one is superior, each preceding one being more significant than the next.
Otherwise, one obtains a contrary result, and it becomes a source of famine and misfortune;
therefore, one should diligently perform the bali offering according to the ritual for Viṣṇu.
Whether at the foot of a tree, at the base of a mountain, against a wall, or within a cave—there is a certain distinction regarding this; listen to that sequence, O Nārada. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 20.331)
Having prepared a pavilion with its furnishings before the gods as previously described, one should there smear the ground on all sides to the extent of one cubit according to the prescribed rite.
Having invoked the Śakti into that [liṅga] which is joined with the pāduka in the vessel,
one should offer the seven items beginning with arghya, followed by the individual offerings of pādya and so forth, in due order.
Having arranged the retinue specifically around the pavilion,
one should circumambulate the pavilion in sequence according to the path of a single enclosure.
O divine sage, one should perform the offering of oblations for fish and other such creatures in this very same manner; O best of sages, one should perform the remainder as previously described.
Otherwise, the performer obtains a contrary result and the patron perishes;
however, I shall explain the ritual offering of the bali alone—listen in due order.
O best of sages, if the practitioner is devoid of the fire-offering festival,
[he should worship] all fifteen gatekeepers, beginning with Caṇḍa.
O tiger among sages, one should worship [them] in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
at that gate, they say there is an offering (bali), which is recited as the lowest [grade].
One should perform the highest [offering] for the highest [deity], the middling for the middling,
and even the lowest for the lowest, in accordance with one's available resources.
O best of sages, one should especially perform the offering of the bali-oblation to the east of the Nityotsava pavilion; thereafter, one should circumambulate the deity.
They say that [a gift] devoid of attendants is the lowest of the low;
however, one known as "with a view to the recipient" (dattāvalokyaka) brings prosperity to that very village.
One should perform all the ornaments for this [deity] as before;
thus have I fully described the ritual procedure for the offering (balikarma) beginning with the supreme [level].
Thus, O Sage, the procedure for the perpetual festival has been briefly explained;
one should perform it here in a single manner according to the desire of the practitioner.

O Sage, for one's own sake, one should worship the supreme Hari according to either the Vedic or the Tantric method; for the sake of others, however, one should worship him according to the Tantric method alone or with the two combined.
The wise man should worship as before for the increase of the king and his kingdom;
however, he should by no means perform it for the sake of another using Vedic rites alone.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the invocation for one's own purpose using a Tantric mixture, whether from a fruit or even from a cloth painting.
Either from the center of the solar disc for the sake of another, or from the primary image (*mūlabera*),
one should perform the dismissal (*udvāsana*) and invocation (*āvāhana*) while setting aside the single image.
O best of sages, one should perform [this] for one's own sake and for the sake of others, especially for an image made of stone; likewise for an image in a child’s house.
One should not recall the invocation or the dismissal; one should perform the remainder of the rite.
This applies even to one who is incapable, lacks the requisite qualification, or has the ritual performed for his own sake by another.
In the future, that entire family will deliver their own kin;
everything offered to Viṣṇu is indeed dear to me as well.
Having removed the floral remains from the fingers of both hands using one's own thumb and ring finger, one should mentally perform breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Therefore, that garland and those auspicious materials which bring me joy should be given to my devotees.
One should cause that very garland and those very materials to be bestowed upon the faithful.
O best of sages, if my worship is performed in that temple without [the image], that worship shall become fruitless and will bring misfortune to the village. (Viṣṇudharmottara 20.353)
[It is forbidden] for those such as crows and dogs, for heretics,
for those who sell the Vedas, and likewise for those who revile the Vedas.
One should not provide such things for the consumption of those devoted to the food of Śūdras, and especially of atheists, nor for the consumption of [those of] such castes.
Or, out of delusion, by giving [the remains] without discernment, one would go to the Raurava hell;
nor, O Supreme Person, should one even step over my *nirmālya*.
But whoever, out of delusion, should transgress [this], great will be his fault;
submerged in the fire of the Mahāraurava hell, he shall bear the burden of that fault.
It is the place for the performance of vows for those of the three castes beginning with the twice-born, especially for Vaiṣṇavas,
for those maintaining the three sacred fires, and for ascetics of tranquil mind.
For those who have been initiated, for ascetics, and likewise for those who are barren and so forth—
one should cause such things to be given to the devotees in the presence of the deity.
Therefore, one should not cause those who have avoided all such efforts to perform it;
thus, he who performs this unsurpassed worship of Viṣṇu with devotion [attains the fruit]. Vis_20.360.
It bestows liberation upon those desiring liberation, wealth upon those longing for wealth, and food upon those seeking food; it is the auspicious granter of all desires.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varieties of Worship," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-One. Nārada said:
"O Blessed One, there is indeed nothing for a person that brings about the attainment of the Supreme equal to this mode of worship."
Is there any praise offered that is free from words faltering due to excessive agitation, and which concerns neither oneself nor another? (Viṣṇu 21.1)
Viṣvaksena said: Listen, Nārada, to this supreme hymn of praise to my form, as it was spoken by my supreme Guru;
since you are devoted, I shall now relate it to you.
For what man here would ever be satiated with virtuous deeds?

I always bow down with reverence to the Supreme Self, the Guru, who has Vinatā’s son as his vehicle, who is the god of the thirty [deities], who wears golden armlets, who possesses eight arms, who resembles a white mountain, who has two feet, and who is of beautiful countenance. Vis_21.3 //

I always bow down to him who holds a lotus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus in his hands, who is adorned with every ornament, whose face resembles the snowy mountain, whose pair of feet is served by the four-faced Brahmā, and who bears the name "Supreme" (Para). Vis_21.4.

I always bow down to the wielder of the plow, who resembles the rising sun, whose feet are worthy of worship by the thirty gods, whose eyes are delicate, who strikes with his mace, who is clad in crimson garments, who is peerless, and whose face is like the moon. Vis_21.5.

I always bow down to him who has four limbs and very thick, long arms, who is served by one of monkey-like complexion with palms joined in reverence, and by Garuḍa on the right and the lotus-born Brahmā on the left as he delivers his blow. (Vis 21.6)
In this regard, there is a specific distinction in the ritual procedure for worshipping the forms;
by worshipping the ten forms beginning with Matsya here in this world, one shall obtain the fruit.
I shall now declare its fruit; listen, O Nārada! It bestows long life and health, and one certainly attains union [with the Divine]. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 21.8)
Whoever worships the Fish [incarnation] with devotion according to the stated sequence attains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Having propitiated the Tortoise with devotion, a person whose impurities have been shaken off shall attain all desires and reach union with Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Varāha with devotion according to this sequence, the wise man,
liberated from sin and disease, attains the supreme goal.
Having propitiated Nārasiṃha, endowed with supreme devotion,
one whose every desire is fully accomplished attains the fortune of victory.
By worshipping Vāmana with devotion, the man of knowledge attains the same world as Viṣṇu;
by propitiating Paraśurāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, one attains the same form as Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, one attains longevity, fame, happiness, and glory; having obtained every desire, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
By propitiating Balarāma, one obtains strength, health, and wealth;
by worshipping Kṛṣṇa, one obtains every desired object and its fruit.
Having attained Kalki, who is the embodiment of knowledge,
as well as prosperity, long life, and fame,
he rejoices with the attendants of Viṣṇu in the realm of Viṣṇu.
O Sage, the meritorious worship of the ten forms is more secret than the most secret;
it is for the benefit of practitioners who are devoted and wise.
I have proclaimed the declaration of the fruits, especially regarding the Fish and other [incarnations].
Now, hear the supreme secret application of the Tantras.
And it has been said: "It should never be taught to one who lacks devotion, nor to the arrogant, nor to the hypocritical, nor to the atheist, nor to the deceitful. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 21.19)
One should not give it to one who does not wish to listen, nor to one who is impure or lacking in compassion;
however, one may give it to one devoted to the deities and the guru, for otherwise the teacher would incur a fault.
O great sage, [he saw] Jānakī, Rukmiṇī, Bhāmā— with Lakṣmī, Puṣṭi, and Vidyā respectively— and also Lakṣmaṇa, Bharata, and Śatrughna.

One who knows the Rāghava-mantra should worship with the Praṇava at the beginning of his own name, ending in the dative case, followed by "namaḥ," using the even-numbered verses; this is the deity of the sage's meter.
O Sage, one should employ this mantra for all the retinues; with these [syllables], gold is to be employed, ending with "svāhā" in its entirety.
In the internal service,
[the mantra] ends with "āgaccha" (come) when making [the deity] face [oneself];
it ends with "kṣamasva" (forgive) at the dismissal, and it ends with "namaḥ" (homage) in the rite of worship.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Worshipping [the Fish-Form and Others]," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-Two. Viṣvaksena:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme procedure for the ritual bathing.
O best of sages, one should cause a pavilion to be constructed on the roof of the palace in due order.
O Brahmin, it should be thirty cubits in length and half of that in width;
having understood this, O best of sages, one should construct an excellent and auspicious pavilion.
One should perform the remaining rites in this [consecration] according to the rules of the treatises on arts (śilpaśāstra),
or otherwise, one should construct the pavilion (maṇḍapa) in front as far as possible.
Having divided the pavilion into three parts, one should place the water-pots in its center;
however, in the third part toward the west, one should prepare the bathing altar.
One should have it constructed according to what is seen in the scriptures;
now hear its sequence:
having understood the measurement here as being either two cubits or one cubit.
O Sage, one should first have a pedestal constructed, equal in width and length [to the temple], or half a cubit high, or half of that; such is the characteristic of the pedestal.
Its height and thickness are said to be four finger-breadths;
above that, one should place a girdle (mekhalā) all around the altar-railing (vedikā).
In the center, one should have an excellent eight-petaled lotus made together with a pericarp;
to its north, one should arrange a bathing channel in due order.
The bathing channel, together with its girdle, should be made according to the measurement of a palm-tree;
one should fashion the girdle as before and provide a stream in the middle.
On the northern side of the altar, one should cause a bathing pit to be made;
one should construct the altar using stones, bricks, or clay.
Thus has it been briefly declared; now I shall tell you the specific details regarding both the regular and occasional rites, which bring about all prosperity and happiness.
Having taken up [an image] made of gold, or silver, or copper, or likewise bell-metal,
or even of mixed metal, with the Astra-mantra, O Nārada.
O Sage, one should have an altar constructed there, provided with four sides, properly made by artisans under the authorization of the preceptor.
One should prepare the altar with wood according to the procedure previously described.
Thus has the method for laying out the lines been briefly explained; now listen to [the rest].
O Sage, one should first draw the Brahma-sūtra from east to west;
by relying on that central portion, that sūtra bestows the increase of Brahman.
For a Kṣatriya, it serves the purpose of victory; for a Vaiśya, it grants the increase of happiness; and a Śūdra attains a good rebirth through it. Therefore, one should practice that Sūtra.

Having cast out from all sides the lines of the sun, smeared with well-prepared rice-flour paste, which run eastward and northward starting from the lotus and extending to the edge of the darkness; Vis_22.17.

Having wiped clean the four streets for the sake of the processions, you shall also have rows on both sides; the threads for the pavilions shall measure nine finger-breadths in length for each square.
Having prepared them, one should subsequently sprinkle them with the *praṇava* for the purification of the ground;
then, filling each jar with a *prastha* measure of *śāli* rice.
Then, having placed all the pure substances along with the *kūrca* grass and their lids—
whether full or not full to the measure of an *āḍhaka*— one should worship them with perfumes and other offerings until the end of the day.

Having wrapped each sacrificial post with new cloths, one who knows the true meaning of the scriptures should again perform the ritual bathing of Rāma with water containing barley and other offerings, beginning with the water for the feet.

Because they lack these characteristics, because of hostility toward gods or humans, because their [alleged] location is untenable, and because of their lack of skill even in the casting of the thread (sūtra). // Vis_22.22 //
Nārada said: "As the ceremonial bath approaches, what should be done by the three devotees of Hari?
For the benefit of the world, may the Blessed One explain this question regarding the ritual bath."
Viṣvaksena said: "O virtuous one, for the benefit of your devotees, I shall give an answer to this; listen.
Even in that place where there is no rice, [it is found] there as well. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 2.24.24)
In the place where the rice was, he should write the seed-syllable of Viṣṇu together with the nasal bindu;
then, reciting the Praṇava with a serene mind, he should place the water-pots upon it.
One should perform the ritual bathing with the eight-syllable mantra; thus one becomes an accomplisher of all aims.
Thus has this essential ritual bathing been taught by my guru for you.
The measure of substances called *dravya* is said to be an *āḍhaka*; O Sage of the Thirty-three, in the absence of that, half of it, or even three *raṇas*, is prescribed. Vis_22.27.
... likewise, three bundles of dry sacrificial fuel;
and a new cloth, very smooth, five cubits long, made of fine thread. // Vis_22.28 //
At the conclusion of the bathing ceremony, having drawn the previously mentioned lotus there, one should place the seed-syllable of Hari upon the *kūrca*,
filling it with an *āḍhaka* measure of turmeric powder.
Having sprinkled it as previously described— or even half an *āḍhaka*—
while reciting the *praṇava*, one should churn that very substance face-down with the *kūrca* brush.
Having cast [the image] inside with its lid closed and worshipped it, one should perform the consecration as before,
or perform a partial bathing with sand, trees, mangoes, and white clay.

O Sage of the Thirty-three, having covered [the deity] with the finest silken garments and worshipped with offerings beginning with *arghya* up to the lamps, and having presented the great sacrificial oblation, the practitioner becomes perfected. (Vis 22.32)
O best of sages, I shall describe to you in brief, according to their sequence, the characteristics of the substances and the deities for this ritual bathing.
O tiger among sages, having taken one āḍhaka of the most excellent ghee from tawny cows, one should consecrate the Lord of Gods.
Having collected pure water and prepared it properly with fuel from milk-tree wood in a temple, one obtains unsurpassed hot water.
Vajra and pearl, as well as maṇi and lapis lazuli,
coral and crystal, and likewise the fruit of the plantain tree.
The bilva, the āmalaka, and the kadalī fruit,
as well as the coconut, the havya, and the bījapūraka.
Likewise, the juice of the fruit of the jackfruit and mango is proclaimed as the "eightfold water" (aṣṭāṅga-phalāmbhaḥ),
consisting of gold, silver, copper, brass, and iron.
Trapuṣa, iron filings, rajanī, sahadevī, śirīṣa, and sūryavartanī are recited as the ingredients for the liquid metal.
Kuśa grass tips and *sadābhadra* are said to be cleansing materials;
likewise saffron, agallochum, sandalwood, and uśīra.
Haribera, mura, and koṣṭha are recited as māṃsī;
these are declared to be fragrant substances, and akṣata-water is also mentioned.
O Sage, having washed it with pure water while reciting the five mantras in sequence, the wise one should place half a *prastha* of unbroken rice (*akṣata*) into the jar. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 22.42.
O best of sages, having taken twenty-five barley grains, or half of that, or even half of that again, one should cast them into the midst of the water.
Śyāmāka, viṣṇuparṇī, dūrvā, and ambuja— these,
O great-minded one, are declared to be the substances for the water for the feet in brief.
Having taken curd mixed with ghee while knowing the mantra, the knower of mantras should fill the central jar with the first mantra; the substances for the *arghya* offering are now described here.
In this way, fragrance, fruit, flower, white mustard seeds,
unbroken rice grains, tips of kuśa grass, and sesame seeds are said to constitute the eightfold arghya offering.
One should place milk mixed with clarified butter in the central jar,
along with unbroken rice, nutmeg, kakkola, cloves, and sesame seeds.
One should place the ritual substances into the water in the vessel intended for the *ācamana* rite;
having taken fresh honey derived from trees, one should take exactly one *āḍhaka* of it.
In the absence of that, however, there should be clarified butter; thus the characteristic is stated:
one-quarter-prastha of ghee and twice as much curd.
Three parts of milk, four parts of cow dung,
and six parts of cow urine constitute the characteristics of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, bilva, audumbara, as well as vaikaṅkata, śamī, and jambu—
these are traditionally known as the components of the decoction. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 22.51.
In the absence of tawny cow's clarified butter, however, other cow's ghee is prescribed;
in the absence of warm water, however, water infused with flowers is recommended.
If even jewels cannot be obtained, a single pearl is praised;
if even fruits cannot be obtained, the plantain fruit is considered supreme.
If even metals are unavailable, gold is highly recommended;
for cleansing, Sahadevī is praised when other materials are lacking.
Likewise, uśīra is recommended among fragrant substances when the others are unavailable;
and in the absence of unbroken rice (akṣata), one should act according to what is possible.
In the absence of barley, however, there should be rice, or else bamboo seed;
but when even these substances are unavailable, dūrvā grass is recommended for the foot-washing water.
But if even these are not available, white mustard seeds are supreme for the water of honor (arghya);
if the remaining items are unavailable, kakkola is recommended for the water for rinsing the mouth (ācamanīyaka).
In the absence of the five products of the cow, cow dung and the rest are recommended;
curd, cow dung, milk, and ghee are recommended according to what is available.
In the absence of the remaining substances for a decoction, the aśvattha tree would be recommended;
however, if even those materials are unavailable, one should prepare it with flowers alone.
All new garments are equal to all other substances;
therefore, with every effort, one should not accept them when no other clothing is available.
O best of sages, the characteristics of substances beginning with ghee and ending with clothing have been declared; indeed, one should deposit as many substances as there are.
As for all the remaining jars, they are filled with pure water;
here, seventeen are specified as those which are the principal jars.
One should establish all of them individually with the Viṣṇugāyatrī,
and the remaining sixty-four others with the knowledge-mantra consisting of twelve syllables.
Facing either the east or the north, one should place all the jars while recollecting the mantra of the [respective] forms, covering them all with new cloths.
Above those [pillars], the practitioner, facing eastward, should worship all the archways and the pitchers with fragrances, flowers, and other offerings. (Vis 22.65)
Free from skin diseases and the like, and devoid of worms and insects, the practitioner, having placed the grains in a mortar that is naturally free of dust, should proceed.
Again and again, O best of sages, having adorned courtesans and others with the twelve-syllable vidyā and accompanied by auspicious recitations, [one should perform the rite].
Accompanied by conch shells, kettledrums, and other instruments, he should have him killed together with the Vaiṣṇavas;
he should take up a club there and strike him again and again.
Then, having collected the pollen, one should gradually fill the jar;
at the end of filling the jar, O best of sages, one should consecrate the Lord of Gods.

Thus, O Sage, the substances have been fully described; now follows the extraction [of the mantras]. One should first offer the water for the feet (pādya), and the second is called the water of honor (arghya). Vis_22.70.
One should know that the third is water for sipping (ācamanīya), the fourth is the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
the fifth is clarified butter (ghṛta), and likewise the sixth is curd (dadhi).
Then the seventh is milk, and likewise the eighth is honey;
the ninth is a decoction, and warm water is recorded as the tenth.
On the eleventh day,
it is fruit-water; on the twelfth day, it is cleansing water.
The thirteenth is Sāṃbhaja, and the fourteenth is Ratnatoya.
Iron is to be known as the fifteenth, and fragrant water as the sixteenth;
barley-water is the seventeenth—such is the sequence for extraction.
In each respective group of nine, one should extract eight together with that [central deity],
excluding the middle nine, according to the sequence beginning with Indra.
One should extract all the middle jars with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
the remainder [of the ritual] should be performed with the eight-syllable mantra alone, and one should release the garment with that very same mantra.
Then, O best of sages, one should offer [the gifts] with the Puruṣasūkta;
or, recollecting the God of gods, one should offer the water for the feet and the other offerings in due order.
Having bathed [the image] with the ninefold water for the feet and so forth, one should perform the secondary bathing (upasnāna).
Then, having offered a garment, one should cause the water for the feet and other offerings, as well as perfumes and the like, to be presented.
At the end of the nine [sections], the wise one should likewise act;
in the middle nine as well, he should cause the water-pots to be offered.
Thus has the extraction been declared; now I shall describe the presiding deities:
Viṣṇu is the deity of the ghee, and the Sun is the deity of hot water.
Brahmā is the presiding deity of gems; Kubera of fruits and water;
the Vasus of iron-water; and the Viśvedevas of the ritual rinsing.
The Gandharvas [are the presiding deities] of the fragrant water; Nirṛti of the unbroken rice grains;
the Āpyas of the barley-water; and likewise the Pitṛs of the water for the feet.

O God, the deity of the milk-offering (arghya) is Sarasvatī; Dakṣa is the deity for the water for sipping (ācamanīya); and Śakra is the presiding deity of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and of curd. Viṣṇu 22.83.
Soma is the deity of milk, and likewise Mahendra of honey;
Yama is the deity of astringent decoctions, while Varāha is the deity of water mixed with treacle.
Likewise, Narasiṃha is the deity of sugarcane juice;
Śrīdhara is the deity of coconut water; and Hayāsya is the deity of the water used for pacification rites.
The four forms beginning with Vāsudeva are for the auspicious waters;
for all the pure waters, the goddesses beginning with Śānti are assigned in sequence.
The Aśvins are the supreme deity of all the water-pots (kalaśas), while the Seven Mothers are the deity of all the small bowls (cakrikās). || 22.87 ||
Vāsava for the gods, Viṣṇu for all, or indeed Viṣṇu alone—
the one skilled in mantras should perform everything with the root mantra.
This bathing rite is proclaimed as both inferior and superior;
as for the pitchers in the corners, there are thirty-two of pure appearance.

However, that bath which is devoid of those [elements], as well as that which is lacking all the water-pitchers of pure water according to their respective directions, would be considered inferior or middling.
That which is performed with only seventeen [mantras] is the lowest of the low;
however, in the ritual bathing and other rites, the binding of the *kautuka* (protective thread) must be performed in due order.
A thread joined with a woolen cord, consecrated upon rice,
along with a golden vessel containing one āḍhaka or more of turmeric powder.
Having prepared a powder of one āḍhaka, half an āḍhaka, or half of that,
according to the prescribed rite,
one should finally place it upon the head of the deity at the conclusion of the successive ablutions.
Then, having performed the ritual bath and adorned Him, one should worship Hari;
having again offered water for sipping, one should show him the mirror in due order.
Accompanied by dance and song, joined with the study of the Vedas,
provided with parasols and fly-whisks, and endowed with incense and lamps.
Having circled eight balls of rice together with a lamp around the head of the deity, one should cast the balls, starting from Indra and ending with Īśāna, while reciting the weapon mantra.

The supreme preceptor should lead the deity to the great pedestal (mahāpīṭha) in a manner appropriate for its increase; then, as before, he should offer the great oblation (mahāhavis) upon the sacrificial altar.
One should perform the oblation either in the eastern or the northern fire, or indeed in the perpetual fire (nityāgni),
using sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice, according to the number of jars.
Thereafter, one should honor the teacher with new garments and finger-rings;
one should cause the materials used therein to be presented to the teacher. (Vis 22.99)
With barley, bamboo seeds, wild rice, white mustard,
and blue *tulasī* leaves, the water for the *dhātrī* [tree] should be prepared in sequence.
But if even these are not available, then the excellent *tulasī* leaf, as well as the sprouts of *indravallī* and the sprouts of the *aśvattha* tree [are to be used]. (Viṣṇu 22.101)
There should be a single vessel containing a lotus and auspicious water; however,
if even these are unavailable, the sprout of an aśvattha tree is excellent.
O best of sages, if those are unavailable, one should use the sprouts of *indravallī*;
and one should employ a single lotus or a lotus according to what is available. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 22.103)
Thus has the ablution, which bestows all accomplishments, been briefly described.
[Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O Viṣṇu, O Lord of beings, O Sovereign of Viṣṇu’s attendants!
O Lord, I wish to hear about the ablution with one thousand and one hundred jars;
for I have previously heard much regarding the ablution from the mouth of Viṣṇu.
And since you have indeed spoken thus regarding this very method,
therefore, O mighty-armed one, if there is any affection for me, [act accordingly].
Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the thousand-plus pot [offering];
a pavilion must be constructed according to the rules at the front of the temple.
Thirty-two cubits in length and twenty cubits in width,
with forty rows [of pillars],
each eight tālas apart.
In that portion, at the place for the pitcher, there are twenty-five rows;
in its central part, however, it measures twelve *tāla*s.
It was provided with four pillars and its height was exactly that much;
it was surrounded by seven palm trees and joined by twelve pillars.
Outside of that, at a distance of seven tālas, there is a section for bathing consisting of one-fifteenth of the whole, which is provided with twenty pillars.
In its middle portion, however, a space of twelve tālas is prescribed,
provided with eighteen pillars and a bathing altar according to the rules.
The remaining rows are measured by the seven-beat time-measure (*tāla*);
for all the *tālas*, there are sixty-four [units] in due order.
Its width is measured at forty palm trees,
and it is proclaimed to have fifty-four pillars.
This is declared to be the ground portion; now I shall describe the remaining parts to you:
it should be four *tāla*s in width and half of that in length.
Half of that is the *upapīṭha*, and above it is the *upānaha*;
the *jagatī* and *kumuda* are likewise beautifully adorned upon the *paṭṭikā*.
A wise person should make the pedestal there level and smooth;
furthermore, one should have a bathing trench constructed on the northern side of the altar.
A channel for drainage should be made, or a trench upon the altar;
the binding [of the cloth] should extend from the base to the middle and the tip, according to the proper measure.
One should fashion a circular base upon the footstool;
then one should make that vessel either round or square.
It should be four finger-breadths in height and of equal width; it should be connected by a channel within the range of a water-filled pit.
The characteristics of the pedestal have been declared; I shall now describe the remaining parts in their entirety:
it is to be provided with four gates and adorned with four archways.
The knower of mantras should hang chowries, palm-leaf fans, bells, and various banners, as well as strings of pearls, at the locations of the doors. (Vis 22.122)
Thereafter, having adorned [the site], one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made there;
then, the ritual cleansing (*mārjana*) should be performed correctly according to the rules, followed by the smearing of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
The practitioner, most skilled in mantras, should sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow;
thereafter, he should worship the gatekeepers at all the entrances.
One should worship two jars each according to the rules for the gateway locations;
then, one should likewise worship the arches and the banners as well.
Having worshipped them in due order with their own names using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings,
one should wrap the pillars of the archways with woolen cloths and silks.
Having reached the location of the pitcher, one should decorate it with rice flour;
the central portion is for Brahmā, and immediately following that is the portion for the gods.
One should place the third human portion as a single step in sequence;
one should set down a step in the Brahma-square according to the rule of eighty-one parts.
Clarified butter, warm water, jewel-water, fruit-water, iron-water, cleansing water, scented water, and indeed unbroken grains.
And [the substances] beginning with barley-water—these one should place in the middle ninefold group;
one should arrange them all around that very [group] in the eight directions on every side.

Then one should place the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), the water for sipping (ācamanīya), the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), curd, milk, honey, and decoctions in the directions beginning with Indra.

One should place the items beginning with water for the feet and ending with the five products of the cow in the cardinal directions; and those beginning with curd and ending with astringent decoctions in the intermediate corners.
Thus the substances have been described; one should deposit them in each of the nine [squares], placing the substances in their proper order from the center outward.
One should cause all the remaining sixty-four [pots] to be filled with pure water;
then, the practitioner should place a footprint upon the divine portion.
In each direction as well as in each corner, the wise one should sequentially place the seventeenth [vessel]; likewise, he should place the substance-vessel in the very center.
One should place a paste of sandalwood in the central portion of the eastern quarter,
and one should place a paste of saffron in the central portion of the southern quarter.
One should place a paste of camphor in the central part of the western quarter;
one should place a paste of uśīra in the central part of the northern quarter.
One should place sesame oil in the middle portion of the southeast;
one should place emblic myrobalan oil in the middle portion of the southwest.
In the central portion of the northwest, one should place mustard oil;
in the central portion of the northeast, one should place camphor oil.
Sandalwood is both mud and water, as is saffron;
camphor is both mud and water, and ushira root is likewise mud and water.
The wise practitioner should arrange [the offerings] starting from Indra and ending with Soma;
likewise, he should offer sesame, myrobalan, oil, and mustard oil.
Likewise, one should place camphor oil in the directions beginning with the southeast;
and [the deities] Puruṣa, Satya, Nara, Nārāyaṇa, and Acyuta.
Aniruddha, Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and the eight deities beginning with Candana—
these twenty-eight remaining [deities] should all be honored in their respective order with pure water.
Thereafter, the preceptor, being well-composed, should fill [the area] on all sides;
in the third human portion, he should [place] the sixteen [deities] beginning with Indra in due order.
The wise one should arrange forty-nine individual squares, and having placed the vessel of substances in their center.
One should place sugar in the east;
spit-water in the south;
coconut water in the west; and water for pacification in the north.
The Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayaśīrṣaka,
as well as the four beginning with Gulā, each have their respective presiding deity.
One should place the Maṅgalas in the corners beginning with the southeast;
the four forms, Vāsudeva and the others, [should be placed] in the waters of the Maṅgalas.
One should place water with rice in the middle portion between Indra and Agni;
and one should place water with sesame seeds in the middle between Dharma and Pāvaka.
One should place rice-water between Yama and Nairṛti,
and mountain spring water between Nirṛti and Varuṇa.
One should place the water of rain between Varuṇa and Vāyu,
and one should place the water of kuśa grass between Vāyu and Soma.
One should pour tulasī water between Īśāna and Soma;
likewise, one should pour sea water between Īśāna and Indra.
Then, one should properly fill seventeen northern jars with sixty-four [units], as before, with water scented with fragrances. *Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa* 22.153.
Thereafter, the knower of mantras should worship with the root mantra;
having worshipped all the jars according to the rule and in accordance with the ritual procedure.
Having wrapped all the jars in order with cloths,
one should [recite] the Puruṣasūkta mantra for all the items, beginning with the water for washing the feet.
One should perform this with either the root mantra or the three verses beginning with "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
the wise one should worship the Lord of the gods and bathe him with ritual substances.
Then, at the second enclosure, the wise practitioner should perform the ritual bathing with sandalwood water and other substances, using the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 22.157)
One should perform this either with the root mantra or with the three verses beginning "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ";
and one should bathe [the image] in the four directions by means of the four [priests] in sequential order.
With the four substances beginning with sesame oil, using the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* mantra and so forth,
the wise one should thus perform the ablution in the corners of the second enclosure.
Afterwards, with substances such as cow dung and water, one should perform four auspicious ablutions using the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ" and the three verses beginning with "viṣṇornukaṃ."
One should bathe [the image] in the eight directions with mantras in due order:
with the four waters beginning with snow, and with the three verses beginning with "āpo asmāt."
One should bathe [the image] in sequence with the four [verses] beginning with "agnim īḷe" and with water mixed with sesame seeds;
furthermore, one should provide all the substances for the foot-water (pādya) and so forth in great detail. (Viṣṇu 22.162)
Listen with a secret mind; it shall now be told in brief:
*tulasī*, lotus, *dūrvā* grass, *śyāmāka* grain, and *viṣṇuparṇikā*.
The bilva leaf— these are said to be the six components of the water for washing the feet (*pādya*).
[The other ingredients are] rice, husked grain, and white mustard.
Fragrance, flowers, fruit, and milk.
Sesame seeds, barley, and *kuśa* grass are said to be the ten components of the *arghya*; along with camphor, nutmeg, *kakkola*, flowers, cardamom, and cloves.
These six components are indeed prescribed for the water used for sipping (ācamanīyaka):
the Nyagrodha, Aśvattha, Śamī, Plakṣa, Jambū, and Kapittha. (Viṣṇu 22.166)
Khādira, udumbara, madhūka, vikaṅkata, bilva, and palāśa— these are recorded as the twelve [trees] for the decoction. Vis 22.167.
Vajra, coral, pearl, beryl, emerald, and mani-gem; puṣyaka, brahmarāga, sapphire, and garuḍa-gem.
The substances for the water of jewels consist of a collection of ten gems,
as well as jackfruit, mango, wood-apple, plantain, and emblic myrobalan.
The bilva, the havya, the mātuluṅga, the coconut, the pomegranate, and the fruit of the badarī and kuṭaja— these are said to be the twelve fruits.
Śirīṣa, kuśa grass, rājasūrī, vivartanī,
bhūstṛṇa, sadābhadrā, asana, and the two types of tulasī.
And Sahadevī— these are the ten ingredients for cleansing;
likewise uśīra, kuṣṭha, saffron, and sandalwood.
Aloe-wood, deodar, spikenard, and *mura*,
as well as *hari*, *bera*, camphor, *nāṭara*, and pearl; // Vis_22.173 //
These twelve fragrances of scented water are thus described:
[the wood of] bamboo, barley, palāśa, and likewise the lotus.
Tulasī leaves, nīvāra grain, and white mustard seeds—
these are briefly stated to be the ingredients for the water of pacification (śāntyudaka).
The sprout of indravālī, the sprout of bamboo,
the sprout of the aśvattha tree, and likewise the single lotus.
The sprout of the palāśa tree and likewise the lotus flower—
these eight sprouts one should place in the auspicious water.
Gold, silver, copper, iron, as well as tin, gold dust, and likewise bronze; Vis_22.178.
In brief, the eight components of iron-water are said to be:
wild rice, bamboo seeds, barley, mustard, and black gram.
Priyaṅgu grain, rice, and unbroken grains are said to constitute the eightfold offering;
regarding materials such as bowls and garments, one should likewise provide the necessary ritual substances.
Once it has been accepted by the patron, one should begin the ritual bathing;
otherwise, it must not be performed, for the rite would be fruitless.
One should perform this same procedure for all other objects as it has been proclaimed;
indeed, for all the water-pots, the deity is traditionally held to be Nārāyaṇa.
For all those belonging to the Cakrika sect, Brahmā Parameṣṭhin is the deity;
for all other objects as well, the eternal Lord Viṣṇu is the deity.
Having performed the ceremonial bath according to the rules, the preceptor, most skilled in the tantras,
should subsequently bathe [the disciple] with powders mixed with fragrant substances.
One should then rub the powder and bathe [the deity] with scented water;
thereafter, one should worship the deity, beginning first with garments and ornaments.
Then one should devoutly offer the madhuparka to the God of gods;
with devotion, one should worship Puruṣottama like a king with sacrificial porridges (caru).
In front [of him were] many kinds of foods, such as milk-rice and rice with molasses,
as well as various diverse dishes and numerous side-dishes.
The knower of mantras should offer to the deity all kinds of edible foods, cakes, and things that are sweet and flavorful, along with fragrant clarified butter.
One should offer two pieces of jaggery and a plantain fruit;
likewise, one should present a jackfruit and a mango in this same sequence.
Then the preceptor should offer curd-rice both outside and inside;
and whatever substance has been offered, whether it be a flower or even a fruit.
Having placed [the object] before me, the knower of the tantra should give it into my right hand;
the best of mantra-knowers, having honored it with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, should do so while reciting its own name.
Having offered the remainder, he should cause it to be given to all the Vaiṣṇavas;
likewise, the preceptor, being pure and facing the east, should consume the remnant of the oblation.
An elephant or a horse, a village, a group of female slaves,
as well as cattle, various garments, or even gold, according to one's ability.
Gifts should indeed be given to the teachers according to one's wealth;
thus, by the prescribed method, with a thousand auspicious jars.
Having properly bathed Hari with devotion, one obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Bathing Ritual," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-three. Viṣvaksena said:
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the supreme limb of the worship of Hari.
And he [described] the location of that flower garden and its very construction.
Listen with a secret mind to these and other [teachings], ending with the protection of the twilight [periods], for the benefit of practitioners indeed. (Vis 23.2)
O Sage,
one should establish an excellent grove around the temple, either in the northwestern direction, or in the east, or even in the south.
As before, the sacrificer, having honored the preceptor with the permission of the Brahmins, should perform the rite joined by Vaiṣṇavas according to the injunctions. (Viṣṇu 23.4)
Having gratified Hari with a ring, garments, and other offerings,
one should mentally recollect the Imperishable One through that very mind, from the offering of water (arghya) up to the ritual bath.
Having worshipped the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who resides in the center of the solar disc, upon that ground accompanied by conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.
Having inspected that ground together with Vaiṣṇavas, the knower of mantras should have it ploughed with ploughs by Śūdras and Vaiṣṇavas in due order, using the Astra-mantra.
Then, O twice-born one, the patron, having remembered Hari, should cause that ground to be prepared with clay, water, and tools, and should again honor the preceptor. (Vis 23.8)
Having fed the brahmins, he should have a declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) performed there;
then, on that auspicious ground, he should plant flowering trees and so forth in due order.
O best of sages, one should place karavīra, jati, mallikā, and likewise vakula flowers for the worship of the God of gods.
The *campaka*, the *karṇikāra*, and likewise the *nandyāvarta*,
as well as a single leaf from a *tulasī* bush, are said to be equivalent to a lotus.
The vṛkṣavakula tree of Magadha, as well as the kramuka, the panasa, and likewise [others].
As well as plantain and āmalaka, and likewise madhuka and mango.
The coconut, the *ta-thośīra*, sandalwood, *hariberaka*,
the *puṃnāga*, the *vaṃśapuṃnāga*, and also the *kṣudrapuṃnāga*. Vis_23.13 //
He saw pomegranates, sacrificial offerings, and palāśa trees,
as well as other such sights in the celestial grove.
In a flower garden, a Brāhmaṇa should indeed perform [the rite] in due order,
having invited Brāhmaṇas who are endowed with knowledge, devoted to Viṣṇu, and masters of the Vedas.
Having gathered them and adorned them, together with all kinds of drums,
he should first worship Vighneśa, accompanied by ritual offerings.
Having honored the Brahmins with betel leaves and fine garments,
the knower of mantras should likewise remember the Praṇava for these and other such offerings to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Having worshipped [the deity] thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, one should then present betel-leaves in due order;
therefore, O best of sages, it should be done by the most excellent of the twice-born in a grove.
One should sow seeds in the ground, joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and end, while recollecting the mantra of Viṣṇu and the *Viṣṇugāyatrī*. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 23.19)
Likewise, one should plant sprouts and so forth upon the ground in a grove according to the sequential order,
starting from Śakra in the east and extending to Īśāna in the northeast, planting karavīra and other species in succession.
The mantra-practitioner should place [the vessel] as before and sprinkle water with the *praṇavas*;
having brought it by means of the *yantra*, one who is truly pure should perform this daily with Vaiṣṇava mantras.
One should satisfy flowering trees with various kinds of leaves and other such things, up to and including fruit-bearing trees. (Vis 23.22)
One should avoid the *tāla*, the *nimba*, the *rājavṛkṣa*, and the *khadira* tree in a temple of Viṣṇu, as well as in a garden or in one's own house.
If that which is to be avoided is not avoided, there will be no growth; Hari becomes displeased.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid tāla and the other [faults].
O Mahāmati, for the sake of honoring brahmins in this world and for the sake of others, a flower garden dedicated to the imperishable Viṣṇu must be established by brahmins alone.

O Sage, in that very same way, through the worship of Viṣṇu by the king and the Vaiśyas, and through the worship of the God by the Śūdras, there was a gradual [transformation] of Nandavana by the Śūdras.
O Sage, one should cause the great austerity of the Brahmins to be performed through the sequential method;
on this earth, there is joy in the propitiation of the Brahmins, just as before.
Just as a Brahmin plants flowering trees and the like in due order, one may likewise plant them according to one's desire using mantras and water; however, these tasks should be avoided by Śūdras.
Until the time for flowers arrives, one should perform [these rites] right here day after day;
when the time for flowers arrives, [one should offer] sprouts and various kinds of leaves.
Having washed his hands and cut those [flowers], he should have the Śūdras fill the vessel; then,
having taken the vessel containing flowers, a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas [should proceed].
Having lifted it up with the *praṇava* and remembering Hari as being provided with a lid,
one should reach the flower pavilion and fill the flower-vessel.
Afterwards, the practitioner, having sprinkled [the area] with pure water using the mantra, should cover those [faces] and,
having gone outside, [protect] the outer region with the Astra-mantra.
Then, on that wooden plank, the minister, recollecting the Wind deity, should sweep it with a bundle of *kuśa* grass and sprinkle it with water while reciting the *praṇava*.
Having washed the wooden plank with fragrant water while reciting the Viṣṇugāyatrī,
and having washed his own hand with that same water, he should consecrate it with the Praṇava.
O Sage, having taken [the vessel] from the flower-vessel with both hands while reciting the *praṇava*,
one should fill it up to the edge of the fruit, or else with new cloths.
In the same manner, one should sequentially sprinkle all these sprouts and leaves with fragrant water, while recollecting the Praṇava.
Constantly recollecting the deity with a concentrated mind,
one should offer flowers according to the sūtras, even if devoid of physical prostrations.
One should likewise offer blue lotuses and other flowers, as well as the two types of *tulasī*, and garlands endowed with various colors. (Vis 23.38)
Then, having uttered the *praṇava* and recollecting the six-syllable mantra,
the wise one, having filled the flower-vessel, should lift it up with the *praṇava*.
Having remembered Hari slowly and without performing prostrations,
one should approach the side of the deity and place [the offering] in front of the right [hand].
Afterwards, the practitioner should sprinkle those [substances] in sequence with the weapon-mantra;
then, having bowed mentally while recollecting the root-mantra.
Having gone outside, the Vaiṣṇava twice-born man should indeed recite [the mantra];
he should not construct a flower-pavilion in an area outside the temple.
O Sage, he who out of delusion offers external flowers, garlands, and the like, does not obtain the fruit of worship; therefore, one should avoid that.
O great sage, neither Śūdras nor Vaiṣṇavas who are not true devotees should ever, under any circumstances, wear a garland, whether for daily or occasional rites.
And especially for the sake of others through the propitiation of Brahmins,
one should worship Viṣṇu, the imperishable Self, according to one's desire even for the sake of one's own self. (Vis 23.45)
That worship leads to both enjoyment and liberation; therefore, it is distinguished for one's own benefit.
Yet, if a Śūdra out of delusion makes a garland for the worship of a Brāhmaṇa... [23.46]
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, that worship becomes fruitless;
that village goes to its destruction. Therefore, one should avoid it with effort. (ViS 23.47)
O Sage, during the morning, midday, and evening— especially at the six periods of twilight— for both obligatory and occasional rites, as well as for the worship of Brahmins.
One should have all the mantra-offerings of flowers and so forth performed by Brahmins alone;
the merit of sweeping [the temple] is one hundredfold, while that of anointing it is a thousandfold.
A garland of hundreds of thousands [of lamps] is called an infinite lamp;
therefore, O best of sages, among them, the garland of lamps is preeminent.
Having worshipped the God of gods with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and delightful garlands, one should perform the twilight protection rite.
For the sake of protecting the world, and especially for that village,
the wise should perform [this rite] day by day using a vessel made of copper or other materials.

Having filled [the vessels] with flower-pots, as well as dūrvā grass, garlands, and so forth, along with sesame and mustard seeds, one should place lamps upon the eight petals of this [maṇḍala] while reciting that weapon-mantra.
Mixed with cotton-wool, cow-ghee, and sesame oil,
combined with camphor and agallochum, and accompanied by lamps in the eight directions.
Having gathered [the materials] with the *praṇava* alone, one should worship with flowers using the *astra-mantra*,
accompanied by a great lamp and provided with a parasol and chowries.
The knower of mantras should cause it to be whirled above his head with the six-syllable mantra;
after that, together with male and female servants and Vaiṣṇavas.
The wise one should bring the protective lamp, accompanied by the sounds of various conch shells and provided with various musical instruments, either at the front of the seat or outside.
Having joined the six-syllable mantra with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end,
one should subsequently offer a great lamp in front of the inner sanctum.
In this same manner, one should perform the protection of the *sandhyā* during both the obligatory and occasional rites;
especially so in the evening, or at the conclusion of one's adornment.
One should cause it to be performed according to the sequential method, which brings about all prosperity and happiness.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, titled "The Rule for the Limbs of Worship," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-four:
Viṣvaksena—
Now, O Sage, I shall explain specifically the worship of Viṣṇu.
The supreme secret ritual procedure for consecrating with water, perfumes, and so forth.
Having consecrated in due order those Brāhmaṇas who are well-versed in the Vedas, devoted to Viṣṇu, and born of noble families, he should sprinkle them while [the water] is upon their heads.
The knower of mantras should subsequently have a reservoir of water constructed using that very same root mantra, either to the north or to the south of the gateway (gopura).
To the south or to the north of the temple itself, according to the prescribed measure,
one should adorn that place and constantly recite the Praṇava.
Having smeared it with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with scented water while reciting the twelve-syllable mantra, joined with the *praṇava* at the beginning and the end. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 24.5)
Having adorned it on all sides with perfumes and the like, with incense and lamps,
provided with strings of pearls, and beautified with canopies.
The practitioner should thereafter adorn that place with garlands of flags and decorations made of rice flour, using the twelve-syllable vidyā-mantra.
Having sprinkled it with water and fumigated it with incense made of guggulu and agaru, O Sage, one should place the water-jars and other vessels in that delightful spot.
One should place each of these while recollecting Hari with the *praṇava* (the syllable Om):
the water-vessel, the *kumbha*, the *vardhanī*, and many others.
One should place [the vessel] together with a garland and an incense burner while remaining composed;
likewise, one should gradually place other such items upon that ground.
Fragrant divine water for bathing, as well as water itself;
likewise, fragrant substances, uśīra, māñja, and malayaja.
O Sage, having gathered these and other such fragrant substances, one should consecrate them with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra, joined with the Praṇava at both the beginning and the end.
O Sage, having thoroughly cleansed all water-vessels and other items with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī,
and having well-sprinkled others that are filled with filtered water, [one should proceed].
One should fill [the vessels] with the *praṇava* alone, covering each one individually;
[placing therein] cardamom, campaka flowers, ketaka, and blue lotus.
Having taken these flowers— uśīra, mallikā, jasmine, and likewise vakula— one should scatter them individually.
But if even these are not available, O best of sages, one should collect whatever is obtainable from the waters and cast in fragrant flowers.
Having extracted the flower with the *trimātra* [mantra], one should dismiss it with the *praṇava*;
one should wrap it with very fine and firm cloths while reciting the *astra-mantra*.
Then the wise practitioner should grind camphor mixed with sandalwood,
as well as fragrant substances, mālatī flowers, and turmeric, together with the Praṇavas.
Having thus prepared [the offerings], the wise man, recollecting all the gods,
should separately offer to Vardhanī and to Viṣṇu accompanied by Lakṣmī using the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
Having taken water from a water-vessel, one should fill it with the *praṇava*;
having thus filled it and covered it with fine cloths, [one should proceed].
