O best of sages, at the commencement of the worship, one should raise the *uddharanī* and *vardhanī* vessels with the Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra, joined by the *praṇava* (oṃ) at the beginning and the end. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 24.21)
Recalling the Praṇava, one should place excellent water for the daily worship of the deity on the northern side of the pavilion.
Thus, day after day, [one should prepare] the supreme water for the worship of the god.
In the same way, one should offer sandalwood and other substances mixed with camphor,
as well as dūrvā grass, unbroken rice, collyrium, and measured grains of rice.
He offered sesame, cows, gold, curd, and clarified butter as a honey-mixture (madhuparka) oblation;
likewise, for the purpose of bathing, he provided ground turmeric and myrobalan with oil.
Having consecrated all such other articles of worship in every respect with the *praṇava*, one should remove them with the *astra-mantra*.
O best of sages, constantly reciting the Praṇava as an oral purifier,
one who is pure and restrained in speech should, at the end, perform the consecration according to the rules and then lift [the vessel].
Every day, accompanied by the three conch shells (and musical instruments),
one should place [the vessel] on the right side of the deity with the *praṇava* and the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).

One should perform it in this very same way during the six periods of time, beginning with the morning twilight; O best of sages, such is the purificatory rite for both the obligatory and the occasional duties.
In brief, I have described the sequence beginning with water and fragrance;
otherwise, there will undoubtedly be a great fault.
Famine shall arise and there will be a depletion of wealth and grain;
therefore, with every effort, one should have [the rite] performed as enjoined by the rules.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Consecration of Water-Deposits and the Like," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-five.
Nārada said:
O Blessed One, O Viṣṇu, O Lord of Beings, O Viṣvaksena, salutations be unto you!
I wish to know everything regarding the planting of the sprouts of auspiciousness.
What are the characteristics of the *pālikā* and likewise the *ghaṭikā*, and how is the *śarāva* described? And what would be the number of these measures?
What would be their color, their names, and their substances;
and what would be their presiding deities, and the auspicious or inauspicious nature of their sprouts?
"Explain all of this to me, for my curiosity is indeed great. Viṣvaksena said:
"Henceforth, I shall proclaim the expansion of the sprout of auspiciousness."
One should make a golden *pālikā* vessel and a silver vessel in the shape of a water-jar;
the shallow bowl (*śarāva*) should be made of copper, or all of them may indeed be made of copper.
Alternatively, the wise one, having fashioned all [the images] out of clay according to his means,
should proceed.
Or one may fashion small earthenware vessels and the like.
The height is thirty-six finger-breadths, its width half of that,
and the base is known to be twelve; this is proclaimed as the measurement for *pālikās*.
The height should be twenty-four finger-breadths and the width twelve;
the five-faced water-clock (ghaṭikā) should be made with a width of five finger-breadths.
One quarter [of the height] is known to be eight finger-breadths; this is proclaimed as the measurement for the *ghaṭikās*.
The height is twelve finger-breadths, and the width is likewise the same.
O Sage, the base of all the shallow bowls should be known to be six finger-breadths; however, the stem should be made according to their specific form or at the discretion of the craftsman.
One should have it made according to the sequential method, smooth and provided with apertures;
or one may make the *pālikā* vessels and so forth in sequence as desired.
Knowing this, O best of sages, one should perform the rite of offering the seed-sprouts during the consecration and other festivals,
as well as during ritual ablutions and the witnessing of sacrifices.
O Sage, [one should do so] at the equinoxes, at the solstices, during eclipses, as well as when there is a conjunction with an auspicious lunar mansion, or even under the lunar mansion of the Sun.
One should cause the rite of offering the sprouts to be performed in every ritual;
however, performing it without the offering of sprouts brings misfortune and inauspiciousness.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have the offering of sprouts performed;
there should indeed be sixteen auspicious plantings of sprouts for each [deity].
And I shall tell you their names as well, O best of sages:
Sundara, Asundara, Vikrama, and Muraśāsana.
Vīrasena, Virāma, Somadatta, Mahāhanu,
Yajñabhuk, Sarvabhuk, Manuja, and likewise Mardana.
Agnigrīva, Hayagrīva, Vāyugrīva, and Mahāhanu—
these sixteen are declared here by name as the Pālikās.
I shall now describe the *ghaṭikās* exactly as they are, O Nārada:
Vega, Avega, Suvega, and likewise Vāyuvega.
Lord of Fire, Lord of Wind, Lord of the Oblation, Lord of Horses;
the consumer of all, the sustainer of all, the all-pervading, and likewise the devourer of all.
Subhuja, Durbhuja, Bhujaga, Vahnija, and Īśvara—
these sixteen are declared by name to be the lords of the ghaṭikās.
I shall now state, in due order, the names of the Śarāvas:
Rājarāja, Virāja, Suketu, and Kīrtivardhana.
He whose deeds are like those of Indra, whose deeds are great, whose deeds are divine, O wise ones;
he is the lord of sacrifice, the lord of oblations, the auspicious conjunction, and the delighter of the gods.
Maṇipriya, Mahāmāya, Devamāya, and Sukhapriya—
these sixteen are declared to be the names of the Śarāvas.
I shall now explain the colors in their proper order:
the four beginning with Sundara are proclaimed to be white in color.
Vīrasena and the others are red; Yajñabhuja and the others are dark-complexioned; all the remaining Pālikās are proclaimed to be black in color.
O Sage, all sixteen *pālikās* (or perhaps all of them) may be white in color; indeed,
their colors may be exactly like this.
And of all the ghaṭikās in every respect.
White and red is prescribed for all types of shallow bowls;
alternatively, all shallow bowls may indeed be of red color.
The *pālikās* are white in color, while the *ghaṭikās* are indeed black;
it is traditionally taught that the *śarāvas* are sixteen [in number] and red in color. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 25.29.
The expansion of the phonemes has been explained; now hear the procedure for the deposition of the seed-syllables (bīja), whether in a temple, a pavilion, or a wall, O best of sages.
There, having smeared the ground according to the rules, one should fashion a square mandala;
situated therein, one should indeed draw the forty-eight positions in sequence.
Having smeared the thread with rice flour mixed with water while reciting the root mantra,
one should stretch out a new thread from east to west and strike it upon the ground.
In that very same way, O best of sages, one should cause the twelfth thread to be drawn from south to north, having struck it with the mantra of the weapon.
O best of sages, one should properly wipe the footprints for the sake of the path;
having skipped every second footprint, one should gradually sweep the third.
O Best of Sages, having recognized this, one should have well-proportioned steps made here, measuring either one and a half tālas or even just one tāla in height.
Furthermore, one should properly worship those receptacles with fragrant water;
thereafter, one should fill them with grain consisting of śāli rice.
Having arranged all of them in three rows, one by one in sequential order,
one should place them starting with grain and ending in the northeast (Īśāna) direction.
Having first established [the deities] with the twelve-syllable mantra,
one should then establish all of them individually and separately, each in their proper order.
Then one should properly fill them with soft sand and dried cow dung;
having filled them all equally, one should then worship them in due order.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the wise one,
the knower of mantras, should then take up the seeds after having performed the worship.
Sesame, mung beans, as well as black gram, neem seeds, flat beans, rice, barley, śyāmāka, nīvāra, kuluttha, kaṅgu, and mustard seeds.
These twelve are prescribed for the rite of auspicious sprouts;
first, one should wash them with milk using the Parameṣṭhin seed-mantra.
Furthermore, one should wash it afterwards with the seed-syllable of the Puruṣa-self;
then, one should slowly perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the mantra "jitam te."
From the southeast (Āgneya) to the northeast (Īśa), one should proceed in order along each row;
then, one should perform the offering of ghee together with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass.
Then, having wrapped each of the *pālikās* individually in unwashed cloths,
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homayet*) either in the eastern or the northern part of the field.
One should offer sixteen oblations each of fuel sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice;
then, having specially sprinkled the clay pots and other items with the residual drops of clarified butter.
In a windless place, one should perform [the rite] in the northeast corner of a pavilion;
for nine days or seven nights, one should worship with fragrant water.
O best of sages, having wrapped each [image] individually with garlands beginning with *śirīṣa* sprouts, one should then wrap them individually with *dūrvā* sprouts, or perhaps wrap them first.
Having honored the auspicious day (puṇyāha) with perfumes and other offerings along with unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
one should present oblations (bali) in all directions throughout the eight quarters.
One should worship with oblations, perfumes, and flowers day after day; this is declared to be the "Placement of the Seeds" (bījanyāsa). Now I shall tell you of the deities.
Likewise, the four divine forms beginning with Vāsudeva, as well as the eight weapons beginning with the conch, are the deities of the *pālikās*. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 25.51)
Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, Hayaśīrṣaka,
Rāma the son of Jamadagni, Vāmana, and Yadunandana.
Nara and Nārāyaṇa, as well as Hari and Kṛṣṇa;
the Fish, the Tortoise, Tārkṣya, and Ananta, the best of serpents.
Thus these sixteen deities of the ghaṭikās have been declared:
the twelve beginning with Viṣṇu, as well as Haṃsa and Bala.
Kapila and Hala are the deities of the earthenware dishes;
others, however, say that the three deities are indeed Candra, Agni, and Āditya.
O Lord of Sages, by drinking yellow sprouts one attains Viṣṇu, and by white ones, Brahmā and Rudra; one obtains auspiciousness, and by drinking white ones, one may attain divinity.
Both black and red colors always indicate an inauspicious outcome;
one will swiftly meet death, especially if the wound is still unhealed and accompanied by suppuration.
The destruction of the substance from the dark sprout shall belong to both the doer and the instigator;
for these [acts], I have declared a healthy festival. (Vis 25.58)
Thus has this been correctly explained to you in great detail regarding the sprouts.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Planting of Sprouts," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-Six:
Viṣvaksena—
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme rite of raising the banner (dhvajotthāpana).
By which misfortunes are destroyed, and all prosperity and happiness are brought forth.
Without a banner, the sacrifice to Viṣṇu will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
On the twenty-seventh day prior to the day of bathing at the sacred ford, [one should perform it].
Or it may take place on the twenty-first day, at which time one should perform the raising of the banner;
or else, on the very day of the commencement, it may occur immediately.
One should perform the raising of the banner during the day, and the planting of the seed-sprouts at night;
however, on a single day for the sacrifice, the hoisting of the banner is not desired.
The second [rite] is proclaimed as being preceded by the offering of the sprouts;
one should fashion the pedestal for the banner between the gateway and the location of the path.
Alternatively, leaving a space of one cubit either from the sacrificial pedestal or from the [image of] Vainateya, [one should place it] within the area of the sacrificial pedestal.
One should fashion the base for the banner; they declare its measurement to be as follows:
one may fashion the base for the banner by setting aside half of that [measurement].
Having established it in the middle of the pillar, four cubits or half of that in width and length, and one cubit or two cubits in height, all equal in its proportions.
The wise one should likewise fashion an auspicious pit one cubit deep in the ground beneath the pedestal,
and around the pillar, he should construct three tiers of molding.
Whether circular, square, or sixteen- or eight-cornered, its interior and so forth, as well as its height, should be [measured] in finger-breadths according to the sequence.

The height and width of each of the enclosures (mekhalā) shall be four finger-breadths; having left a space of one palm (tāla) all around on the altar-platform (vedikā), [the next enclosure is placed]. Vis_26.11.
Thereafter, the best of those who know mantras should properly fashion the girdles;
above the girdles, one should construct a circular altar.
With a height of four finger-breadths, one should draw a lotus petal (or lotus) above that,
having either sixteen, twelve, or eight petals.
O Sage, it should be known that the thickness, including the pericarp, is two finger-breadths;
its height is three finger-breadths, and its thickness should be two finger-breadths.
Thus has the procedure for the lotus petals been declared, categorized as superior, inferior, and middling;
one should construct the pillar surrounded by all manner of ornaments.
In the manner thus described, one should fashion the pedestal for the banner;
one may fashion this excellent pedestal either before or after [the installation].
Otherwise, if the sacrificial altar (vedi) should be useless and bring about inauspiciousness,
therefore one should have it constructed with every effort according to the injunctions.
O great sage, I shall describe the banner-pole in its pure form:
it may be made of sandalwood, or campaka, or bilva, or even arjuna wood.
The teka tree, the khadira, the sāla, and the tinduka;
the campaka, the aṣṭaka, the betel nut, and the coconut.
In this case, one should likewise have the palm and the flute made according to their proportions;
the best, middling, and lowest sizes are respectively half and half again of one hundred *tālas*.
Some maintain that it should be eighty *tāla*s in height, or even half of that;
it may be shaped like a city gate (*gopura*), or the pillar itself may be one and a half [units].
The height of the pillar should be equal to the measurement of the temple, or even one and a half times that; its elevation should be free from cavities and other defects.
O Nārada, the base of the staff should have a circumference of thirty finger-breadths;
the middle part twenty-eight,
and its tip should be twenty-six.
For below the Garuda-abode, one should place a perforated machine;
there, one should install a Garuda made either of iron or wood.
Seated facing the gods, with body small and hands joined in reverence,
[the image] should be sixteen finger-breadths or likewise twelve finger-breadths in height.
O Sage, having measured eight finger-breadths, one should fashion Garuḍa;
or likewise, O Lord of Sages, having prepared a wooden plank, one may do so according to one's desire.
Having drawn Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā, in his own place in the center of that [mandala],
one should then install the Lord of the Sky (Kheśa) with his respective mantra.
Upon the altar, the knower of mantras should fashion a beautiful flight of stairs,
adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass and provided with strings of pearls.
One should attach banners there at the eastern side of the water-shed,
measuring ten cubits, seven cubits, or even five cubits.
One should attach another eight-fingered staff to the pillars and the mechanical devices;
regarding that, I shall tell you the specific characteristics of the cloth-painting.
Listen attentively to that which brings about all prosperity and happiness:
it may be twelve cubits, ten cubits, or nine or seven cubits in length.
The length has thus been fully described; now the width is being stated:
the width of the door is said to be sixty-seven tālas.
The length of the face should be two tālas; the head is said to be equal to that.
The arms should be known to be equal to the head, or indeed half of it.
Or this painting may be distinguished by being devoid of two arms;
if it has the form of a small palace, there should be nine or seven cloths.
Indeed, anything less than nine cubits is not permitted for a great residence;
if one builds it out of delusion, all ritual activity therein becomes fruitless. (Viṣṇudharmottara 26.35)
There, one should draw Garuḍa, golden-hued and radiant;
from his fixed gaze down to his throat and navel, such is the desired height of Garuḍa.
Measured by nine palm trees according to its height, width, and circumference,
he had slightly elongated and rounded eyes, red eyes, and a blue nose.
With his left foot raised and his right placed behind,
he begins to move through the sky, accompanied by the flapping of his wings.
He holds his hands joined in a gesture of flower-offering, possesses a fierce majesty, and is the son of Vinatā;
he is adorned with serpent ornaments, has a smiling face, and wears golden armlets.
Wearing a crown and a blue garment, he was pleasing to behold;
the palms of his hands and the soles of his feet were deeply red, and his face shone with two fangs.
Ananta is his left armlet, while Vāsuki is his sacred thread;
Takṣaka is his waistband, and Karkoṭaka is likewise his necklace.
Padma is on the right ear, while Mahāpadma is on the left;
Śaṅkha is in the region of the head, and Gulika is between the arms.
Adorned by these eight primordial and supreme serpents, there are two brahmins,
Ananta and Gulika, who are red in color and born from fire.
Vāsuki and Śaṅkhapāla are yellow; the two kings born from the Moon are yellow;
Mahākṣa and Takṣaka are the courtesans; and those born from Water are white.
Having drawn Padma and Karkoṭaka, who are Śūdras, dark in color, and born from Vāyu,
one should place Garuḍa there and arrange a parasol above him.
Furthermore, one should draw a jar of nectar and a lotus here;
on both sides of these two, one should place two lamps of auspicious appearance.
The best of mantra-knowers should cause the installation of the variegated manifestation;
the preceptor, having gathered water, should perform the preliminary consecration of the image.
Having then laid [the image] upon the altar, having withdrawn it and generated it according to reality,
one should deposit a heap of grain all around the center of the altar.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Ananta upon the kalaśas of the altar;
furthermore, one should arrange auspicious objects such as conch shells around it in due order.
One should place the conch in the east, and likewise the discus in the southeast;
one should set up the banner in the south, and prosperity in the southwest.
A mirror in the western quarter, a bull in the region of Vāyu (the northwest),
a pair of fish in the northern quarter, and a jar in the region of Īśāna (the northeast).
Having thus deposited the auspicious symbols in the sequence beginning with the east,
one should worship the eight auspicious signs in the jars according to their proper order.
When these have been wrapped in garments and gold has been placed within them,
one should spread the garments out in the middle and lay Garuḍa there.
Then, having covered the Lord of Birds with cloths so that his neck faces inward,
one should place a water-pot upon rice to the south of him.
It was filled with water and well-covered with a pair of soft,
very beautiful white garments— new, unwashed, and of excellent quality.
In that [vessel], which is adorned with jewels, joined with gold, provided with a lid, and equipped with a wick-holder,
one should invoke the god Garuḍa, the son of Vinatā.
O great sage, I shall correctly explain the procedure for invocation:
[one should use] a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 26.57)
Having invoked the deity from the sky into that vessel filled with either milk or water to the capacity of one āḍhaka, the most excellent knower of mantras [should proceed].
Come, come, O Lord of Birds, Vainateya of great strength!
Grant your presence together with your attendants; homage, homage to you!
The knower of mantras should bring that deity, fallen into the vessel, into the water of the jar by means of the root mantra; that mantra is now being stated.

Oṃ! Homage to Garuḍa, who is adorned by the serpents of the eight families, who is the son of Vinatā, whose limbs are smeared with the blood of the *nāgas*, the fair-winged one, who dwells in the seven underworlds, the king of birds, the vehicle of the Blessed One, the agitator of the three worlds, the seed of the end of the age,
the destroyer of grief for his mother— slay, slay!
"Vighnanāśāya svāhā!
Having praised the Lord of Birds with this, his own mantra,
one should always invoke the presence of the King of Birds there.
Having thus addressed Garuḍa, one should display the banner mudrā:
placing the right hand level upon the left.
One should move the thumb there and display the banner mudrā;
thus one should perform the mudrā of Garuḍa, who is adorned with serpents.
Having worshipped it thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings, indeed up to incense and lamps,
one should then [visualize] the image on the cloth as lying upon Garuḍa.
Having withdrawn [the elements] by way of dissolution, one should again generate them in sequence:
the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth, starting from the seed-syllables (bīja) and so forth, in their proper order.
Having placed the [mantras] together with their respective designations, the preceptor should fashion the mantra-body;
having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, he should do so by way of meditation.
One should sprinkle him with water contained in the pitcher using one's own vidyā;
likewise, one should sprinkle Ananta and the others with the waters from the pitchers situated in the east and other directions, using their respective names.
One should sprinkle [the offerings] in sequence with kuśa grass, using mantras beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*,
while praying for their presence until the conclusion of the sacrifice.
Then one should worship the Lord of Birds with all the ritual offerings;
one should present as the food offering (naivedya) mung-bean rice soaked in ghee.
Having first offered mouth-perfume, one should then commence the rite of fire-oblation (homa),
having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there according to the rules in the four directions.
Having established the Vaiṣṇava fire there, one should commence the rite of oblation (homa),
offering one hundred and eight oblations each of fuel-sticks (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), and sacrificial porridge (caru).
Four Brahmins,
having been initiated, wearing upper garments and well-adorned, should offer oblations simultaneously.
The teachers have declared that there are four forms of the King of Birds;
all the guardians of the forms, meditating upon those forms, should offer oblations ending with "svāhā."
Having thus completed the fire sacrifice, they should touch the Lord of Birds (Khageśvara) on his feet,
belly, mouth, and head, in that order.
Alternatively, O Sage, the one most skilled in the tantras, having approached the eastern direction, should perform a single oblation with the root mantra.
Or, O Sage, one may perform the installation of Garuḍa even without a fire sacrifice;
except for the banner, it should be performed with fourfold gold according to the sequence.
Having thus completed the fire sacrifice (homa) and the installation of Garuḍa,
or else, O best of sages, the supreme consecration (adhivāsana) in this [rite].
I shall explain in brief, preceded by the rite for an auspicious day;
having caused the auspicious day to be performed together with Brahmins, one who knows the mantras [should proceed].
Thereafter, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) with the mantra of Vainateya;
and upon the altar, one should fill it with grain measuring one bhāra.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus and cover it again with cloth;
then one should place half as much rice and half of that amount of sesame seeds.
Having spread cloths upon the altar, one should cover it again;
having strewn red flowers, one should worship with fragrant flowers.
There, one should cause the deity to lie down according to the previously mentioned procedure;
there, one should worship Garuḍa with all offerings up to incense and lamps.
One should place the supreme pitcher on the right side of the deity;
into that pitcher, one should invoke the mighty Vainateya.
The lord of the sky, fallen from the heavens, was established indeed in the form of a banner:
"Come, O lord of the sky, mighty-armed Vainateya of great strength!"
"Be present, O Lord of Birds; be gracious here; homage be to you!
Having thus invoked [the deity] with this very mantra, the preceptor—
Then one should worship Viṣṇu in the jar with substances such as perfumes and flowers;
thereafter, one should place eight jars around that central jar.
One should install Indra and the others, from Indra up to Īśāna, in sequence;
having worshipped the world-protectors in the jars with perfumes and flowers.
Outside of that, one should place the eight auspicious symbols all around;
then, having performed worship, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) in due order upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the east.
The preceptor should duly offer one hundred and eight oblations each of fuel sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice to Vainateya, using the root mantra.
Having first uttered the *praṇava*, then the salutation (*namaskāra*) in sequence,
and afterwards the twenty-fourth [letter], which is the third consonant.
One should likewise utter the twenty-ninth [syllable] joined with the first vowel,
and afterwards, the sixteenth [syllable] joined with the eleventh vowel.
The wise know the root mantra to be the word *vainateya*, followed by the dative case ending and joined with the utterance *svāhā*. Vis_26.92.
Having completed the fire sacrifice according to the rules, one should invoke [the deity] upon the cloth from the ritual jar;
then, having sprinkled that cloth with the three-verse hymn beginning with "haṃsaḥ śuciṣad," [one should proceed].
Having invoked Garuḍa, who is adorned with serpents, by means of the root mantra,
one should sprinkle him according to the ritual rules that night and worship him with perfumes and flowers.
One should worship that Lord of Birds with parched grain flour mixed with sugar-cane juice, with mung bean rice and rice cooked in molasses, and with various other kinds of edible foods.
Then one should offer mouth-perfume and satisfy [the deity] with a hymn of praise;
one should worship Indra and the other deities starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
O best of sages, the sequence of activities such as dissolution is not accepted in this system;
rather, I have taught the two-fold sequence of the ritual for consecration.
In this case, one should perform it in a single manner according to the teacher's wish;
then, during that night, the invocation of the deities should be performed with their respective mantras.
O tiger among sages, for the sake of protecting the world,
one should have it constructed on the upper part of the temple so that it faces toward Garuḍa.
Filled with two *droṇas* of water, red in color,
and wrapped with three threads of string, it should be adorned with five jewels and sprouts.
Equipped with two bundles of kūrca grass, adorned with red garlands,
wrapped in a pair of cloths, and filled with perfumes and flowers.
In a jar endowed with these characteristics, the wise man should invoke Indra,
Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, and likewise Varuṇa.
Vāyu, Soma, and likewise Īśāna, the Moon, the Sun, and the hosts of Maruts;
the eight Vasus, as well as the eleven Rudras, and Vināyaka.
Kārttikeya, Vīrabhadra, those known as the twelve Ādityas,
the three-eyed god, the five-faced deity, Nīlakaṇṭha, and Umāpati.
Then he should likewise summon all the lords of beings together with their hosts,
as well as the Mothers, Durgā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Sarasvatī.
One should lead Kānti, Śānti, Śuci, Mudrā, Umā, and likewise Lakṣmī,
together with their hosts and retinues, into the water of the pitcher.
Then, O Nārada, one should invoke the gods, Kumuda and the others,
and with great care, one should bring their retinues into the jar.
One should invoke [the deities] from Indra to Īśāna into the water of the pitcher;
then, one should perform the worship of the deities residing in the pitcher-water with perfumes and flowers.
Having thus concluded with incense and lamps accompanied by the sound of a bell,
one should afterwards present the sacrificial offering for the sake of pleasing all the gods.
It would be equivalent to having committed a different [offense], and a great fault will arise; he who destroys that village, or even one who remains there, shall go to hell.
Therefore, with every effort, one should place the attendants in that jar;
and in the northeast quarter of the pavilion, at a measurement of four cubits.
Having smeared it with cow dung, one should prepare an altar of rice using eight *droṇas*, or half of that, or half of that again, or even half of that once more. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 26.112.
One should fill the center of the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and draw an eight-petaled lotus;
then, reciting the Praṇava, one should cover the lotus with a new cloth.
One should lay [the corpse] down with its head to the south, following the sequence starting from the south;
having placed a new, well-characterized drum (bherikā) in the middle of that.
The preceptor, the most excellent knower of mantras, wearing an upper garment and a turban,
should face west and worship that drum in due order.
Having worshipped thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings while recollecting Hari with the primordial mantra,
one should strike it throughout that night until the end of the night.
Afterwards, accompanied by dance and song, one should proceed with the five great sounds;
then, joined with the uṣṇīṣa, [one receives initiation] from the Yāmalācārya in due order.
One should have all the members of the assembly, beginning with Vainateya, depicted in due order;
having thus made the proclamation, one should be joined by the teacher of the Yamala.
One should especially perform the "five great sounds" until the end of the night for the sake of pleasing all the gods; this always increases auspiciousness. (Viṣṇu 26.119)
There shall be prosperity for both the village and the king, and likewise for the cities and so forth;
therefore, one should strike that drum at night with every effort.
Otherwise, there will certainly be great calamity and the ruin of the kingdom;
that village will surely meet its destruction and be afflicted by diseases.
Having performed it in this manner according to the ritual injunctions, one should then carry out the festival of the banner (dhvajotsava).
Then, at the clear dawn, [the area] will resound with the noise of conchs and drums.
Having adorned [the image] with all ornaments, one should wander through the village;
at the time of wandering, one should offer the oblation with a concentrated mind.
One should first worship the gods, beginning with Indra and ending with Lakṣmī, right there with rice mixed with saffron powder, milk, and curd.
A coconut fruit, likewise provided with the five substances,
combined with these as an offering of food (balyanna), should indeed be presented as a bali-offering during the festival.
Thereafter, one should perform the rites in sequence as before, preceded by the fire offering (homa).
One should raise the banner during the day and perform the invocation at night.
One should perform the invocation of the deity upon the banner especially at midday;
one should carry out the hoisting of the banner during the day and the planting of the sprouts at night.
Having offered the bali-oblation with sacrificial food at the two door-sills and the pedestal,
one should worship the gods in the center upon an altar measuring one cubit in the middle.
Having commenced the offering of the bali, one should perform it in the dwellings of villages and so forth;
one should then place [the deities] beginning with Indra and ending with Brahmā in the cardinal and intermediate directions in due order.
Having invoked the deity into that jar, one should worship with its water;
there, one should properly worship the gods beginning with Indra in the east and ending with Lakṣmī.
Then, having joined them with their respective hosts in the dwellings of villages and other places,
one should worship Kumuda and the other deities in their proper sequence.
The preceptor, wearing washed garments and standing facing north,
should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, [the directions] beginning from Indra and ending with Īśāna.
Having uttered their names, the wise one should offer the bali-oblation;
for as long as the sacrifice lasts, the deities of the bali remain present.
In this regard, there is a specific distinction concerning the sequence of offerings to the deities,
particularly at the time of hoisting the banner and during festivals.
O Sage, from the conclusion of the sacrifice until the end of [the worship of] Indra and the others,
and until the end of Lakṣmī at midday, one should proceed according to the sequence.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, as well as with oblations, in the center of the altar;
one should present the sacrificial food (bali) as it is obtained, at midday and during the nights, in due order.
O great sage, for them there are auspicious offerings to Viṣṇu that bring him delight, intended for the festival at the conclusion of the festival of sprouts.
For the sake of accomplishing the sacrifice, one should perform the worship of the sacrificial pavilion;
at the conclusion of that worship, O best of sages, one should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rule.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should perform the bali offering, beginning with Kumuda and the others,
extending as far as the end of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and likewise throughout the dwellings of villages and other settlements.
Otherwise, the offering for the carrying away [of the deity] would be performed as a flag-sacrifice;
through the destruction of the flag-sacrifice, the festival would become fruitless.
Through the destruction of the festival, the daily worship becomes fruitless;
indeed, the cessation of daily worship is the cause of universal destruction.
Therefore, with every effort, perform the invocation offering;
having summoned Garuḍa to the dwelling, perform a circumambulation.
Having remembered the ritual procedure for the time and subsequently made the proclamation of the auspicious day (puṇyāha),
one should lay the flagpole on the southern side of the pedestal.
Having placed its tip toward the south, one should set its root toward the north;
at the western gate of the temple, the preceptor should likewise cause it to lie toward the north.
O Great Sage, if it is thus at the southern gate,
one should place the head of Indra upon the eastern side of the pedestal near the flagstaff.
Having placed its base in a pit while recollecting the root mantra,
the northern gate should likewise be prepared for the hoisting of the banner.
Otherwise, O best of sages, there would be great harm causing the lack of prosperity for both the village and the king; day by day, the path of Dharma would perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have that which is enjoined by the ritual rules performed;
having washed the pillar with water from the great jar while reciting the mantra.
Taking up that banner, the wise one, most skilled in mantras, should sprinkle it with the root mantra and then fasten it to the flagpole.
Having made it steady, the preceptor should lift it up with a flagpole,
or he may lift it with a mechanical device together with a rope.
One should construct the altar as previously described, endowed with the proper characteristics;
having thoroughly smeared the altar and performed the recitation for auspiciousness (svastivācana), [one should proceed].
The practitioner, having wrapped *darbha* grass from the tip of the staff down to its base,
and indeed having encircled it with a garland of *darbha* and so forth, [proceeds] precisely from the tip of the staff to the end of the base.
Water for the feet, water for sipping, perfume, flowers, and likewise incense,
as well as a lamp according to the requirements, accompanied by the sounding of a bell.
One should worship Garuḍa and subsequently offer him the sacrificial oblation (caru),
consisting of rice mixed with fruits and parched barley flour, along with boiled mung beans soaked in ghee.
Having placed [the food] in a separate vessel, one should offer it to Garuḍa;
likewise, having given water for drinking and sipping, as well as mouth-perfume.
Having thus worshipped the auspicious Garuḍa, who is dear to all the gods,
one should then worship his retinue, beginning with the guardians of the directions and ending with those who are without beginning or end.
Then, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) at the base of the altar;
one should worship them individually by their own names, according to the sequence starting from the east.
In this manner, one should perform [this] every day at both twilights;
and whatever substance has been offered—whether food, flowers, or fruit.
That should be known as the *piṇḍa*; one should cause it to be offered to women who are auspicious, virtuous, pure, and devoted to auspicious vows. (Viṣṇu 26.159)
Remembering that as "Prasāda," having bathed and fasted, the woman of auspicious countenance should, while meditating on Garuḍa, consume it; thus a barren woman gives birth to a son.
One afflicted by disease shall be freed from disease; one who is bound shall be released from bondage;
one in peril shall be freed from fear, and one shall attain perfect knowledge.
For the purpose of invoking the gods, one should place Garuḍa upon the cloth;
on that cloth, one should invoke all the gods day after day.
A banner is established either with an image made of metal or wood, or even without one;
provided that an image of Garuḍa has been fashioned upon the cloth of the banner.
Having fashioned a variegated banner equipped with flags and pennants,
and having placed an image upon it, the supreme guide should install it.
When the Vaiṣṇava sacrifice has been completed according to the rules at the conclusion of the ritual bathing,
one should offer the *bhūtabali* at night and, in due order, dismiss the attendants (*pārṣada*).
One should perform the flower sacrifice according to the prescribed ritual;
O Śakra, the procedure for the flower sacrifice has been declared by me in this manual.
Having likewise drawn the maṇḍala, one should worship it according to that procedure.
O bull among sages, I shall now describe the ritual for the flower-sacrifice in brief. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 26.167)
That which is the sacrifice to the Lord of Gods within a mandala filled with flowers is called the Flower Sacrifice (puṣpayāga); one should perform it at the conclusion of the festival.
Alternatively, on the roof of a palace, or in the southern, western, or northern direction,
having constructed the previously described pavilion, one should draw [the mandala] within that pavilion.
Either in a pleasure pavilion or wherever the mind finds delight,
one should likewise draw the great infinite mandala, as well as the lotus within the wheel.
Or else, the layout of the lines should be auspicious and performed according to the rules;
it may be one cubit, two cubits, or equal to the inner sanctum.
Having made it square and even with the cord itself,
the preceptor [should lay] twenty-one cords running east-west and north-south.
One should strike out [the lines] so that there are four hundred squares here;
in the center, sixteen squares are declared to be the field of the lotus.
Then, having released the outer row, one should thereafter cause the triple row to be grasped;
one should release it all around in sequence, distinguishing between the feet and the limbs.
The wise one should project six [units] inside and six outside, with a square in the middle, for the sake of the limbs in the four directions.
One should perform six lines inside and five outside, including half of the corner-lines;
then, one should erase two rows all around on the outside for the sake of the pathway.
And [one should place] two at the vicinity of the door-neck, two for the external beauty,
four inside, and four outside for the sake of the doors in the four directions.
One should cleanse three lines internally and one externally; by reversing this order, one should cleanse one line internally and five externally, marking the corners.
One should rotate the mandala for the field as previously described for the lotus;
however, the outer portion measuring half the size of the lotus-field should be divided into twelve parts.
Having released [the breath], one should rotate the head; the field of the petals is circular.
First is the field of the pericarp, and the second is that of the filaments.
The third [line] is for the joints of the petals, and the fourth for the tips of the petals;
having struck the diagonal lines, one then [marks] the intermediate directions from the corners.
Having fixed [the thread] at the tips of the filaments, one should then rotate it to the edge of the petal;
then, one should place the thread at the joint, measuring the distance between the edges of the petals.
One should rotate the tip of the petal there, and immediately after that, its point;
this is declared to be the common [method] for the lotus-wheel. Now listen to that [specific method]. Vis_26.183.
One should rotate the axle-field with a measurement of twelve finger-breadths;
the nave should be equal to the axle-field, and one should draw two outer lines.
Outside of that, the field of spokes (ara-kṣetra) measures one finger-breadth;
there, one should fashion a lotus as previously described, complete with a pericarp and filaments.
The width of the non-axle-field is equal to that of the two axle-fields;
the circular rim at the end of the wheel-field shall be half the extent of the axle-field.
One should cause spokes to be made there, placing two spokes for each petal;
having divided the field of the spokes into three parts according to the arrangement of the three qualities (guṇas).

The first is indeed characterized by goodness (sāttvika), the second is of the nature of passion (rājasa), and the third is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa); one should perform them with equanimity, O best of the twice-born.
The *sāttvika* [seat] is shaped like a water-jar; the *rājasa* is shaped like *dūrvā* grass;
the *tāmasa* is shaped like a tortoise; and likewise, above that, it is shaped like a pedestal (*pīṭha*).
One should also act as if forming a wrist-joint behind the seat;
the vessel with its opening downward is the navel-field, which is the middle [of the three].
It should have the form of a crest up to the rim; the remainder may be according to one's preference.
In this very manner, the lotus-wheel is described.
One should fill the mandala with flowers, starting from the pericarp and proceeding in due order;
for the flower-sacrifice, flowers of five colors are auspicious.
White, red, yellow, black, and green—
these are the pure colors, as well as others that are mixed.
Having cut flowers from among the various groups of blossoms, the wise one should fill the pericarp with yellow substances and the filaments with red ones.
O best of the twice-born, the pericarp-circle should be red or green;
one should fill the circle at the end of the filaments with white flowers.
On the bases of the petals, the best of instructors should fill them with white and red [pigments] mixed together; from the tips of the petals, he should fill them with red flowers.
O best of Brahmins, one should fill the junctions of the petals with dark-colored flowers,
and the lines between the petals with green flowers.
One should fill the navel line with beautiful white flowers,
O best of sages, and one should fill the middle line with yellow flowers.
The knower of mantras should likewise mark the boundary lines with red flowers,
and the spokes and the northern line with green and red flowers.
O twice-born one, one should fill the lines beginning with the rim up to the rim with black [pigment],
the rim with white flowers,
and then with red or yellow flowers.
The Flower Mandala is specifically prescribed for the Flower Sacrifice;
thus, a wise person should have a lotus within a wheel constructed according to these characteristics.
Whatever penance there may be for acts beginning with hoisting a banner and ending with visiting a sacred site,
one should perform a flower sacrifice (puṣpayāga) for the purpose of destroying those faults.
O best of the twice-born, one should construct a pavilion in front of the temple, either to the south, the west, or the north, following the same sequence as before.
In its center, the wise one should draw a lotus within a wheel, endowed with all the proper characteristics;
and at each door, he should place two small jars.

In the same manner, one should place shallow bowls (śarāva) in the directions starting from the east in due order; likewise, one should place small jars (pālikā) in sequence, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna.
Having placed auspicious objects such as the conch and so forth at its sides in due order,
one should fill the mandala with flowers, starting from the pericarp, in the proper sequence.
One should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the four directions beginning with the east;
one should place Śrī and the others upon the lotus in the intermediate directions in due order.
One should also worship the retinues beginning with Indra in their respective directions in due order, and Viṣvaksena and Garuḍa right there in that same vicinity.
Thus should the wise one practice yoga in the mandala of flower arrangements; he goes to the same world as Viṣṇu and should perform sacrifice through the sacrifice of knowledge.
O Śakra, I have declared the ritual procedure for the flower-sacrifice in this manual;
having drawn that maṇḍala, one should worship it according to that same procedure. Vis_26.210.
Having offered the *bali* for the cruel spirits (*bhūtakrūra*), and having gradually dismissed the attendants (*pārṣada*),
one should bathe, sip water, become pure, and worship the Lord of Birds (*khageśvara*).
One should dismiss the deities who were invoked there in the prescribed order;
this establishment of the banner is intended for the obligatory, occasional, and optional rites. (Viṣṇu 26.212)
Thereafter, being composed, one should worship the teacher according to one's ability.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Hoisting the Banner and Other Rites," in the Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
The twenty-seventh chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme procedure for the festival.
It brings about all peace, is meritorious, and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
It removes all sins for men and brings about auspiciousness in all actions;
it is the glorious ornament of the three worlds, intended for the prosperity of kings and kingdoms.
The festival, O Brahmin, may last for one night, or even three nights,
or five nights, or even seven nights.
One should perform the festival either for nine nights or with full elaboration;
a one-night festival is called Brāhma, while a three-day festival is said to be Śaiva.
The festival lasting five days is to be known as that of Indra; that of seven days belongs to the Ṛṣis; and that of nine days is declared to be divine. Thus, the festival is said to be of five kinds.
The *daivika* [mantra] is for the sake of allaying all calamities; the *ārṣaka* increases the kingdom;
the *aindra* is for the destruction of famine; and the *śaiva* is for the eradication of disease.
The increase for a Brahma-consecration shall be fivefold as its fruit, whether it lasts for one day, three days, seven days, or nine days. (Viṣṇudharmottara 27.7)
This festival, which begins with five days, should not be shortened; rather, one may extend it as desired. Shortening it brings about the destruction of the kingdom.
It will also cause confusion regarding the seasons and bring about the fear of famine;
therefore, one should perform festivals in accordance with the specific nature of the agent.
And when there is an auspicious conjunction of constellations, having observed the lunar day and the day of the week,
or during the constellation of consecration, or the constellation of the city or village.
O divine sage, perform [the rite] on the king’s birth star according to the sacrificer’s desire; O Hari, listen as I shall explain that procedure to you. 27.11.
Know that everything inauspicious is [overcome] by this; its removal is a festival.
Furthermore, it is said to consist of fifteen limbs; these shall now be described in sequence.
First is the sowing of the seedlings, then the hoisting of the banners;
the third shall be the pure ablution, and after that, the ceremonial bath (snapana).
Afterwards, there should be a festival for the sprout, then the fire-oblation (homa), and then the adornment;
one should know the eighth to be the offering (bali) and the ninth to be the great festival (mahotsava).
After that, there is the consecration of the sacred site (tīrtha), followed immediately by the ritual bath at the sacred site;
one should know that the twelfth rite is the ceremonial bathing, which follows the flower sacrifice.
The presentation of sacrificial fees and the lowering of the banner—
this festival is proclaimed to consist of fifteen parts.
The worship of the Vaiṣṇavas, accompanied by oblations performed both morning and evening and joined with sacrificial fees, [is prescribed].
This collection of food for the festival extends down to the very Cāṇḍālas;
on those days, as well as on other days dedicated to Brahmā and Śiva, it is offered to the bhūtas, pitṛs, and yakṣas.
One should offer the Vaiṣṇava remains as a bali offering both at dawn and at dusk;
for seven days, the wise practitioner should perform the bali with materials suitable for sacrifice.
The Brahmakādi rite should be performed over five days, while the Vaiṣṇava and others over three days;
however, the wise practitioner should perform the fire-oblation preceded by the procession with offerings.
The procession of the festival image should take place twice daily, or at the final time; or else, the one most skilled in the tantras may perform it once a day.
One should perform the offering of the bali at either forenoon or midday;
during the time of the bali procession, one should circumambulate very slowly.
From the conch up to the water-pot, these are the eight auspicious symbols in sequence;
[they are to be offered by] one who is a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant.
The wise man should separately bear upon his head the various auspicious Vaiṣṇava emblems;
this sequence has been declared by me, and now the materials for the bali offering are described.

On the first day, during the period known as Bhūta, the sage offered a satiating oblation consisting of white flowers, night-lotus pollen, parched grain, and white sandalwood paste, mixed with saktu, which was even more excellent than those offerings. Vis_27.25.
On the second day, the offering should consist of sesame, saffron, water, and blue flowers mixed with milk;
O Sage, it is said that on the third day, there is likewise an offering that brings satisfaction to the ancestors.

Red flowers, ghee, cakes, and parched grain—or in autumn, mixed with *karambha*—should be offered daily by wise and learned masters of sages for the sake of satisfying the Yakṣas; this was the ritual of Bali.

The most excellent of the noble ones say that on the fourth day, the offering (*bali*) for the Kākodarās consists of boiled rice, blue lotuses, coconuts, milk, rice-flour cakes, and parched grain flour.
On the day of the Lotus-Seated One, this offering is proclaimed by the sages: unbroken lotuses, water scented with blue lilies, along with heaps of flowers resembling gold.

On the sixth day, there shall be the worship of Hari on the sacred day as enjoined by the Purāṇas, consisting of offerings of water scented with fragrant *pāṭala* flowers, heaps of perfumed blossoms, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and cakes with molasses. *Viṣṇudharmottara* 27.30.
On the seventh and most excellent day, which is the festival of Viṣṇu, the offering that brings him satisfaction consists of dark flowers, rice mixed with jaggery, and jasmine-scented water;
on the eighth day, there should be milk-rice (pāyasa) scented with nutmeg, and Nārada says that for the day of Mahāviṣṇu, the flower should be deep blue.

O Sage Nārada, on the ninth day, for the constant satisfaction of Viṣṇu, this ritual of offering (balividhi) should be performed according to rule with rice cooked with sesame (kṛsara), heaps of fragrant substances, lamps, cool water, and flowers of all colors; and the offering should be accompanied by parched grain flour (saktu). This rite of offering leads to the increase of the king and his people.
O best of sages, I shall now explain, in brief and in due order, the names of the Kumuda and the others, as well as their retinues.
Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, Vāmana, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sarvanetra, Sumukha, and Supratiṣṭhita.
The gods and their enemies, the asuras; the gandharvas, yakṣas, ancestors, and serpents;
the yakṣas and those of the piśāca species; and the sixth class of deities known as the grahas.
One should present the bali offering within the mandala according to the sequence beginning with the altar,
as well as at crossroads, corners, and at places where three paths or a single path meet.
In a temple, or at an anthill, on the bank of a well, or on a mountain; at a pond, at sacred trees, or in the vicinity of a mountain.
In such places as these, one should have archways constructed,
properly established all around the eight types of sites, beginning with villages.
Having raised the banners individually at the archways,
or else, O best of sages, [one should raise] the banners here in the villages and other dwellings.
One should arrange the offering pedestal (balipīṭha) in the eight directions as appropriate,
measuring two tālas in width and length.
Each of the two girdles should be four finger-breadths wide;
in their center, one should fashion a pericarp, either circular or square.
O best of sages, the pericarp should be four finger-breadths in width;
thus the ritual for the pedestal has been declared. Now hear concerning the attendants of Hari.
Nārada said:
O preceptor of the preceptor of all the gods, tell me in due order of the attendants of Hari stationed in every direction,
including the crows and those headed by Kumuda, who act as priests in the construction sites for the great festivals of Hari.

Viṣvaksena: Indeed, I [shall describe] the colors, forms, vehicles, weapons, retinues, mantras, and modes of worship for Kumuda and the others stationed in the directions beginning with Indra, during the great festivals and other occasions of Hari— the source of all cosmic eggs, the sovereign of all intellects, the immeasurable one who is eternally blissful— within villages and other dwellings.
I shall describe it according to my understanding:

furthermore, the attendant Mukunda is white like a night-lily, clothed in jasmine-white garments, three-eyed, and bearing a conch and a discus; with palms joined in reverence, mounted upon an elephant, he stands facing the village in the midst of the hosts of gods and grahas.
Utkaṭa, Prakaṭonmukha, Vimukha, Aśvagrīva, Aśvavadana, Aśvajihva, Hastivaktra, Kumuda, Hastipāda, Keśava, Vāmana, Naraka, Naramardana, Mandadṛṣṭi, and Kaṇḍu.

Having recollected him surrounded by fifty gentle attendants of various forms— named Kanduka, Locana, Paṭaha, Akṣa, Viśālākṣa, Kṣāmaka, Kṣama, Pāṇḍara, Pāṇḍu, Pṛṣṭha, Durdina, Sudina, Vāmadeva, Mahādeva, Mahāgni, Madhusūdana, Kanaka, Kālakabhāvana, Bhavana, Bhānumat, Bhānuvega, Bhāskara, Abhāskara, Viśvasena, Visena, Viṣvaksena, Visārin, Vistāra, Nistara, Vidaṇḍin, Daṇḍaka, Amada, Kāmuka, Kāmabhṛt, and Kāmanāśana— and having worshipped him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for washing the feet (pādya), water for sipping (ācamana), perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, immediately thereafter...

Having offered the oblation prepared on that day, one should present the *bali* offering; having shown the *añjali* gesture and provided mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) for Hari, one should cause conchs, drums, dance, song, and so forth to be performed for the sake of satisfying that deity.
Furthermore, one should [visualize] Kumudākṣa, who stands in the southeast, is clothed in blue, has three eyes, a crow-like face, four arms, and hands engaged in the act of fist-fighting.
Holding a sword and a mallet, mounted upon a buffalo, facing toward the village, and situated in the midst of a host of asuras and grahas.

[He was accompanied] by Āgneyanidhana, Agnijihva, Hutāśana, Agnirūpa, Agnikeśa, Agnivarṇa, Agnyagnivaktra, Mahāvaktra, Mahāsena, Mahodara, Karālaka, Kākajihva, Kākavaktra, Agnivaktra, Maṇḍu, Maṇḍūkavaktra, Devadevalaka, Śarvaka, Śapaka, Śaṅku, Śaṅkuśrava, Mārīca, Droṇamārīca, Mahiṣa, Māhiṣaka, Kumbhanāsa, Vināsa, Kumbhakarṇa, Vikarṇa, Vidāri, Vikrama, Maskari, Maskarasūkarasūkarāsya, Śaśa, Śaśamukha, Siṃha, Siṃhamukha, Narasiṃha, Narakāladhṛk, Kālasūtra, Sūtrasūtravinālin, and Nālakarṇa.

Having worshipped that [deity] surrounded [by his retinue] as before, having offered the sacrificial materials for that day's *bali*, having given water for sipping (*ācamana*), and having displayed the *añjali* mudrā, one should perform the rites up to the mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) at the *balibara*;
then, for the sake of satisfying the deities of that direction, one should cause musical instruments to be sounded.

[He beheld] a white lotus situated at the end of the quarters, possessing the luster of a white lotus, with a face like a white lotus, three eyes, four arms, holding a conch and a discus, with palms joined in reverence, mounted upon a horse facing the village, standing in the midst of the hosts of ancestral spirits and planetary deities,
[surrounded by] Yama, Dharmadhara, Dharmarāja, Dhanurdhara, Vinaya, Praśraya, Niśreyas, Nirguṇa, Alasa, Kuṇapa, Krūra, Bāhu, Kuñjara, Prāṃśu, Damana, Niṣkopa, Niranukrośa, Nirmama, and Vivāha.

Having worshipped as before the one surrounded by Vibhava, Hutāśa, Hyū, Bahūr, Dhvara, Rakṣaṇa, Saṃjñaika, Lapākalaka, Kaṅka, Kaṭaka, Āvaṭa, Śaṅkhin, Cakrin, Gadī, Khaḍgī, Śārṅgin, Śārṅgadhara, Vāsudeva, Bhadraketumat, Ketuka, Kṣamī, Jvalana, Kiṃnara, Aśvattha, Supta, Sujapana, Japa, Paścimakaikṣika, Svañja, Bāḍava, and Kṣamī; and having offered the daily oblation (*taddinabali*) and given water for sipping (*ācamana*), he should show the *añjali* gesture, and thereafter perform the offering at the *balikautuka*.
Having provided mouth-perfume (or having offered it), one should sound conch shells and other instruments for the sake of satisfying the deity of that direction.
One should [visualize] Vāmana, stationed in the direction of Nirṛti, smoke-colored, dressed in smoke-colored garments, three-eyed, four-armed, and bearing a trident, a sword, and a mallet.

He whose hands are engaged in fist-fighting, who has mounted a cart and is proceeding toward the village, who stands within the *yātu* and *graha*, who possesses strength, who is the original and modified nature, the doer of good deeds, the fierce tamer, the protector, the one characterized by the hundred-fold, the Lord of Spring (*Mādhava*), the one harsh with meat, the one of harsh speech, the long-hanging one, the one who breathes life, the one of affection, the hero of the army, the one who speaks with distinction, the terrifying one, the red-eyed, the blood-eyed, the red-tongued, the one who abandons the wise, the one with hair like lightning, the large-eyed, the one who flows forth, the one who utters the cry of "Hā" for heroes, the one who sprinkles, the one who bestows, the one who takes any form at will, the deformed, the all-pervading, the all-knowing, the golden one, the one born of non-existence, the source of origin, the one belonging to Varuṇa, the one who crushes wealth, and the one who intoxicates.

Having worshipped as before the one surrounded by Vaikartana, Vikartṛka, Pardi, Prthukandaki, Kandaka, Nakī, Varuṇa, and Aruṇa, having performed the day’s offering and the sipping of water (ācamana), and having offered the joined palms (añjali),
one should provide mouth-perfume (mukhavāsa) for the deity in the sanctum (kautuka); thereafter, one should cause the musical instruments to sound.

One should visualize [the deity] whose abode is the direction of Varuṇa, who has spike-like ears, is yellow in color, possesses three eyes, wears yellow garments, has four arms, and holds a conch and a discus;
who stands with palms joined in reverence, faces the village, is mounted upon a tiger, and is situated in the midst of the host of ancestral spirits (Pitṛ-grahas);

and who is accompanied by Varuṇa, Vāruṇa, Pāśī, Pāśadhara, Gurukṣepaṇa, Kṣobhaṇa, Nārada, Sarvadaravi, Sumana, Naman, Haṃsa, Vaikuṇṭha, Paramaparahu, Matvasumat, Bhadra, Bhadravapra, Bhava, Mahākarṇa, Vikarṇa, Śaśaka, Śalaka, Kapika, Vānara, Naraka, Kārṣṇīkarṇa, Dhara, Aṃśumat, and Cakrṛbhṛt.

Having worshipped as before the one surrounded by Ugra, Vajrī, Vajranābha, Vinābhaka, Karapa (or -bha?), Kurabhadākṣiṇadakṣiṇa, Suhṛd, Durgandha, Pūtigandha, Tārkṣya, Garuḍa, Virodha, Rodhakara, Rodhakaṅkaṇa, and Vṛkodara, and having offered the daily bali and water for rinsing the mouth, one should join the palms in *añjali* and offer mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) to the *baliberam*.

Having offered these, one should sound the conch and other instruments. Then, moreover, [one should visualize] the deity residing in the direction of the wind (the northwest), resembling molten gold, with eyes like a serpent’s, three eyes, four arms,
clad in turmeric-colored garments, holding an axe and a noose, with hands bound in fists, facing the village, and mounted upon a deer.

Adorned with serpent-ornaments, situated amidst hosts of Gandharvas and planetary deities, [it was] filled with Maruts, Mārutas, cows, the earth, mice, the sons of Vāyu, winds, throats, seasons, birds, Kaṅkas, arrows, courtyards, mountains, armies, treasures, heroes, adversaries, obstructors, ordinances, Siddhas, Vasus, barley, mixtures, the steadfast, garlands, the ritual of garlanding, objects capable of purpose, assemblies, festivals, bracelets, armlets, fragrances, the wind, those sprinkled with [perfumes],
those anointed, the sick, servants, service, all medicinal herbs and remedies, the sick, wombs, causes, instruments, agents, heroes, and the wicked.

Having honored [the deity] as prescribed while surrounded by powerful, well-bred, and beautiful horses, having offered water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), and having made the gesture of joined palms (*añjali*), one should provide fresh garments for the images of the offerings (*balibimba*). Then,

having offered mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) and the day’s offering (*taddinabali*) to the images of the offerings, one should cause conch shells and other instruments to be sounded for the sake of satisfying the deities of the directions.

Immediately thereafter, [one should meditate on] the one who dwells in the quarter of the Amṛtakara (the Moon), possessing a dark complexion, wearing dark garments, three-eyed, four-armed, holding a lotus and a discus, with palms joined in reverence, facing the village, situated in the midst of hosts of Yakṣas and Grahas, fair-faced, mounted upon a ram; he who is Soma, Somaka, Soma, the knower of the Sāmans, the leader of the Sāmans, the maker of nectar, the creator of nectar, the Lord of the nectar of the Kālakūṭa poison, the wielder of power, the master of the Wheel of Time, the bearer of the Kali age, the bracelet-wearer, the solitary one, the powerful one, Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa, and the one whose limbs are tawny.

Surrounded by clever leaders capable of dispatching thousands of *rākṣasas*—who were like lines, drawings, or sketches; like *pikas*, *śukas*, *lūbakas*, *śukas*, *śyenās*, and *śyenamukhas*; like cats, desert-dwellers, *vālagulmakas*, *kaṇavakas*, and those whose remains were but fragments of grain; who possessed bodies as foul-smelling as mud; and who bore the speed of the winds that carry the force of the *sāmba-saṃvatsara* year—he was worshipped with meditations upon his retinue as before, and the sacrificial offerings for the door were presented while meditating upon him and his assembly.

Having worshipped as before, having offered the bali-offering substances at its entrance, and having shown the añjali-gesture, one should provide (and offer) mouth-perfume (*mukhavāsa*) to the bali-image and cause conch shells and other instruments to be sounded for the sake of satisfying the local deities (*śādevatā*).
Then, furthermore, [one should worship] the well-established Lord Śiva, mounted upon a lion, silver-colored, and clad in silver garments.

[He is] three-eyed, four-armed, holding a sword and a mace, with hands ready for hand-to-hand combat, facing the village, standing in the midst of a host of *piśāca* spirits and seizing demons (*graha*), surrounded by Īśāna, Īśvara, Vyāpin, Vyasana, Vinasa, Budha, Dhara, Baka, Viśavāda, Śakuni, Śakaṭa, Ghaṭa, Vṛkṣaka, Kṣaka, Kṣamī, Kṣānti, Mātṛ, Romaka, Piñjala, Brahmaṇya, Brahmavit, Brahmo, Brahmātman, Brahma-sādhana, Vedī, Vedavid, Udbandha, Śaṅkara, Śaṅkaradhīmat, Visṛṣṭi, iṣṭātman, Duṣṭātman, Duṣṭakarmakṛt, Vinetṛ, Govinda, Gopati, Goptṛ, and Maheśvara.

Having worshipped the [deity] as described while surrounded [by the retinue], having offered water for rinsing the mouth (*ācamana*), having given the daily offering (*balidāna*), and having performed the gesture of joined palms (*añjali*) to conclude the offering to the image,
one should cause conch shells and other instruments to resound for the sake of satisfying the deities of the directions.
[One should meditate upon the deity] stationed on Ananta, namely Pṛśnigarbha, accompanied by the hosts of Siddhas and Grahas, resembling molten Jāmbūnada gold, and four-faced.
Four-armed, holding a rosary and a water-pot, holding a handful of flowers, mounted upon a swan, facing west, born from a lotus, and seated upon a lotus throne.

[He was accompanied] by Siddha, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Dhātṛ, Prajāpati, Lokeśa, Lokakṛt, Kartṛ, Sraṣṭṛ, Brahmā, Ātmabhū, Sutāpati, Tulyarītivardhana, Avyaktaguṇavat, Gauṇaguṇabhuk, Udgītha, Praṇava, Hiraṇyagarbha, Viriñca, Puṣkarabhāsana, Bhāsa, Vikarṇa, Vijaya, Rathantara, Chandas, Yajus, Ṛk, Atharvan, Marīci, Aṅgiras, Pulaha, Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Pracetas, Alabha, Bhīṣma, Hemanta, Śiśira, Kusumākara, Kalaha, Virāhi, Amarṣa, Roṣaṇa, Śoṣaṇa, Gati, Harṣaṇa, and Vardhana; [and] by Pṛśnigarbha and Vaśānuga, who were of terrifying form and massive body, with countless retinues.
With tiger faces, ram faces, rabbit faces, swastika faces, serpent faces, boar faces, cock faces, crane faces, swan faces, peacock faces, swastika mouths,
ruddy goose faces, pigeon faces, with one eye, two eyes, three eyes, [and many eyes].
Having meditated upon [the deity] standing in the midst of the hosts of Viṣṇu’s attendants— surrounded by countless beings with one foot, two feet, many feet, one face, or many faces—

and having worshipped him with arghya and other offerings, presented the materials for the bali offering, shown the añjali for the ācamana, turned [the image] toward the liṅga, and performed the flower-añjali, the practitioner should pay homage and provide (or give) all auspicious musical instruments and mouth-perfume.
For the satisfaction of that deity, one should sound conch shells and other instruments.
Nārada says: "Is there any [need for] festivals, the offering of arghya, and so forth, for Caṇḍa and the others in the case of the Guru?"
O Lord, is there a distinction even in general terms regarding the mantra, or rather, the ritual procedure?
Viṣvaksena said:

Having performed the meditation on the deities beginning with Caṇḍa at the mouth of the Lord, one should then offer arghya into the right hand, ācamana likewise, and pādya for the feet. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 27.45)
One should apply perfume to the forehead, place a flower upon the head,
offer incense to the right side of the nose, and then a lamp to the eyes.
One should offer the sacrificial substance, water for drinking, and likewise water for sipping (ācamana) upon the right hand; now hear the proportions for those.
The quantity for the water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is considered to be as desired;
the fragrance should be exactly six drops, and the flowers should fill a closed fist.
One should offer incense that is filled with fragrance, rising with calm flames,
possessing many lines, and reaching a height of ten finger-breadths.
One should offer a lamp seven finger-breadths high, lit with ghee and camphor,
to the deity as an act of service, performing it like the incense offering.

The display of the mudrā with three finger-measures in the right eye, having performed it in this manner for [the prescribed] times, brings about the increase of the king and the kingdom. (Viṣṇudharmottara 27.51)
Otherwise, during the ritual for the worship and festival of the retinue,
it would lead to the destruction of the king and the kingdom, and would bring about famine and misfortune.
Next, the characteristics of the mantras beginning with Caṇḍa are now described:
that which begins with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ends with *namaḥ* is known as a name-mantra (*nāmamantra*). (Viṣṇupurāṇa 27.53)
Having offered the bali-oblation at each sacred seat (pīṭha), one should conclude it in the middle of the village with the words:
"Homage to the creators of beings; and let there be homage to all beings."
One should utter the mantra "Homage be to all beings";
this is known as the mantra for that area extending from the sacrificial altar to its boundaries. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 27.55)
But those who, filled with curiosity, follow here out of curiosity, obtain at every step the fruit of a sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Having become pure, having cleansed his teeth,
eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and with self-restraint, the teacher should perform the bali offering.
At the conclusion of the offering of oblations at night, one should immediately perform a bath,
especially during the consecration, festivals, fire-offerings, and bathing ceremonies.
Having begun, one should observe what is not mentioned in the tantra and have other [details] performed;
otherwise, if one were to employ [the rite] by looking at only a single tantra, it would be incomplete.
Without forgetting that summary, which prevents total destruction through delusion,
one should perform the consecration (adhivāsana) on the night preceding the day of the pilgrimage site.
Having prepared an altar in the center of the sacrificial pavilion, or else in front of the deity,
using eight *droṇas* of rice grains.
Having placed half that amount of rice, one should draw a lotus in its center;
having strewn kuśa grass over it, one should place cloths around its middle.
Having strewn it evenly with perfumes and flowers, one should sprinkle it with the root mantra;
it should be provided with lamps in the eight directions and fumigated with camphor and agarwood.
Having fumigated the altar, one should then bring the deity into its center;
having honored him with the water for the guest-offering, the water for the feet, and so forth, one should cause the sacrificial oblation to be given to him.
On the eastern side of the deity, one should place a full water-jar,
wrapped in fine cloths and adorned with gold and jewels.
In that [vessel], one should invoke the sacred fords, rivers, and lakes;
having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, one should then honor the deity.
Having prostrated, the preceptor should request for the sake of the pilgrimage:
"O God of gods, Lord of the world, salutations to you, O Creator of the universe! (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 27.67)
"Perform a pilgrimage; be gracious, O Puruṣottama!
Having thus entreated the Lord of Gods, one should sprinkle [the image] with water from the jar. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 27.68)
The knower of mantras should likewise [worship] with the five mantras and the Puruṣasūkta,
as well as the Nārāyaṇasūkta, which sets forth the process of creation and so forth.
This auspicious hymn of the Atharvaveda bestows all desires;
it likewise purifies the preceptor, himself, the Vaiṣṇavas, and the Sāttvatas.
They obtain the entire fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā;
then one should sprinkle [them]. Having again given water for sipping (ācamana), one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. // Vis_27.71 //
One should present the sacrificial offering, as well as cakes and fruits;
having given water for drinking and rinsing the mouth, one should likewise provide an aromatic for the mouth.
One should present all that which has been offered to the preceptor;
the preceptor’s satisfaction brings about the attainment of supreme success. (Vis 27.73)
One should present [the offering] to the Sāttvatas in accordance with the teacher;
having taken a small portion, one should cause it to be given to the members of the assembly.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should then tie the protective amulet (*kautuka*).
Thereafter, one should display the auspicious objects of the God of Gods in their proper sequence.
At an auspicious moment, one should present a parasol, a fly-whisk, and a mirror;
one should cause the deity to lie upon a divine bed with the root mantra-vidyā.
Having bound the protective amulet upon himself, he should complete the remainder of the night;
then, when the day has arrived at the sacred ford (tīrtha), he should perform his daily rites.
One should smear the northeastern portion of the middle section of the pavilion;
in its center, one should construct an altar of rice, and in the middle of that, an excellent lotus.
Having adorned the mortars, one should fill them with powdered charcoal of the *niśā* plant.
One should cause it to be struck again in three ways according to the previously stated procedure.
O Great Sage, in the western part of that place, in the midst of the rice field,
one should arrange powders, perfumes, and so forth for the sake of the sacred bathing site (tīrtha), according to the proper sequence.
Likewise, having ground fragrant powder and the powder of turmeric,
one should place it in the center of the rice, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
O Sage, having wrapped the jars and the mortars in turn with new cloths, one should subsequently fill the jar with the powder of *rajani*.
Having worshipped that deity with water for honor (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, one who is composed should thereafter bathe the head of the God of gods with the root mantra.
Having gathered powders such as perfumes and the like, one should perform them at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha);
thereafter, one should conduct the powder festival accompanied by a ceremonial bath with powder.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise, one should bring [the image] to the sacred site (tīrtha).

There, one should provide the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), the offering of clarified butter (ājyāropaṇa), bathing garments, water for the feet (pādya), the respectful offering (arghya), a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha), and water.
Having provided a mirror, oil, and unguents, as well as the bathing of the *dhātrī* and the preliminary services for the bath,
I shall now describe the sequence of bathing for both the daily and the occasional rites.
Alternatively, for a rite performed out of desire, one should prepare a five-cubit mandala on the eastern side of the god, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, the God of gods.
O Sage, having prepared that [altar] and placed two *droṇas* of *śāli* rice within it,
one should spread half of that amount of rice across the middle of the sacrificial platform (*vedi*).
Therein, the wise one should place twelve jars in sequence in the center;
having placed ghee in the central one, he should place curd in the eastern one.
The practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should place milk in the south, honey in the western direction, and warm water in the north.
In the southeast, one should place scented water; in the southwest, flower-water;
in the northwest, auspicious water; and in the northeast, with pure waters.
Having released the hand from the Navaka, one should place the powders in sequence— either in the Aindra, the Uttara, or by means of the sequential method— according to the sequential application.
One should bathe Puruṣottama with the mantras beginning with *parameṣṭhi*,
and thereafter wipe him with powders using the root mantra for the limbs and other parts of the deity.
Furthermore, one should wipe the supreme image with a bundle of *kuśa* grass;
having thus placed the water jars, the wise practitioner should likewise place the ritual substances from the bundles of *kuśa*.
One should place a circular diagram upon it and scatter fragrant flowers;
having covered it with new cloths, one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Then, for the sake of protection, one should station Kumuda and the others all around:
Kumuda in the eastern quarter and Puṇḍarīka in the south.
One should place Śaṅkukarṇa in the west and Sumukha in the north;
one should place Kumudākṣa in the southeast and Vāmana in the southwest.
Sarpanetra is in the northwest, and Supratiṣṭhita in the northeast;
in this manner, the wise one should place Kumuda and the others in the jars.
Tulasī, Sahadevī, Bilva, Audumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Vakula, and Sadābhadra are proclaimed [as auspicious].
Having taken the sprouts of these [plants], one should place them in the jars in due order;
having worshipped them with flowers and so forth, up to incense and lamps.
Having thus deposited the jars, I shall now tell you of the substances and deities:
rice, nīvāra grain, mung beans, sandalwood, and uśīra root.
Known as the "five-powders," it is the most excellent of all fragrant substances; it consists of sandalwood, saffron, uśīra, and the scents of campaka and utpala.
Known as "scented water," it possesses a luster equal to the waters of the Gaṅgā;
it contains blue lotuses, jasmine, jāti, pāṭala, and red lotuses.
One should place this "fivefold water with flowers," which consists of the five Upaniṣads,
