along with sprouts of *indravallī*, a single leaf of *aśvattha*, and a lotus.
This auspicious rite with auspicious water was previously described;
having taken pure water, one should consecrate it with the mantra of the Supreme Lord.
Having stirred [the mixture] with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, one should consecrate the Lord of Gods;
likewise, [one should use] saffron, uśīra, kuṣṭha, turmeric, and sandalwood.
This meritorious substance consisting of sacred fords is known as *tīrthacūrṇa*; one should take one *droṇa* or even half a *droṇa*, omitting it on one night.
The knower of mantras should prepare a powder weighing one āḍhaka or half of that;
however, if even powder cannot be obtained, the powder of turmeric is excellent.
Or one should bathe all [the images] with śāli rice using the root mantra;
or [one may use] one āḍhaka or even half an āḍhaka of oily substances such as ghee and the like.
But if none of these are available, one should fill [the vessel] with scented water;
with that alone, one should bathe the deity according to one's means.

The knower of mantras should likewise remember the specific defects of whatever flower was prescribed for the festival, and having cast it away, he should offer *tulasī*, blue lotuses, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*).
Thus the substance has been fully described; now I shall tell you of the deities:
the forms beginning with Keśava and ending with Dāmodara.
The deities of the jars containing clarified butter and other substances have been proclaimed;
for the protection of the jars, Kumuda and the others are the presiding deities.

Having established [the deities] in this manner according to the rule, one should subsequently perform purification, by means of which that sequence of extraction and the sequence of the deities have been proclaimed. Vis_27.114.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, one should sprinkle [the image] with water mixed with *kuśa* grass;
having thus sprinkled it according to the rule, one should then perform the ritual bathing (*snapana*).
O Sage, having performed full worship, one should bathe the Lord with ghee, curd, milk, honey, and warm water, as well as with the five powders.
One should offer scented water with the eight-syllable mantra, flower water with the twelve-syllable mantra, auspicious water with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, and pure water with the syllable Om.
Then, having bathed [the image] with holy-site powder using the root mantra, the practitioner,
at the conclusion of the bathing, should place the excellent powder of turmeric.

O Great Sage, one should thus bathe [the deity] in sequence, beginning with clarified butter and ending with powdered incense, and having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, up to the offering of lamps. Vis_27.119.
At the conclusion of the ablution, the knower of mantras, having circled Kumuda and the other guardians around the head of the deity, should cause them to be bestowed upon the devotees.
Having thus performed the ritual bathing, one should then cause the river-bath to be performed;
having brought the deity to the bank, one should cleanse him with a bundle of *kuśa* grass.

Then one should worship the auspicious thread (kautuka), beginning with the water for the feet and ending with the lamp; and having immersed oneself in that sacred ford, one should invoke all the sacred fords from every direction.
Having performed the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite there with the five mantras while composed in meditation,
the preceptor should then engage in water-play and reach the shore.
Having bathed there in the water of the sacred ford, one is liberated from all sins;
having adorned oneself with garments and the like, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having offered either ordinary oblation or a great oblation, one should cause dancing and other performances to be held;
with a concentrated mind, one should present the *bali* offering to the deity in the eastern direction.
Having uttered the mantra, "Homage be to all the gods," and having adorned [the image] with vessels and other ornaments, one should place Hari upon the vehicle.
Furthermore, one should perform circumambulation of a village or a city, or even of one's own dwelling; in the absence of these, however, according to one's means. // Vis_27.127 //
Accompanied by the recitation of auspicious verses, filled with the sounds of conchs and kettledrums,
provided with hundreds of lamps, and attended by dancing, singing, and other such performances.
Accompanied by a rain of flowers, together with unbroken grains and parched rice,
joined with the singing of the Sāmaveda, and endowed with shouts of victory.
Having circumambulated [the site] clockwise, neither too quickly nor too slowly,
and having reached the sacrificial ground, one should perform worship in the proper sequence.
Having performed the ritual bathing according to the rules, one should commence the flower sacrifice;
having fashioned a lotus, a wheel, or a mandala in that place, [one should worship] Vāsudeva and the others.
Śaṅkha and the others, the world-protectors (lokapālas), are indeed outside; Viṣvaksena and Vainateya are also on the exterior.
Bhūteśa and the others are to be worshipped on the outside; and gaudy food (gaulyanna) is indeed to be offered as an oblation to Agni.
The auspicious day offering, a single flower, and the bali-oblation—these should indeed be placed upon the primary image, which is worthy of worship;
as for the remainder, one should apply it to the path characterized by the wheel.
One should perform the lowering of the banner after having dismissed the deities,
having offered them a great bali-oblation consisting of mung-bean rice, cakes, and parched grain.
Having offered groats both outside and inside the village and having asked for forgiveness,
one should dismiss the god Vainateya from the banner with his own mantra.
O Great Sage, one should perform the lowering of the banner after one night, two nights, or three nights; one should not allow it to remain longer than that.
If there is more [available], one should perform the ceremonial bathing (snapana) there in due order; however, for the festival image (utsavapratimā), the bathing may be either inferior or superior.
One should cause Hari to be bathed with either twenty-five or twelve jars, according to one's means.

Thereafter, the one most skilled in mantras should perform the lowering of the banner during the plowing and other rites, the worship, the consecration, the mounting, and so forth. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 27.139)
At the time of raising the banner, as well as at its lowering,
during festivals, and when making offerings, one should cause it to be proclaimed with conch shells and other instruments.
O Sage, the sounding of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments brings satisfaction to the green-hued one (Viṣṇu),
causes the flight of Rākṣasas, and likewise brings peace to kings.
That which brings about the prosperity of the kingdom and correctly bestows happiness upon the sacrificer—
such is the mudrā that is taught for each of the rites beginning with the bathing and installation [of the deity].
If one is unable to do it in that way, one should place the root mantra upon the hand;
by performing all rites with that hand, O bull among sages, [one succeeds]. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 27.143)
This is their third contemplation; at its conclusion, they join their palms in reverence and bring satisfaction to the Lord of the Water-abodes and the Waters.
"One should satisfy [the deities] so as to achieve one's own satisfaction," says the teacher of secret instruction;
through such rites as festivals for the gods, the king gains strength, long life, health, victory, and prosperity.
The prosperity of the kingdom, the acquisition of wealth and grain, and the attainment of happiness by the patron and others are the fruits [of this].
Now, I shall describe the excellent sacrificial pavilion, which is a constituent part of the festival. Vis_27.146.
One should have the sacrificial pavilion constructed to the south of the gateway, or likewise in the southeast, the south, or the north.
To the east of that, one should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) endowed with the proper characteristics;
O best of sages, one should likewise construct an altar (vedi) beside the pit according to the prescribed rule.
One should have an excellent altar constructed measuring four cubits; O Great Sage, the sacrificial altar should be equal in width and length.
One should have an excellent altar constructed, measuring either three cubits or two cubits,
with a height of one ratni or one tāla.
Having thus constructed the unsurpassed sacrificial altar according to the prescribed rite— resembling the surface of a mirror and bestowing the auspiciousness of worldly enjoyment— Vis_27.151.
There, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus above it using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
One should sprinkle it with water purified by *kuśa* grass using that mantra,
[upon] the small earthen vessels containing sprouts and endowed with the eight auspicious symbols.
O Sage, one should place auspicious items such as conch shells according to the sequence starting from the east;
this is declared to be the supreme sequence for the characteristics of the altar.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited and having sprinkled [the site] with water mixed with *kuśa* grass,
the knower of mantras, together with the Brahmins, should then chant the *Svastisūkta*.
Therein, O best of sages, one should construct an altar in the center using rice,
measuring five bhāras, or half of that, or even half of that again.
Having spread out [the materials] in the center of the altar, or using red śāli rice,
one should draw an eight-petaled red lotus as before.
There, having placed nine jars in order in the center, provided with three threads and filled with filtered water; Vis_27.158.
Having adorned them with pairs of garments, provided with perfumes and flowers, endowed with the five precious gems, and furnished with three tufts of kusha grass; Vis_27.159.
Having covered [the vessels] with wheels joined by Aśvattha sprouts,
one should invoke [the deities] in sequence into the jars endowed with these characteristics.
O great sage, one should lead the Śakti from the Mahābera vessel into the central jar;
then, one should worship Vāsudeva and the others in the eight jars starting from the east.

O best of sages, having honored the deity residing within the water-pot with offerings of water for the guest and for the feet, and so forth, one should present the sacrificial oblations and mouth-freshener.
And with the remainder of that [offering], one should cast the bali-oblation into the eight jars starting from the east;
having recognized Vāsudeva and the others, one should do so individually by their own names.
Then, one should worship Kumuda and the others around Kumbha,
accompanied by the sound of a bell, with [offerings] the size of a hen's egg.
Accompanied by the recitation of auspicious verses and provided with incense and lamps,
the supreme practitioner should perform the offering of the bali-oblation under his own name.
One should offer a coconut fruit and worship in this manner during the two twilights;
at the conclusion of that worship, the knower of mantras should commence the rite of fire-oblation (homa).
The best of practitioners should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or half of that, or even half of that again, beginning with sacrificial fuel-sticks and ending with sesame seeds.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, one should perform the offering of bali in the village dwellings;
thereafter, on the day of the pilgrimage site, the fire-oblation and worship should be performed in the forenoon.
The practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should perform [the rite] correctly as before;
at the conclusion of the fire offering, he should bring that eye from the vase into the primary image.
Then, O Brahmin, one should lead Vāsudeva and the others as before in the enclosure; this supreme auspicious rite should be performed year after year.
For one who has been deprived of the daily worship, the expiation is a great festival;
thus one should worship the God during the festival in the sacrificial pavilion.
One should worship in due order for as many days as the duration of the *tīrtha*,
during the worship of the sacrificial pavilion and the rite of sowing the ritual sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*).
Whatever remains of the sacrificial offering, whatever remains of the oblation, and likewise whatever remains of the vessel—
all that which has been offered in this [rite] should be presented to the teacher.
Otherwise, it becomes fruitless for the patron and causes disease;
therefore, with every effort, one should have [the rite] performed as enjoined by the scriptures.
The wise person who causes this to be done shall obtain that same fruit;
however, if one performs the festival without the worship of the sacrificial pavilion, [the result will differ].
Merely by means of this oblation, it is sufficient for a great festival;
it is auspicious, conducive to fame and long life, and the destroyer of all sins.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Festival," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
The twenty-eighth chapter. Viṣvaksena said:
O Lord of Sages, I shall describe the festival of the new moon (Amāvāsyā), which occurs month after month.
Or on the birth asterism of the deity, or on the asterism of the consecration, or even on another asterism.
Having first determined the auspicious time for the sprouts during the birth asterism of the patron, or even that of the king, or during the solstice or at the time of the equinox; Viṣṇu 28.2.
On the ninth day, or on the seventh or fifth day, or even on the third or first day—
the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) performed on these occasions brings all prosperity and happiness.
O best of sages, one should cause it to be performed properly according to the rules in the evening;
the offering of sprouts should not be done, as it brings about misfortune and inauspiciousness.
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) to be performed;
in this rite of offering the sprouts, one need not observe the specific times and so forth.
O Sage, in this great tantra, during the festival, three types of vessels—the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*—are taught in succession for the sixteen [offerings]. (Vis 28.6)
O Nārada, regarding the individual characteristics of the *pālikā* and other vessels, is there any distinction among them? Listen to that distinction in due order.
Either twelve for each, or likewise only the individual *pālikās*;
or sixteen *pālikās*, or twelve, or nine.
One should thoroughly wrap the *pālikā* vessels and others with *dūrvā* grass and *śirīṣa* flowers;
[one should also place] the ten seeds beginning with sesame, or even just a single mung bean.
One should wash [the seeds] with milk or indeed with water while reciting the five mantras;
having thus thoroughly washed the seeds, one should perform the offering of the sprouts.
In this rite of planting the sprouts, one should not perform the laying out of the lines;
I shall explain the specific detail here—listen to the procedure for the lotus threads.
One should smear an area measuring three cubits with cow dung;
having spread rice grains over it, one should then draw a lotus in its center.
O best of sages, during a three-day or single-day festival, at the ceremonial bathing,
and in rites such as those on the new moon day, one should perform sixteen or twelve [recitations].
Having drawn the pericarp and the other petals, one should place [the mantras] there individually,
O Sage, during the consecration, the festival, and the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa).
Likewise, according to the procedure for initiation, one should cause sixteen,
twelve, or all [the vessels] such as the *pālikā* and others to be made in sequence.
One should draw all the remaining rites and the unsurpassed lotus;
hear now, O great sage, the number of petals of that lotus.
If the pedestal has sixteen [petals], one should draw the fifteenth petal;
if the pedestal has twelve, one should draw a lotus of that same kind.
O tiger among sages, one should cause the first syllable to be placed upon these petals starting from the pericarp; or else, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus.
As before, one should draw the seed-syllable and the eight syllables starting from the east;
O Sage, one should sprinkle [the site] with that mantra, or with the root of a branch.
The wise one should place nine small vessels at the ends of the directions, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna;
with that mantra, he should sprinkle them with scented water.
On that occasion, O Nārada, one should have the Brahmins who are masters of the ritual manuals recite the *puṇyāha* formula,
after having worshipped sesame seeds and other grains upon the rice.
One should sow all the seeds with the mantra "jitanta," worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and place them in a well-protected location in due order.
The specific detail here has been fully declared; the remainder shall be common [to all].
One should perform this bali offering either in the evening or in the forenoon.
One should offer a bali-oblation with sacrificial food, or with unbroken grains, or even with flowers;
and the sowing of sprouts is prescribed for occasions such as the festival of the new moon.
Or even a festival image, or likewise an image for bathing and worship,
or a bali-image, or even a single disc-image.
Having taken that, the knower of mantras should perform a pure ablution;
the binding of the thread must be performed according to the ritual rules during the first part of the night.
O Sage, having performed the consecration with perfumes as if for a dwelling,
let there be an ornamentation of the pavilion four fingers in height and four cubits in measurement.
Having properly constructed an altar with śāli rice in the center of the pavilion,
one should perform the rite in its middle using an altar made of half that amount of rice.
In the absence of grain, the sacrificial altar (vedi) is praised according to what is available;
one skilled in the ritual procedure (tantra) should construct the altar according to the desire of the sacrificer.
As before, having drawn a lotus, one should place the eight-syllable mantra in its center;
in the middle of the eight-syllable mantra, however, one should place the seat consisting of four lines.
One should sprinkle [the site] with the root mantra and install Dharma, Jñāna, and the others;
having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should invoke Hari into their midst.
One should worship Puruṣottama with offerings beginning with water for the feet and ending with a lamp;
thereafter, one should bind the marriage-thread (kautuka) with the Puṇḍarīkākṣa-vidyā.
The wise man, having taken one portion of excellent śāli rice, filling three āḍhakas, in vessels made of gold or other precious materials; Vis_28.33.
One should fill [the vessel] with pure rice that has the luster of jasmine or the white moon;
above the rice, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp.
O Nārada, having tripled a cord made of gold, or silver, or even linen thread, or even a cotton thread, [one should proceed].
Having tripled the threefold [line], one should place it in sequence upon the pericarp;
one should lay down the excellent thread from east to west.

One should worship the auspicious thread (kautuka), beginning with perfumes and ending with lamps, in due order; thereafter, one should bind the auspicious thread on the right hand of the Blessed One.
Then the preceptor, reciting the mantra with his thumb and ring finger,
takes ashes from the incense and performs a protection rite accompanied by the mantra.

Having performed the binding of the eight directions on the forehead of the deity all around in sequence, the practitioner should afterwards present the sacrificial offering with the Parameṣṭhin mantra.
One should cause all the offerings, such as cakes and so forth, to be presented;
then one should give water and offer mouth-perfume. (Viṣṇu 28.40)
The practitioner should present a parasol, a fly-whisk, and a mirror to the Lord of Gods,
and should perform the binding of the directions within that [mandala] using the Cakra-mantra.
One should present all that has been offered to the preceptor;
O Sage, everything not presented to him is equal to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).
Therefore, with every effort, one should assemble [the deities] in the presence of the god;
for the sake of the prosperity of the village and its settlements, one should worship them starting from the east and proceeding all around.
May Kumuda and all the others accept this supreme offering,
accompanied by the sound of bells and provided with incense and lamps.
One should perform the offering of oblations (bali) accompanied by the recitation of benedictions (svastivācana), combined with dance and song,
using flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and water with kuśa grass.
This which is spoken here for the purpose of pleasing the God of Gods:
one should subsequently dismiss [the deity] at night with the extensive array of substances previously mentioned.
And one should properly worship the Lord of Gods with the Puruṣasūkta,
having diligently adorned him with garments, ornaments, flowers, and other offerings.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering and likewise the betel leaf;
having adorned himself, the preceptor should commence the rite of fire-oblation.

One should perform, as prescribed by the rules, the oblation of sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, and parched grain twenty-five times each, either in the perpetual fire or in the festival fire.
One should perform the offering of fuel sticks and so forth upon one’s own respective tongue in the proper sequence:
the fuel sticks with the root mantra, and the clarified butter indeed with the root of the meter.

Then, having offered an oblation of *yava* grain with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī mantra for the measure of an *akṣa*, the one most skilled in the ritual procedure should offer parched grains (*lāja*) with the mantra beginning with "The Vedas" (*vedādi*).
O Sage, one should offer the sacrificial materials with [mantras] ending in the dative case,
and one should offer the expiatory oblations (prāyaścittāhuti) in sequence with the five Upaniṣads.
Then, having offered the full oblation with the twelve-syllable vidyā,
[one should perform it] during the eternal great festival, as well as at the new-moon festival and others.
O best of sages, even fuel prepared by a Brahmin is not permitted for you;
thus has the fire-oblation for the new moon festival and other occasions been described to you.
At the conclusion of the fire offering (homa), the one most skilled in the tantras should perform the offering of the sacrificial bali;
the bali offering in the temple should be performed according to the sequence as before.
O tiger among sages, for the sake of pleasing all the gods, one should have it constructed in a village, a city, a town, or even in a hermitage. (Viṣṇu 28.56)
In such places as these, one should cause the supreme bali offering to be performed;
having first ensured the purification of the path, one should present the bali in the forenoon.
O Brahmin, the bali-rite performed at midday would be inferior;
if it is performed in the forenoon, there will be prosperity for the village and it shall bring all forms of wealth and happiness.
At midday, however, it brings about the destruction of clouds and prosperity for cities and other places;
therefore, one should perform the bali offering with every effort during the forenoon.
As before, having diligently adorned the Lord of the Gods with perfumes and other offerings,
he was made most beautiful and gratified by the ritual measures.
Having placed that image upon a palanquin or similar vehicle, being composed in mind,
[he should mount] either a chariot, a palanquin, an elephant, or a noble horse.
One should sprinkle [the offerings] with the Gāruḍa mantra and adorn them while recollecting Garuḍa,
along with parasols, banners, canopies, and so forth, accompanied by dance and song.
Accompanied by the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, and surrounded by a great multitude of people,
he should wander through the center of the village and its streets.
One should worship the kumuda and other [deities] in villages and other inhabited places,
in all temples, and in the abodes of the Great Teacher.
O best of sages, one should place the hosts of all beings in wells, in tanks, at confluences, along the roads, and in various locations throughout that region.
In the presence of the deity, one should perform the offering of oblations (bali) there,
consisting of milk-rice mixed with jaggery and joined with Tulasī leaves.
It should be provided with *karavīra* flowers, combined with white and red unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
accompanied by sesame seeds and water, and joined with the substances for the bali offering.
O best of sages, if this sacrificial substance is touched by worms, insects, moths, or the like through negligence, it must be discarded during the worship of the deity.
One should worship with unbroken grains or flowers, as available, while recollecting the respective mantras for each of the sites of the dwelling. Vis_28.69.
Wearing the upper garment and the turban, the preceptor should perform the bali offering;
at the conclusion of the bali, he should worship the Supreme Self with water for honoring and water for washing the feet, and so forth.
O Lord of Sages, having gone to the temple at the third pressing of the day, perform the auspicious invocation for this rite of all auspiciousness.
Having offered the seven items beginning with water for the feet, one should then commence the ritual bathing;
having beautifully decorated the pavilion, one should prepare the altar with rice.
There, in the center, the wise one should place the jars,
resembling the flowers of the śālmali and kiṃśuka trees, and wrapped with thread.
O best of sages, having placed [the vessels] upon the altar according to the mantras beginning with the four Vedas, one should deposit the ritual substances in their midst.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) should be in the middle section, the water for the guest-offering (arghya) in the eastern section,
the water for sipping (ācamanīya) in the southern section, and the fragrant substances (gandha) in the western region.
One should place water with flowers in the north (Soma), rice-water in the southeast (Kṛśānu),
curd in the southwest (Nairṛta), and milk in the northwest (Vāyavya).
O Sage, one should place auspicious clarified butter mixed with fragrance in the northeast;
having thus established the group of nine, one should insert bundles of kusha grass into them.
One should place small bowls upon them and deposit fragrant flowers;
then, one should place powdered turmeric either in the east or in the north.
Having placed them there, one should worship them in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains;
then, one should wrap the jars with new cloths while reciting the Praṇava.
O Nārada, one should properly recite the *puṇyāha* formula exactly as it is;
having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should place eight jars at the archway.
One should place two jars each at the points starting from the east and ending with the north;
having filled them with scented water, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
O bull among sages, the practitioner who knows the supreme reality should recollect the six-syllable mantra for all of them by means of their own names. (Vis 28.82)

The knower of mantras should consecrate the Lord of Gods with all the jars containing water for the feet and other offerings; at the conclusion of the bathing ceremony, he should then consecrate the night.
Then, having performed a pure bath and having adorned Janārdana,
the wise one should take the bathing water and sprinkle the Vaiṣṇavas with it.
Having taken that, one should place it upon the heads of all devotees;
it yields the merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā and destroys all sins.
"The certainty of the scripture is that there shall be the perfection of all prosperity; as before, the knower of mantras, having placed the deity within the vehicle, [proceeds]. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 28.86)
O Sage, having brought the God of gods to a pond mentioned in the Purāṇas or else to the bank of a river, the practitioner [should proceed] with the root mantra.
O bull among sages, one should bathe her in the middle of that [river] as before;
having summoned the great multitude, one should bestow this unsurpassed sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Accompanied by the recitation of benedictions and the sounding of conchs and drums,
O Nārada, he proceeded in due order to the temple and stood at the entrance.
Having honored [the deity] with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, the knower of mantras should perform protection;
or else, he should present an offering to the eight directions with food or flowers. (Viṣṇu 28.90)
Having taken refuge in the temple of the gods, one should proceed in due order starting from the east and so forth with the Sudarśana mantra, preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions.
Having worshipped the deity as before, one should offer a great quantity of food;
thereafter, O Nārada, one should honor the preceptor according to one's ability.
One should cause other offerings, such as cakes and the like, to be presented;
afterwards, one should cause betel to be offered according to the rule by the Supreme Lord.
All remaining rites should be caused to be performed like those for a king;
the wise man who causes them to be performed shall obtain prosperity in this world.
He attains the same world as Viṣṇu and even the same form as Viṣṇu;
or else, O tiger among sages, listen to the procedure for bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha).
One should have a pavilion constructed in due order on the bank of a river's sandy shore;
or else, having prepared a fine water-staircase provided with four gates.

The supreme characteristics of a water-shed for the perfuming of robes have been declared; O Lord of Sages, having constructed a water-shed endowed with such characteristics, [one should perform the rite].
One should smear the area from the east to the northeast with cow dung,
spread the previously mentioned rice grains upon it, and decorate it with canopies and other ornaments.
One should place the jars in their midst, adorned with flower garlands and the like; having established the group of nine as before, one should perform the ritual bath as before.
Then, O Brahmin, accompanied by a great multitude, one should perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha) in a river,
a lake, or a pond, and worship the Lord of Gods.
Having brought the deity to the bank, one should perform a pure bath;
having adorned the deity with effort, one should worship the deity with the *arghya* and other offerings.
One should perform all remaining rites in this regard as previously described.
O Lord of Sages, I have thus declared to you the two types of ritual bathing at sacred fords.
One should perform [the rite] according to the practitioner's desire and as is appropriate;
thus has the procedure for bathing at sacred sites (tīrtha) been declared, each preceding one being more important than the next.
Thus has the supreme festival of the new moon been briefly described;
otherwise, it becomes fruitless, resulting in the increase of disease and the depletion of wealth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have it performed according to the prescribed ritual.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the New Moon Festival," in the Śrī Pañcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Twenty-nine:
Viṣvaksena says— I shall likewise describe the rites for the birthday of Rāghava.
The rite should be performed under the asterism Punarvasu, in the month of Caitra, on the ninth lunar day.
Or else, O Brahmin, having performed the Rāghava-utsava in the month of Māgha,
one should first perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) and thereafter conduct the festival.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing of Rāghava according to the rules in the evening,
one should afterwards honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.

The gift of a cow, the gift of land, as well as gold and silver, the gift of cattle, clarified butter, and sesame seeds, and the offering of a morsel of food to a cow according to the prescribed rule.

Thereafter, the supreme practitioner should bind the auspicious thread (kautuka) preceded by a most meritorious day, and he should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rule. Vis_29.5.

One should offer the fuel sticks with the root mantra and the clarified butter with the *praṇava*, twenty-eight times for each; then one should perform the oblation of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
The Puṃsūkta consists of sixteen verses; from that, the Devāḥ section has six verses;
likewise, there are five Upaniṣads, and the "viṣṇornuka" section consists of three verses.
One should perform the fire oblation with the twelve-syllable mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*.
Having offered these full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should complete the remainder of the fire ritual.
Then, at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should perform the *puṇyāha* rite in due order;
thereafter, one should cause the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *puṇyāha* of the fire sacrifice to be given there.
The knower of mantras should place fire within himself and offer himself to Hari;
thereafter, he should worship Rāghava with the Rāma-mantra.
Thereafter, one should offer the sacrificial oblation in five ways with the *parameṣṭhin* mantra:
boiled rice, rice mixed with sesame, sweet rice, milk-rice, and barley meal with curds.
One should cause to be given water rich with fragrance, mouth-perfumes,
and various kinds of foods and various kinds of fruits.
There, one should feed Vaiṣṇava brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
one should spend the remainder of the night with the diversions of song, dance, and other entertainments.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should cause ornaments to be distributed;
having adorned all the people who are most dear to Viṣṇu, they should be made equal.
With oils, sandalwood pastes, and unguents for the body in every way;
with turmeric powder, flowers, and likewise various kinds of garments.
And hundreds of them, filled with water and mixed with water,
all accompanied by dance and song, splashed one another here and there.
With variegated banners and canopies, with yak-tail whisks and palm-leaf fans,
with the sounds of conchs and drums, and even with shouts and the slapping of arms.
One should celebrate a great festival accompanied by dances, songs, and instrumental music, as well as by devotees of the Blessed One and the sounds of shouts of "Victory! (jaya).
Having mixed it with oil, fragrance, and water, and combined it with the powder of *rajanī*, they should wander through the village and then return to their own abode. *Viṣṇupurāṇa* 29.19.
One should bathe that God of gods according to the extent of one's wealth,
having diligently adorned him with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and other such items.
Then, having offered the great oblation and performed the worship of the devotees, whoever should thus cause the festival to be celebrated with devotion during the king's birth— Vis_29.21.
He goes to the world of Viṣṇu (Viṣṇusālokya) and gradually becomes a lord among the attendants.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Festival of Śrī Rāma's Birth," in the Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā of the glorious Pāñcarātra.
Chapter Thirty. Viṣvaksena:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the festival of Kṛṣṇa’s birth-day,
which arose for the benefit of all the worlds within the Yādava clan.
Out of a desire for the welfare of the gods, he was born to Vasudeva and Devakī in the month of Śrāvaṇa,
during the dark fortnight, on the eighth lunar day under the asterism Rohiṇī.
Having first performed the ritual of offering the seed-syllables (aṅkurārpaṇa), on either the seventh or the fifth day,
at midnight, one should [prepare] the unsurpassed black image in the east.
O Sage, on that day one should worship him as the Dancer of Butter, or as the Dancing Serpent, or likewise as the Four-Armed One.
To the east of the palace, however, there was a square pavilion,
provided with a canopy and banners, and encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass.
Having adorned it with flower garlands and decorated it with strings of pearls,
one should perform the cleansing from Indra to Īśāna with the syllable *praṇava*.
One should sprinkle it with scented water using the twelve-syllable vidyā,
having smeared it with cow dung according to the sequence starting from the east.
The practitioner should then light lamps in the four directions in sequence,
adorning the entire perimeter of the pavilion with lamp-stands.
And in the center of the pavilion, one should place a four-legged seat;
there, one should provide a covering on top and scatter white flowers.

One should worship with perfumes and flowers according to the sequence beginning with Dharma; then, having had the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions (*svasti*), one should install the image there.
Having tied the protective amulet with the permission of a Brahmin,
[he should do so] with the thumb and ring finger, using the twelve-syllable vidyā.
Then one should offer mouth-freshener and fan him with palm-leaf fans, accompanied by parasols and chowries, and provided with dance and song. (Viṣṇu 30.12)
One should perform the auspicious rite for Hari accompanied by lutes and flutes,
together with conchs and drums, preceded by the recitation of benedictions.
One should place the pair of sandals upon the bed;
having prepared the bed as before, one should bring the Deity into its center.
To the south [he should place] Balabhadra, and afterwards he should perform the consecration there;
the most excellent practitioner should effect the binding of the directions with the eight-syllable mantra.
In the same manner, the practitioner should install the deity Viṣṇu with his mantra,
as well as the water for the feet, the respectful offering, the water for sipping, and likewise fragrance and flowers.
There, one should have the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited by Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas;
the preceptor (*ācārya*), moreover, should be dressed in white garments and wear a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
Wearing the vertical sectarian mark (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) and likewise holding the purifier (*pavitra*) in his hand,
he should wash his feet up to the knees and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice, twice.
On the right side of the deity, seated on a throne facing north,
one should perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) as well as the creation-arrangement (sṛṣṭinyāsa).
In the same way, O Sage, having installed the deity and recited the eight-syllable mantra,
the knower of mantras should take a vessel made of gold or other materials and fill it with pure water.
O Sage, one should thereafter wash that vessel with the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī;
it should be filled with water, scented, and provided with a thread and a cloth.
O Great Sage, having placed [the image] within a heap of grain, one should then meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the deity, from the perspective of the *mūlabera*. 30.22.
Recalling the dark-complexioned image of Kṛṣṇa with a youthful body,
one should sprinkle that water upon the head of the image while reciting the root mantra.
Having joined his palms in reverence and bowed again and again,
he laid that deity upon the bed with the root-mantra.
In the same manner, one should have Balabhadra laid down with his mantra;
one should cover the deity with cloths and worship him with white flowers.
Then the best of practitioners should recite the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta,
accompanied by the sounding of conchs and drums, and joined with the study of the Vedas.
Accompanied by lutes and flutes, joined with cymbals and drums, and attended by courtesans and attendants, the teacher recites the mantra. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 30.27)
Then, accompanied by the sounding of conchs and other instruments, one should raise up the deity,
having offered fragrant flowers and prostrated again and again.
One should cause [the offering] of rice mixed with ghee to be given to Bhavabhadrā;
one should also cause it to be given to the Vaiṣṇavas and to all the members of the assembly.
One should offer milk, curd, and ghee to Bala and Kṛṣṇa,
as well as plantains, jackfruit, and fruits such as rose-apple.
At the end of that, one should cause the oil and the powder of turmeric to be offered to the God of Gods with the root-mantra; both of these he should sprinkle upon the head.
And he should give the remainder to the devotees of Viṣṇu, or indeed give everything;
accompanied by the sounds of conchs and kettledrums, along with trumpets and flutes.
Accompanied by dance and song, and with the Brahmins reciting benedictions,
Rāma and Kṛṣṇa were then established upon seats strewn with flowers.
Having honored [the deity] with water for the guest-offering, water for the feet, and so forth, one should perform the rite of fire-oblation;
O great sage, one may do so either in the perpetual fire or in the previously mentioned [fire]. Vis 30.34.
The knower of mantras should offer sacrificial fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice into the Vaiṣṇava fire twenty-five times with the root mantra.
But for each [deity], O best of sages, one should subsequently perform the rite of pacification (śānti) with honey, milk, curd,
and ghee.
In that same manner, one should offer oblations with mantras and then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, one should bathe the Lord of the Gods according to the prescribed rite.
With black fragrant wood, uśīra, and sandalwood, as well as with the powder of the two types of turmeric and black sesame seeds; (30.38)
O best of sages, the practitioner, having ground all grains together with *siddhārtha* mustard seeds into powder, should sprinkle them at the conclusion of the ritual bathing.
Then, one should bathe the head of the deity with powdered rajani;
having offered a flower and paid obeisance, perform the auspicious recitation.
Then, having performed a pure bath with fragrant water, the practitioner, having applied fragrant unguents, should adorn himself with garments, ornaments, and garlands. (Vis 30.41)
One should worship the deity according to the prescribed rite with perfumes, flowers, and so forth;
then, having adorned the deity, one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).
One should then give to the brahmins, in due order, the gift of a cow, the gift of land, gold, clothing, ornaments, and all other gifts.
At the conclusion of that, one should honor the Vaiṣṇavas with food, clothing, and so forth,
as well as with betel for everyone, according to one's means.
Gold, or clothing, or cows, or even grain—
these should be given to the teacher as a cause for his great satisfaction.
Immediately after the gift, one should worship the deity with water for the hands, water for the feet, and so forth;
[one should offer] milk-rice, rice mixed with sesame, sweetmeats, and pure food, each separately.
One should offer plantains and breadfruit to the Lord of Gods;
and with devotion, one should give water for drinking and water for sipping to the God.
Quickly removing the seat for the food, one should lead the deity to the seat of enjoyment;
one should offer water for rinsing the mouth to the deity and cause a fragrant mouth-freshener to be presented.
Having first removed the previous garland, one should then cause another garland to be offered;
having adorned the God of gods, one should further present an aromatic mouth-freshener.
Accompanied by dance and song, and provided with lutes and flutes,
one should circumambulate the temple of the deity and lead Hari into the inner sanctum.
When the night has turned to dawn, one should then cause a festival to be held;
whether in a village or even in a city, one should also cause the purification of the roads to be performed.
Having adorned a palanquin, or a chariot, or even an elephant or a horse, with garments, flowers, and various kinds of garlands, [one should offer them]. 30.52.
Having thus adorned the deity, one should place it in the middle of the vehicle;
then, accompanied by song, dance, and the like, one should perform a circumambulation of the village.
Having prepared a drum accompanied by rhythmic clapping, one should wander through the village;
likewise, one should prepare oil mixed with *candana* and the powder of *rajanī*.
One should cause gifts to be given to the Vaiṣṇavas, especially to the members of the assembly;
then, having performed circumambulation once more of the unsurpassed temple of the deity, [one should proceed].
Having performed the ceremonial bathing according to the rules for the eternal God of gods, and having offered the great oblation, one should then lead Hari into the inner sanctum.
Thus has been briefly described the festival of Kṛṣṇa’s birthday,
which destroys all sins and bestows the fruit of all sacrifices.
One attains the fruit of union; this is the truth, there is no doubt about it.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Jayantī Festival," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-one.
Nārada said:

At the time of the investiture of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), the flower-sacrifice (*puṣpayāga*), the consecration and other festivals, and during the procedures for initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth;
As was said previously, "O gods, at that time, how was the maṇḍala drawn there by the castes? (Vis 31.1)
Viṣvaksena said:
O Sage, although [the ritual] is devoid of restrictions regarding place, time, recited syllables, and so forth, the action must nevertheless be performed according to the will of the agent.
O Sage, I shall explain to you the means for its accomplishment by those who seek success; listen to that which is truly secret from the beginning.

The practitioner, having smeared a lotus with his ring finger on a clean patch of ground as wide and long as the span of his own hand, and strewn it with a *droṇa* measure of unbroken grains of *śāli* rice, should draw an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp according to his desire.
Nārada said:
"O Lord of the Vāhinīs, having heard from you through the distinction of bliss the infinite rites of worship and so forth,
my mind, O Guru, desired to hear of the power of the root-mantra of the Cause of the Universe, by your grace."
Viṣvaksena said:

Listen, O Sage, to the power of this eight-syllabled mantra, the root of bondage, which is even inconceivable to Padmāsana; such is its nature that it possesses the power to speak, O Bhoh! (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 31.5)

Out of such grace that the God of gods himself, the remover of the suffering of his devotees, has shown for the sake of destroying my delusion— O Sage, because of your Vaiṣṇava nature, I shall tell you the power of the Root-Vidyā as he commanded it.
Seated in a purified place for the sake of worshiping himself and others, he remained absorbed in that pair [of mantras].
Then, as a means, men [should worship] the ocean of the reality of devotion, the seed-syllable, the meters, the sages, the fields, and the deities.

Or, having himself recited [the mantra] according to his ability, if he touches the region of his eyes and his body with all his fingers, he shall be cleansed of sin; having achieved his purpose, he will be a master of wealth and honored by his devotees like a god himself.
Endowed with the constituent parts of worship beginning with invocation, and freed from sin through the power of the root mantra,
this worship of the daughter of Viriñci has been performed, bringing delight to Ananta Viṣṇu, the source of all cosmic eggs.
Nārada said:
"Āvāhana" (invocation) is the act of bringing Lakṣmīdhara, who is present and engaged in the ritual, into one's presence by means of a mantra.

For the one whose self is the mantra and who performs the mantra-rite, the rites of *saṃsthāpana* (establishment) and so forth for his beloved [consort] are accomplished by this very [invocation]. 31.10.

Since Hari, as the Lord of the moving world, remains eternally present for their invocation at the proper time, why was it that Vāsudeva, stationed in the primary image, was not perceived by Nara during the festival and other occasions? How could this be?
"O Lord of the armies, O Guru, you have asked about a profound and supreme secret;
for one so devoted to Viṣvaksena, O Sage, who else but you would dare to ask such a question? Being pleased by him, I shall explain it to you."

O Sage, as you were intent upon the ritual services for the worship of Hari, a doubt arose whether your invocation was for the sake of manifesting His presence simultaneously or in succession. Vis_31.13.
O Sage, just as a garland of lamps arises simultaneously from a single lamp when lit, so too Vāsudeva will grant his presence when one draws his image; such is the conviction.
Then another [rite] bestows great wealth and yoga upon living beings, as well as prosperity and liberation;
having meditated upon it with the supreme root mantra and touched the five fingers of the image's heart-mudrā.
Having prostrated at the feet of the Sage with a gesture of the fingers clearly visible, or having scattered unbroken rice grains or flowers,
one should again offer the arghya, water for the feet, water for sipping, and perfumes and flowers, using the eight-syllable vidyā.
Then, having offered incense and lamps, and having presented the *bhūtānna* food, one should properly arrange the inner enclosure (*antarāvaraṇa*).
Likewise, for the [other] enclosures, as before, one should offer flowers with this very mantra, beginning with the *arghya* water.
Then, having offered betel-leaf to Acyuta and having performed the offering of food (bali) and the fire-oblation (homa) at the conclusion,
one who excels all others, bestows all accomplishments, and is beloved by kings and others, shall attain the perfection of yoga.
Nārada said:

"O Guru, O Viṣṇu, O General, how is it that Vāsudeva alone is worshipped as the foremost while his own seat remains covered? You ought to explain this to me in its entirety for the sake of dispelling my doubt. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 31.19)
Viṣvaksena:

Just as the single sacrificial fire is worshipped by the best of the twice-born in various sacrifices according to the distinction of its locations, so too is Vāsudeva called Ananta when seated upon his own throne; thus, the distinction arises from the difference in location.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Maṇḍala and Other Rites," in the Śrī Pañcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-Two:
Viṣvaksena—
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the characteristics of Hetirāja.
Listen, Nārada, to the secret [teaching] in the sequence beginning with the highest.
The great wheel may have a thousand spokes, or a hundred, or even fifty;
or the wheel may have sixteen spokes, or even twelve.
O tiger among sages, one should have it made according to the sequence of gold and so forth—
whether with gold, silver, copper, or iron, O sage.
One should have the King of Weapons fashioned as superior, inferior, or middling;
first, hear the characteristics of the superior King of Weapons.
Measuring twelve finger-breadths in length according to the measurement of one's own thumb, one should rotate it in the form of a wheel, with its width and length being the same.
Alternatively, O best of sages, the path for the measuring line is prescribed here;
one should have it made under a lunar mansion that is favorable to the village and the king.
One should have it fashioned by the most skilled artisans according to the treatises on the arts;
one should then draw [the deities] in the form of blazing fire, either facing the six directions or the four directions.
Having doubled it with a circle, it should become extended in the shape of a staff;
its width should be six finger-breadths, while the lotus is eight finger-breadths in height.
It should always measure twenty finger-breadths in length for each foot;
one should fashion the pericarp, which is twelve finger-breadths wide, so that it is most beautiful.
One should cause the great Vaiṣṇava discus to be fashioned in the center; having meditated upon it as being contained within a perfect circle, in accordance with the specific form [of the deity].
Ravi, Agni, Rudra, Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu,
as well as Kāla and the submarine fire (Vaḍavāgni), and indeed the fire in the crest [are present].
The staff is the form of Time (Kāla), and its radiance is the wheel of light;
that wheel, endowed with eight powers, is the very embodiment of the God.
Thus have I described the characteristics of the King of Weapons;
now listen, O observer of noble vows, to the characteristics of the middling King of Weapons.
One should rotate it in sequence like a wheel, provided with ten finger-breadths;
its length, including the handle, is correctly said to be eight finger-breadths.
That lotus is four finger-breadths in width and five finger-breadths in height;
the extent of the base of the lotus from there is fifteen finger-breadths.
O best of sages, having fashioned the pericarp in proportion to the petals, this is declared to be the medium [size];
one should perform the remainder as previously described.
One should fashion the form of a wheel with a width of eight finger-breadths;
one should likewise have the form of a mace made with a length of four finger-breadths.
Its circumference should be three finger-breadths, and its height likewise;
the lotus should be fourteen finger-breadths in size, equal to the width of the foot.
One should have the size of the pericarp made according to proportion;
or otherwise, one should fashion the characteristic of the staff-shaped [handle] as before.
In this middle and lowest wheel, perform the sequence starting from the highest according to the power of the agent; what has been taught as the highest and so forth shall be common to the rest.
The wise man should likewise fashion the very beautiful discus, which is the characteristic of the King of Weapons, for the purpose of being seen by devotees.
O great sage, for the purpose of the ritual worship and so forth, one should have the King of Weapons fashioned from gold or silver; alternatively, one may have it made from copper.
Or one may make it of mixed metal according to the prescriptions seen in the scriptures, O Nārada;
likewise, O great sage, for the sake of wealth, one should perform the offering of oblations and the festival for the purpose of the ritual bathing.
The form of the Discus is declared here to bring all prosperity and happiness;
alternatively, the knower of the Tantras should have it fashioned from the *baliberam* (the sacrificial image).
During the day, one should perform [the ritual] with the *bimba*; at night, one should have it performed with the *cakra*.
In the absence of the *cakra*, during the two twilights, one should have it performed with the *baliberam* (offering image).
Thus it has been briefly explained; it is impossible to describe everything regarding the consecration of the sacred thread and the flower sacrifice in its entirety.
Likewise, at the conclusion of the initiation, during the well-established self-worship,
the mandala of the wheel must be drawn upon the ground in this very same manner.
Without the form of a staff, one should worship that [mandala] with powder during the night;
first in the center of the wheel, and second in the beautiful middle.
The wise one should then place the third outer circle;
thus, having adorned it with powders, the supreme wheel-maṇḍala is complete.
In this [rite], Mahāviṣṇu is not desired; one should cause Hari to enter the center, and then, with the measure of a palm-clap, bring about satisfaction and wisdom.
With rice grains, one should fashion a form white as a jasmine flower or the moon on both sides,
and construct four doors in the four directions, each measuring one *tāla* in height.
The wise person who performs the ritual procedure for consecration— which brings happiness to the king and the kingdom,
and bestows fortune, fame, long life, as well as victory in battle—
shall attain all desires.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Rule for the Characteristics of the Weapon-King," in the *Śrīpāñcarātra* as compiled by Viṣvaksena.
Chapter Thirty-three. Viṣvaksena:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme procedure for the purification of substances.
Jewels, gold, garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as those made of copper.
Food, water, curd, milk, ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth;
the madhuparka offering, flowers, mouth-perfumes, and ritual gifts.
The Lord of the Gods should offer these and other such things;
now hear indeed about the substances that have been offered, whether pure or impure.
O best of sages, one should avoid those offerings such as food;
however, items ranging from gems to those made of base metals are indeed pure, of this there is no doubt.
Jewels, gold, garments, ornaments, and iron objects that have been offered become pure; one should wash them with the recitation of mantras.
One should wash them three times again with the mantra beginning with "astarāja";
likewise, one should wrap the copper jars with cloth.
By the mere majesty of the mantra, they are purified; of this there is no doubt.
This applies to food, water, curd, milk, ghee, honey, and likewise molasses. (Viṣṇu 33.7)
The honey-mixture (madhuparka), flowers, and offerings for refreshing the mouth—
these should be known as "nirmālya," which are auspicious and pleasing to me.
O Brahmin, one should cause the betel, the honey-mixture, and likewise the food of the sacrificial offering—
which has been consumed— to be presented to the preceptor.
Having taken a portion of one-fourth, he should place it before me in due order;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he should offer it, intending it for me.
One should give that flower-offering and that which has been eaten by Him to the Vaiṣṇavas.
Thus, O Sage, the purification of substances has been briefly described by me.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the presiding deities of the *sruk*, *sruva*, and other implements:
the *sruk* and *sruva*, as well as the *darvī*, are traditionally held to have the Earth as their deity.
The water-jar has the moon as its deity;
the *praṇītā* vessel has Varuṇa as its deity;
and the tongue has heaven as its deity.
The intermediate space and likewise the sacrificial porridge.
The *gandharva* has the fragrance as its presiding deity;
the flower has semen (*śukra*) as its presiding deity;
the unbroken rice grains (*akṣatāḥ*) have Lakṣmī as their presiding deity.
And the incense, which has the deity of the arghya offering as its presiding divinity.
One should know that the sun is the root of the lamp, and the moon is its presiding deity;
Vihaṛi is the deity of Vāsudeva,
and the fuel has Brahmā as its deity.
Clarified butter has Rudra as its deity;
food has Rudra as its presiding deity; and so too does the wood for the sacrificial fuel.
And likewise the classes of ancestors in their proper order.
All products of the cow are present there, with Gaṇeśa as the presiding deity;
Sarasvatī the goddess resides in the vowels, and all powers reside in the *praṇava*.
The essential nature of all things indeed belongs to Viṣṇu;
whether remembered or unremembered, everything has Nārāyaṇa as its self.
I shall describe the deities in the pitcher; listen, O Nārada, according to the truth:
the goddess Vāgīśvarī is the mouth, and Lakṣmī is likewise the ear.
Likewise, Śānti is on the two sides, and Pṛthivī is remembered on the back;
in the same way, one should meditate upon the full water-jar as the presiding deity.
Thus has been briefly declared the presiding deities for the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements,
in all these Viṣṇu sacrifices, whether they be regular (*nitya*) or occasional (*naimittika*).
Having understood the presiding deity therein, the practitioner should employ it;
he should cause the presiding deity of the mantras to be invoked in the sacrifices to Viṣṇu.
If one performs [the rite] out of ignorance or delusion, it remains as unperformed even though it was performed;
therefore, the practitioner who knows the ultimate truth should exert every effort [to avoid this].
Having recognized them for those tasks, the best of mantra-knowers should cause them to perform them.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Purification of Substances and Other Matters," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena-saṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-four. Viṣvaksena said:
O Lord of Sages, I shall describe the characteristics of temples in brief.
On the bank of a river, by a lake, on a mountain peak, or on level ground.
At the confluence of the ocean, on its shore, at ponds and at junctions of rivers;
in sacred fields, in great forests, and at holy fords, O great sage.
Whether in a village or a city, or even in a town or a hamlet; whether in a wretched village, a great village, a medium-sized one, or even a remote one.
One should cause a temple of Viṣṇu to be built at a site that is pleasing to the mind;
a stone structure is said to be the best, while one made of wood is called middling.
The wise man should construct a small temple for Viṣṇu according to his means, or he may have it made of clay, following the prescribed sequence.
The hand is of three kinds and each of those is threefold—superior, inferior, and middling;
that which consists of thirty cubits is called the most excellent of the excellent.
They know that the twenty-one-cubit [image] is of three kinds and is the best;
that which is fifteen cubits is called the middle-best.
The middle [size] is proclaimed to be eleven cubits,
while the smallest among the middling is said here to be nine cubits.
That is declared to be the best; here it is said that [the medium] is seven cubits, while the middle is five cubits and the smallest is three cubits.
According to his respective wealth, he should perform each of these with a concentrated mind.
At the base of the little finger, within a square, he should install the vehicle in the proper sequence.
Having placed a lion, or a garuḍa, or even the son of the Wind (Hanuman) upon the top of the celestial chariot, [he should place them] in the four directions starting from the east.
One should have [images of] Vārāha, Nārasiṃha, Śrīdhara, and Hayaśīrṣaka fashioned according to their own respective forms, or indeed Ananta in the north.
One should cause Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa to be placed in the four directions starting from the east, in due order.
Having had that constructed, one should then have a pinnacle and a mandala made upon it by a skilled artisan, in accordance with the scriptures.

O best of sages, the knower of the tantra should, according to the procedure for the crown-brick, have it constructed in sequence above that; having installed the *stūpa* pinnacle, he should place it in the center of that [structure].
Having drawn a lotus in the center of the stūpa, one should well fashion it with a pericarp and filaments,
having twelve, eight, or sixteen petals.
Above that, one should have a pitcher (kumbha) made, either one cubit in height or double that;
or even less by a quarter of its size—one should have it made very beautiful.
Then one should perform the whitening rite and have the painting work carried out;
having done this, one should then cause the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) to be constructed and the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) in due order.
O tiger among sages, one should have a wall constructed with two, three, or one gate-tower, and the kitchen should be built in the southeast.
O Lord of Sages, one should arrange the flower-stand and the water-stand within the enclosure wall,
either in the northwest, the southwest, or the northeast.
Having constructed a pavilion for recreation, endowed with all ornaments,
one should employ here that which has not been mentioned in other tantras after having examined it.
Thus has the characteristic of the temple (prāsāda) been briefly declared here;
now I shall speak of that called the vimāna—listen to it in its true essence, O Nārada.
Mandara, Niṣadha, and Nāgara,
along with Drāviḍa and Vesara— thus it is proclaimed as having five varieties.
Equipped with peaked halls and possessing nostrils facing all directions,
with a vast expanse above its neck, it is known as Mount Mandara.
That mountain which is square and very extensive, extending from Pāda to Siṃha,
and is devoid of peaks or halls, is known as Niṣadha.
From the wooden base up to the stūpa, if it is square on all sides, that is declared to be the Nāgara style; now the Drāviḍa style is being described.
From the neck upwards,
an eight-sided temple is Drāviḍa;
however, O best of sages, for a bedchamber, the form of a gopura is prescribed.
Or one should have it constructed here joined with three, four, five, or six pitchers;
[the shape] from the base of the kumuda-lotus up to the top of the stūpa should be either sixteen-sided or eight-sided.
Or one may have it made with thirty-two corners, O best of sages; describe that temple, for it will certainly possess the Dravidian style. (Vis 34.29)
From the neck upwards, it should be circular; that vesara [style] should be equal [to that].
The temple, possessing three full domes (pūrṇakumbha), takes the form of the vesara shape.
For the sake of increasing the prosperity of the king and the kingdom, this supreme celestial palace, the glorious ornament of the three worlds, is proclaimed as extending toward the east.
That which is constructed with burnt bricks or with stone is indeed called "puruṣa" (masculine);
that which is supported by materials consisting of stone, wood, and brick is to be understood as "napuṃsaka" (neuter).
The threefold vimāna known as *aṅganā* consists solely of a firm wooden structure;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*).
O best of sages, one should construct it to the north or the east of the palace,
provided with sixteen pillars and adorned with four archways.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
endowed with all ornaments, and possessed an altar-platform made of rice.
One should prepare eight *droṇas* combined with all manner of beautiful ornaments;
half of that amount should be rice, and half of that again should be sesame seeds.
One should construct a most beautiful altar (vedikā) higher and higher;
there, one should strew kuśa grass in sequence, with the tips pointing toward the north and the east.
Having wrapped it with new cloths, one should place [the materials] above it in sequence;
having prepared the bricks as before, four should be placed in the same order as previously described.
Having established the image with the image-mantra, the knower of mantras should establish the stūpa there with the root-mantra, while recollecting the primary form.
Having placed it in the center of each of those and again covered it with a cloth,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the four directions, or else in the western direction.
Or, having established the single fire, one should perform the oblation at night as before, offering fuel-sticks, clarified butter,
and sacrificial porridge entirely with the Mūrti-mantra.
O tiger among sages, upon the sacrificial ground they offered one hundred oblations for each [deity] with the fourth mantra, and then they performed the final full oblation.
The knower of mantras, having placed a very firm jar in the eastern direction, filled with various jewels or else combined with gold; Vis_34.43.
One should consecrate the jars— provided with lids, cloth, and firmly wound with thread—
around the eight Lords of the Vidyās in their proper order.
They were provided with cloths and lids, accompanied by gold and brushes,
joined with *aśvattha* sprouts, and filled to the brim with a *droṇa*.
There, one should have the Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
one should spend the remainder of the night there accompanied by song and dance.
When the night has turned to dawn, the preceptor, who knows all mantras, should bathe, adorn himself with garments and other ornaments, and then worship the astrologer.
O Sage, because Takṣaka is fit for the ritual action, one should worship the Takṣakas in due order with new garments and finger-rings, with the permission of the preceptor.
Indeed, no action whatsoever exists here without Takṣaka;
he alone, because of his performing all things, is celebrated as the Creator.
The supreme task that was previously undertaken by Takṣaka must indeed be performed by Takṣaka, and never by anyone else.
Since its very fitness for action has been ordained by the Creator,
it is therefore enjoined that one should strive with every effort together with that [discipline] alone.
Having determined the base and the summit, one should lay down the four square bricks;
having established the stūpa in the center, one should then recite the declaration of an auspicious day.
The practitioner of mantras should place the crown-brick in the east with the Puruṣa mantra;
having placed it in the south with the Viśva mantra, he should place it in the west with the Nivṛtti mantra.
Having placed sovereignty (aiśvarya) in the upper [part] with [the mantra] "sarveṇa," and the pinnacle (stūpī) with Parameṣṭhin,
the wise one should bathe [the image] with water-pots while reciting the Puruṣasūkta.
And one should place the water-pot upon the top of the stūpa with the root mantra;
there, one should feed Brāhmaṇas who are devotees of Viṣṇu and masters of the Vedas.
The Ṛgveda is in the eastern part, the Yajurveda in the south,
the Sāmaveda chanting in the west, and the Atharvavedins in the north.
Having fed them in due order according to the rules, he should then have the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited;
in this very same manner, he should also perform the rite for the temple of the retinue.
One should perform the ritual placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) for the enclosure wall itself, even without the formal sequence;
likewise, for the gate-tower (gopura) and the pavilion (maṇḍapa), it may be done without the image-consecration fire-sacrifice (mūrtihoma).
This supreme procedure for the crown-brick has been declared in brief;
in the manner thus described, one should cause an excellent temple to be built.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra, O best of sages, or even Takṣaka himself, [he should act] according to the injunctions of the scriptures. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.8.60)
One should have the artistic works executed, each preceding one being more important than the next;
all [works], beginning with the first brick, should be carried out according to the proper sequence.
But if a carpenter cannot be found at all, one should follow the supreme rule for the head-brick (mūrdheṣṭakā),
as well as the application of lime, the half-painting, and likewise the appearance of painting.
One should have the installation of the root image, as well as the temple for the retinue and so forth,
constructed by others such as potters and the like, according to the proper sequence.
The procedure for the main temple, extending up to the base of the stūpa, must be carried out by a carpenter alone; otherwise, it will cause the destruction of the kingdom. (Viṣṇudharmottara 34.64)

Thus, with the desire for the welfare of the king, the kingdom, the patron, and himself, the preceptor should cause the placement of the crown-bricks (mūrdheṣṭakā) to be performed in the proper sequence.
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter [titled "The Rules for the Characteristics of Temples, etc. in the Śrīpāñcarātra Viṣvaksenasaṃhitā;
[now begins] the thirty-fifth chapter.
Viṣvaksena said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare the characteristics of the retinue;
listen, O best of divine sages, to that which concludes with the great seats (mahāpīṭhas). 35.1.
The wise one should leave aside two *tāla*s or half of that from the temple for the retinue, and then arrange it at a distance of two, three, or even four cubits.
O Great Sage, having set aside four cubits or five cubits [for the central image],
one should arrange a space of one cubit all around for the retinue.
O Sage, with stones or bricks, according to the measurement of the teacher’s finger,
one should make a height of four fingers, with a lotus and its pericarp in the center.
One should have a pedestal constructed all around, joined with two tiers;
or one may make the offering-pedestal on all sides to the height of one palm-span.
In the same way, the measurement of the enclosure walls for the retinue should be determined here;
thus one should then arrange the pedestal for the entire retinue in every respect.
O great sage, having set aside sixteen cubits from the pavilion or from the enclosure wall, [the site] begins from the tip of the preceptor's fingers at the great pedestal.
O Great Sage, having extended it to eight cubits or half of that at the end, one should have a great pedestal constructed; each preceding one is more excellent than the next.
I shall proclaim the auspicious characteristics of the *tāla*, which bestow both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
O Nārada, listen to this supreme secret in its true essence in a secluded place. (Viṣṇudharmottara 35.9)
Or it may be three, four, or five cubits in width and length;
and from the footstool up to the lotus seat, it should be arranged according to the sequence of the superior and other grades.
One should have it constructed by a skilled artisan according to the instructions of the treatises;
for an excellent [image], one should make an excellent [image], and for a middling one, make a middling one.
One should construct even a lowly [shrine] in a manner that is lowly, in accordance with one's means;
it should be six or seven cubits in length, and its width should be equal to that.
Having understood this, one should fashion a most beautiful great seat (mahāpīṭha);
by means of skillful means and specific reasoning, one should have the offering altar (balipīṭhaka) constructed.
Listen, O observer of noble vows, to that sequence consisting of twenty-one parts: with one part [is made] the pedestal,
and likewise the base with five parts.
The *kumuda* is three parts, and the fillet (*paṭṭikā*) is one part;
the neck (*gala*) is four parts, and the upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*) is one part.
The *valabhī* (arched roof) should have three parts, and the height of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) should likewise have three parts;
having thus constructed the great pedestal (*mahāpīṭha*), it should be skillfully adorned by a wise artisan.
At the conclusion of the ritual work, the one most skilled in the tantra should perform the sprinkling;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sprinkling upon the sacrificial pedestal.

During the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day in the first fortnight of the month, on a favorable weekday and under a good lunar mansion, the wise one should perform the rite; on the preceding day, he should have the preparations made.
Then, having completed the work of carving, the one most skilled in the ritual system should sprinkle it;
he should cause a declaration of auspiciousness (*puṇyāha*) to be made there and sprinkle it with the five mantras.
Between the seat of the gods and the seat of the supreme deity, the wise one should have a pavilion constructed;
according to the rules for the pavilion, the archways (toraṇas) should be made as before.
Having properly prepared [the site] as before, one should construct an altar in the center,
measuring four cubits or two cubits [in length], and one cubit in height, O Sage.
One should have it made very smooth there, resembling the surface of a mirror;
then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should sprinkle it with scented water.
Between that [altar] and the pedestal, one should have either a circular or a square pit constructed;
there, in the center, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).
Upon the sacrificial altar, one should place two *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, together with a tuft of grass,
a lid, gold, and cloth, and filled with river water.
The wise one should place many attendants of Viṣṇu in the middle, together with their sūtras, free from defects, filled with a *droṇa* measure, and very beautiful.
One should place the water-jars separately from Indra to Īśāna;
[namely] Kumuda, Kumudākṣa, Puṇḍarīka, and Vāmana.

Having worshipped Śaṅkukarṇa— who has eyes like serpents, a beautiful face, and is well-established— with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with a joyful heart.
One should offer one hundred oblations each of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, curd, honey, milk, barley, and water mixed with white mustard seeds.
With either the eight-syllable mantra or the twelve-syllable mantra,
the wise one should pass the remainder of the night with dance, song, and musical instruments.
When the auspicious moment had arrived, with the permission of the Brahmins,
he went around the palace clockwise while reciting verses of benediction.
Having sprinkled [the substances] in their respective places while the wise one recollects those specific locations,
he should consecrate the remainder of the water from the pitcher upon the great pedestal.
The best of practitioners should call to mind all the attendants of Viṣṇu,
[offering] milk-rice, rice-and-pulse, sweetmeats, and turmeric-rice— these four kinds of food.
One should offer clarified butter mixed with curd and milk, as well as coconut water,
upon the great pedestal while recollecting the Primordial Form.
Having offered the remainder and collected it, one should cast the bali-offering to Caṇḍa and the others,
accompanied by conch shells, kettledrums, and the like, and joined with song and dance.
One should complete the *balikarma* accompanied by the study of the Vedas;
at the conclusion of the *bali*, one should bathe the Supreme Self, whether it be the lowest or the highest.
Then, having offered the great oblation, one should again perform the rite for an auspicious day;
there, one should feed the Vaiṣṇava Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas.
Thereafter, one should honor the teacher with gold, jewels, and rings;
this is auspicious, brings renown, and shall bring about all forms of peace.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Installation of the Great Seat," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
The thirty-sixth chapter.
Viṣvaksena said: ...
[the knower of mantras] should cause the Brahmins there to pronounce an auspicious day (puṇyāha) together with them.
It should be five bhāras in measure, or half of that, or even half of that again.
One should certainly not make that excellent store of rice deficient;
there, the wise man should scatter half of it upwards and likewise half of the rice grains.
