Having placed an excellent eight-petaled lotus upon the rice,
one should write the seed-syllable in its center and arrange the eight syllables on the petals.
The most excellent practitioner should place nine jars in the center,
equipped with threads and cloths, and adorned with garlands of jewels.
Filled with scented water and wrapped in a pair of cloths—
this applies to each of the eight jars starting from the east, or else a single cloth for each.
One should place the eight [deities] such as Diṅmūrti and the others, either on a single cloth or separately;
one should place a pitcher upon the pericarp and eight pitchers upon the petals.
Or, having fashioned a *kūrca* from twenty-one blades of *darbha* grass, one should place it within that full jar;
in its center, one should visualize the temple of the deity.
The Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet;
he is endowed with a thousand locks of hair and possesses a thousand crowns.
Resembling a thousand suns, with a face like a thousand moons,
joined by a thousand vehicles, and possessing a nose directed toward every quarter.

"One should consecrate [the image] during the first part of the night, saying: 'He who holds the conch, the discus, and the mace in his hands, and is endowed with all weapons—he is said to be in the form of a palace.'"
O celestial sage, through that very meditation one attains the perfect bath;
the seeker of liberation attains liberation. Therefore, meditation is preeminent.
In all [structures] such as the pavilions, meditation is thus proclaimed;
in the center of that, the wise one should lead [the visualization], recollecting it as belonging to the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin).
One should contemplate his form starting from the east and ending in the north;
one should then install Vainateya and the others in the corners beginning with the southeast.
One should place a lion, the lord of the Mṛgagaṇa and a portion of Vainateya, in the center of that full jar; therein one should practice the Pauruṣa Sūkta.

O Nārada, one should recite the respective mantras for the deities of the directions and others within the pitchers, in due order, having extracted the essence of the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda.
One should recite [the names] from the east up to Soma with a melodious voice;
then, one should worship the full jars and other items with that mantra.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering with the Parameṣṭhin mantra;
then, having performed protection against the eight directions, one should offer mouth-freshener.
Accompanied by the sound of a bell and together with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
one should perform the offering of oblations with sacrificial food in the eight directions.
O best of sages, all the kumuda and other lotuses receive this supreme offering, while the sound of conchs and drums resounds here.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, the practitioner who knows the ultimate truth,
having paid homage to all [the deities] without exception, should recite the auspicious verses in their proper order.
When the night has turned to dawn, the teacher should perform his bath,
either with the Puruṣasūkta or with the mantra of Parameṣṭhin.
The practitioner should worship the Lord of Gods, Puruṣottama, with [offerings] contained in a water-pot, beginning with perfumes and ending with lamps, each with its respective mantra. (Vis 36.22)
One should worship the jars of the eight directions, starting from the east and ending with the northeast;
then, having taken up the great jar and others, one should circumambulate the temple.
Accompanied by the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, together with dance and song,
and joined with the recitation of auspicious verses, one should cause [the image] to enter the inner sanctum.
O Nārada, having placed the supreme Lord of Lords within the great jar upon the rice in front of the deity, according to the prescribed rite.
Having placed the jars in sequence upon rice on its eastern side,
one should worship them with the offering of water for honor (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), and so forth, ending with the mouth-freshener (*mukhavāsa*).
Having thus worshipped, the wise one, uttering the words "May you forgive me," [should pray]:
"O Janārdana, [whatever was done] deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in devotion..."
"O Lord of Gods, you should forgive me; may that [rite] be complete for me.
Having done this, the knower of mantras should recite auspicious verses.
The preceptor, having taken a flower and paid homage to Lord Hari,
should join it to the primary image (mūlabera) of the Lord of Gods situated within the pitcher.
In the same manner, one should install the power from the eight jars into that body;
first, one should deposit Parameṣṭhin with the [mantra] of the quarters, the forms, and so forth, using one's own vidyā.
One should sprinkle those [drops] with three drops from the top of the head of the root image;
then, having repeatedly offered flowers with both hands at the feet of the deity...
Then, together with the Brahmins, he should recite the Puruṣasūkta;
at that time, O one of great wisdom, he should honor the preceptor with wealth.
With new garments, rings, bracelets, and other ornaments,
one should sprinkle the excellent house with water contained within the pitcher.
The substance used here, excluding the ornaments for the deity,
should be given to the preceptor along with garments, rice, and other offerings.
One should present all that which has been offered to the Sāttvatas;
there, one should honor the artisan and subsequently honor the astrologer.
There, the wise man should feed Vaiṣṇava brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
at the conclusion of the rite, he should have a painting executed.
One should perform the fire-oblation (havana) in the pavilion and other locations in this very same manner;
in the manner thus described, one should carry out the consecration (adhivāsana).
O Sage, in the perfuming of the garments, the sprinkling of the palace,
and the rite of planting the sprouts, no fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed here.

O divine sage, one should construct the house for a child according to the previous sequence; however, in the case of a young man's residence, one should omit the *jagatī* and the *kumuda* and so forth.
During the consecration of the abode of the child, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
one should cause the preliminary rites such as the preparatory consecration (adhivāsa) and those pertaining to Vāsava and the other deities to be performed.
O Nārada, having thus dismissed the Śakti in the manner described,
one should then perform the restoration of the dilapidated [temple] by means of a skilled artisan.
If one acts otherwise out of delusion, there will be the destruction of the village, the loss of wealth, and the ruin of the dwelling; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should first, according to the prescribed rite, transfer the supreme Hari residing in the celestial chariot (vimāna) into the great image (mahābimba) in due order.
Therefore, with every effort, one should begin the rite of awakening the power (śaktyudvāsana),
having united it with the presiding deity of the temple by means of a single path.
Likewise, [he should construct] pleasure pavilions, as well as embankments and ramparts;
and in the surrounding dwellings and so forth, as well as outside the rampart.
One should perform the consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the manner thus described;
having thus briefly explained this, one should then commence the restoration of the dilapidated (*jīrṇoddhāra*).
After this, O great sage, I shall explain the supreme procedure for the restoration of a dilapidated [temple], concerning the preceptor, the patron, and the master carpenter.
When an earthen image has decayed, its staff, clay,
and ropes should be replaced with new earthen materials, or one may have it made of stone.
When an image made of stone has been consumed, [the substitute] should be made of iron or likewise of stone;
when an image made of jewels has been consumed, it should be made of gold or silver.
Wood, clay, stone, metal, and so forth, as well as gold, jewels, and the like, should be known as superior in sequence, each subsequent one being more excellent than the preceding.
"Some wise ones say that gold and gems are equal,
while others, O divine sage, say that stone and iron are similar."
"Gold, silver, and copper are equal, O Nārada;
having designated them by the term 'iron' (loha), one should perform festivals and other rites. (Viṣṇu 36.52)
O best of eminent sages, if the sacrificer so desires, [the image may be made] according to his means, provided it is made without tin and iron.
O Sage, in the making of an image for one's own sake or for the sake of others,
even if it is accomplished with inferior materials, the work performed for another is unsurpassed.
The wise declare that the task appropriate for one's own station is the "middling" one;
however, by performing a superior task through delusion, one is ruined by those who are inferior.
"The entire kingdom and its people [are at risk]," such is the certainty of the scripture;
there is only a discrepancy regarding the goods themselves, in terms of weights, measures, and standards.

O Sage, if there is neither deficiency nor excess in the procedure for the restoration of ruined temples, such as those containing the original or primary images, then one attains success for oneself. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.36.57)
Whether for one's own sake or for the sake of others, O best of the twice-born, this is equal:
for one's own sake there would be the destruction of one's lineage; for the sake of others, the destruction of the kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort, one should have constructed, as prescribed by the rules,
a celestial palace (vimāna), or a statue, as well as a rampart and a gate-tower.
One should construct a pavilion as before for the application of new work and plastering;
if the temple has been destroyed, one should perform it upon that ground according to the ancient teachings or the traditional rites of the sages.
One should cause it to be built according to one's desire, whether divine or human; right here, one may construct either an excellent abode or even one that is most excellent of all.
O best of Brahmins, O most excellent of sages, if the temple is dilapidated,
one should have it rebuilt according to either the middle or the lowest standard.
If the sacrificer so desires, it may likewise be in the middle [region];
however, in that case, there would be either a lowly abode or one that is both lowly and supreme.
Furthermore, for the rite of restoring what is ruined, it should be of the lowest-of-the-low type,
provided with an *upapīṭha*, and consisting of either two or three stories.
One should construct [the temple] with a single story according to one's means;
having understood the sequence beginning with the most excellent, one may increase it according to one's desire.
By increasing [the merit], O Nārada, one obtains the prosperity of the king, the kingdom,
as well as the cities and so forth, especially that of the royal residence.

O Sage, if one should cause a dwelling here in this world to be built in the shape of a gateway, with turrets and the like, or if it is dilapidated, one should have it restored to the form of a water-shed.
Having designated the city and so forth, one should build a house according to the king's favor, in accordance with one's wealth, and as one pleases.

Alternatively, one may construct an unsurpassed temple in accordance with the layout of the village; furthermore, within that very place, one should fashion an image according to the proportions of the temple itself.
O Sage, in the rite for restoring what has been lost, one should act according to the measurement of the door or the measurement of the inner sanctum, categorized as superior, inferior, or middling.
To the west or south of that house, an exit-like form is not desired;
O best of sages, one should perform the restoration of what is dilapidated as previously described.
If, out of delusion, one should cause the exit [of the image] toward the west or the south,
it will cause strife for the village and the path of Dharma will perish.
That kingdom and the sacrificer will surely perish; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not create the form of an exit.
If the patron so desires, one should increase the size of the eastern gatehouse, the pavilion, and so forth, in due order, according to his wish.
O Sage, everything from the intermediate directions to the west is not intended [for this]; rather, for a house with an eastern gate, the pavilion and so forth should be arranged in due order.
O best of sages, in the restoration of what is decayed, one should perform everything as before;
therefore, with every effort, one should cause it to increase according to one's desire.
By increasing [the size], one obtains prosperity for that house day by day;
however, damage to the ornaments on the walls and other parts is a cause of misfortune.
The sages, Nārada and others, declare that [the merit] would not be so;
there is even greater devotion at the city gate, and especially within the enclosure wall.
Having thus examined [the site], the wise one should proceed in due order with the new construction, the plastering, the restoration of what is ruined, and the renovation of what is decayed.
O best of sages, if the primary image (mūlabera) should become cracked or broken, the practitioner, accompanied by a master craftsman, should subsequently have it repaired.
O great sage, if that image should crack, one should first abandon it;
thereafter, one should swiftly withdraw the deity from the image and perform a rite of pacification.
Having duly installed the imperishable Hari in a water-pot before him,
one should bring Hari from the original image into the middle of that pot by means of the root mantra.
Then, having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma) with the Cakra-mantra,
the knower of mantras [should recite] the great Sudarśana mantra, which brings about all peace.
One should perform the invocation and dismissal from the water-pot as before; having prepared the locus of the Child (Bāla) in due order, one should install it as prescribed by the ritual rules.
O best of sages, the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) for him is not required;
one should install the imperishable Hari by means of immediate consecration (sadyo 'dhivāsana) alone.
O best of sages, in the restoration of a dilapidated temple, one should disregard considerations of time, hour, and so forth,
after having observed the many defects that arise day by day at the time of worship.
Afterwards, one should worship the God if he has become free from defects; however, if he is thus possessed of defects, one might worship Hari out of delusion or greed.
That worship goes to waste; the performer and the patron perish.
That village will go to ruin, and there will be an increase in disease.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the restoration of what has decayed;
even after the banner has been raised, if any defect is subsequently observed.
And having reached the place where the child resides, O best of sages, one should perform a festival there accompanied by a peace-offering (śānti-homa).
Otherwise, there would be great fault and it would bring about the destruction of the king;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform the remaining rites.
O Nārada, the wise one should perform the rites such as the perpetual festivals even in the place of a child as before; this is the certain conclusion of the scripture.
One who knows the mantras, is endowed with a noble lineage, is of good family, has mastered the scriptures,
knows the tantras, recites the Vedas, and is devoted to the rites of installation and so forth.
With all his limbs complete and free from all diseases,
he is perfectly tranquil, skillful, self-controlled, and content with whatever comes by chance.
Free from envy, having conquered anger, avoiding impurity and confusion, distinguishing between what is to be avoided and what is not, grateful, proactive, and full of devotion.
Whether he be a descendant of that lineage, a disciple, or a grand-disciple who has mastered the tantras;
or one who possesses the tantras, is initiated, virtuous, or the most excellent among those who know virtue.
One afflicted with consumption,
one with leprosy, one with abdominal tumors, one suffering from piles, one who is bald, one who is very old, a child, and one with disease of the testicles. Vis 36.97.
A Brahmin who has a short stature yet is excessively tall, whose chin is thin, who is deaf, whose limbs are deformed, and who is afflicted by defects of the teeth; Vis 36.98.
One who has deformed nails should especially avoid [participating] in rites for the gods;
know this, O Nārada, to be the characteristic of both the Sthāpaka and the Ācārya.

The wise one, having thus examined [the candidates] for the rites of consecration, propitiation, and so forth, should appoint an ācārya and likewise an *sthāpaka*, both endowed with the characteristics of the *saṃgraha*.
Especially during the restoration of a ruined temple,
the consecrator, accompanied by carpenters, should observe the auspicious characteristics at a favorable moment and a propitious conjunction.
O Nārada, the plowing and other such rites should be performed with a single thread;
whatever has been commenced with a particular thread, one should carry it through to completion with that same thread.
O best of sages, one should observe what has not been mentioned in other tantras and apply it here, as well as the specific details; otherwise, it will cause the destruction of the kingdom.
Endowed with the four castes, devoted to virtuous conduct,
of noble lineage, a knower of all scriptures, one who understands the world, and a knower of all dharmas.
He is devoted, wealthy, eloquent, endowed with the fulfillment of all his intentions,
virtuous, handsome, full of faith, and pure in mind.
Ācārya, Takṣaka, Vaṃśaga, Sumukhottama, Śāstraprāmāṇyaka, Dīna, and Subahubhṛtyavat.
The wise one who acts according to what has been taught is skilled in all activities;
he is a predecessor, a member of that lineage, a disciple, or even a grand-disciple.

"O Sage, one who belongs to that same class or a different class, provided he possesses superior qualities than the previous one, may take it; but only upon the relinquishment of the former, not otherwise."
If one should take [it] through delusion, there would be a confusion of agents for him;
by the fault of this confusion of agents, it causes disease for the king and his kingdom.
Therefore, with every effort, one should act according to the perspective of the scriptures,
like a skilled carpenter who knows the carpenter’s line and is proficient in all crafts.
One who is light-handed, handsome, very peaceful, and divine; one endowed with a noble lineage and its continuity, skillful, and devoted to the supreme goal.
One who is a Vaiṣṇava, knows the proper time for the thread ceremony, is skilled in ritual action, is a pioneer in practice,
compassionate, tranquil in mind, possesses a true lineage, and is honored by the virtuous.
But if those are unavailable, one should instead invite members of their lineage, their disciples, or their grand-disciples;
one should not, in this manner, cause a confusion of castes.

O Great Sage, in the primordial age, that which was undertaken by one caste and performed out of delusion by another caste brought about the destruction of kings and their kingdoms. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.6.114)

O best of sages, having thus undertaken the ritual according to its characteristics, if one should out of delusion cause it to be performed by another path contrary to the performer's intention, [the rite fails].* *Note: The final clause of the verse is elliptical; the full sense is that the ritual becomes fruitless or leads to undesirable results. The translation provided reflects the standard interpretation of this technical injunction.*
"Sin would accrue to the preceptor, the patron, and even the carpenter.
Having thus reflected extensively with his eye of wisdom, he remained constantly single-minded through his faculty of discernment.
And let him cause the restoration of what is decayed to be carried out by the master architect; for he is the teacher of the worlds, the supreme Guru Viṣvaksena.
Henceforth, I shall describe specifically the characteristics of the temple.
The sprinkling of chariots, palanquins, and other such vehicles is supremely auspicious;
it brings peace to all men and bestows the fruit of visiting all sacred fords.
In the pure pavilion previously described, endowed with all auspicious things,
one should construct in its center an altar measuring one cubit, either circular or square.
One should have it constructed according to the prescriptions of the scriptures; its name is now stated:
a perfectly beautiful circular shape, or a very auspicious square.
O Nārada, for the sake of increasing the king and the kingdom, it should always be circular; however, for the sake of increasing villages and settlements, it should be square.
The circular and the square should be known as the forms;
the altar (vedi) may be made with either unbaked or baked bricks— thus one should construct an unsurpassed altar.
One should smear the altar— which is one cubit high or half that, and resembles the surface of a mirror—
as before, and sprinkle it with water in the same sequence as previously described.
There, with the permission of the Brahmins, one should have them recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha);
O best of sages, having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as before with rice.
Having prepared half that amount of rice, either with *śāli* rice or other grains,
one should place a pedestal upon the altar and then draw [the design] again.
One should prepare the altar with rice grains all around the railing;
O best of sages, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus in the center of the rice.
One should write the statement beginning with "chandomūla" in the middle of that petal;
it should be covered with thread and cloth, and endowed with all the auspicious characteristics.
One should place [the deity] within the center of the moon-maṇḍala by means of that mantra;
then, one should cast a white flower into the middle of the water from that jar.
Having adorned it with flower garlands and embellished it with a pair of garments,
it should likewise be provided with the nine jewels and equipped with nine tufts of wool.
In the center of that temple, one should invoke the presiding deity;
and one should place a water-pot in the center, with [the other pots] situated around it on the petals of the eight directions.
The wise one, having covered eight jars in sequence with new cloth, each with its respective mantra, and having provided them with thread, flowers, and water; Vis_36.131.
Equipped with two bundles of kuśa grass and adorned with flower garlands,
one should bring it to the jar as before, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.
The preceptor, having adorned himself with gold, garments, and finger-rings,
stands facing north on the right side of the water-pot.
Having formed a hollowed palmful of flowers, the wise one should recite this mantra,
namely the hymn beginning with "Sahasraśīrṣā" from the Puruṣa-sūkta.
O tiger among sages, one should then bring the deity in the form of the temple into the pitcher, or else one should bring it by means of the *parameṣṭhin* mantra.

The wise one, the best among those who know mantras, should bring [the offerings] into the eight jars at the cardinal points with their respective mantras, and should perform the offering of the bali oblation as before.
In the same manner, the wise one should sprinkle [the site] with the Puruṣasūkta;
having likewise sprinkled the inner sanctum (garbhageha) both inside and out on all sides.
One should join the Lord of Gods with the water remaining in the pitcher for the celestial chariots and other vehicles;
having worshipped him with the offering of water (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and so forth, no sacrificial oblation (havis) is required there.
One should offer the bali-oblation there in all eight directions;
at that time, the highly wise master should perform the worship in due order.
Then one should worship [the deity] like a god with golden garments and rings;
there, one should honor the artisan with new garments and rings.
One should feed Brāhmaṇas there who are devotees of Viṣṇu and have mastered the Vedas;
in this very same manner, one should likewise perform the rites for the three palanquins.
The knower of mantras should bring power for chariots and other vehicles from the Lord of Birds; with that mantra, he should sprinkle them in the prescribed sequence as before.
O Lord of Sages, if there should be contact with Caṇḍālas, outcasts, menstruating women, Niṣādas, carpenters, and the like— whether out of greed or through delusion— [what is the remedy? Vis_36.143.
In this case, the temple is indeed purified simply by sprinkling it with water;
or else, O tiger among sages, one should bring the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having anointed a space one cubit in front of the deity with focused concentration,
he should spread out a *droṇa* of *śāli* rice and likewise half that amount of husked grain.

There, in the center, the practitioner should draw a lotus according to the previously mentioned procedure; having placed the five products of the cow there, [he should do so] with that seed-syllable.
