One should offer sixteen oblations each of the fuel sticks (*samidh*) with the root mantra, the clarified butter (*ājya*) with the *praṇava*, and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) with the *Puruṣasūkta*.
Having performed the oblation in this manner according to the ritual procedure, one should again offer oblations with clarified butter;
and out of devotion to Viṣṇu, one should perform the fire-sacrifice with the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, O best of sages, having correctly understood the Nārāyaṇa-sūkta which sets forth the creation and other [cosmological] matters, one should offer oblations into the fire for Kālī in due order.
One should offer oblations again and again with the five Upaniṣadic mantras;
furthermore, one should perform the pacifying homa according to the ritual rules as previously described.
Having performed the oblation in this manner, O best of sages, one should bind the protective amulet (kautuka) of Hari;
then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship the Lord who has the sacrificial offering as His end.
O Great Sage, one should indeed perform [the rite] there with either the twelve-syllable mantra or the form-mantra, using either linen thread or cotton.
One should sprinkle that thread repeatedly with the root mantra;
at night, one should hold a great festival with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments.
Having decorated the auspicious amulet, O Nārada, and placed it upon rice,
one should thereafter wander through the village accompanied by a multitude of great lamps.
Thereafter, one should bind the protective thread (kautuka) according to the previously mentioned procedure;
the fire offering (homa) should be performed at night, and the sprinkling with water during the day.
One should not perform the sprinkling at night, nor should one perform the fire-oblation during the day;
therefore, with every effort, one should arrange the fire-oblation at night.
At dawn, during an auspicious moment, one should perform the ritual sprinkling with water in due order;
one should sprinkle according to the prescribed rule from the image up to the surrounding deities.
Then one should invoke the god Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment—
the god who bears the conch and the discus, who is clad in yellow garments, and who is infallible.
Adorned with all ornaments and resplendent with a forest garland,
he resembles a rājāvarta gem and is decorated with necklaces and armlets.
With the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, wearing beautiful earrings shaped like sea-monsters,
with a neck like a conch shell, mighty-armed, and with a face slightly smiling.
Having thus meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu seated upon Garuḍa,
together with his twelve and ten forms.
Likewise by the world-protectors, the Ādityas, the Rudras, and the Vasus;
and by the ṛṣis, the cāraṇas, the siddhas, the kinnaras, and the hosts of apsarases.
Having thus meditated upon Mahāviṣṇu, the flawless Nārāyaṇa,
and having installed him with his respective mantra, one should sprinkle him with fragrant water.
With the remaining water, the wise one should sprinkle the retinue;
he should sprinkle all the members of the retinue without exception using their own mantras preceded by the *praṇava*.
Having taken the jars from the east and other directions, one should perform the consecration upon the great pedestal;
thereafter, one should worship Puruṣottama with the Puruṣasūkta.
Thereafter, one should present the sacrificial offering according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should also give the bali-oblation to Caṇḍa and the others in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should perform the circumambulation with the *bali* offerings joined with the image;
in this manner, one should present the *bali* in sequence, accompanied by conch shells, trumpets, and other instruments. (Viṣṇudharma 38.72)
Then one should perform a circumambulation, prostrate, and ask for forgiveness;
having given the teacher’s fee, one should thereafter feed the Brahmins.
Having thoroughly honored the *hotṛ* priests, he should again worship the preceptor (*ācārya*) with necklaces,
armlets, a waist-band, and finger-rings.
One should present various garments to the teacher and give an excellent sacrificial fee, having also given a milch cow.
Or else, half of the wealth should be given to the officiating priests who desire his welfare;
to the practitioners, three-quarters less; and to those who have received initiation, half of that.
And one should give food offerings to all in the presence of the deity;
O Sage, in the same manner, one should cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given during the Pavitrāropaṇa rite.
Thus has the procedure for the ritual sprinkling with water been correctly explained;
having reflected upon this, it should be performed by those proficient in the Pañcarātra.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Sprinkling [Water] Based on Omens such as the Shaking of the Throne," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
Chapter Thirty-nine:
Viṣvaksena said—
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the supreme procedure for expiation.
O best of sages, in all activities such as worship and the like, [one should act with mindfulness].
If one fails to perform the morning twilight worship, one should perform it twice at midday;
if one fails to perform it both in the morning and at midday, one should perform it three times in the evening.
If the worship is omitted for a single day, one should observe a fast;
having bathed [the deity] with nine jars according to the previously mentioned procedure, [one should proceed].
There, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), and three Brāhmaṇas should indeed be fed,
having honored them according to rule by means of the procedure previously described.
In the second [period] one should perform twice as much, and in the third, three times as much;
in this very manner it should be carried out until the end of twelve days.
In that case, it would be deficient in its wings; one should bathe the lowliest and the most excellent there, and feed twelve Brahmins with milk-rice (pāyasa).
If it should be deficient by one month, one should perform the Vāstu-homa there;
then, according to the inferior or superior method, one should cause the ceremonial bathing of Hari to be performed.
There, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited and perform worship in the prescribed sequence;
there, one should feed the learned Brahmins, numbering more than fifteen.
Having performed this in sequence, especially until the end of three months;
[this applies] in the event of a lapse in worship for a period starting from three months up to six months.
Having swept the interior and exterior of the house, having washed it according to the rules,
and having perfumed it with agallochum incense, one should then cause a day of merit (puṇyāha) to be proclaimed there.
Or indeed, by means of the most excellent path, or according to the sequence of eighty-one [substances], one should bathe the Lord of the Gods of gods in accordance with one's wealth. // Vis_39.11 //
There, one should feed the Brahmins and perform the fire-oblation as before;
then, having offered the great sacrificial oblation, one should worship Puruṣottama.
Thereafter, O tiger among sages, before three years have passed, one should perform the most excellent bathing ceremony according to the previously mentioned procedure.
One should feed Brāhmaṇas there according to one's means;
beyond that, but within twelve years, the expiation is prescribed.
Then, having gazed at the inner sanctum with the *praṇava*,
the practitioner, having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in due order, should purify the interior of the shrine.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with either the highest-of-the-high path or the middle one, according to the extent of one's available wealth.
One should feed Brahmins there according to one's means;
having performed a peace-offering (*śāntihoma*), one should worship Hari as before.
Thereafter, O best of sages, an expiation is prescribed:
one should perform a sprinkling with water, preceded by the proclamation of an auspicious day.
One should feed Brahmins there; by that, peace will be attained.
Even if the materials for the components of the worship—from the *arghya* offering up to the sacrificial oblation (*havis*)—are lacking.
One should worship the Lord of Gods again with double the effort even if using inferior materials;
one should mutter the eight-syllable mantra a hundred times before the deity.
To avoid those faults, this expiation should be performed;
one should perform the expiation day by day with that same substance in due order.
This has been declared in brief, O Nārada, regarding the omission of worship;
if the temple collapses there, one should have a place for the Child (Bāla) constructed.
Having installed the Lord of Gods according to the prescribed rule, one should worship him day after day;
having prepared the sanctuary as before, one should then perform the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
But when the original foundation has crumbled, one should construct a structure of stone or wood in its place;
provided with bricks and mortar, one should have new works carried out.
There, in that abode of variegated appearances, one should perform the work of painting;
there one should perform the ritual bathing and cause the fire-oblation for the image to be performed.
Then, one should have the Brahmins who are devotees of Viṣṇu partake of a meal;
having offered the great sacrificial oblation, one should then worship Puruṣottama.
I shall now declare the sequence of the rules for expiation regarding the burning of a temple,
a pavilion, a rampart, or likewise a gate-tower.
Or even inside a palace, or indeed in a kitchen,
or in a pleasure pavilion, or even in a sacrificial pavilion.
If, through negligence, [the image] is burnt by fire while it is in a flower-vessel, a water-vessel, or any other such place, one should properly restore it as before.
One should have the ceremonial bathing performed before three nights for the inferior and superior [types of images];
there, one should feed the Brahmins and likewise cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made.
One should recite the Nārāyaṇa Upaniṣad according to the sequence of the Tantra;
one should offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter with the eight-syllable mantra.
If the celestial palace has been burnt, but the image alone remains;
or if only a portion of that which was burnt remains, one should properly restore it as before.
One should perform the supreme ablution, or indeed the inferior or intermediate one;
one should bathe the Lord of the God of Gods and worship Him according to the previous sequence.
If the temple has been extensively burnt, one should designate it as a place for novices;
having constructed a new house in due order, one should have the remaining rites performed.
Nārada said:
"The defect of the place has been described by you to me in detail;
now tell me, without omission, about all the exceedingly wonderful defects."
Whatever defects indeed arise in the abode of the God of gods, as well as whatever defects exist in the sacrificial oblations and in the ritual implements; [all these are removed by this].
Viṣvaksena: Well asked by you, O Lord; and I must now speak.
I shall tell you of those defects that exist in the abode of the God of gods.
O Lord of Sages, upon seeing an anthill, as well as a snake, or other creatures that possess venom, one should likewise [act].
In the case of eating honey, of intentionally throwing oneself into fire, and likewise in the falling of lightning and thunderbolts, as well as the falling of meteors; // Vis_39.39 //
If, through negligence, the image should become split in two, or if it should dwell in an owl or arise from trees; Vis_39.40.
And when a celestial palace is broken, when all things are brought to destruction, when hair, insects, and the like fall [into water], and when aquatic creatures are cast down; Vis_39.41.
And likewise for other living beings, at the time of their downfall, during sacrificial offerings,
in the inner sanctum of Viṣṇu, and similarly during ritual presentations.
In the pavilion of the God of Gods, either in the first enclosure,
or in the second, or in the third, on all the offering pedestals (balipīṭha).
In the fire-hall, in the water-hall, and likewise in the flower-hall,
as well as in the assembly pavilion and the ornamentation pavilion.
O Lord of Sages, I shall describe the faults that arise when cows become loose in other places of recreation as well as in their own stalls. (Viṣṇudharmottara 39.45)
The sight of an anthill portends disease; the sight of a snake, death; the sight of a Madhu tree, drought; and the sight of others, famine. (Viṣṇudharmottara 39.46)
If a king sees a statue of Hari with its pedestal (or *śilīndhra*) loose,
he will meet with death or the loss of his kingdom.
He will either contract a great disease, suffer defeat at the hands of enemies, or experience separation from his children and wife; of this there is no doubt.
The destruction of villages, cities, the country, and the army will occur either completely or there will be an immediate minor affliction.
In the throne hall, in the inner sanctum, and likewise in the sacrificial chamber,
as well as among the faults of ministers, counselors, and the subjects.
But when those who have become lax are seen everywhere in other places,
faults will arise in the kingdom, resulting from famine and disease.
Or by dogs, or even by monkeys, by vultures and by worms and insects;
or by tawny-colored crows, and by birds such as cocks and the like.
If the image is touched by other such beings,
it suffers destruction of its location and brings misfortune to the village.
I shall now declare the expiation for the sight of an anthill and the like;
that same rite applies if it occurs on an image, provided one performs the procession according to the prescribed rule.
Having purified that place until it becomes perfectly firm,
and having performed the ritual arrangements as before, one should re-establish [the deities] again in their proper order.
Alternatively, a wise practitioner of mantras should perform a sprinkling with water if the other image has been defiled by contact with living beings.
Having cleansed it with *kuśa* and *darbha* grass, one should cause a declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made there;
afterwards, one should perform the ritual bathing of the ritual image according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer one hundred oblations for each of the five mantras;
then, when the pedestal or even the inner sanctum has become loose, [the rite should be performed].
Having purified that place and made it firm with great effort,
one should perform the ritual bathing according to the rules in the sequence of eighty-one [mantras].
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one becomes purified by the declaration of a "meritorious day" (puṇyāha);
this applies whether the defect occurred in the celestial palace (vimāna), in the honey-plant (madhūka), or within the inner enclosure wall.

Having washed it inside and out on all sides with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having performed the ceremonial bath, one becomes pure through the rite of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha).
However, for all those [offenses] not mentioned, an expiation is prescribed as either the highest,
the middle, or even the lowest-highest.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods and worship him according to the prescribed rites;
then, having performed a fire-oblation for peace, one becomes pure through the *puṇyāha* rite.
One should have dance, song, and instrumental music performed in the presence of the deity;
at the conclusion of that, having performed worship, one should recite the mantra of the form according to the prescribed order.
Having fed the Brāhmaṇas, and especially the Vaiṣṇavas,
and having performed the rite of adornment, one should present the food offering and the great sacrificial oblation.
However, if the perpetual lamp is extinguished, an expiation is prescribed:
one should place Kapila-ghee in a shallow bowl while reciting the Astra-mantra.
Having kindled [the fire], O best of sages, one should display the lamp-mudrā;
in the perpetual fire, oblations are offered separately with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge.
One should cause him to perform one hundred oblations, or half of that, or half of that again, in sequence;
he should offer each one individually in order with the Mūrti-mantra.
O Nārada, when hair, insects, or similar things fall into any of the sacrificial offerings (havirādya), the expiation must be performed in exactly this same manner.
Having first performed the pure bath for that image by means of the Supreme Lord,
one should cause the ceremonial bathing to be performed in sequence according to the lower and higher paths.
Having offered one hundred oblations for each with the five Upaniṣadic mantras and having had the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) proclaimed, through that there will be peace.
Thereafter, one should worship the Lord of Gods according to the previously mentioned procedure;
thereafter, one should worship the preceptor so that he will be satisfied.
One should offer the materials used here to the preceptor;
I shall now declare the expiation for death in a temple of the deity.
O Lord of Sages, when the death of outcasts, those who have fallen from their caste, and others occurs within the inner chamber or even in a half-maṇḍapa; ||| Vis_39.74 |||
In front of the pedestal situated within the palace, as well as in the inner pavilion,
one should dig that spot to the depth of one bow (dhanus) if it is indeed free of stones.
Having filled [the vessel] with sand and earth and washed it with water,
one should purify the abode both inside and out with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should offer a thousand oblations each of fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and cooked rice,
in the eight directions according to rule, with the root mantra.
Thereafter, one should feed the brahmins all around the palace;
one should have them proclaim an auspicious day there and perform the rites from the lowest to the highest.

A wise man should cause the ritual bathing to be performed according to the rules and properly, in accordance with his wealth; however, for a Śūdra, he should have half of this performed at the time of death.
But half of that [penance] applies to the death of the twice-born in a temple of the gods,
a pavilion, or a city gate, when their death has occurred there.
Having performed the purification of the ground as before, one should likewise cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made;
the wise man should then perform a single fire-oblation (*homa*) to the north of the temple.
O Nārada, if that house, including the inner sanctum and other parts, is made of stone,
the knower of mantras should take cow dung from a tawny cow while reciting the root mantra.
One should smear the inner sanctum and all other areas with the wind-mantra;
having sprinkled them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the remaining rites as previously described.
In a place protected by the earth, or one burnt by fire, or one flooded by water, or one that is desolate,
or where the Lord of Mantras has long been neglected, one should perform the re-consecration.
Thereafter, one should begin the ritual installation of the image according to the rules; however,
if the image (bera) should be deficient in a limb, [the procedure for] that deficiency must be performed.
Then, having fashioned that limb with gold, one should join it firmly;
having performed this according to the ritual procedure, one should begin the re-installation once more.
One should perform the remaining rites as before according to the procedure for dwelling in water;
or else, O best of sages, one may simply perform the sprinkling with water here.
One should have [an image] of the God of Gods made; by that, there will be peace.
A wooden image should be discarded, and it should be replaced with one made of clay.
If the face [of the image] is thus broken or split due to negligence regarding the primary icon (mūlārcā),
one should then fashion [a replacement] for the Lord of Gods according to the sequence of the "position of the child" (bālasthāna).
One should have it made sturdy by artisans using logic and specific methods of reasoning;
having performed the decoration with colors, one should then commence the consecration.
But when a golden image has its face cut or broken,
one should melt it down, pour [the liquid] over it once, and then re-establish it.
Then one should cast the copper, divided into many parts, into water;
and that which is divided into one part or two should be joined with copper itself.
Having performed all that as before, one should fashion a new, auspicious image;
by installing a copper image, the daily worship proceeds perpetually.
If an image made of silver, endowed with the auspicious marks, should be obtained,
then all the rites such as the preliminary consecration in water (jalādhivāsana) and so forth should be performed for it in every respect.
Having carefully placed the Śakti within a copper image,
one should eventually set aside the copper image and install the silver one in its place.
In the same way, having abandoned the silver one, he should gradually establish the golden one;
one who desires prosperity should never, at any time, abandon the golden one.

O twice-born one, even from those of low conduct who are born into their own dharma, O Brahmin, the primary [image] is always superior; likewise, the image made of excellent materials is likewise superior. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.9.97)
A golden image is praised as the foremost for all;
having installed it in its own place, one should worship it day after day.
One should not move the image situated in the place of Brahmā, which is the object of ritual worship;
for if it should move, there will be the displacement of the kingdom.
That place goes to ruin, and the ruin of the entire village shall follow;
therefore, with every effort, one should move it at the time prescribed.
O best of sages, at the solstices, at the equinoxes, at the transits of the sun, as well as during eclipses, at the time of the morning twilight worship, and at the time of bathing— 39.101.
If the bathing image is absent, however, one should perform the movement [of the deity];
but outside of the second enclosure, one should not move the ritual image (karmārcā).
O Lord of Sages, if there should be a lapse due to negligence or delusion,
one should perform a sprinkling with water, preceded by a declaration of an auspicious day.
One should bathe the supreme image by means of the lower and higher paths;
however, in the case of the ritual for a single image, an expiation is prescribed.
The ceremonial bathing (snapana) of a stationary image should always be performed according to the rules;
however, having constructed a new temple, one should purify it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should bathe the Supreme Person by means of the lower and higher paths;
in this very manner, it should be performed until the end of twenty-six years.
Henceforth, I shall explain the ritual sprinkling with water in due order;
through that alone, purification will occur and all-pervading peace shall come to pass.
If the image should become deficient in a limb, one should produce it again as before;
having established it according to the rules as previously done, one should perform the rite of re-consecration.
Nārada said:
"O General, O one of great wisdom, be gracious to me regarding this bathing;
tell me, without omission, all the great faults of what is contrary to the scriptures."
By those defects arising from the bathing ceremony, the king and his kingdom perish,
as do the cattle, the subjects, and the destruction of crops and other provisions.
Viṣvaksena said:
O Lord of Sages, I shall declare the great faults of bathing: by means of moths and those corrupted by foul odors, all human beings would become defiled. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.9.111)
If the consecrated jar is broken, one should fill it again with those same materials;
for all human beings are deficient when their jars are deficient, as are their resources.
If one should fall upon substances such as worms, insects, or moths,
one must always avoid all of that entirely during the sacrifices to Viṣṇu.
If one performs the worship of the Lord of Gods using substances that are forbidden,
one falls into hell for sixty thousand years.
Any substance containing hair that falls upon the head of Viṣṇu will destroy a consecrated king; of this there is no doubt.
O Great Sage, regarding others as well who are wicked or fallen,
the Lord Nārāyaṇa himself has declared that this very same fruit [accrues].
One should not fill jars with water that has been left standing overnight;
if one should take it out of greed, one will go to a hundred births as a crow.
If one bathes the deity with aged ghee out of greed,
one shall go to a hundred births as a vulture, and at the end of that, become a pig.
If one bathes the Lord of Gods with buffalo-ghee out of delusion,
he shall go to a hundred births as a vulture, and at the end of that, become a cock.
If one bathes [the image] with ghee in any other manner, one will become a hundred lizards;
but if, out of greed, one bathes it with milk mixed with curd, [the same fate awaits].
A man who uses mineral substances and honey derived from wild plants will become poor and undergo a hundred births in the human world.
O Brahmin, if that [substance] is honored, one may go through a hundred births as a bull;
if it falls upon objects belonging to worms, insects, or moths.
One should always avoid all of that in every respect during the sacrifices to Viṣṇu;
even if such a substance is seen to have been prepared, one should nevertheless abandon it.
Once the jar has been consecrated, one should not touch any of those [substances] again;
rather, it should be observed in that manner, and then other [substances] should be placed therein.
If it is seen again [to be defiled] by dogs, chickens, or outcastes (caṇḍāla),
one should then set aside those others and consecrate the water-pots once more.
If it is seen again that [the site] has been prepared by outcaste women or those of the lowest castes,
then the wise man should abandon it and establish another one instead.
For that which has been gazed upon by the wicked, or even touched by their feet— whether it be a king, a royal official, or even a sacrificer— [is likewise defiled].
In the consecration with wicked substances, it destroys the kingdom along with its retinue, its herds, its stores of wealth, its ministers, and its cities. Viṣṇu 39.128.
And there will be fierce diseases as well as drought;
likewise, there will be bhūtas, vetālas, rakṣasas, piśācas, uragas, and dānavas.
For these constantly afflict both the king and the kingdom;
one should therefore avoid [the area] by a distance of an āḍhaka, half of that, or even less than that.
The practitioner, most skilled in mantras, [should employ] all types of oily substances;
however, if lacking cloth or thread, he may do so even with archways and the like.
Or likewise, by means of dance, song, and so forth, as well as perfumes, flowers, and the like,
[one should worship] the God of gods, the wielder of the Śārṅga bow, even if he is devoid of ornaments.
O best of sages, in whatever kingdom such a ritual bathing might ever take place,
that kingdom will become overrun with thieves and will be destroyed by enemies.
Therefore, one who desires prosperity and the supreme goal should have Viṣṇu bathed with every effort, according to the scriptures and in the proper sequence. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.9.134)
It brings about the pacification of the humors and all diseases whatsoever,
as well as for the appeasement of malevolent planets and for victory over enemies.
For the sake of increasing longevity and health, for the increase of sons and grandsons,
and for the fulfillment of all desires of people of every caste.
Whatever substance is deficient in ritual procedure, deficient in action, and likewise deficient in material;
whatever substance is deficient in measure, and whatever is deficient in worship toward the Guru.
If it is performed at the wrong time, lacks progeny, or is done by any agent in any location whatsoever,
it will immediately bring about malevolent magic against the village or the city.
The person who thus causes the aforementioned ritual bathing to be performed is liberated from all sins, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water.
The killer of a cow, the killer of a father, the killer of a mother, the destroyer of an embryo, the violator of the Guru’s bed,
the drinker of liquor, the stealer of gold, and the one who violates another's wife.
These and others are indeed liberated from sins by means of this ritual bath;
for there exists a preeminent merit in the ritual bath, O best of sages.
Whatever purification of the body one might achieve by performing a thousand horse-sacrifices, that one obtains through bathing Viṣṇu; of this there is no doubt.
O Nārada, I shall now declare the expiation for the place where the banner stands:
[the use of] a painting on an unauthorized cloth, or indeed a bamboo staff.
One should diligently avoid what is either unstated or redundant; if it is performed with such omissions or excesses, it will undoubtedly be fruitless.
At the time of the consecration of the banner, when the deity has been invoked into the jar and onto the vehicle, as well as in the event of that jar falling, shaking, or breaking; (Viṣṇu 39.145).
If there is a cracking around the image, that village shall perish;
in that case, an ablution for the Lord of Gods must be performed with the most excellent materials.
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma) that cuts away the evils of the village,
one should establish the ritual jar (kumbha) according to the prescribed rite and produce it anew.
If the banner, or especially the Garuḍa, is devoid of the proper marks, there will be the destruction of both the maker and the owner; one situated therein shall go to hell.
Having quickly removed the banner there, the preceptor, with a concentrated mind,
should immediately raise a banner endowed with all the auspicious characteristics.
One should properly undertake the remaining ritual according to the previously stated procedure,
even when the time for circumambulating the village has arrived and the wind has been stirred up.
A famine prevails there, and the people are afflicted by disease;
to avoid those evils, one should perform ablutions, both inferior and superior.
O tiger among sages, one should have the Brahmins recite the "auspicious day" formula there and provide them with a meal; the remainder should be performed as previously described.
Thereafter, one should worship the preceptor according to the path prescribed in the scriptures;
however, in the event of a fall or a breach [of the vow], one must abandon the banner at that very moment.
Having performed the supreme ceremonial bathing (snapana) of the Wheel-bearing God of gods,
one should then perform the Vāstuhoma sacrifice and thereafter cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
Having raised it, one should properly hoist the banner endowed with the auspicious marks;
at the time of circumambulating the village, if the offering of oblations should be lacking.
That village goes to its destruction, and one staying there shall go to hell;
to avoid that fault, an expiation is prescribed.
One should bathe the Lord of the Gods with fifty jars as one proceeds;
having thus worshipped the God, one should then wander again through the village.
One should subsequently raise the bird-banner (the banner of Garuḍa) accompanied by the offering of a sacrificial victim;
however, one may also perform the offering of a sacrificial victim alone, accompanied by the beating of drums.
At this very time, however, one should not look at the tides and so forth;
having duly raised the banner, one should perform the remainder of the rite as before.
If, at the time of raising the banner, it then trembles in the sky,
the performers will encounter disease and also total destitution.
To avoid those faults, one should perform either an inferior or a superior ritual bathing;
by having the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited, his fault is pacified.
If the banner falls, the king himself and that village shall perish;
now the expiation for the falling of the banner will be declared.

Having recited the *puṇyāha* (day of merit) formula, one should then feed the Brahmins; this is the ritual for the ablution (*snapana*) of the God of gods, categorized as inferior or superior according to the prescribed rule.
Having established it according to the rules, one should thereafter worship it according to the prescribed rite;
and in the event of its falling or breaking, one should raise the banner once again.
If [the image] falls during its installation, that kingdom shall perish;
therefore, one should perform the supreme consecration bath and the festival according to the prescribed ritual.
Having performed the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rule, one should then have the proclamation of an auspicious day made;
for if [the image] is stolen by thieves, that kingdom will perish.

Having performed the supreme ceremonial bath (snapana), preceded by a peace-offering homa, whether during the time of the ritual circumambulation with offerings, or in the daily rite, or during a festival; Vis 39.167.
And in the event of the falling of any substance, such as incense, flowers, and so forth,
one should perform the rite of pacification according to the prescribed procedure, sequentially with the five Upaniṣads.
One should again produce all the ritual substances, beginning with the perfumes, in their proper sequence;
however, in the absence of these substances, one should offer the *bali* with cooked rice (*caru*) or with unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
If it has been touched by wicked people, Śūdras, or those of other castes,
one must perform a propitiatory fire-offering (śāntihoma) and then display auspicious signs.
O Sage, an expiation is prescribed at the time of confusion regarding the offerings,
or when they are presented without reflection, or when they are devoid of the [proper] image.
There will be an increase in disease for both the village and the king;
as a means to avoid that fault, an expiation is prescribed.
One should bathe the *bali* and the *kautuka* by means of the lower and higher paths;
having performed the *śānti-homa* in due order, three Brahmins should indeed be fed.
If the image of the deity falls, or is carried away, or even if it sinks into the ground,
that village shall go to its destruction, as will the maker and the owner alike.
One should lead the deity into the ālaya and perform the ablution, both inferior and superior,
followed by the performance of the peace-offering (śāntihoma) preceded by a great worship (mahāpūjā).
There, one should cause the Brahmins to recite the "Auspicious Day" (puṇyāha) and satisfy them;
then, whether in a village or a city, one should perform the remaining rites.
If it falls or is missing a limb, the king and the kingdom perish;
one should then gradually withdraw the power from the food-image or the flower.
One should place the Śakti within the ritual image (karmārcā), and the bathing ceremony shall be most excellent;
one should perform the peace-offering (śāntihoma) in the four directions with the five mantras.
Having invoked [the deity] into another image, one should perform the remaining rites;
having performed the reconnection as before, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics.
Having performed the installation as before, one should not expect [the result] at this time;
rather, one should apply its power to the image and perform the remaining rites.
Whether standing, sitting, lying down, or in the presence of the bali-offering vessel,
or if one falls or has a limb impaired, the atonement is as previously prescribed.
On the day the festival begins, even those rites that were arranged by the officiating priests must likewise be performed by those very same individuals until the very conclusion.
But if, O best of sages, one should insert others in the middle out of delusion, those rites become fruitless; therefore, one should perform the propitiatory rite (śānti).
An expiation must indeed be performed for the removal of that fault;
even the officiating priest who presided previously should perform the concluding rite.
O Lord of Sages, one should bathe Hari with fifty, or even with twenty-five, jars, following either the inferior or the supreme path.
In that case, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) and perform a fire-offering for peace (śāntihoma);
likewise when [the image] is afflicted by disease, or dead, or lacking the scriptures, or defiled by others.
Likewise, in the rite of consecration and in festivals,
one should appoint another person who is a seeker of the ultimate truth as the preceptor, provided that he has mastered the tantras.
When the sacrificial fire has been extinguished and the festival has come to an end,
that kingdom will perish, and the performers will be afflicted by disease.
To avoid those faults, one should perform the bathing ceremony— both the inferior and the superior—
after having supplicated the Lord of the Gods of gods, preceded by a great oblation.
Having produced fire by friction, or else using a common worldly fire,
it should be consecrated with the Vaiṣṇava mantras, preceded by a most auspicious day.
A wise person should perform this rite to sever that fault when the worship of the Lord of Yoga has been omitted during a festival in the sacrificial pavilion.
If the deity has entered the water-pot in the middle [of the rite], especially during a festival,
that sacrifice becomes fruitless and the performers will be afflicted by disease.
Therefore, for the sake of accomplishing that fruit, one should perform both the inferior and superior ablutions,
as well as a peace-offering (śānti-homa), and offer a hundred oblations.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), his fault is pacified,
whether it concerns the jar of the Lord of Sacrifice (*yāgeśakumbha*) or the surrounding jars (*parikumbha*).
In the case of breaking or falling [upon] the altar, the atonement is as previously stated;
likewise when the eight auspicious symbols are missing or when the worship is deficient therein.
Otherwise, auspiciousness would perish and the performers would be afflicted by disease;
therefore, one should worship the Lord of Gods, whose nature is auspicious, according to the prescribed rites.
Then, having performed a peace-offering (śāntihoma), one should thereafter cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
[this applies] in the event of a festival, daily worship, a lapse [in ritual], or a failure in the fire-oblation (homakarma).
Those who remain there go to hell; therefore, no increase occurs.
To avoid that fault, however, one should perform an expiation as previously described.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa), as well as during festivals;
at the end of the homa, however, one should offer the sacrificial bali according to the prescribed ritual. // Vis_39.199 //
In the event of the omission of either the daily festival or the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali),
one should offer a hundred oblations into the perpetual fire with the root mantra.
But when these two times have passed, one should likewise perform the ritual bathing thereafter;
having offered oblations with the eight-syllable mantra, one should subsequently perform the daily rite.
If, through the deficiency of a daily festival, a great festival should occur,
one should bathe the unsurpassed image of Bala with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Thereafter, one should perform the ceremonial bath (snapana) with twenty-five [substances] in sequence;
having performed the adornment in order, one should worship [the deity] ending with the sacrificial oblation (havirantaka).
One should perform the bali offering in the temple according to the procedure for constant festivals;
one should carry out the circumambulation of the bali offerings in the morning, at midday, and in the evening.
Furthermore, O Sage, if the ritual of offering (balikarma) is performed when the midday has passed,
that offering should be made at a single time.
In that case, the festival will be fruitless and the destruction of the village will certainly occur;
therefore, for the sake of attaining its fruit, one should perform the bali offering twice a day.
O best of sages, one should cause the offering of bali to be performed at two times: the morning bali, the midday bali,
and the evening bali, accompanied by circumambulation.
This ritual offering of oblations is the cause for the destruction of spirits, rākṣasas, piśācas, and pannagas.
O Nārada, whoever out of delusion offers a bali-oblation during even a single twilight—
To avoid those faults, an expiation is prescribed:
one should cause Hari to be bathed by means of both the lower and the higher path.
Afterwards, one should feed the Brahmins preceded by a great oblation;
thereafter, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited, and perform the fire-offering (homa) as before.
Thereafter, one should perform the offering of the bali-oblation at the appropriate time;
however, if the vessel for the consecration of sprouts is lost or has fallen, [one should act accordingly].
If it is touched by those who are untouchable, it may blow away or arise again in succession;
or when the dark, red, or fully grown [wound] has been gnawed by a mouse, [it may likewise recur].

The knower of mantras should offer oblations with each of the five mantras using sacrificial fuel sticks and other materials; having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Viṣṇu-mantra, he should proceed.
O Nārada, if the sacred ford has not been visited on the designated day due to divine or human obstacles, one should begin the festival again.
If a transposition occurs regarding the days or the substances when the offering (bali) has been made,
one should offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
If, however, during the great festival, the sequence of the deities of the directions is reversed,
one should subsequently perform them in the proper order as before, preceded by the fire-oblation (homa).
O Nārada, I shall now declare the expiation for when the offering of the bali-oblation— whether performed once a day or on a festival— is obstructed.
One should offer one hundred oblations with that substance using the root mantra;
thereafter, if the single daily rite is obstructed, one should perform it twice.

Having first performed everything according to the rule with the previous substance, as was done previously during the first part of the night, one should thereafter proceed with the subsequent [substance] in due order.
If the day and night are obstructed, one should perform [the rite] on the following day;
likewise, having prepared the night, one should also offer that bali.
If the great festival is obstructed for more than one day, one should cause the ritual circumambulation and the fire offering to be performed twice as much.
But if that sacred site has been obstructed, one should perform all of that again, beginning with the offering of the sprouts,
on the following day.
Having performed the ceremonial bathing according to the rules, and having performed the fire sacrifice there as before,
having thus completed everything according to the ritual, one should perform the remainder as previously prescribed.
O Lord of Sages, I shall explain the expiation regarding the consecration of an image that lacks the proper measurements, or one that is deficient in its clothing and ornaments.
One should not perform the installation at an improper place or at an inauspicious moment;
for if the installer performs the installation out of great delusion, both he and his patron shall perish.
To avoid those faults, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed the journey according to the rule, one should begin the re-installation once again.
O Lord of Sages, if the ritual action is interrupted between the preliminary consecration with water and the formal installation,
an expiation is prescribed.
Having obtained the permission of the Brahmins, on the following day he should offer oblations of clarified butter, one hundred times each, with the five Upaniṣadic mantras.
Having completed the remainder according to the rules, one should install Puruṣottama;
likewise, one should cause everything to be performed if it has been protected for three days.
A water jar, or a full vessel, or even the eight auspicious symbols—
whether touched by those who are untouchable, or broken, or consecrated with mantras.
Having produced another [vessel] as before, one should establish it in the same sequence as previously described;
for the Brahma-vessel that has been lifted up, or is defiled, or has fallen, [is no longer fit].
Having likewise prepared another jar and consecrated it according to the rules, the wise one [should do so] with the five Upaniṣadic mantras and likewise with the Praṇava.
There, one should offer one hundred oblations for each [deity] with clarified butter;
having performed the proclamation of an auspicious day, one should install them in the previous sequence.
Deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, and likewise deficient in materials; with inverted order, deficient in time, as well as faltering and likewise extraordinary.
And for these [faults] which have not been mentioned, an atonement is prescribed:
one should offer one hundred oblations of clarified butter with the root mantra.
If at that time there should occur impurity, illness, or even death of the teacher, I shall describe the procedure for the installation [of the deity].
Or, O best of Brahmins, even one who is uninitiated but is a Vaiṣṇava well-versed in the Vedas—
the wise man, having bathed him and adorned him so that he is pure, should install him by means of that very [image].
Then, with the *puruṣasūkta* and the *praṇava*,
and thereafter with the two root mantras, the wise one should establish [the image] for a short while.
Then, having observed the preceptor, one should diligently have him perform everything— beginning with the ritual placement of mantras (*mantranyāsa*)— just as before, within ten days.
From that time forward, after the bathing of the deity on the fourth day,
one should then worship the preceptor with abundant wealth.
O Nārada, if the teacher’s fee has been omitted, one should perform worship through an expiation on the fourth day after the installation of the deity.
O Nārada, if the ceremonial bathing and worship have not been performed for that [image],
then a penance is prescribed within twelve days thereafter.
The ablution may be either supreme or intermediate-supreme;
having first performed the ablution, one should provide a meal for the brahmins.
Having offered a hundred oblations each with clarified butter using the five Upaniṣad mantras,
one should then perform the ceremonial bathing according to one's means.
One should worship the Lord of Gods day by day according to one's capacity;
at the conclusion of the worship, O Nārada, one should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) day after day.
For the benefit of practitioners and for the welfare of the king and his kingdom,
one should therefore always cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given with every effort.
If this [rite] is devoid of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is entirely fruitless;
when the preceptor’s fee is lacking, an expiation is prescribed.
Then, one should bathe the Lord of Gods by way of the lower and higher paths;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas and cause them to pronounce a declaration of auspiciousness.
One should worship Puruṣottama according to the previously described procedure;
thereafter, one should worship the teacher in accordance with one's wealth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should provide the best sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
as well as the large and small ladles (sruk-sruva) in the pavilion, along with the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the mandala, and the archway (toraṇa).
O best of sages, if one should construct the altar and other features out of proportion through negligence,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra joined with the root syllable.
O great sage, the preceptor should indeed offer oblations into the Vaiṣṇava fire in the midst of the flames, using fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge for each one.
By making him a Vaiṣṇava, peace will be attained for him;
therefore, one should perform that rite which is most dear to Hari.
O Nārada, I shall now describe the expiation for the state of being a child (bālasthāna):
one must not worship the image used for the primary shrine in the child’s shrine.
The knower of mantras should worship the image from the child’s station at the root station;
however, if out of greed, he should worship an image that is to be avoided.
That worship becomes fruitless, and the performer—the master—is destroyed;
for one who, out of delusion, should worship such an image, an expiation is prescribed.
O best of sages, one should bathe the image used for worship according to the inferior, superior, or middling path; this is the eradication of that fault.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas who are Vaiṣṇavas and masters of the Vedas;
having performed the peace-offering (śāntihoma) in due order, one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited.
The worshipper should properly perform worship at the root [shrine] in the house of the Child;
however, the worshipper of the Child’s house should not perform worship there at the location of the Root.
If one should worship [it] out of delusion, it will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
That village will go to its destruction, and the path of Dharma will perish.
Therefore, with every effort, one should not worship [the deity] in a root-house;
yet, O Nārada, if out of greed or delusion one should worship the Lord of Gods there, [it is a grave offense].
To achieve the perfection of the fruit of that worship, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed a sprinkling with water, preceded by the auspicious declaration of a holy day (*supuṇyāha*).
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at the root and the consecration within the pavilion,
O Best of Sages, one should cause the lower or the superior path to be constructed.
Thereafter, one should feed the Brahmins according to one's means;
one should honor them in the house of the child until the entry of the *mūla* constellation.
And even by not doing it in this way, there occurs a transgression of the proper time;
[namely,] the ceremonial bathing, the fire-offering for the image, and the preparatory consecration (*adhivāsana*) in the pavilion.
Having performed [the rite] correctly according to the rules, one should install [the image] properly in the prescribed sequence;
however, if more than a year has passed since then, that which will now be described shall apply.
Without the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsa), one should perform everything as before;
having performed the rites of consecration (pratiṣṭhā), one should pray to Hari.
If that image has been carried off by thieves from the young temple,
one should produce another beautiful image made of metal.
Having performed the preliminary consecration of the water, as well as the preliminary consecration in the pavilion,
one should likewise perform the fire-oblation for the image, the rite of pacification, and the ablution, whether inferior or superior.
Having made a proclamation of an auspicious day, one should install [the image] in the child’s chamber;
provided that the previously consecrated image has not been residing in water.
Having thus completed the section on the stage of the child, listen now to the intermingling of the tantras;
indeed, I shall explain the intermingling of the ritual sites (vāstu) according to the sequence of application.
According to the threefold paths taught in their respective scriptures— the Pañcarātra, the Śaiva, and the Vaikhānasa— the collection of building materials and other rites are performed.
In that very same manner, temples, images, and so forth should be constructed;
having indeed completed them properly according to the rules, one should perform the consecration and subsequent rites in their proper sequence.
In their dwelling, however, due to such intermixture, there is the destruction of the kingdom and the loss of wealth;
therefore, one should avoid the intermingling of dwellings with every effort.
In this regard, there is a certain distinction; listen, O observer of noble vows, as I shall explain it.
First, the plowing and other preparatory rites should be performed according to the rules prescribed for the Vaikhānasas.
One should establish Puruṣottama according to the Pañcarātra scripture,
while the collection of the site (vāstusaṃgraha) should be performed according to the rites of either the Śaiva or Vaikhānasa traditions.
One should install the deity in that place according to the Sāttvata rite,
in accordance with the customs of the village or kingdom, and with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.
If there is a desire for worship within five nights,
it should be performed according to the path taught in that scripture, having been previously installed and consecrated.
O Lord of Sages, one should never worship [the deity] through the Śaiva or Vaikhānasa traditions,
because both the Vaikhānasa and the Śaiva are non-Vedic.
The Śaiva and Vaihānasa systems are described as being non-saumya;
however, the Sāttvata is indeed saumya, and for that reason, the saumya is superior.
There, one should worship Puruṣottama according to the Sātvata path;
however, worship performed by means of the Śaiva or Vaikhānasa traditions results in fierce [retribution], fire, and disease.
One should practice the ritual injunctions of that Saumya Sāttvata Tantra;
whether due to divine or human causes, or even out of greed, delusion, or negligence.
While [the image] was being established by way of the Raudra path and worshipped day after day, [he],
out of a desire for the welfare of all, abandoned the Raudra ritual.
It is meritorious, increasing the prosperity of the village and causing the advancement of kings and Brahmins;
therefore, with every effort, one should abandon that fierce [deed] at that very moment.
One should establish [the image] and then worship Hari according to the Sāttvata rite;
therefore, with every effort, one must not cause a confusion of the Tantras.
This quintessential work known as the Pañcarātra, heard directly from the mouth of Viṣṇu himself,
is to be practiced by the best of the twice-born, the Vaiṣṇavas who have mastered the Vedas.
The Pañcarātra, the great knowledge that bestows virtue, pleasure, wealth, and liberation,
and the Śaiva [scripture] proclaimed by Śambhu— these are pure, while the Laiṅga is of two kinds.
O best of sages, the foremost of the twice-born should not perform [this] for the sake of others; rather,
O excellent sage, one should worship the pure and supreme [deity] for one's own sake.
O best of sages, day after day a wise man should not forget the scripture composed by Bhārgava for the sake of achieving the goals of the Vaikhānasa, which pertains to the Liṅga.
The best of the twice-born should not perform [this] for their own sake or for the sake of another;
rather, for the benefit of those born in the inverse order of castes, they should worship Puruṣottama.
O best of sages, that worship is for the sake of increasing the wealth of Śūdras and causes a loss of power for the twice-born; it should not be performed day after day—of this there is no doubt.
And because that worship is Vedic, it should not be performed by the best of the twice-born.
Nārada asks:
"Those called Vaikhānasas—what are they intended to mean here?"
"Are those forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) of two kinds? Are they *sūtas*, or what do you intend them to be?
Viṣvaksena replied:
"Those born of a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa mother are *sūtas*, as are the *vaikhānasas*."
"Sūtakas, rathakāras, and likewise paurāṇikas—
these are synonymous terms for those born of inverse unions who are honored."
These are declared to be the Vaikhānasas, worshippers of the Bhārgava scriptures;
the Tantra was proclaimed by Bhṛgu for the benefit of those born in the inverse order (pratiloma).
O best of sages, it is the settled conclusion of the scriptures that the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprasthāśrama) is prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras of Manu and others in due order.
The wise declare that the mixing of these [practices] therein must be avoided;
through the fault of mixing the tantras, everything is destroyed without a doubt.
By the king who desires to protect the world with every effort,
intermixture must be avoided for the sake of the happiness of the kingdom and the monarch.

O Brahmin, one should not even mentally conceive of a field that has been prepared according to the prescribed rites through plowing and so forth as belonging to any deity other than the one for whom it was intended.
If, however, he is established [in office] out of delusion, he is to be punished or even executed as a partaker of evil;
for he is the creator of confusion for both the king and his kingdom.
The Pañcarātra is indeed Śaiva, following the Vaikhānasa injunctions; due to the intermixture of their rules regarding the site and other matters, there is only a slight distinction between them.
The Sāttvata [system] is for the sake of all prosperity; the Śaiva [system] brings about the destruction of all; the Vaikhānasa [system] leads to misfortune; therefore, one should avoid that.
Some [images] have been installed in improper places or deprived of their own proper locations;
due to the wrath of two deities, everything will undoubtedly perish.
Confusion is said to be of two kinds, which brings about the destruction of all living beings:
namely, confusion of caste and likewise confusion of the Tantras.
By the intermingling of castes alone, the world falls into the state of outcasts;
by the intermingling of Tantras alone, the king and the kingdom perish.
The kingdom is the body, while the king is said to be the life-force;
when the kingdom perishes, the king perishes. Therefore, the wise should protect both.
When the world had fallen into the state of being outcastes (caṇḍāla), all the Vedas disappeared;
and when the Vedas had disappeared, so too did the sacrifices and other ritual acts.
The entire world would become a single caste and all things would be devoid of activity;
through the fault of the confusion of castes, the twice-born would meet their death.
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid confusion;
for there is nothing higher than the God of gods, since all spiritual accomplishments depend upon him.
Reflecting thus upon all beings, we worship the Divine;
for the Blessed Viṣṇu, the creator of beings, is composed of all the gods.
For the sake of the welfare of all living beings, not even one other is seen besides him—
neither Brahmā, nor Rudra, nor Śakra, nor the Vasus, nor Varuṇa.
Yakṣas, gandharvas, and siddhas; bhūtas, vetālas, and rākṣasas; as well as the śaktis and all other such powers—all these are manifestations of Viṣṇu.
And all of them become propitious toward men who seek their goals,
provided they are constantly worshipped according to the specific rites for each.
O bull among sages, for the benefit and welfare of all living beings, the compassionate sages have composed various treatises suited to their respective capacities.
Vedic, Tantric, and likewise Vaidika-Tantric—action is declared to be of these three kinds, the nectar of the ocean of the Pañcarātra. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.9.315)
For Brāhmaṇas, however, it is Vedic; for kings, it is both Vedic and Tantric;
for Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it is Tantric; or indeed, for all, it may be Tantric.
One should perform rites such as those in the reverse order according to the dharma taught by Bhārgava;
that which is devoid of prosperity and lacking in gentleness is for the possession of non-Brāhmaṇas.
Because it is non-Vedic, that Vaikhānasa tradition is inferior;
therefore, this intermixture must be avoided by Brāhmaṇas who seek the welfare of the world.
In the construction of the temple, in the worship of the image, and for the worshiper,
any confusion must be avoided by all means through various kinds of expiatory rites.
Nārada said:
"Explain the expiation for the mixing of images and other such acts,
by performing which all faults that cause inauspiciousness are destroyed."
Viṣvaksena said:
"Neither the lunar day nor the asterism, nor the specific time of day, is required.
Indeed, for the benefit of all living beings, this [rite] should be performed quickly, setting aside all such considerations."
The expiation for a mixture [of castes] must be performed immediately; thereafter,
through that expiation,
one brings about the great prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
It brings all prosperity and happiness to both the village and the city;
therefore, with every effort, one should quickly perform rites for peace.
Whatever has been commenced with a particular tantra should be performed with that very same tantra;
otherwise, there will be great fault, causing the destruction of the king and the kingdom. (Viṣṇupurāṇa 3.9.324)
Therefore, with every effort, one should not cause a confusion of tantras;
even if the worship is omitted for a single day, one should perform it according to the procedure prescribed in one's own kalpa.
Having performed the ablution according to the sequence of eighty-one [verses], the supreme practitioner,
having performed the pacifying homa in due order, performs the ablution once more.
Having performed the *śāntihoma* in due order, and likewise the *vāstuhoma*,
one should afterwards feed one hundred and eight Brahmins in sequence.
Whether it be half of that or half of that again, according to one's means,
one should remember the ritual for the fourfold form and abandon the ritual for the fivefold form.
One should place all the attendants in their proper order as before;
having performed the placement of the principles (tattva-nyāsa) in sequence, one should likewise perform the placement of emanation (sṛṣṭi-nyāsa).
Then the wise one, recollecting the primary form [of the deity], should constantly perform worship with the root mantra according to the previously described procedure.
Then, having offered the great oblation, one should perform the worship of the Guru;
even if there has been a lapse in worship there, one should worship again by that very same means.
In that regard, while worshipping day after day according to the Sātvata path,
one should never at any time worship the Lord of Gods according to another tantra.
If one should worship [it] out of delusion, it will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
Furthermore, that worship performed day after day will bring about the destruction of that village.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, one should worship that with every effort;
first, however, one should perform a pure bath prior to the rites of worship and so forth.
One should employ the rites of sprinkling with water and so forth upon the root image;
one should employ the rites of bathing and so forth upon the action image.
O Lord of Sages, one should cause a festival to be held during that time, preceded by offerings and fire oblations, for either one day, three days, or seven days.
One should cause a festival to be celebrated there according to one's capacity and in accordance with propriety;
this should be performed in sequence until the end of twelve years.
In the first year, it is the abode of Rākṣasas;
therefore, one should perform a rite of pacification.
In the second year, it is the dwelling of Yakṣas, and in the third year, it is crowded with Bhūtas.
In the fourth year, it is the abode of the Piśācas; in the fifth year, the dwelling of the Dānavas;
and when five years have passed, it is the residence of the Brahmarākṣasas.
Therefore, with every effort, one should quickly effect pacification;
before twelve years have passed, one should perform it by means of sprinkling with water.
In this very manner, however, it must be performed until the end of twenty years.
Beyond this, O Nārada, I shall proclaim the expiation.
One should perform the sprinkling with water preceded by a stay in the water;
afterwards, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas preceded by a great sacrifice.
Before thirty-six years have passed, one should have it performed by that very person;
after thirty-six years have elapsed, an expiation is prescribed.
Having prepared the five products of the cow in sequence, one should purify the inner sanctum;
then, with the permission of the Brahmins, one should have them recite the benediction for an auspicious day.
One should perform the preliminary consecration with water and the other rites exactly as previously described;
likewise, one should give gifts of cows, land, gold, and clothing.
Then one should perform all kinds of gifts to the Brahmins in due order;
having thus increased that [merit] until the end of fifty years.
After fifty years have passed, an expiation is prescribed;
one should then begin the re-installation, starting with the preliminary consecration in water and other rites.
One should feed Brahmins there and perform the remaining rites as previously described;
this should be carried out in sequence until the end of one hundred years.
After a hundred years, that empty place will certainly become desolate;
that village goes to its destruction, and those dwelling there shall go to hell.
That village goes to its destruction; therefore, one should perform a rite of pacification.
Having performed the pacification according to the prescribed rule, one should worship for five nights.
If there is an omission of worship in this regard, one should worship again with that very same [rite];
therefore, with every effort, one should swiftly perform pacification.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for Expiation," in the Śrī Pāñcarātra Viṣvaksena Saṃhitā.
